AI-Native Video Content Creation

In this program, AI is the production medium. You use it to write, design, generate, edit, finish, and deliver video. You also learn how the models work inside, how to connect them into pipelines that agents operate, and how to run the infrastructure under them.

The program is for adults with IT experience. You already use a command line, Python, APIs, and cloud services. You do not need any experience with video, film, or design.

How each module works: read the concept text, look at the diagram, listen to the summary, and watch the selected videos. Then follow the worked example and do the lab. Use the quiz to check yourself, and compare your result with the model answer. Mark the module complete. Your progress stays in this browser.

Start here: How to study · Requirements by level · Tool landscape, October 2026 · Next steps and specializations

Concepts last; tools change. The concept text uses no product names. The labs name the best current tools as of October 2026. One example: OpenAI removed the Sora 2 API on 2026-09-24, so any pipeline that used only that API stopped. In this program you learn to design for change.

About this course

You will use generative models in every other course. This course shows you what happens inside them. You do not need to train a large model. You need a correct mental model, so that you can predict what a model can do, why it fails, and which setting to change.

The labs use Python notebooks. They run on a laptop or in Google Colab. Some labs call hosted APIs.

tools/promptlog.py The prompt log for every generation (M03, M05)

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M01 From data to model

Study time: 7 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain the difference between training and inference.
  2. Explain what parameters, a loss function, and gradient descent do.
  3. Explain why training data decides what a model can make.
  4. Estimate the memory that a model needs from its parameter count and precision.

Key words

model parameter training inference loss gradient descent weights

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 01. From data to model. After this module, you can: 1. Explain the difference between training and inference. 2. Explain what parameters, a loss function, and gradient descent do. 3. Explain why training data decides what a model can make. 4. Estimate the memory that a model needs from its parameter count and precision. A model is a large function with many numbers, called parameters. Training changes the parameters so that the function output gets closer to the training data. The loss function measures the error. Gradient descent changes each parameter a small amount to make the loss smaller. Inference is when you use the trained model. A model can only make what is similar to its training data. The memory that a model needs is about the parameter count multiplied by the bytes for each parameter.

Learn

A model is a function

A generative model is a function. It takes an input, for example a text prompt and some random noise. It gives an output, for example an image or a video. The function has many internal numbers. These numbers are the parameters. A current open video model has between 5 and 30 billion parameters. The file that stores them is the weights file.

Training

Training sets the parameters. The process is a loop:

  1. Take a batch of examples from the training data.
  2. Let the model make a prediction.
  3. Measure the error with the loss function.
  4. Calculate, for each parameter, the direction that makes the loss smaller. This is the gradient.
  5. Change each parameter a small step in that direction. This is gradient descent.

The loop repeats millions of times. Training a large video model uses thousands of GPUs for weeks. You will not do this. In C14 you will do a small version: fine-tuning with a LoRA.

Inference

Inference is the use of a trained model. The parameters do not change. You give an input and you get an output. Every time you generate a video, you run inference. Inference cost depends on the model size, the output size (resolution × duration), and the number of steps. With the same input, seed, settings, and software, a run usually gives the same output again; this makes tests repeatable (M07).

The data decides what the model can make

A model learns the patterns of its training data. It can combine those patterns in new ways. It cannot reliably make things that are rare or absent in the data. This explains many failures:

  • Hands, text, and fast complex motion were rare or hard in older data, so older models failed on them.
  • A model trained mostly on stock footage makes "stock-looking" shots.
  • A model trained with good captions follows prompts better.

When a model fails, ask first: "Was this pattern common in the training data?"

Generalization and overfitting

A model is useful only if it works on inputs that it did not see in training. This is generalization. When a model learns the training examples too exactly, it fails on new inputs. This is overfitting. Large models trained on very large data generalize well. But they still overfit rare items: a model can copy a well-known image or logo if it saw it many times. Fine-tuning a small adapter on a few images overfits easily (C14).

Captions teach the prompt

A text-to-video model learns from pairs: a clip and its caption. What the captions describe, the prompt can control. Model makers now write detailed captions with other AI models: subject, action, camera, light, style. This is a main reason why prompt following improved. When a word has no effect, the captions probably did not use it. Write prompts in the style of the captions, in the order of subject, action, scene, camera, and light (C02·M06).

Memory estimate

Weights memory ≈ parameter count × bytes per parameter.

Precision Bytes per parameter 14B model
FP32 4 56 GB
FP16 / BF16 2 28 GB
FP8 / INT8 1 14 GB
4-bit (NVFP4, GGUF Q4) about 0.5 about 7 GB

At inference, the GPU also needs memory for activations. These grow with resolution and video length. This is why a 720p, 5 s clip can fit on a GPU where a 1080p, 10 s clip does not. C01·M06 and C13 explain this in more detail.

  • 3Blue1Brown — But what is a neural network?Watch all (19 min). Good visual model of parameters and layers.
  • 3Blue1Brown — Gradient descent, how neural networks learnWatch 0:00–12:00. The idea of the loss landscape.
  • Andrej Karpathy — Intro to Large Language ModelsWatch 0:00–20:00. Parameters file + run file; training vs inference at scale.

Worked example

Task: Decide if Wan 2.2 14B can run on a 24 GB GPU.

  1. Weights in BF16: 14 × 2 = 28 GB. This is more than 24 GB. It does not fit.
  2. Weights in FP8: 14 × 1 = 14 GB. It fits, with 10 GB left.
  3. The text encoder (a large language model) also needs memory. Typical: 5–11 GB in FP16. The VAE needs about 0.5 GB.
  4. Decision: use FP8 weights for the video model, and offload the text encoder to the CPU after it encodes the prompt. ComfyUI does this offload automatically.
  5. Activations: start at 480p and 81 frames. Increase only after a successful run.

Result: it runs. The cost is some quality loss from FP8 and slower model loading. This matches the reported requirement (24 GB class with FP8).

Lab

Deliverable: C01/M01/memory.ipynb and a one-page note.

  1. Write a Python function weights_gb(params_billion, bits) that returns the weights memory in GB.
  2. Make a table for these models: 1.3B, 5B, 14B, 22B, 27B. Use 16, 8, and 4 bits.
  3. Add a column "fits on 24 GB / 32 GB / 80 GB" (weights only, plus 6 GB headroom).
  4. Train a tiny model to understand the loop. Use the notebook cell below. Plot the loss for 200 steps.
import torch, torch.nn as nn
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 256).unsqueeze(1)
y = torch.sin(x)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 1))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
losses = []
for step in range(200):
    loss = ((model(x) - y) ** 2).mean()   # loss function
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward()     # gradients
    opt.step()                           # gradient descent
    losses.append(loss.item())
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), "parameters")
  1. Write 5 sentences: what changed during training, and what stays fixed at inference.

Result checklist

  • [ ] The table has 15 rows and correct numbers.
  • [ ] The loss plot goes down.
  • [ ] The note uses the terms parameter, loss, gradient descent, inference correctly.

Self-check quiz

1. What changes during training?

Training changes the parameters so that the loss gets smaller. At inference, the parameters stay fixed.

2. A model has 14 billion parameters in FP16 (2 bytes each). About how much memory do the weights need?

14 × 10^9 × 2 bytes = 28 GB. Activations, the text encoder, and the VAE need more memory on top of this.

3. Why can a video model fail to make a rare dance move correctly?

A model learns the distribution of its training data. Rare patterns are learned badly or not at all.

4. What does the loss function do?

The loss is one number for the error. Gradient descent uses it to know in which direction to change each parameter.

5. A tiny model reaches a loss of 0.001 on its training data, but fails on new inputs. What is the name of this problem?

Check a model on data it did not see in training. In C14, you will see the same problem with a LoRA trained on too few images.

6. Why do newer video models follow prompts better than models from 2023?

The prompt can only use what the captions taught. Read the data statement in a model card (M04).

7. A 22B model is offered as a 4-bit file. About how much memory do the weights need?

22 × 10^9 × 0.5 bytes ≈ 11 GB. Add the text encoder, the VAE, and activations.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)
  • 14B at 16 bit = 28 GB, at 8 bit = 14 GB, at 4 bit = 7 GB. With 6 GB headroom: 14B 8-bit fits on 24 GB; 14B 16-bit needs 80 GB class (or 32 GB with offload tricks).
  • 27B (for example a large MoE video model) at 8 bit = 27 GB. It does not fit on 24 GB. It fits on 32 GB only with offload. Note: in an MoE model, only some experts are active for each step, but all weights must still be in memory or offloaded.
  • The tiny model has 193 parameters. The loss falls from about 0.5–1.0 (it depends on the random start) to below 0.01; in our run with torch.manual_seed(0), from 1.04 to 0.031 after 50 steps and 0.0044 after 200. During training, the 193 numbers change. At inference, they stay fixed, and the model maps each new x to a y.

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M02 Tokens, embeddings, and attention

Study time: 9 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain how text, images, video, and audio become tokens.
  2. Explain what an embedding is and why similar meanings are near each other.
  3. Explain self-attention and cross-attention in one paragraph each.
  4. Explain why attention cost grows fast with video length and resolution.

Key words

token embedding transformer attention context window patch

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 02. Tokens, embeddings, and attention. After this module, you can: 1. Explain how text, images, video, and audio become tokens. 2. Explain what an embedding is and why similar meanings are near each other. 3. Explain self-attention and cross-attention in one paragraph each. 4. Explain why attention cost grows fast with video length and resolution. A transformer works on tokens. A token is a small piece of the input: part of a word, a patch of an image, or a small block of video in space and time. Each token becomes an embedding, a list of numbers that holds its meaning. Attention lets every token look at every other token and take the information it needs. Self-attention connects tokens of the same input. Cross-attention connects the video tokens to the prompt tokens. Attention cost grows with the square of the token count. This is why long, high-resolution video is expensive.

Learn

Tokens

A transformer does not see words or pixels directly. It sees tokens.

  • Text: a tokenizer cuts text into pieces. "Cinematic" can be one token or two. A 100-word prompt is about 130 tokens.
  • Image: the image is first compressed (see M03). Then it is cut into small squares. Each square is a patch, and each patch is a token.
  • Video: the compressed video is cut into small blocks in space and time. One block can be 2×2 latent pixels over 1 latent frame. Each block is a token.
  • Audio: the sound is compressed into a sequence of short frames. Each frame becomes a token.

Embeddings

Each token becomes an embedding: a vector of, for example, 3,072 numbers. Training places tokens with similar use near each other. So "dusk" and "sunset" are near, and "dusk" and "spreadsheet" are far. A position signal is added, so the model knows where each token is in the sequence, in the frame, and in time.

Attention

Attention is the core operation. For each token, the model asks: "Which other tokens are important for me?" Each token makes three vectors:

  • a query (what I look for),
  • a key (what I contain),
  • a value (what I give).

The model compares each query with all keys. High similarity means high weight. The token then takes a weighted mix of the values.

  • Self-attention: tokens of the video look at other tokens of the same video. This keeps a face the same from frame 1 to frame 120. It also keeps motion smooth.
  • Cross-attention: video tokens look at the prompt tokens. This is how "red umbrella" in the prompt becomes a red umbrella in the frame. Some new models do not use separate cross-attention. They put text and video tokens in one sequence (joint attention). The effect is the same.

The cost of attention

Full attention compares every token with every other token. If there are N tokens, the cost is about N². A 5 s, 720p clip has tens of thousands of tokens. Double the duration and the cost is about 4×. Double the width and height and the token count is 4×, so the cost is about 16×. This one fact explains:

  • why clip length is limited (5–15 s, now up to 30 s in the best models),
  • why high resolution is often made by upscaling (C09),
  • why "extend" and multi-shot features exist (C05).

Blocks and layers

A transformer is a stack of identical blocks. Each block has two parts: an attention layer (tokens exchange information) and a small feed-forward network (each token is changed on its own). Each part adds its result to its input (a skip connection) and normalizes the numbers. A large video model has 30–60 blocks with embeddings of 3,000–5,000 numbers. The number of blocks and the embedding size set most of the parameter count (M01). In diffusion models, each block also receives the noise level (the timestep), so the same blocks work at every step (M03).

Saving attention cost

Because full attention grows with N², model makers save cost in several ways:

  • windowed or sparse attention: each token looks only at tokens near it, or at a chosen subset;
  • separate space and time attention: first within a frame, then across frames at the same position;
  • efficient kernels (for example FlashAttention) that compute the same result with less memory traffic. The first two can weaken long-range consistency: a detail at second 1 may change by second 9. Efficient kernels give the same result, only faster.

Context window

An LLM also has a limit on tokens: the context window. In C03 you will use it to hold a whole script, a style guide, and a shot list at the same time.

Worked example

Task: Estimate the token count of a video clip.

Settings: 1280×720, 5 s at 16 fps = 81 frames. Typical video VAE compression: 8× in width and height, 4× in time. Patch size in the transformer: 2×2 in space, 1 in time.

  1. Latent size: 1280/8 = 160, 720/8 = 90, time (81−1)/4+1 = 21 latent frames.
  2. Tokens per latent frame: (160/2) × (90/2) = 80 × 45 = 3,600.
  3. Total tokens: 3,600 × 21 = 75,600.
  4. Attention pairs: 75,600² ≈ 5.7 billion for each attention layer and step.

Now change to 1920×1080: tokens = 120 × 67.5 × 21 ≈ 170,000. That is about 2.25× more tokens and about 5× more attention cost. This is why many models make 720p natively and then upscale.

print(len(enc.encode(p)), [enc.decode([t]) for t in enc.encode(p)])

  2. Make a table of tokens and relative attention cost for: 480p/5 s, 720p/5 s, 720p/10 s, 1080p/10 s, 4K/10 s.

  • [ ] The explanation uses the terms token, attention, and upscale.

Self-check quiz

1. In a video transformer, what is a typical token?

Video models cut the (latent) video into small blocks in space and time. Each block becomes one token.

2. What does cross-attention do in a text-to-video model?

Cross-attention is the bridge between the prompt and the picture. Weak cross-attention = weak prompt adherence.

3. You double the duration of a clip. Full attention cost grows by about:

Token count doubles. Full attention compares every token with every other token, so cost grows with the square: 2² = 4×.

4. Why are words with similar meaning near each other in embedding space?

The embedding is learned. Tokens that behave in a similar way get similar vectors.

5. A model uses windowed attention: each token looks only at tokens near it in space and time. What is the typical cost of this saving?

Sparse and windowed attention trade global consistency for speed. Test long shots with returning details (M07).

6. You double both the width and the height of a clip. How do tokens and full attention cost change?

Tokens grow with the area; full attention grows with the square of the tokens: 4² = 16.

7. What does a transformer block contain?

Depth (the number of blocks) and width (the embedding size) set most of the parameter count.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)
Setting Tokens (approx.) Attention cost vs 720p/5 s
480p, 5 s 33,600 0.2×
720p, 5 s 75,600 1×
720p, 10 s 147,600 3.8×
1080p, 10 s 332,000 19×
4K, 10 s 1,330,000 310×

A vendor limits clip length because attention cost grows with the square of the token count. A 4K, 10 s clip with full attention costs hundreds of times more than a 720p, 5 s clip. For this reason, most systems generate at a lower resolution and then upscale. Some use sparse or windowed attention to reduce the cost, and this can reduce long-range consistency.

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M03 Latent space, diffusion, and flow matching

Study time: 10 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain why generation happens in a compressed latent space.
  2. Explain the forward (noise) and reverse (denoise) process of diffusion.
  3. Explain flow matching as a straight path from noise to data.
  4. Connect steps, sampler, and scheduler to quality and speed.

Key words

latent VAE diffusion flow matching sampler step

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 03. Latent space, diffusion, and flow matching. After this module, you can: 1. Explain why generation happens in a compressed latent space. 2. Explain the forward (noise) and reverse (denoise) process of diffusion. 3. Explain flow matching as a straight path from noise to data. 4. Connect steps, sampler, and scheduler to quality and speed. Pixels are too many to work with directly. A VAE compresses each image or video into a smaller latent, and decodes it back at the end. Diffusion training adds noise to latents and teaches the model to predict that noise. At generation time, the model starts from pure noise and removes noise step by step. Flow matching learns a direct velocity from noise to data, so fewer steps are necessary. The sampler and scheduler decide how big each step is. More steps usually give more detail, but cost more time.

Learn

The latent space

A 5 s, 720p video has about 75 million pixel values. Attention over all of them is impossible. So the system first compresses the video with a VAE (variational autoencoder).

  • The encoder makes a small latent. A typical video VAE compresses 8× in width, 8× in height, and 4× in time. It keeps 16 to 48 channels per position.
  • The decoder turns the latent back into pixels.

All generation happens in the latent. The decoder runs once at the end. VAE quality sets an upper limit on detail. Small text and fine textures often fail in the VAE, not in the transformer.

Diffusion: the idea

Training:

  1. Take a clean latent from the training data.
  2. Add random noise at a random strength.
  3. Ask the model to predict the noise (or the clean latent).
  4. Use the error as the loss.

Generation:

  1. Start from pure random noise. The seed decides this noise.
  2. The model predicts the noise in it.
  3. Remove a part of the predicted noise. This is one step.
  4. Repeat until the latent is clean.

Early steps decide the composition and layout. Late steps add detail and texture. This is useful in practice. If you like the composition but not the detail, keep the seed and change late-step settings. If the composition is wrong, change the seed or the prompt. Do not spend late-step settings on a layout problem.

Start from an image: denoise strength

You do not have to start from pure noise. In image-to-image (and video-to-video), the system encodes your input to a latent, adds noise to a chosen level, and runs only the remaining steps. The denoise strength (0–1) sets that level:

  • 0.2–0.4: same composition and shapes; new texture, light, or style details;
  • 0.5–0.7: same rough layout; new forms and details;
  • 0.8–1.0: little of the input remains. This follows directly from "early steps decide composition". It is the basis of restyling, upscaling with detail (C09), and many editing workflows.

The VAE in practice

  • Decode memory: decoding a long, high-resolution latent needs a lot of GPU memory. Tiled decoding decodes overlapping tiles in space and time; it uses less memory but can show seams.
  • Each model family has its own VAE. A latent from one family cannot be decoded with another family's VAE.
  • Round trips lose detail. Encode and decode a frame several times, and it gets softer. Keep your masters in pixels, not in latents. Encode once, edit, and decode once.

Flow matching

Classic diffusion follows a curved path from noise to data. Curved paths need many small steps (25–50). Flow matching (and rectified flow) trains the model to predict a velocity along a straight line from noise to data. A straight path tolerates large steps. Most 2025–2026 image and video models use flow matching. With distillation (C01·M06), some models make good output in 4–8 steps.

Sampler and scheduler

  • The sampler is the method that takes a step (for example Euler, DPM++, UniPC).
  • The scheduler decides the noise level at each step (for example linear, Karras, "shift" for flow models).

Rules of thumb:

  • Use the sampler and step count from the model card first. Change one setting at a time, and log it.
  • Too few steps: soft, unfinished detail.
  • Too many steps: more time, small gain, sometimes over-sharpening.
  • Flow models often have a "shift" value. A higher shift spends more steps at high noise. This helps the global structure at high resolution.

Watch

  • Welch Labs / 3Blue1Brown — But how do AI images and videos actually work?Watch all (about 40 min). The best visual explanation of diffusion and guidance.

Worked example

Task: Understand the step budget of an open video model in ComfyUI.

Model card default for a distilled LTX-type model: 8 steps, Euler sampler. Full model: 30–40 steps.

The times below are illustrative orders of size, not measurements; measure your own in the lab.

  1. Run 1: distilled model, 8 steps, seed 1234 → 720p, 5 s. Time: about 40 s on an RTX 5090 class GPU.
  2. Run 2: full model, 30 steps, same seed → about 4× the time. Better fine texture on fabric; same composition.
  3. Run 3: full model, 12 steps → texture between run 1 and run 2; time about 1.6× run 1.
  4. Decision: use the distilled model for exploration (many seeds, fast). Use the full model only for selected shots.

This "explore fast, finish slow" pattern appears in every pipeline in Level 4.

Lab

Deliverable: C01/M03/ with images and a short report.

Use any hosted image model that exposes steps and seed (for example a FLUX model on fal.ai or Replicate), or ComfyUI if you have a GPU.

  1. Fix one prompt and seed 42.
  2. Generate at steps 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 (or the model's allowed values).
  3. Put the results in one contact sheet (use ffmpeg tile filter or Python PIL).
  4. Change only the seed (3 values) at the best step count.
  5. Report: at which step does the composition stop changing? At which step does detail stop improving? What does the seed change?

Result checklist

  • [ ] The report names the step where composition is fixed and the step where detail saturates.
  • [ ] Every image has a line in your prompt log (model, seed, steps, cost).

Self-check quiz

1. Why do models generate in a latent space instead of pixels?

A video VAE compresses about 8×8 in space and 4× in time. The transformer then works on far fewer tokens.

2. What does a diffusion model learn in training?

Training adds known noise. The model learns to predict it. At generation, it uses this skill to remove noise step by step.

3. Main practical benefit of flow matching / rectified flow?

A straighter path can be followed with larger steps. This, plus distillation, makes 4–8 step generation possible.

4. Same prompt, same model, same seed, same settings, same hardware. The result is:

The seed fixes the start noise. With the same settings, the result is usually reproducible. Some GPU kernels add small non-determinism.

5. You run image-to-image with a denoise strength of 0.3. What do you expect?

Strength (denoise) chooses where on the noise path you start. Low strength keeps layout; high strength (0.7–1.0) re-invents it.

6. A 1080p video decode fails with an out-of-memory error after all steps finished. What is the usual fix?

The decoder needs a lot of memory at full resolution. Tiling trades a little time for much less memory; check the tile seams.

7. Small text on a sign is unreadable in every take, even at high step counts. Where is the likely limit?

Detail that the VAE cannot represent cannot appear, whatever the transformer does.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Typical result with a flow-matching image model:

  • Steps 1–2: blurry color fields; the main layout is already visible.
  • Step 4: the composition is fixed. Further steps do not move objects.
  • Steps 8–16: edges, skin, and fabric detail improve.
  • Step 32: very small gain over 16; time doubles.
  • Seed change: composition changes (pose, camera, layout); style and palette stay similar because the prompt is the same.

Conclusion: the seed and the early steps control composition. Late steps control detail. For exploration, vary seeds at low steps. For final output, fix the seed and use more steps. Write the measured times next to each step count: in the report, "step 16 took 2.1× the time of step 8 for a gain that 2 of 3 viewers saw" is a decision that others can check.

Go deeper

  • Ho et al. (2020) — Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
  • Rombach et al. (2021) — High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
  • Lipman et al. (2022) — Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
  • Liu et al. (2022) — Flow Straight and Fast (Rectified Flow)

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M04 Diffusion transformers for video and audio

Study time: 9 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Describe the main blocks of a current video model (text encoder, video VAE, DiT, decoders).
  2. Explain how a model generates audio and video together.
  3. Explain what a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is and why video models use it.
  4. Read a video model card and find the information that matters for production.

Key words

DiT text encoder MoE joint audio-video model card

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 04. Diffusion transformers for video and audio. After this module, you can: 1. Describe the main blocks of a current video model (text encoder, video VAE, DiT, decoders). 2. Explain how a model generates audio and video together. 3. Explain what a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is and why video models use it. 4. Read a video model card and find the information that matters for production. A current video model has four main parts. A text encoder turns the prompt into embeddings. A video VAE compresses the frames. A diffusion transformer, or DiT, removes noise from the space-time tokens. Decoders turn latents back into video and sound. Joint audio-video models put audio tokens and video tokens in one transformer, so speech and lips match. Mixture-of-experts models have several expert networks and use only some of them for each step. This gives more capacity for the same compute.

Learn

Four main parts

  1. Encoders. The text encoder turns the prompt into embeddings. Current models use a large language model for this, so they understand long, detailed prompts. Image and video references go through image encoders or the VAE. Audio references go through an audio codec.
  2. Video VAE. It compresses frames into a latent (M03).
  3. Diffusion transformer (DiT). This is the large part: 5 to 30 billion parameters. It removes noise from the space-time tokens. Each layer has self-attention (video ↔ video), conditioning on the text (cross-attention or joint attention), and a feed-forward network.
  4. Decoders. The VAE decoder makes frames. In joint models, an audio decoder makes the waveform.

Joint audio-video generation

Since 2025, top models generate sound with the picture, both hosted and open models (examples in the Tool walkthrough). The method: audio tokens and video tokens are in the same transformer, or in two streams that attend to each other ("dual-stream"). The effects:

  • Lip movement and speech match.
  • Footsteps, impacts, and doors match the action.
  • Room acoustics match the space.

The limits: the voice can change between clips, the music is generic, and the mix is not controllable. In C06 and C10 you will often replace or layer the generated audio.

Mixture of experts (MoE)

A mixture-of-experts model has several "expert" sub-networks. A router chooses which experts run for each token or each step. Only a part of the parameters run each time, so the model has more capacity for the same compute. Some open video models use MoE. One common split: a high-noise expert for layout and motion, and a low-noise expert for detail. All experts must be in memory (or offloaded), so MoE does not reduce VRAM need.

Positions in space and time

Attention itself does not know where a token is. The model adds position information for three axes: frame (time), row, and column. Most current models use a rotary method (RoPE) for this. It explains two practical facts. A model works best at the resolutions, aspect ratios, and durations that it was trained on. Quality falls when you go far beyond them (for example 4× the trained duration). Read the native values in the model card.

References as tokens

Many models take reference images or clips (a character, a product, a style) as extra tokens in the same sequence. The video tokens attend to them like to the prompt. This is "in-context" conditioning: no training is needed, and identity follows the reference closely. Limits: each reference adds tokens (cost), and many references can conflict. C04 uses this for consistency; C14 trains an adapter when references are not enough.

How to read a model card

Check these items first:

Item Why it matters
License Commercial use, or research only?
Modes T2V, I2V, V2V, reference, editing, audio?
Native resolution, fps, max duration Output that does not need upscaling or extension
Parameter count, precision variants VRAM need (M01)
Distilled variant, recommended steps Speed
Text encoder Prompt understanding, extra VRAM
Known limits Text in frame, hands, fast motion, faces
Training data statement Legal risk (C16)

Tool walkthrough

Model families by architecture (as of 2026-10)

Feature Examples
Joint audio-video generation Veo 3.1, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.x, LTX-2.5 (open weights)
Mixture of experts (high-noise and low-noise experts) Wan 2.2, Wan 2.7
LLM text encoder LTX-2.5 (Gemma 4 12B), Wan (umT5), HunyuanVideo 1.5
Many references as tokens Seedance 2.5 (up to 50 references), Kling 3.0, Wan 2.7 reference-to-video

Check each claim against the model card on the day you use it; versions change monthly.

Decision for a 32 GB GPU: use the distilled FP8 or NVFP4 build. Generate at 720p. Upscale selected shots. Use audio-to-video for music-driven shots.

Lab

Deliverable: C01/M04/model-cards.md.

  1. Choose 3 video models: one hosted (for example Kling 3.0 or Veo 3.1), and two open (for example Wan 2.7 and LTX-2.5 or HunyuanVideo 1.5).
  2. Fill the model-card table for each one. Use only the vendor page, the Hugging Face card, or the technical report.
  3. Mark each fact with its source URL and date.
  4. Write a 5-line recommendation: which model for (a) a commercial ad, (b) a private local pipeline, (c) a dialogue scene with lip sync.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 complete tables with sources.
  • [ ] License is clearly stated for each.
  • [ ] The recommendation uses the model-card facts, not opinions from social media.

Self-check quiz

1. Which component turns the prompt into embeddings?

Modern video models use a large language model as text encoder (for example Gemma 4 12B in LTX-2.5). A better encoder = better prompt understanding.

2. Why do joint audio-video models give better lip sync than adding audio later?

In one transformer, the mouth tokens and the speech tokens exchange information at every step.

3. In an MoE video model with a high-noise expert and a low-noise expert, what does the low-noise expert mostly do?

Early (high-noise) steps decide layout and motion. Late (low-noise) steps add detail. Splitting experts by noise level gives each a specialized job.

4. Which model-card item matters most to decide if a model can be used for a paid client project?

License decides commercial use. Apache 2.0 allows it; 'research only' does not.

5. A model card says '720p, 5 s native'. You ask for 1080p, 20 s in one generation. What do you expect?

Work at the trained resolution and duration, then use upscaling (C09) and extension (C05).

6. You give a model 3 reference images of a character as extra tokens. What is the main benefit, and the main cost?

In-context references are the first tool for consistency (C04). Train an adapter only when they are not enough (C14).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)
  • (a) Commercial ad: a hosted top model (Kling 3.0, Veo 3.1, or Seedance 2.5). Reasons: best quality, native audio, vendor terms allow commercial use on paid plans. Risk: vendor change (compare Sora 2 API shutdown on 2026-09-24).
  • (b) Private local pipeline: Wan 2.7 (Apache 2.0, local weights, no data leaves the company) or LTX-2.5 (LTX-2.x Community License: free below US$10 million annual revenue). Reason: control and privacy. Check the license of every file in the workflow, not only the model (the VAE and the text encoder can differ).
  • (c) Dialogue with lip sync: a joint audio-video model (Kling 3.0 with voice lock, Veo 3.1, or LTX-2.5). Alternative: generate silent video, then use a dedicated lip-sync model (C06).

Every recommendation names its source and date, and states the main risk, so that a reader can re-check it when the facts change.

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M05 Conditioning, guidance, and control

Study time: 9 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain the main types of conditioning (text, image, reference, structure, audio).
  2. Explain classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its effect on output.
  3. Use seed, steps, CFG, and denoise strength on purpose.
  4. Choose a control method for a given production problem.

Key words

conditioning CFG seed denoise strength ControlNet reference

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 05. Conditioning, guidance, and control. After this module, you can: 1. Explain the main types of conditioning (text, image, reference, structure, audio). 2. Explain classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its effect on output. 3. Use seed, steps, CFG, and denoise strength on purpose. 4. Choose a control method for a given production problem. Conditioning is all the information that guides the denoising: text, images, reference videos, structure maps, and audio. Classifier-free guidance, or CFG, makes the model follow the conditioning more strongly. Too low gives weak prompt adherence. Too high gives burnt, over-saturated output. The seed fixes the start noise, so you can reproduce a result. Denoise strength decides how much of an input image or video the model keeps. Structure controls, like depth or pose, fix the layout while the prompt changes the look.

Learn

Conditioning

Conditioning is all the information that guides the denoising. In 2026, a video model can take many types at the same time:

  • Text: the prompt.
  • Frames: a first frame, a last frame, or key frames in the middle.
  • References: images or short videos of a character, product, place, or style. Some current models accept dozens of references.
  • Structure: depth maps, pose skeletons, edge maps, camera paths, or a 3D "white box" scene.
  • Audio: speech or music that the video must follow.
  • Input video: for video-to-video edits.

Each type fixes some things and leaves others free (see the diagram). Good direction is the right combination: the fewest conditions that fix what the shot needs, and nothing more.

Classifier-free guidance (CFG)

During training, the model sometimes sees no prompt. So it learns two predictions: with the condition, and without it. At generation time, CFG takes the difference between them and multiplies it:

output = unconditional + CFG × (conditional − unconditional)

  • CFG near 1: weak adherence, natural but may ignore the prompt.
  • CFG in the model's normal range: good balance.
  • CFG too high: over-saturated, high contrast, artifacts.

CFG doubles the compute per step (two predictions). Distilled models often bake guidance in and use CFG = 1. The negative prompt is the "unconditional" side. It works only when CFG > 1.

Seed and steps

  • The seed fixes the start noise. Log it for every shot you keep, with all other settings and the model version.
  • More steps: more detail, more time (M03).

Denoise strength

For image-to-image and video-to-video, you do not start from pure noise. You add noise to your input up to a level, and then denoise. That level is the denoise strength.

  • 0.2–0.4: keep structure and most detail; change grade or style a little.
  • 0.5–0.7: keep layout and motion; change materials and look.
  • 0.8–1.0: keep only rough motion; new content.

Strength and timing of a control

Structure controls (depth, pose, edges) usually have two settings:

  • strength: how much the control pushes the result (for example 0.4–1.0);
  • start and end: the part of the steps where it is active (for example from 0 % to 60 % of the steps). Because early steps set the composition (M03), a control that is active only in the first half fixes the layout and leaves the detail free. A control that is active to the end can force its own errors into the detail: a noisy depth map makes noisy surfaces.

When conditions conflict

Conditions can disagree: the prompt says "a woman with short hair", the reference shows long hair; the first frame is daylight, the prompt says "night". The model then follows one, mixes them, or makes artifacts. Rules:

  • Decide which condition is the master for each property (identity → reference; layout → structure or first frame; light and mood → prompt).
  • Remove words from the prompt that disagree with the master conditions.
  • Add one condition at a time, and test after each.

Choose a control method

Problem Control
Same character in every shot Reference images or a character LoRA (C14)
Exact start and end of a shot First/last frame
Exact camera move Camera-path control, or 3D layout (C07)
Copy motion from a performance Pose or video reference
Restyle real footage Video-to-video + depth/edge control
Product must not change shape Product references + structure control + low denoise

Watch

  • Sander Dieleman — Guidance: a cheat code for diffusion models (blog)Read the first half. The clearest explanation of CFG.
  • ComfyUI docs — ControlNet tutorialLook at the example images for depth, pose, and canny control.

Worked example

Task: A sneaker ad. The shoe must stay exactly the same. The background and light change in each shot.

  1. Make a product sheet: 6 clean photos of the shoe (front, back, sides, top, 3/4).
  2. Shot 1 (hero): image-to-video. Start frame = a composite of the real shoe photo on a generated background. Prompt only the camera move and light: "slow orbit left, soft rim light, dust in the air".
  3. Shot 2 (on foot): reference-to-video with all 6 product references + one model reference. Prompt the action.
  4. Check every frame for logo and stitching changes. If they drift, reduce motion, shorten the clip, or use first/last frame both from real photos.
  5. Log seed, model, CFG, references, and cost for each kept shot.

Lesson: for products, give the model as little freedom as possible on the product, and full freedom on the rest.

Lab

Deliverable: C01/M05/ with 4 short clips or 4 images per test, plus a report.

Use one model that exposes CFG, seed, and an image input (hosted on fal/Replicate, or ComfyUI).

  1. CFG sweep: one prompt and seed; CFG at 1, 3, 5, 8, 12. Note the effect.
  2. Denoise sweep: one input image; denoise 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8.
  3. Control test: make a depth map of a photo (any depth estimator, for example Depth Anything). Generate 3 different styles with the same depth control.
  4. Write a table: method → what it fixed → what it left free → when you will use it.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Three labeled contact sheets.
  • [ ] The table has at least 5 rows.
  • [ ] All runs in the prompt log.

Self-check quiz

1. CFG is set very high (for example 15 on a model that expects 4). Typical result?

High guidance pushes the output too far toward the condition. Distilled and flow models often need low CFG (1–5).

2. You want the motion of a real dance video but a new character and style. Best control?

Pose control fixes the motion; the reference fixes identity; the prompt sets style.

3. Video-to-video with denoise strength 0.3. What happens?

Low denoise keeps most of the input. High denoise (0.7–1.0) keeps little more than the rough motion.

4. Why does a producer log the seed for every chosen shot?

Same seed + same settings = same start noise. You can re-render at higher steps, or make small variations.

5. A depth control makes the room geometry right, but the walls get a noisy, bumpy surface. What do you change first?

Early steps fix the layout; late steps make detail. Controls active to the end force their errors into the detail.

6. The reference image shows a red jacket; the prompt says 'blue jacket'. The result mixes both. What is the rule?

Conflicting conditions give mixed results or artifacts. Decide which input controls which property.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)
  • CFG 1: soft, low saturation, the "neon" in the prompt is weak. CFG 3–5: best. CFG 8: higher contrast. CFG 12: burnt highlights, color banding, and repeated patterns.
  • Denoise 0.2: almost the input. 0.4: new grade and texture, same layout. 0.6: new materials, same layout. 0.8: same rough composition only.
  • Depth control kept the room geometry and camera in all 3 styles; materials and light changed freely.
  • Use: depth for restyling a real location; pose for performances; references for identity; first/last frame for exact transitions.
  • Depth control active only for the first 60 % of steps gave the same geometry with cleaner surfaces than control to the end.

A strong report states the settings next to each observation, so that another person can repeat the test and see the same effect.

C01 · Generative Model Internals

C01·M06 Small and fast models - quantization, distillation, LoRA

Study time: 8 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain quantization and compare FP16, FP8, INT8, NVFP4, and GGUF.
  2. Explain step distillation and why distilled models are fast.
  3. Explain how a LoRA changes a model with few parameters.
  4. Choose a model variant for a given GPU, speed, and quality target.

Key words

quantization distillation LoRA offload GGUF

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C01, module 06. Small and fast models - quantization, distillation, LoRA. After this module, you can: 1. Explain quantization and compare FP16, FP8, INT8, NVFP4, and GGUF. 2. Explain step distillation and why distilled models are fast. 3. Explain how a LoRA changes a model with few parameters. 4. Choose a model variant for a given GPU, speed, and quality target. Three methods make large models practical. Quantization stores each parameter with fewer bits, so the model needs less memory and often runs faster, with some quality loss. Distillation trains a student model to do in 4 to 8 steps what the teacher does in 30 or more. A LoRA adds small trainable matrices to a frozen model, so you can teach a character, product, or style with a file of tens or hundreds of megabytes. Offload moves parts of the model between GPU and CPU memory when VRAM is too small.

Learn

Quantization

Quantization stores each parameter with fewer bits.

Format Bits Notes
FP32 32 Training reference. Not used for inference.
BF16 / FP16 16 Standard full-quality inference.
FP8 (E4M3) 8 Hardware support on NVIDIA Ada/Hopper/Blackwell. Small quality loss.
INT8 8 Integer; needs a scale per block or channel.
NVFP4 4 Blackwell (RTX 50, B200) hardware format. Fast and small.
GGUF Q4–Q8 4–8 Block quantization format from llama.cpp, widely used in node-graph tools for low VRAM.

Rules:

  • Start with FP8 on a 24–32 GB GPU.
  • Use 4-bit only when necessary, and check faces, text, and fine textures.
  • The speed gain needs hardware support. FP8 on an old GPU saves memory but may not run faster.

Distillation

Step distillation trains a student model to match the output of a teacher in far fewer steps. Methods include consistency distillation and adversarial distillation. Results:

  • 4–8 steps instead of 30–50.
  • Often CFG = 1 (guidance is baked in), so each step is also cheaper.
  • Less variety between seeds, and sometimes less fine detail.

Use distilled models to explore. Use the full model to finish (pattern from M03).

LoRA

A LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the base model. It adds two small matrices A and B next to some weight matrices W. The change is W + B·A. If W is 3,072 × 3,072 (9.4 M numbers) and the rank is 32, A and B together have only about 197,000 numbers. So:

  • training needs much less memory,
  • the file is small (tens to hundreds of MB),
  • you can load several LoRAs and set a strength for each one.

Uses: a character, a product, a style, a camera move, or a speed-up (some "lightning" LoRAs distill steps).

Offload and block swap

When VRAM is too small, parts of the model live in CPU RAM and move to the GPU when needed. This makes it run, but slower. Text encoders are good offload candidates because they run once. "Block swap" moves transformer blocks in and out during each step; it is slower, but allows large models on 16–24 GB.

Caching and reuse

Some work does not need to be done again:

  • Text embeddings: the text encoder output for a prompt is the same in every run. Cache it, and you can even unload the encoder.
  • Step caching: consecutive denoising steps often change the result very little. Caching methods reuse part of a step's computation in the next step. They save 30–60 % of the time with a small loss of detail. Test them like a quantization.
  • The same seed and start frame across variations: you change only what you test.

Speed is not only the model

Measure the whole job: model loading (tens of seconds for large files from a slow disk), text encoding, denoising, VAE decoding, and the video encode. On a cold start, loading can take longer than generation. Keep models loaded between jobs (a warm worker, C13) and put model files on a fast local disk.

Decision table

Situation Choice
32 GB GPU, final quality FP8 full model, 25–40 steps
24 GB GPU, exploration FP8 or GGUF Q8 distilled, 4–8 steps
16 GB GPU GGUF Q4–Q6 or a small (5B) model, offload the text encoder
Same character in 40 shots Train a LoRA (C14)
Cloud API Variant is chosen by the vendor; you pay per second

Watch

  • Hugging Face blog — Exploring quantization backends in DiffusersRead the comparison tables of memory and quality.
  • Edward Hu — LoRA explained by the author (Microsoft)Optional. The idea of low-rank updates.

Worked example

Task: Same Wan 2.2 14B I2V shot on three set-ups. Reported orders of size; your numbers will differ.

Set-up Variant Steps Result
RTX 5090, 32 GB FP8 full 30 Best detail; several minutes per 5 s clip
RTX 5090, 32 GB FP8 + "lightning" step LoRA 4–8 Under a minute; slightly less micro-detail
16 GB laptop GPU GGUF Q5 + text encoder offload 8 Runs; slower; soft detail on hair

Decision: explore with the step LoRA. Re-render the 10 selected shots with the full model at 30 steps, same seed.

Lab

Deliverable: C01/M06/variants.md.

  1. Choose one open model available in several variants on Hugging Face (for example Wan 2.2, LTX-2.5, or FLUX.2).
  2. List all official and popular community variants: precision, size in GB, recommended steps, license.
  3. If you have a GPU (or rent one for 1 hour): run the same prompt + seed on 2 variants. Record time per run and peak VRAM (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv -l 1).
  4. If you have no GPU: use a hosted API that offers "fast" and "pro" versions of one model. Record time and cost.
  5. Write your decision table for a 24 GB GPU and for a 32 GB GPU.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Variant list with sizes and sources.
  • [ ] Measured time and memory (or cost) for 2 variants.
  • [ ] Decision table with reasons.

Self-check quiz

1. A LoRA file for a video model is usually:

A LoRA stores only small low-rank matrices for some layers, not the full weights.

2. Main benefit of a distilled model?

Distillation teaches a student to jump in large steps. It is ideal for exploration and real-time use.

3. Your GPU has 16 GB. The model in FP8 needs 14 GB for weights, plus a 9 GB text encoder. Best option?

The text encoder runs once per prompt. Offloading it after use frees VRAM for the DiT.

4. Which quantization is most likely to show visible artifacts in fine textures?

Fewer bits = more rounding error. 4-bit is very useful, but check fine detail.

5. A job takes 3 minutes: 70 s to load the model, 90 s to denoise, 20 s to decode. Which change helps most for 50 similar jobs?

Measure every stage. Loading is often the largest fixed cost per job.

6. A step-caching method saves 45 % of the time. How do you decide to use it?

Every speed-up trades some quality. Measure the trade on your eval set (M07).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A good report has: (1) a list such as "BF16 28 GB / FP8 14 GB / GGUF Q8 15 GB / Q4 8 GB / distilled LoRA 600 MB"; (2) measured numbers, for example "FP8 full 30 steps: 6 min, 29 GB peak; FP8 + 6-step LoRA: 1 min 10 s, 27 GB peak"; (3) a decision: "24 GB: GGUF Q8 or FP8 with text-encoder offload, step LoRA for exploration. 32 GB: FP8 full for finals." It also says what quality loss was visible (for example "Q4 changed small text on a sign").

A strong report also separates the stages: load time, denoise time, and decode time for each variant. Without this split, a reader cannot tell if a faster variant is faster at generation or only faster to load.

C01, module 07. Evaluate models - arenas, benchmarks, your own eval set. After this module, you can: 1. Explain how arenas rank models with blind human votes (Elo / TrueSkill). 2. List the limits of public leaderboards and benchmarks. 3. Design a small eval set for your own production needs. 4. Run a blind comparison and calculate cost per usable second. Public arenas show two outputs for the same prompt and ask people which is better. Many votes give a ranking such as Elo or TrueSkill. This is useful, but it measures general taste on general prompts. Your work needs specific things: the same character, exact product shape, a camera move, or clean speech. So you also need your own small eval set: fixed prompts and references that match your real jobs. Score each model blind, and calculate the cost per usable second, not the cost per generated second.

Learn

Arenas

An arena shows two anonymous outputs for the same prompt. A person votes for the better one. A rating system (Elo, Bradley–Terry, or TrueSkill) turns many votes into a ranking. The top of the ranking changes almost every month. The top few models are often inside each other's error range (see the Tool walkthrough for a dated example).

Arenas are good for a first short list. Their limits:

  • General prompts, general voters. Your clients are not general.
  • Short clips. They do not test 10-shot consistency.
  • They do not include cost, speed, license, or API stability.
  • Vendors can tune for arena-style prompts.

Benchmarks

Automatic benchmarks (for example VBench) measure many dimensions: motion smoothness, subject consistency, aesthetic quality, and prompt adherence. They are reproducible, but metrics do not always match human taste.

Your own eval set

Make 10–20 fixed cases that match your real work. Each case has:

  • a prompt (and references, if your work uses them),
  • the criteria that matter, with a 1–5 scale,
  • a "usable" rule: for example "all criteria ≥ 4 and no critical defect".

Write the criteria before you see any output; criteria written after viewing tend to favor the clips you already like. Typical criteria: prompt adherence, identity consistency, motion quality, physics, text/logo accuracy, audio sync, artifacts.

Blind scoring

  1. Generate each case with each model (same number of tries, for example 2 seeds).
  2. Rename files with random IDs. Keep the key in a separate file, and do not open it until all scores are written.
  3. Score without the names.
  4. Join scores with the key.

How many clips

A usable rate from a few clips is very uncertain. With 8 clips, "5 usable" means a true rate somewhere between about 31 % and 86 % (a 95 % interval). Two models with 5 of 8 and 2 of 8 are not shown to be different (p ≈ 0.16 in a one-sided Fisher test). Use the small first set (2 seeds per case) to find large problems and to build the habit. To decide a route, use about 30–40 clips per model per shot type (C17·M02 shows the numbers).

Judge models

A vision-language model can score some criteria automatically: "is the label text correct?", "does the clip show two people?". This saves time on many clips. Check it first: score 30 clips yourself, let the judge score the same clips, and measure how often you agree. Use the judge only for the criteria where agreement is high (for example over 85 %). Keep taste, story, and acting for human scores (C03·M03).

Keep the set alive

Version the set (v1, v2, …). Add a case for every real production failure. Retire cases that every model passes. Keep old results, so that you can show progress over time.

Cost per usable second

cost per usable second = total generation cost / total seconds that pass the usable rule

This number decides production budgets. A cheap model with a 10% usable rate can cost more than an expensive model with a 50% usable rate.

Tool walkthrough

Arena example (dated)

As of 2026-10-02, one blind-vote video arena (llm-stats, "best AI for video creation") ranked Kling v3 first (1934), then Happy Horse 1.0 (1816), then Seedance 2.0 Fast (1747). Use such lists to choose which models to test, then test them on your own set.

Scoring and analysis

Use the blind-rename script in the lab, a spreadsheet or CSV for scores, and starter/tools/model_trial.py (C17·M02) to compute usable rates with intervals and cost per usable second per shot type.

Watch

  • LMArena — Text-to-Video leaderboardLook at the video and image arenas. Note the number of votes and the confidence intervals.
  • Artificial Analysis — Video arenaCompare its ranking with LMArena. Note the differences.

Worked example

Eval set "Coffee brand", 4 cases × 3 models × 2 seeds, 5 s clips.

Model List price/s Clips Usable Usable seconds Cost Cost per usable s
A (hosted, premium) US$0.10 8 5 25 US$4.00 US$0.16
B (hosted, fast) US$0.05 8 2 10 US$2.00 US$0.20
C (open, rented GPU) about US$0.02 8 3 15 US$0.80 US$0.05

With 8 clips per model, these rates are rough (5 of 8 → 31–86 %); they show the method and the large differences, not a final ranking.

Decision: model C for background and B-roll (cheapest per usable second, private). Model A for hero shots with the product, where its higher usable rate matters most. Re-run the eval when a new model appears.

Lab

Deliverable: evals/v1/ in your repository: cases, outputs, scores, and a report. You will reuse this set in C05, C17, and the capstone.

  1. Choose a domain you care about (for example a product, a story world, or explainer videos).
  2. Write 10 cases. At least 3 must test consistency between two shots.
  3. Define criteria and the usable rule.
  4. Run 3 models (at least one open model, if possible).
  5. Score blind. Calculate usable rate and cost per usable second.
  6. Write a decision of 5–8 lines.

Starter script for blind renaming:

import random, shutil, json, pathlib
src = pathlib.Path("raw"); dst = pathlib.Path("blind"); dst.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
key = {}
for f in src.glob("*.mp4"):
    rid = f"{random.getrandbits(32):08x}.mp4"
    shutil.copy(f, dst / rid); key[rid] = f.name
json.dump(key, open("key.json", "w"), indent=2)

Result checklist

  • [ ] 10 cases with criteria and a usable rule.
  • [ ] Blind scores for 3 models.
  • [ ] Cost per usable second for each model.
  • [ ] A decision with reasons.

Self-check quiz

1. Two models differ by 10 Elo points with wide confidence intervals. Conclusion?

Small Elo differences inside the error range do not mean a real difference for your job.

2. What is 'cost per usable second'?

If only 1 in 5 clips is usable, the real cost is 5× the list price per second.

3. Why score blind?

When you know the model name, you see what you expect.

4. Which case belongs in an eval set for a beverage-ad studio?

Eval cases must match real jobs and their failure modes.

5. Model A has 5 of 8 usable clips, model B has 2 of 8. What can you say?

Small samples show large problems, not small differences. C17·M02 gives the clip counts for a decision.

6. A judge model agrees with your scores on 'label text correct' in 93 % of 30 clips, and on 'good acting' in 61 %. How do you use it?

Measure agreement per criterion before you trust a judge. Taste and performance need people.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong report shows a table like the worked example. It also says why clips failed (for example "model B: logo text changed in 5 of 8 clips"; "model C: hand deformation in fast motion"). It ends with a routing rule: which model for which shot type. It records the date and the model versions, because the result will be old in 3 months. It states the sample size and the intervals, and it says which results are only rough (small samples) and which justify a routing decision now. It lists two new cases for v2, taken from the failures that the run showed, and the date of the next run. A reader can repeat the whole test from the folder.

Go deeper

  • Chiang et al. (2024) — Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference
  • Huang et al. (2023) — VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models
  • llm-stats — Best AI for video creation (blind-vote leaderboard)

Program · Level 1

C02 Screen Language for AI Directors

50 h · Prerequisites: none

M01M02M03M04M05M06

About this course

A model makes exactly what you describe, and invents the rest. A director who knows screen language describes more, so the model invents less. This course gives you the vocabulary of film and the reasons behind it. You will use this vocabulary in every prompt, every shot list, and every review.

There is no camera work in this course. You analyse existing films, and you make the shots with image and video models.

Course outcomes

  1. Name and use shot sizes, angles, and composition rules on purpose.
  2. Use lens language and camera movement to create a specific feeling.
  3. Describe light and color in precise, reproducible terms.
  4. Plan continuity and cuts so that generated shots join into one scene.
  5. Structure a story for 15 s, 60 s, and 3 min formats.
  6. Turn any shot idea into a precise prompt and judge the result against it.

Modules

  1. C02·M01 Shot sizes, angles, and composition 8 h
  2. C02·M02 Lens language and camera movement 8 h
  3. C02·M03 Light and color language 8 h
  4. C02·M04 Continuity and cutting 8 h
  5. C02·M05 Story structure for short formats 9 h
  6. C02·M06 Write the shot as a prompt 9 h

C02 · Screen Language for AI Directors

C02·M01 Shot sizes, angles, and composition

Study time: 8 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Name the 7 main shot sizes and the effect of each.
  2. Use camera height and angle to change how strong or weak a subject looks.
  3. Use rule of thirds, lead room, headroom, and depth layers.
  4. Analyse the shots of a real scene in a shot table.

Key words

shot size camera angle rule of thirds lead room coverage

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C02, module 01. Shot sizes, angles, and composition. After this module, you can: 1. Name the 7 main shot sizes and the effect of each. 2. Use camera height and angle to change how strong or weak a subject looks. 3. Use rule of thirds, lead room, headroom, and depth layers. 4. Analyse the shots of a real scene in a shot table. Shot size tells the viewer what is important. Wide shots show place and relation. Close-ups show emotion and detail. Camera height changes power: a low angle makes a subject strong, a high angle makes it weak. Composition places the subject on purpose. Use the rule of thirds, give lead room in the direction of a look or movement, and build depth with foreground, middle ground, and background. When you prompt a model, name the shot size, the angle, and the composition every time.

Learn

Shot size

Shot size decides what the viewer sees, and so what the viewer thinks is important. See the diagram for the 6 main sizes, plus the full shot (head to feet, between WS and MS). Rules:

  • Start a scene wide enough to show where we are (establishing shot), unless confusion is the goal.
  • Move closer as emotion grows.
  • Use the closest shots rarely. They lose power if overused.
Abbr. Full name Typical framing
EWS Extreme Wide Shot (also Extreme Long Shot, ELS) The subject is tiny; the setting dominates
WS Wide Shot (also Long Shot, LS) Whole body with plenty of surroundings
FS Full Shot Head to feet, filling the frame
MS Medium Shot (also Mid Shot) Waist up
MCU Medium Close-Up Chest or shoulders up
CU Close-Up The face fills most of the frame
ECU Extreme Close-Up (also XCU) A single detail: eyes, mouth, hands

Camera height and angle

  • Eye level: neutral.
  • Low angle (camera below, looking up): power, threat, heroism.
  • High angle (camera above, looking down): weakness, being watched.
  • Overhead / top shot: pattern, distance, a "god's view".
  • Dutch angle (tilted horizon): unease. Use rarely.
  • Over-the-shoulder (OTS): dialogue; connects two people.
  • Point of view (POV): we see what the character sees.

Composition

  • Rule of thirds: place the subject or eyes on the lines that divide the frame in thirds.
  • Lead room: leave space in the direction of a look or a movement.
  • Headroom: a small space above the head in MS; cut the forehead a little in a tight CU.
  • Depth layers: foreground, middle ground, background. Something in the foreground (a glass, a branch) makes the image deep.
  • Leading lines: roads, rails, and walls lead the eye to the subject.
  • Symmetry: order, control, sometimes threat.
  • Negative space: empty area that makes a subject feel alone or calm.

Shots by content

Shot size says how close; these names say what is in the frame:

  • Single: one person. Two-shot: two people in one frame, which shows their relation. Group shot.
  • Insert: a close detail of an object or action (a hand on a key, a message on a phone). Inserts carry information and make cuts easier.
  • Cutaway: a shot of something outside the main action (a clock, a passer-by, the street). It shows time or context, and hides a jump in the main action.
  • Reaction shot: a listener's face. Reactions often carry the emotion of a dialogue more than the speaker. Plan inserts, cutaways, and reactions on purpose. In AI production they are cheap to make and they solve many editing problems (C02·M04).

Where the viewer looks

The eye goes first to faces (especially eyes), then to the brightest area, the area of highest contrast, sharp focus, warm colors, and movement. Use this to lead attention: put the important thing where these meet, and keep competing bright or moving areas out of the frame. When you review a generated frame, ask: where did my eye go first? If it is not the subject, change the light, the focus, or the composition.

Aspect ratio

The frame shape changes composition. 16:9 for YouTube and TV; 9:16 for Shorts, Reels, TikTok; 2.39:1 for "cinema" look; 1:1 or 4:5 for some feeds. Compose for the delivery ratio from the start. A model that generates 16:9 and is then cropped to 9:16 loses the composition.

Safe areas

Platforms put buttons, captions, and profile names over the picture, mostly at the bottom and the right side of vertical video. Keep faces, text, and products inside the safe area of the delivery format (C10·M03 gives the exact margins). For TV, keep text inside the title-safe area (about 90 % of the frame).

Why this matters for AI

A prompt without shot size and angle gives the model's default: usually a centered medium shot at eye level. Every professional shot list names size, angle, and composition. Your prompts must too.

Watch

  • StudioBinder — Ultimate Guide to Camera ShotsWatch all. Note each shot size and the example films.
  • Every Frame a Painting — Akira Kurosawa: Composing MovementWatch all (8 min). Composition is also about movement inside the frame.

Worked example

Scene: a delivery rider arrives at night at an old apartment block. Goal: tension, then relief.

# Size Angle Composition Purpose
1 EWS High, overhead drone Rider small in lower third; wet street as leading line Place, isolation
2 MS Low, slight Rider on left third, lead room to building Determination
3 ECU Eye level Finger on a broken doorbell, shallow focus Tension detail
4 CU Eye level Face in the doorway light, right third Reaction
5 MCU OTS from the rider Old woman opens the door, warm light Relief

Prompt for shot 3: "Extreme close-up, eye level, a gloved finger presses a cracked, rusty doorbell button, shallow depth of field, rain drops on the metal, cold blue night light, 9:16 vertical."

Lab

Deliverable: C02/M01/, with a shot table and 6 generated frames.

  1. Choose a 2–3 minute scene from a film you like.
  2. Make a shot table: number, size, angle, composition, purpose (at least 15 shots).
  3. Write 6 prompts for a new scene of your own, each with a different size and angle.
  4. Generate them with any image model. Keep the same character description in all 6.
  5. Score each frame: did the model give the size, the angle, and the composition you asked for? (yes/partly/no)

Result checklist

  • [ ] Shot table with 15+ rows and purposes.
  • [ ] 6 frames, each with its prompt.
  • [ ] A score table and 3 sentences on which terms the model followed best.

Self-check quiz

1. You want the audience to feel a character is small and alone in a city. Best shot?

A tiny subject in a large space + high angle = isolation and weakness.

2. A character looks to the right of frame. Where do you place them?

Lead room (look room) in the direction of the look feels natural.

3. Low-angle shot of a CEO in a product launch. Effect?

Camera below eye level, looking up = power.

4. What is 'coverage' in a scene?

Coverage gives the editor choices. With AI you must plan and generate coverage on purpose (C05·M06).

5. A dialogue scene feels flat: only the speaker is ever on screen. What shot type is missing?

Emotion often reads in the listener. Reactions also give the editor places to cut.

6. In a generated frame, your eye goes first to a bright window behind the actor, not to the actor's face. What do you change?

Attention goes to faces, brightness, contrast, focus, and motion. Make them agree.

7. Your 9:16 ad has the product name in the bottom 15 % of the frame. What is the risk?

Compose for the delivery format, including its overlays.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Typical finding: models follow shot size well (wide, close-up), follow "low angle" and "high angle" most of the time, and often ignore "rule of thirds" and "lead room" (they center the subject). Fixes: describe the position ("subject on the left third of the frame, looking right, empty space on the right"), or give a reference image or a rough sketch as the composition guide. Extreme close-ups of hands still show defects in some models; keep them short or use a real insert shot.

Example score table (shape):

Frame Asked Size Angle Composition
1 EWS, high yes yes partly (subject centered, not lower third)
3 ECU, eye level yes yes yes
5 OTS MCU partly (became a single MCU) yes no

"OTS failed in 2 of 3 tries; adding 'the back of a man's shoulder and head out of focus in the left foreground' fixed it."

Go deeper

  • StudioBinder — Camera shots, angles and movements (free guide)
  • Mercado — The Filmmaker's Eye (book, composition rules with examples)

C02 · Screen Language for AI Directors

C02·M02 Lens language and camera movement

Study time: 8 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain how focal length changes perspective, space, and feeling.
  2. Use depth of field to guide attention.
  3. Name the main camera moves and the meaning of each.
  4. Write camera instructions that video models follow.

Key words

focal length depth of field camera movement dolly motivated movement

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C02, module 02. Lens language and camera movement. After this module, you can: 1. Explain how focal length changes perspective, space, and feeling. 2. Use depth of field to guide attention. 3. Name the main camera moves and the meaning of each. 4. Write camera instructions that video models follow. Focal length changes how space looks. A wide lens makes space deep and close faces distorted. A long lens compresses space and isolates the subject. Depth of field decides what is sharp. Shallow focus guides the eye. Camera movement must have a reason. A push-in raises attention or emotion. A pull-out reveals or isolates. A tracking shot follows action. A handheld camera adds urgency. In prompts, name the lens, the focus, and one clear camera move per shot.

Learn

Focal length

Focal length (in mm, for a full-frame camera) changes perspective.

  • Wide (14–24 mm): deep space, strong perspective lines; faces close to the lens look distorted. Use for spaces, action, and unease.
  • Normal (35–50 mm): close to human vision. Neutral and honest.
  • Portrait (85 mm): flattering faces, background soft.
  • Telephoto (135 mm+): compressed space, isolated subject, a "watching from far" feeling.

Video models understand these numbers. "24 mm" and "135 mm" give visibly different perspective.

Depth of field

Depth of field (DOF) is the zone that is sharp. Shallow DOF (wide aperture, long lens, close subject) isolates the subject and guides the eye. Deep DOF (small aperture, wide lens) shows the whole scene. A rack focus moves focus from one subject to another during the shot. It moves attention. Models can do rack focus when you name the start and end subject.

Camera movement

See the diagram. The rule: every move needs a motivation. Good motivations:

  • The subject moves (follow it).
  • The story reveals something (pull out, pan to it).
  • The emotion changes (push in).

A move without motivation feels like a demo reel. Also decide speed (slow, steady, fast) and direction (left, right, toward, away).

Stabilized vs handheld

  • Gimbal or dolly: smooth, controlled, "cinematic".
  • Handheld: shake, breath, urgency. Real documentary feeling.
  • Locked-off (tripod): stillness. Lets the action speak. Often the best choice for AI shots, because fewer things move.

Frame rate, shutter, and motion blur

Film and most drama use 24 fps; TV and online video also use 25 or 30 fps; sport and games use 50–60 fps. Each frame is exposed for a time set by the shutter. The common rule is a 180° shutter: exposure = half the frame time (1/48 s at 24 fps). It gives natural motion blur. A short shutter (1/500 s) gives sharp, stuttering frames: tense, "war footage". A long shutter gives smeared, dreamy motion. Generated video imitates this blur from its training data; ask for "natural motion blur" or "crisp, fast shutter" when it matters. Slow motion is filmed at a high frame rate and played at 24 fps.

Parallax and speed

A camera that moves sideways makes near objects pass faster than far ones. This is parallax, and it is the strongest cue of depth. A slow lateral move with a foreground object (a pillar, a plant) makes a flat scene deep. Fast moves through complex scenes are hard for models: the background can warp. Keep moves slow and the scene simple when quality matters, and add speed in the edit (C02·M04).

Moves that are hard for models

  • Long orbits around a complex subject: the back of the subject and the background must be invented, and they warp.
  • Moves through doors and windows: the model must invent a new space, and it often changes the first one.
  • Combined moves (crane up while panning and pushing in): choose one.
  • Fast whip pans: the blur hides the cut; generate two shots and join them with a whip-pan transition in the edit instead. For these, use first and last frames or a 3D layout (C05·M05).

Camera language in prompts

Write the camera like a camera operator: [move] [direction] [speed], [lens], [focus] Example: "Slow dolly in toward her face, 85 mm, shallow depth of field, focus on the eyes."

Model behavior (as of 2026-10, from practitioners): some models need short camera words; some need detail. Many tools also offer separate camera-control parameters or camera paths (see C05·M05). Use them when they exist, because they are more exact than words.

Watch

  • StudioBinder — Ultimate Guide to Camera MovementWatch all. Note the reason for each move.
  • Every Frame a Painting — Edgar Wright: How to Do Visual ComedyWatch for camera moves and cuts that are timed to action.

Worked example

Same moment, three lenses: a runner on a bridge at sunrise.

  1. "Wide shot, 16 mm, low angle, the runner passes very close to the lens, strong perspective lines of the bridge rails, fast tracking shot following from the side." → energy, speed.
  2. "Medium shot, 50 mm, eye level, steady tracking shot, runner centered, natural perspective." → neutral, documentary.
  3. "Wide shot, 200 mm telephoto from far away, the runner small, the bridge and the sun compressed behind, locked-off camera." → loneliness, scale.

Each prompt has one move (or none), a lens, and a reason.

Lab

Deliverable: C02/M02/ with 6 clips and a review table.

  1. Choose one action (for example "a person opens an old letter").
  2. Generate 3 clips with the same prompt except the lens: 16 mm, 50 mm, 135 mm.
  3. Generate 3 clips with the same lens but different moves: push-in, orbit, locked-off.
  4. For each clip: did the model follow the lens? the move? Was the motion clean?
  5. Write which version gives which feeling, in one sentence each.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 6 clips with prompts in the log.
  • [ ] Review table: lens followed / move followed / defects.
  • [ ] 6 sentences about the feeling of each version.

Self-check quiz

1. You want a crowded street to look dense and compressed. Lens?

Long lenses compress distance between layers. The crowd looks packed.

2. What does a slow push-in on a face usually mean?

The frame closes in as the character's inner state intensifies.

3. Best practice for camera moves in one AI video generation?

Models follow one clear instruction well. Many moves in one clip give chaotic motion.

4. f/1.4 vs f/11 at the same focal length. Which has shallower depth of field?

A wider aperture (small f-number) gives shallower focus.

5. You want a calm interior to feel deep in a 5 s generated shot. Which move helps most?

Parallax is the strongest depth cue. Slow moves also give cleaner model output.

6. A fight scene should feel harsh and urgent, with sharp, stuttering motion. Which shutter look do you ask for?

Short shutters remove blur and make motion staccato. 180° is the natural default.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Usual results: lens differences are clear in background blur and compression. The 16 mm version shows wide-angle distortion on the hands. Push-in is followed well; orbit is followed well when the subject is simple, and gives background warping when the scene is complex. Locked-off gives the cleanest motion, with fewest defects. Feelings: push-in = discovery; orbit = importance; locked-off = quiet observation; 135 mm = distance, privacy.

Review table (shape):

Clip Lens followed Move followed Defects
16 mm yes (strong perspective) n/a hands stretched near the lens
135 mm yes (flat, soft background) n/a none
Orbit n/a partly (stopped at 3 s) background lamp bent during the move

The strong answer names the defect, the time, and a fix for the next try (for example "a simpler background for the orbit").

Go deeper

  • Brown — Cinematography: Theory and Practice (book)
  • Google Cloud — Veo prompt guide (camera and lens terms)
