C03·M06 Agentic coding tools for media work

Study time: 9 h · Level 1

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Use an agentic coding tool to build, run, and fix small media tools.
  2. Give the tool a project memory file with rules and commands.
  3. Review and test code that an agent writes.
  4. Drive headless creative tools (ffmpeg, ComfyUI API) from an agent.

Key words

agentic coding project memory headless ffmpeg

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C03, module 06. Agentic coding tools for media work. After this module, you can: 1. Use an agentic coding tool to build, run, and fix small media tools. 2. Give the tool a project memory file with rules and commands. 3. Review and test code that an agent writes. 4. Drive headless creative tools (ffmpeg, ComfyUI API) from an agent. Agentic coding tools, such as Claude Code and Codex, run in your terminal. They read your files, write code, run commands, and fix errors in a loop. For a media creator with IT skills, they are a fast way to build small tools: batch renders, contact sheets, prompt builders, uploaders, and ComfyUI drivers. Give the agent a project memory file with rules and commands. Review every change with Git, and require tests. The agent can also drive headless tools directly, for example ComfyUI through its JSON API.

Learn

What these tools do

An agentic coding tool is an agent (C03·M04) with tools for files and the shell. It reads your repository, writes code, runs it, reads the errors, and fixes them. Terminal agents, IDE agents, and cloud agents all work this way (dated names in the Tool walkthrough). For you, with IT skills, this is the fastest way to build the small tools that an AI-native production needs.

Good tasks for an agent

  • Batch jobs: transcode, proxies, contact sheets, loudness normalize.
  • Glue code: shot list → prompts → API calls → downloads → naming.
  • Drivers for headless tools: node-graph server APIs, NLE scripting APIs, MCP servers.
  • Checks: ffprobe spec checks, file naming lints, cost reports.

Project memory

Write a memory file in the repo root (each tool has its own file name; see the Tool walkthrough). Include:

  • the goal of the repo,
  • folder layout and naming rules,
  • commands to build, test, and run,
  • forbidden actions (never delete footage/, never overwrite masters),
  • style rules (Python version, type hints, tests required).

Review and test

  • Work on a branch. Review each diff before you merge it.
  • Ask the agent to write tests first for anything that touches media files.
  • Use permission settings to block destructive commands, by default.
  • Keep secrets in environment variables, never in the repo or the memory file.

Write the task like a ticket

A good task for a coding agent has five parts. Give the goal in one sentence, and the inputs and outputs (file types, a CLI shape). Give the constraints (only ffmpeg, Python 3.12, no network), the test that proves it works, and what it must not touch. Small tasks with a test finish well. "Build the whole pipeline" does not: split it into tools that each do one job, and let the agent build and test them one by one.

What agents get wrong

Agents are fast and confident, and they make typical mistakes. They assume a tool or a font exists. They write a command that works on their example but not on your files (spaces in names, variable frame rate, no audio track). They "fix" a failing test by weakening the test. They add a dependency that you did not want. Review the diff with these in mind, and run the tests yourself. Test on a real file from your project, not only on generated test media.

Media in tests

Make test media in the test itself with ffmpeg's built-in sources (testsrc2, sine, anullsrc): a few seconds at small size, generated in milliseconds. Then tests do not depend on files that nobody can share, and they run in CI. Add one test for each edge case that broke the tool in real use: no audio, odd sizes, 23.976 fps, a long file name with spaces.

Driving headless tools

A node-graph generation tool can run as a server. You export a workflow in "API format" (JSON). A script changes inputs (prompt, seed, image) and sends it to the server, then reads the results. An agent can write this script, call it as a tool, or use an MCP server that wraps it (C11·M04).

Tool walkthrough

Tools (as of 2026-10)

  • Terminal agents: Claude Code (memory file CLAUDE.md, permission settings, MCP servers), OpenAI Codex CLI (AGENTS.md).
  • IDE agents in VS Code and JetBrains; cloud agents that open pull requests.

Reference solutions in the starter kit

Compare your agent's result with the tested versions: starter/tools/spec_check.py (delivery checks, C10·M03) and starter/solutions/C11-M04/comfy_run.py with test_comfy_run.py (a headless ComfyUI client, tested against a fake server).

Watch

  • Claude Code — official docs (overview and best practices)Read the overview and 'memory' (CLAUDE.md) pages.
  • Purz on X — Claude Code operating ComfyUI headlessShort demo: the agent sends workflow JSON to the ComfyUI API.

Worked example

Prompt to the agent (in the repo ai-video-lab):

Build tools/contact_sheet.py. Input: a folder of MP4 files. Output: one PNG per file with 12 frames in a 4×3 grid, timecode burned in, file name in the header. Use ffmpeg only. Add a pytest test with a 3-second test clip made by ffmpeg testsrc. Do not touch footage/.

The agent:

  1. Reads CLAUDE.md (rules, Python 3.12, pytest).
  2. Writes the script with ffmpeg -vf "select=..., drawtext=timecode..., tile=4x3" (it assumes the drawtext filter exists).
  3. Writes a test that makes a clip with ffmpeg -f lavfi -i testsrc=duration=3:size=640x360:rate=24.
  4. Runs pytest; it fails: the installed ffmpeg (9.0.2 in the course tests) has no drawtext filter. The agent switches to Pillow: it renders the timecode labels as PNG images and overlays them with ffmpeg. The test passes.
  5. You review the diff and commit.

Lab

Deliverable: 3 tools in ai-video-lab/tools/, each made with an agentic coding tool, each with tests.

  1. Write CLAUDE.md (or the equivalent) for your repo.
  2. Build contact_sheet.py (as above).
  3. Build spec_check.py: reads a delivery spec YAML (resolution, fps, codec, loudness range) and checks files with ffprobe and ffmpeg ebur128. Exit code ≠ 0 on failure.
  4. Build comfy_run.py: loads a ComfyUI API-format workflow, sets prompt and seed, submits it, waits, downloads outputs. (No GPU? Use a cloud ComfyUI or mock the server in tests.)
  5. Record what you asked, what the agent did wrong, and how you corrected it.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 tools, each with passing tests.
  • [ ] Memory file with forbidden actions.
  • [ ] A short log of agent mistakes and fixes.

Self-check quiz

1. What belongs in a project memory file (for example CLAUDE.md)?

Stable rules and commands. Never secrets.

2. Best protection against a bad agent change?

Version control + review + tests.

3. 'Headless' ComfyUI means:

You send workflow JSON to the server and receive outputs.

4. An agent proposes `rm -rf footage/` to 'clean up'. What should have prevented this?

Use the tool's permission system; deny destructive commands by default.

5. A test fails, and the agent 'fixes' it by changing the expected value in the test. What do you do?

Weakening tests is a typical agent mistake. Review test changes with extra care.

6. Your tool passes all tests on generated test clips, then fails on a client file. What do you add?

Each real failure becomes a test, so it never comes back.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Good results have small, single-purpose scripts with a CLI, tests that make their own test media with ffmpeg lavfi, and a spec checker that prints clear failures ("fps 30 ≠ 24"; "integrated loudness −11.2 LUFS above −14 ±1"). Typical agent mistakes: wrong ffmpeg filter escaping, assuming a font file exists, polling ComfyUI without a timeout. Each was found by tests or by review.

Mistake log (shape): "Task: contact sheets. Agent used drawtext; our ffmpeg has no such filter → test failed → I told it to render labels with Pillow. Task: spec check. Agent read loudness from the wrong ffmpeg output line → my test with a −23 LUFS tone caught it. Task: ComfyUI client. Agent polled forever → I asked for a timeout and a test with a server that never answers." Each entry names the task, the mistake, how it was found, and the correction.

  • FFmpeg documentation

About this course

C04 · Image Generation and Look Development

C04·M01 Prompt and reference control for images

Study time: 10 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Write image prompts with the shot grammar from C02, in a fixed order that you can automate.
  2. Use reference images for identity, objects, style, and composition, and say in the prompt what each reference is for.
  3. Compare 3 image models on your own eval set with a scoring sheet, and route jobs to models from the results.
  4. Log every kept image with model, prompt, seed, settings, references, and cost.

Key words

reference image style reference aspect ratio prompt log

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C04, module 01. Prompt and reference control for images. After this module, you can: 1. Write image prompts with the shot grammar from C02, in a fixed order that you can automate. 2. Use reference images for identity, objects, style, and composition, and say in the prompt what each reference is for. 3. Compare 3 image models on your own eval set with a scoring sheet, and route jobs to models from the results. 4. Log every kept image with model, prompt, seed, settings, references, and cost. Image models accept text and reference images. Text controls subject, action, camera, light, and style. Reference images control identity, objects, style, and composition more exactly than words. Write prompts in a fixed order, so code can build them and you can compare them. Say what each reference is for. Models have different strengths, so test them on your own cases with a scoring sheet and route each job to the best model. Log every image that you keep, with everything that you need to make it again.

Learn

Why start with images

In AI-native video, most shots start as a still image. A still costs a few cents and a few seconds. A video take costs 10–100 times more. The still fixes the things that are expensive to fix later: who is in the frame, where they stand, the lens, the light, and the look. When the still is right, the video model only adds motion (C05).

So the image stage is not decoration. It is the design stage of each shot.

The prompt order

Write every image prompt in the same order. Then code can build prompts from your shot list (C03·M02), and you can see what changed between two versions.

  1. Shot: size, angle, lens look. "Medium close-up, eye level, 85 mm look, shallow depth of field."
  2. Subject: who or what, with the fixed descriptor from the character sheet (M03).
  3. Action: one clear action or state. "She reads a small printed photo."
  4. Place and time: "Hospital locker room, night."
  5. Light: direction, quality, color. "Cold fluorescent top light, warm practical lamp from frame left."
  6. Look: the look suffix from the look bible (M04).
  7. Format: aspect ratio and size, as a setting if the model has one.

Keep each part short and concrete. A model follows "85 mm look, background soft" better than "beautiful cinematic depth".

Text inside the image

Current models can render short text well. Put the exact text in quotes and say where it goes: a sign on the door that reads "STAFF ONLY". Check every letter. Long text and small text still fail often. For logos and legal text, use the real file in a later edit or in compositing (C09·M03). Do not trust generation for those.

Aspect ratio

Set the aspect ratio when you generate: 16:9, 9:16, 4:5, or 2.39:1. A model composes for the frame that it gets. A vertical crop of a horizontal frame usually puts the subject too small or cuts the head. If you need several ratios, generate the main one, then extend the frame for the others (M02).

Reference control

A reference image gives the model exact visual information that words cannot hold:

  • Identity: face, hair, body, clothes. Use 2–3 views from the character sheet.
  • Objects: product shape, logo, packaging, materials.
  • Place: room layout, windows, props.
  • Style: palette, texture, rendering. Use a style reference only for style.
  • Composition: a sketch, a 3D block-out, or a photo with the layout you want.

Most current models accept several references in one request. They do not know the role of each image unless you say it. Write the roles into the prompt: "Image 1 is the character. Image 2 is the room; keep its layout. Image 3 is for color mood only; do not copy objects from it." Without roles, models mix features across images. A common failure is the palette of the place image on the character's clothes.

How references reach the model

There are two common methods inside the models:

  1. Encoded references. The image is encoded (often by the same VAE that makes the output) and attached to the conditioning. The model attends to it at every step. This copies detail well. You will see this method node by node in C11·M02.
  2. Image embeddings. A vision encoder turns the image into a short vector of features. An adapter feeds these features to the model. This copies style and general identity, and fine detail less well. You do not need to know which method a hosted model uses. You need to test how exactly it copies the detail that matters for your shot.

Choose models by test

Model rankings change every month. Your project has its own needs. So build a small eval set and test (C01·M07):

  1. Cases: 6–10 shots from your own shot list. Include the hard cases: night, mixed light, close-ups, hands, text, and your product.
  2. Variants: text only, and text plus references.
  3. Scores: 1–5 for prompt adherence, identity, light, look, and artifacts. Score blind if you can: hide the model name.
  4. Cost and time: per image and per kept image.
  5. Route: choose a model per job. One model can be best for hero key frames, another for edits, and an open model for private client work.

The prompt log

Every image that you keep gets one log line. The line must let you make the image again, change it, and prove where it came from (C16). Use starter/tools/promptlog.py. It appends JSON lines to prompts/log.jsonl, adds a SHA-256 hash of the file, and checks the log for missing fields, typos, changed files, and references without a rights record.

Tool walkthrough

This walkthrough shows one hosted path and one open path (as of 2026-10). Use the landscape page for current alternatives.

Hosted: an image API from Python

The official Gemini image guide (2026-10) shows this shape for text plus one reference image:

from google import genai
import base64

client = genai.Client()  # reads the API key from the environment
ref = base64.b64encode(open("refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png", "rb").read()).decode()
interaction = client.interactions.create(
    model="gemini-3-pro-image",
    input=[
        {"type": "text", "text": PROMPT},
        {"type": "image", "data": ref, "mime_type": "image/png"},
    ],
    response_format={"type": "image", "aspect_ratio": "9:16", "image_size": "2K"},
)
open("out/S07_a.png", "wb").write(base64.b64decode(interaction.output_image.data))

Check the guide before you use this code. Vendors change SDKs and model IDs often. The model IDs listed on 2026-10-04 were gemini-3-pro-image, gemini-3.1-flash-image, gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image, and gemini-2.5-flash-image.

Then log the image:

python starter/tools/promptlog.py add --id S07_a --model gemini-3-pro-image \
  --prompt-file prompts/S07.txt --refs CHAR-MARA-01,LOC-LOCKER-02 --cost 0.13 \
  --file out/S07_a.png --status kept

Open: the starter ComfyUI workflows

If you have a GPU (or rent one), use the C11 starter workflows now. You do not need to understand the graphs yet.

  • 01_t2i_flux2_klein_4b.json: text only, 4 steps.
  • 02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b.json: two references (character and place) plus a prompt. Run them from the editor, or with starter/solutions/C11-M04/comfy_run.py and the map files. The open path keeps client images on your own machine.

The scoring sheet

Use one CSV row per image: shot,model,variant,seed,adherence,identity,light,look,artifacts,cost_usd,kept. A spreadsheet pivot by model and variant gives the routing table.

Watch

  • Google — Gemini image generation guide (prompting and multi-image references)Read the prompt strategies and the multi-image examples. 20 minutes.
  • OpenAI — image generation guideRead the sections on editing with reference images and on quality settings.
  • Black Forest Labs — FLUX.2 announcement and docsLook at the multi-reference examples and the model variants (pro, dev, klein).

Worked example

Key frame for shot S07 (from the C02·M06 shot list): "MCU, eye level, 85 mm look. Mara reads a printed photo. Locker room, night. Cold fluorescent top light and a warm practical lamp. 9:16."

Try Input Result Decision
1 Text only, model A Good light. The face does not match the character sheet. Reject
2 Text + 2 character views, model A Face correct. The photo in her hand is blank. Keep as fallback
3 Text + 2 character views + room, model B, roles named Face and room correct. Light too warm. Edit (M02)
4 Instruction edit of try 3: "make the top light colder, keep everything else" All correct. Keep: KF-S07-v3

Cost: 4 calls at about US$0.04–0.13 each. The log line for KF-S07-v3 has parent: S07_try3, so the edit history is clear.

Routing from a 6-shot test (example of the shape):

Job Model Why
Hero key frames with cast B Identity 4.5 / 5 with references
Small fixes and edits B Keeps unchanged areas best (M02)
Client product shots (private data) Open model on own GPU Data stays inside; identity 4 / 5
Fast exploration Open model, 4-step US$0 per image on own GPU, 3 s each

Lab

Deliverable: C04/M01/ with a scoring sheet, a routing table, and 6 kept key frames with log lines.

  1. Choose 6 shots from your C02·M06 shot list. Include at least one night shot, one close-up, and one shot with text in the frame.
  2. Write each prompt in the 7-part order. Save each prompt as a text file.
  3. Generate each shot with 3 models: first text only, then with references with named roles. Use at least one hosted model and one open model.
  4. Score every image in the CSV. Hide the model names while you score, if you can.
  5. Keep the best frame for each shot. Log each kept frame with promptlog.py. Run promptlog.py check until it passes.
  6. Write the routing table: job → model → reason, with numbers from your sheet.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 36 or more images, all scored in the CSV.
  • [ ] 6 kept key frames, each with a complete log line; promptlog.py check passes.
  • [ ] Routing table with numbers.
  • [ ] One paragraph: what references fixed, and what they did not fix.

Self-check quiz

1. A client must see their real product's logo exactly. What is the correct control, and what is the second step?

Words cannot describe a logo exactly. A reference can, but models still change small details, so a check is part of the method.

2. You give three reference images without explanation. The output copies the color palette of the location image onto the character's clothes. What is the fix?

Without roles, the model mixes features from all references. Name each reference and its job.

3. Model A wins your text-only test. Model B wins with references. Your project has a fixed cast in 40 shots. Which do you use for key frames?

Choose by the job. A fixed cast means reference control is the main requirement.

4. Your eval set has 6 prompts, all bright day exteriors. Model C scores best. What is wrong with the conclusion?

An eval set must look like the work. Include your hardest cases: night, mixed light, close-ups, hands, and text.

5. Which fields must a prompt-log line have so that you can make the image again?

Without the exact model version, seed, settings, and references, you cannot reproduce or vary the image. C16 also needs the log to show where each image came from.

6. You need a 9:16 vertical key frame. When do you set the aspect ratio?

A model composes for the frame that it gets. A crop of a 16:9 frame often cuts the head or leaves the subject too small.

7. A hosted model gives the best results, but the client contract forbids sending their unreleased product photos to third parties. What do you do?

Data rules are requirements. An open-weight model that runs on your own GPU keeps the data inside. Measure its quality before you promise it.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission has a sheet with 36–48 rows and a summary like this:

Variant Mean identity Mean adherence Mean cost per kept image
Text only, all models 2.1 3.8 US$0.31
With named references, all models 4.2 3.9 US$0.12

The text explains the numbers: "References doubled identity on every model. Prompt adherence did not change, because references do not carry action or camera. The cost per kept image fell by 60 %, because fewer takes failed."

The routing table names a model for each job and gives the score that justifies it. It also names a risk: "Model B changed the scar position in 2 of 12 images. Check the scar in every review."

The log passes promptlog.py check. Every kept image has its references by ID, and every reference that you did not make has a rights line.

The paragraph on limits says what references did not fix: hands, small text, and the photo inside the photo. These need edits (M02) or compositing (C09·M03).

C04 · Image Generation and Look Development

C04·M02 Instruction editing, inpainting, outpainting, upscaling

Study time: 9 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Edit images with one-change instructions that name what must not change.
  2. Use masks for local fixes, and extend the canvas for a second aspect ratio.
  3. Measure what an edit changed outside the target area, and reject edits that drift.
  4. Choose between non-generative and generative upscaling, and protect text, logos, and faces.

Key words

instruction editing inpainting outpainting upscaling mask

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C04, module 02. Instruction editing, inpainting, outpainting, upscaling. After this module, you can: 1. Edit images with one-change instructions that name what must not change. 2. Use masks for local fixes, and extend the canvas for a second aspect ratio. 3. Measure what an edit changed outside the target area, and reject edits that drift. 4. Choose between non-generative and generative upscaling, and protect text, logos, and faces. Modern image models edit by instruction: remove the cup, make it night, change the jacket to red. Good models keep everything else the same, but not always, so measure. Inpainting changes only a masked area. Outpainting extends the canvas, for example to make a vertical version. Upscalers add resolution; generative upscalers also invent detail, so protect faces, text, and logos. An edit is often cheaper and more exact than a new generation, because it keeps what was already approved.

Learn

Why edit

A generated key frame is often 80 % right. A new generation can fix the last 20 % and break the 80 %. An edit keeps the approved parts and changes one thing. It is usually faster, cheaper, and easier to review. Treat edits like code changes: one change at a time, with a check after each change.

Instruction editing

An instruction edit takes an image and a text instruction and returns a new image. The model was trained on pairs of images that differ by one described change. So it works best when you describe one change.

Write instructions like a retoucher's notes:

  • One change per instruction. "Change the jacket to deep red wool."
  • Name what must stay. "Keep her face, pose, hair, and the background unchanged."
  • Be concrete. "Deep red wool, same cut" works better than "make it pop".
  • Name the place in the frame when there are several similar objects. "The cup on the left side of the table."

Edit chains drift

Multi-turn editing is convenient. But each turn decodes and re-generates the image. Small losses add up: detail gets softer, color shifts, and faces change a little. After 3–5 turns, compare with the original. If quality fell, go back to the best version and continue from there. Log each edit with a parent ID, so the history is clear.

Inpainting

A mask marks the area that may change. Only the masked area is generated again. The model sees the rest of the image, so the new area matches the light and perspective. Use masks for:

  • removing an object;
  • fixing hands, eyes, or teeth;
  • fixing or adding text;
  • replacing a generated product with the real product photo.

Make the mask a little larger than the object, and soften (feather) its edge by a few pixels. A hard edge can show a seam.

Measure what changed

Do not trust your eyes alone. A color shift of a few values is hard to see in one frame, and easy to see when two shots cut together. Measure each edit:

  1. Mark the area that should change (a box or a mask).
  2. Compare before and after outside that area.
  3. Look at three numbers: the share of pixels that changed, the mean absolute difference, and the signed shift of each color channel, of saturation, and of brightness.

The signed shift is important. Compression noise moves pixels up and down, so its signed mean is near 0. A real drift moves the whole frame in one direction, for example warmer or more saturated. starter/tools/frame_diff.py reports all of these and fails the edit if the outside area drifted.

If an edit drifts outside the target, you have two fixes:

  • redo it with a mask;
  • composite: take only the target area from the edit and paste it onto the original.

Outpainting and reframing

Outpainting extends the canvas and generates the new area. Use it to make a 9:16 version from 16:9, or to add headroom. After the extension, check the composition again (C02·M01). A vertical frame usually needs the subject larger. If the subject becomes too small, generate the vertical frame again from the same references instead.

Outpainting has typical faults: repeated patterns at the edges, a second copy of an object, and lines that do not continue correctly (walls, tables). Check the joins.

Upscaling

Two kinds of upscalers exist:

  • Non-generative upscalers sharpen and enlarge what is there. They cannot invent a wrong letter. They look softer.
  • Generative upscalers use a diffusion model to add detail. They look sharper, with skin texture and fabric. They also invent: pores, threads, and sometimes wrong letters, numbers, or facial features.

Rules:

  1. Upscale only approved frames.
  2. For text, logos, and real people, protect the area with a mask, or restore it from a non-generative upscale.
  3. Check at 200 % zoom. For video, you usually upscale the video, not the key frame (C09·M04). Upscale key frames for posters, thumbnails, and print.

Tool walkthrough

Instruction edit with an image API

Use the same call as in M01, with the approved frame as the input image and the instruction as the text. Example instruction for shot S07:

Make the fluorescent top light colder (more blue). Keep the woman's face, hair, raincoat,
pose, the photo in her hand, and the room exactly as they are.

Mask edit in ComfyUI (open path)

In the ComfyUI editor, right-click a Load Image node and open the mask editor. Paint the area, save, and connect the MASK output to an inpaint-capable graph. The official templates include image-edit and inpaint graphs for current open models. For a hand fix, make the mask about 20 % larger than the hand.

Measure the edit

python starter/tools/frame_diff.py KF-S07-v2.png KF-S07-v3.png --box 410,620,690,980 --heatmap diff_S07.png

Open diff_S07.png: bright areas changed. If the heatmap shows changes far from the box, read the shift numbers.

Non-generative upscale with ffmpeg

For a safe ×2 reference version: ffmpeg -i in.png -vf scale=iw*2:ih*2:flags=lanczos out_x2.png. Compare it with a generative upscale at 200 % zoom.

Watch

  • Google — Gemini image editing (multi-turn) examplesLook at the editing and multi-turn examples. Note how each instruction names one change.
  • Brooks et al. — InstructPix2Pix (project code and examples)The research origin of instruction editing. Look at the example pairs.

Worked example

Calibrate the checker. We tested frame_diff.py on a 960 × 1200 portrait (2026-10-04). The "allowed area" was a 220 × 220 box:

After image Mean abs. diff outside Saturation shift Result
JPEG re-save, quality 90 0.81 −1.21 PASS
Local edit inside the box only 0.00 0.00 PASS
Local edit + saturation +15 % everywhere 0.79 +4.26 FAIL
Warm shift (red +6, blue −6) 3.52 +60.98 FAIL
JPEG re-save, quality 75 2.73 −0.86 FAIL (3.8 % of pixels changed)

The mean difference is almost the same for the quality-90 save and the saturation drift (0.81 and 0.79). Only the signed shifts separate them. Also, heavy compression fails the check. So save edit results as PNG.

Fix plan for KF-S07-v3:

  1. The photo in her hand must show a wet locker. Mask the photo area; instruction "a small printed photo of a wet metal locker, slightly blurred". Outside change: 0.2 % of pixels. ✓
  2. A 16:9 version for the trailer: extend left and right. A second locker door appears in the wrong color. Instruction edit "make the new locker door the same grey as the others". ✓
  3. A 4K poster version: generative ×2 upscale. The locker number "27" became "21". Mask the number and restore it from the lanczos upscale. ✓

Lab

Deliverable: C04/M02/ with before/after pairs, diff reports, and a fix decision table.

  1. Choose 3 key frames from M01 that each have a real problem.
  2. For each frame, do one instruction edit, one mask edit, and one canvas extension to a second aspect ratio.
  3. Measure every edit with frame_diff.py. Save the JSON report and the heatmap. Redo any edit that fails.
  4. Upscale one frame twice: non-generative and generative. Compare text, faces, and fabric at 200 % zoom. Write what the generative upscaler invented.
  5. Log every kept edit with its parent ID.
  6. Write a fix decision table: problem → method → measured result → cost.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 9 before/after pairs, each with a diff report.
  • [ ] At least one failed edit that you found by measurement, and how you fixed it.
  • [ ] Upscale comparison with a list of invented details.
  • [ ] Fix decision table with costs.

Self-check quiz

1. You must change three things in an approved frame: the jacket color, the time on the wall clock, and a cup on the table. How do you edit?

One change per call is followed more exactly and is easy to review. If edit 2 drifts, you go back one step, not three.

2. After an edit, the target object is correct, and the measurement shows saturation +4.3 outside the target area. What happened, and what do you do?

A global shift breaks continuity with neighboring shots. A mask limits the change. A composite keeps the original pixels outside the target exactly.

3. You need a 9:16 version of a perfect 16:9 frame of a person at the table. What is the best method?

Outpainting keeps the subject. But vertical framing often needs the subject larger, so check composition (C02·M01).

4. A generative upscaler changed '27' on a locker door to '21'. Why, and what is the fix?

A generative upscaler draws new detail. For text, logos, and real faces, protect the area or use a method that does not invent.

5. After 6 multi-turn edits, the image is soft and the colors are flat. What is the cause and the fix?

Edit chains drift. Keep a version history (log parent IDs) and restart from a strong version.

6. When is a mask better than an instruction edit?

A mask is a hard limit. An instruction is a request that a model can over-apply.

7. A JPEG re-save at quality 90 gives a mean difference of 0.8 and no color shift. A real edit gives mean 0.8 and saturation +4. Why does the checker fail only the edit?

Mean absolute difference cannot separate noise from drift. Signed mean shifts can.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Fix decision table (shape of a strong answer):

Frame Problem Method Outside change Result Cost
S03 extra finger mask + inpaint, mask 20 % larger than the hand 0.1 %, no shift ✓ US$0.04
S03 cup in wrong hand instruction edit 0.3 %, saturation +3.1 ✗ → redo with mask US$0.08
S05 16:9 needed canvas extension n/a (new area) ✓ after one fix: a doubled lamp at the right edge US$0.05
S07 sign text wrong mask + inpaint with the exact text in quotes 0.0 % ✓ on try 2 US$0.08
S07 poster 4K generative ×2 n/a number "27" → "21"; restored from lanczos US$0.02

The written summary gives three lessons with evidence:

  1. "Instruction edits drifted color in 2 of 6 cases. Masks never did. For approved frames, I now use masks by default."
  2. "Canvas extension made repeated objects at the edges in 2 of 3 cases. I check the edges first."
  3. "The generative upscaler invented 3 details: a number, a button, and an eyelash pattern. Faces looked better, text looked worse."

The log shows each edit with its parent, so anybody can follow KF-S07-v1 → v2 → v3.

C04 · Image Generation and Look Development

C04·M03 Character, product, and environment sheets

Study time: 11 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Make a character sheet with a turnaround, an expression set, wardrobe variants, and a fixed descriptor sentence.
  2. Make a product sheet that protects shape, logo, materials, and exact colors.
  3. Make an environment sheet with several angles, light states, a panorama anchor, and a top-view plan.
  4. Store references in a library that code can read by ID, with source and rights for every file.
  5. Test consistency with references only, and find which details drift.

Key words

character sheet turnaround product sheet environment sheet panorama anchor

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C04, module 03. Character, product, and environment sheets. After this module, you can: 1. Make a character sheet with a turnaround, an expression set, wardrobe variants, and a fixed descriptor sentence. 2. Make a product sheet that protects shape, logo, materials, and exact colors. 3. Make an environment sheet with several angles, light states, a panorama anchor, and a top-view plan. 4. Store references in a library that code can read by ID, with source and rights for every file. 5. Test consistency with references only, and find which details drift. Consistency starts with reference sheets. A character sheet shows one person from the front, three-quarter, side, and back, with expressions and wardrobe variants, on plain light. A product sheet shows the exact object from all sides, with its logo and materials. An environment sheet shows a place from several angles and at several times of day; a panorama can anchor the whole space. Every set gets an ID and a sheet file with its descriptor, source, and rights. Prompts, pipelines, and logs then point to the same IDs.

Learn

Why sheets

A model keeps a character, a product, or a place the same only when it gets the same information every time. Words are not exact enough. "Short black hair" gives a different haircut in every shot. A reference sheet is the exact information, made once, approved once, and used in every shot.

Think of a sheet as a fixed dependency. Every key frame depends on it. If a sheet has an error, every shot gets the error.

Character sheet

Contents:

  • Turnaround: front, three-quarter, side, and back, full body and head. Same light, same plain background, same scale.
  • Expressions: neutral, happy, sad, angry, surprised, and thinking. Close-ups, front view.
  • Wardrobe variants: A, B, C. Each as a full-body front view.
  • Details: hands, a unique mark (scar, tattoo), jewelry, buttons, glasses. Close-ups.
  • Descriptor sentence: one fixed sentence that every prompt uses, word for word. Example: "Mara, early 30s, short black bob, small scar through the left eyebrow, olive raincoat with brass buttons."
  • Voice ID for audio (C06·M01), and height and age for consistency of scale.

Use neutral, soft light and a plain mid-grey background. A sheet with dramatic light teaches every shot that light. A sheet in a kitchen puts kitchen details in every shot.

How to make a character sheet

  1. Generate one strong front portrait. Approve it carefully. It is the root of all other views.
  2. Generate each other view with the front portrait as the reference: "The same woman as image 1. Full body, side view, facing left. Same clothes, same light, plain grey background."
  3. Check each view against the descriptor and the front: the mark on the correct side, the same hairline, the same buttons. Fix errors with a mask edit (M02).
  4. Generate the expressions from the front portrait.
  5. Generate the wardrobe variants. Then generate one view of each variant in the other views if the story needs it.

Short-drama studios keep a large expression library per character, because emotion close-ups are a large part of their shots. Make the expressions that your story needs.

Product sheet

A real product must never be invented or "improved". Use real photos of the product, or the client's CAD renders. If you generate a product (a fictional one), generate it once, approve it, and freeze it.

Contents:

  • 6 views: front, back, left, right, top, and three-quarter;
  • a logo close-up and the logo vector file;
  • material swatches: matte, gloss, metal, glass;
  • exact color values (hex, or the brand's spot colors);
  • do-not rules from the brand guide: no tilted logo, no other colors.

Environment sheet

  • Angles: a wide establishing view, a reverse view, and 3–4 detail views (door, window, the main prop).
  • Light states: the same place at 3 times or moods, for example day, night, and night with emergency light. This is your light plan (C02·M03).
  • Panorama: a 360° image of the space. Make it with a model that supports panoramas, or stitch it from several views. It anchors the layout. Each shot uses the part of the panorama that it needs, so walls, windows, and props stay in place.
  • Top-view plan: a simple drawing with walls, doors, the main props, the action line, and the camera positions (C02·M04).

The reference library

Store references so that code can read them:

refs/
  CHAR-MARA/   sheet.json  01_front.png  02_34.png  03_side.png  04_back.png  10_happy.png ...
  PROD-CAMERA/ sheet.json  front.png  back.png ... logo.png
  LOC-LOCKER/  sheet.json  wide.png  reverse.png  pano.png  plan.png  night.png

sheet.json holds the ID, the kind, the descriptor, the source (generated, photo, licensed), the rights status, a consent file for any real person, and the file of each view. starter/tools/refs_check.py checks the library: required views, files that exist, files that are not listed, rights values, and consent for photos of real people.

Test consistency

A sheet is good when new shots made only from the sheet keep the identity. Test it:

  1. Write 3–5 new short prompts in new places and with new actions.
  2. Generate them with the references only, no long descriptions.
  3. Score each detail: face, hair, mark, clothes, buttons, scale.
  4. The details that drift tell you what to add: a detail close-up, a missing view, or a LoRA (C14).

Tool walkthrough

Turnaround prompts (any model with multi-reference input)

Front portrait:

Studio character reference, front view, head and shoulders, neutral expression.
Mara, early 30s, short black bob, small scar through the left eyebrow, olive raincoat with brass buttons.
Soft even light, plain mid-grey background, no shadows on the background. 3:4.

Side view, with the approved front as image 1:

Image 1 is the character. The same woman as image 1, full body, side view facing left,
same raincoat and buttons, same hair. The scar is on her LEFT eyebrow (the side facing away).
Soft even light, plain mid-grey background, same scale as a 170 cm person in frame. 3:4.

Write the side of a mark in capitals when the view could confuse it. Models often mirror features in side views.

The open path

02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b.json (C11 starter kit) takes two references. For a turnaround, use the front portrait as reference 1 and a grey background image as reference 2. Change only the view in the prompt.

Check the library

python starter/tools/refs_check.py refs/

Watch

  • Bilibili — Seedance 2.0: 360° panorama control for scene consistency (Chinese)Watch the method: one panorama as the anchor for many shots in the same place.
  • RunComfy — Consistent Character Creator workflow (ComfyUI)Look at how one workflow makes a full character sheet.

Worked example

Character Mara.

  1. Front portrait: 8 tries, 1 approved. Approval checklist: scar on her left eyebrow, short bob above the jaw, 4 brass buttons visible.
  2. Turnaround with the front as reference: three-quarter ✓ on try 1, back ✓ on try 2, side ✗ — the scar moved to the right eyebrow. Mask edit on the eyebrow area with the instruction "small scar through the eyebrow". Outside change 0.1 %. ✓
  3. Expressions: 6 close-ups. "Angry" changed her hairline; regenerated with the instruction "same hairline as image 1". ✓
  4. Wardrobe B: hospital scrubs, full-body front. ✓
  5. sheet.json written. refs_check.py reported one problem: CHAR-MARA: file 05_side_v1.png is not listed in sheet.json (an old rejected file). Moved it to rejects/. ✓

Consistency test: 4 new scenes (street, car, kitchen, hospital corridor) from references only:

Detail Street Car Kitchen Corridor
Face 5 4 4 5
Scar side ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓
Hair 5 5 4 5
Buttons (4, brass) 3 2 3 3

Finding: buttons drift most. Fix: a close-up of the coat front added as 11_buttons.png, and the prompt names it. The re-test gives buttons 4, 4, 4, 5.

Lab

Deliverable: refs/ with 1 character, 1 product, and 1 environment set, plus C04/M03/consistency.md.

  1. Character sheet: 4 views, 6 expressions, 2 wardrobe variants, detail close-ups, and the descriptor sentence.
  2. Product sheet: 6 views and a logo close-up. Use a real object that you own (photograph it on a plain background), or a generated object that you freeze.
  3. Environment sheet: 4 views, 3 light states, a panorama, and a top-view plan with the action line.
  4. Write sheet.json for each set. Run refs_check.py refs/ until it passes.
  5. Consistency test: 4 new scenes from references only. Score each detail. Add one fix for the detail that drifts most, and test again.
  6. Log every kept reference image with promptlog.py. Add a rights line for every photo that you did not take.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Three complete sets; refs_check.py passes.
  • [ ] Every view checked against the descriptor (write the checks).
  • [ ] Consistency table before and after one fix.
  • [ ] Prompt-log and rights-log lines for all files.

Self-check quiz

1. Your character sheet has only front views. In video, the character turns her head, and her face changes. Why?

A model can copy only what the references show. Add three-quarter, side, and back views.

2. Why must sheet images have neutral, soft light and a plain background?

References transfer everything they contain. Keep only what you want to carry: the person, the object, or the place.

3. The side view shows the scar on the right eyebrow. The descriptor says left. What do you do?

Errors in references multiply. Check every view against the descriptor before you approve the sheet.

4. For a real product ad, which source for the product sheet is best?

A model must never invent or 'improve' a real product. Use real images and check every output against them.

5. What is the panorama anchor for?

A panorama shows the room in all directions. Each shot can take the part it needs from one source.

6. Why does each reference set have an ID like CHAR-MARA and a sheet.json file?

IDs connect the script tags (C03·M02), prompts, the prompt log, and the rights log (C16).

7. In the consistency test, the face scores 4/5 but the brass buttons change shape in every shot. What is the next step?

Small details drift first. A detail reference often fixes it. A LoRA is the stronger fix.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission is boring on purpose. All sheet images have the same grey background, the same soft light, and the same scale. That is why they work as references.

consistency.md has a detail table before and after one fix, like the worked example, and three conclusions with evidence:

  1. "Face and hair hold with 2 views (mean 4.6 / 5). Small parts drift: buttons 2.75 → 4.25 after I added a close-up."
  2. "The scar flipped sides in 1 of 4 scenes. Side and three-quarter views must state the side in capitals in every prompt."
  3. "The panorama kept the locker room layout in all 4 test shots: the window is always on the left of the door. Without the panorama, it moved in 2 of 4."

The product set uses real photos of a real object (an old film camera), with the logo photographed flat. The sheet has "source": "photo", "rights": "own".

The environment plan is a simple top view with the action line and three camera positions. It is the input for continuity in C02·M04 and for camera planning in C07·M03.

refs_check.py refs/ prints 3 reference sets, 0 problems.

C04 · Image Generation and Look Development

C04·M04 Look bible, key frames, and storyboards

Study time: 20 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Write a look bible as testable rules for palette, light, texture, lens, and camera, plus a fixed look suffix.
  2. Generate a storyboard of 2–4 key-frame options per shot from the shot list with a script.
  3. Review every option in a sheet with the look-bible checks, and decide pick, fix, or redo.
  4. Build an animatic with shot timing, slow moves, and temp audio, and change the plan from what it shows.

Key words

look bible key frame storyboard animatic

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C04, module 04. Look bible, key frames, and storyboards. After this module, you can: 1. Write a look bible as testable rules for palette, light, texture, lens, and camera, plus a fixed look suffix. 2. Generate a storyboard of 2–4 key-frame options per shot from the shot list with a script. 3. Review every option in a sheet with the look-bible checks, and decide pick, fix, or redo. 4. Build an animatic with shot timing, slow moves, and temp audio, and change the plan from what it shows. A look bible defines how the whole project looks, as rules that a reviewer can check: palette with color values, light, contrast, texture, lens, and camera. A fixed look suffix goes into every prompt; the do-not rules go into the review sheet. A script turns the shot list into 2–4 key-frame options per shot. A review sheet records the decision for each shot. An animatic puts the chosen frames on a timeline with durations, slow moves, and temp sound. It tests story and timing before you pay for motion.

Learn

Why a look bible

A project has many shots, often made with several models and on several days. Without written rules, each shot gets a slightly different look, and the cut feels like a collection, not a film. A look bible is the specification of the look. It does three jobs:

  1. It gives code one fixed look suffix for every prompt.
  2. It gives reviewers rules to check every frame.
  3. It gives the colorist the target for the grade (C09).

Write rules, not adjectives

A useful rule has one meaning for every reader. "Moody" has none. Write rules with numbers, named colors, and examples:

  • Palette: 3–5 colors with hex values. Where the accent color is allowed. Example: "Teal-grey base (#3E5A5E), skin warm, one accent: practical amber (#D9922E). Nothing else above 30 % saturation."
  • Light: key direction preferences, contrast, practicals, the night look (C02·M03). Example: "Night interiors: top light cold, one warm practical in frame, faces 1.5 stops under the practical."
  • Contrast: deep blacks or lifted blacks; highlight roll-off.
  • Texture: clean digital, 35 mm grain, 16 mm grain, halation, bloom.
  • Lens: focal length per shot type, depth of field. Example: "Close-ups 85 mm look, shallow; wides 28 mm look; no ultra-wide distortion."
  • Camera: locked, gimbal, or handheld; which moves are allowed (C02·M02).
  • References: 10–20 frames from films or your own tests, each with one line on what to copy from it.
  • Do-not rules: for example "no lens flares, no teal-and-orange look, no pure white backgrounds".

Keep it short: 1–3 pages. A long bible is not read.

The look suffix

Turn the bible into one short text, for example: "muted teal and amber palette, 35 mm film grain, soft halation, deep blacks, motivated practical light". Code adds it to every prompt, word for word. Do not paraphrase it per shot. Small wording changes give visible look changes.

Do-not rules go to review

Do not write "no lens flares" or "avoid lens flares" into the prompt. Many models react to the words "lens flares" and add them. The text encoder does not reliably understand negation. Name what you want in the prompt. Check the do-not rules in review. Some models have a separate negative prompt input. Use it only where your tests show that it works.

The storyboard as a batch job

A storyboard is a key frame for every shot. In this program it is a batch job, not a drawing session:

  1. Input: the shot list from C03·M02 (JSON), the reference library (M03), and the look bible.
  2. Prompt build: for each shot, join the parts in the fixed order (M01): shot, subject descriptors from the sheets, action, place descriptor, light, and the look suffix. Add the reference roles.
  3. Options: 2–4 seeds per shot. Name files by shot ID and option: S07_a.png, S07_b.png.
  4. Log: every option goes into the prompt log with its seed and references.
  5. Review sheet: one row per option, with empty score columns and one column per do-not rule.

The batch job is cheap. A 20-shot storyboard with 3 options is 60 images. On an open model on your own GPU it costs only time. On a hosted model it costs a few dollars.

The review

Review the options of each shot together, then the shots in order. Score:

  • Story: does the frame show the beat clearly?
  • Continuity: does it match the shots before and after? Screen direction, light, props (C02·M04).
  • Identity: does the character match the sheet?
  • Look: does it follow the bible? Check each do-not rule.
  • Composition for the delivery frame: for 9:16, is the subject large enough, and is the subject clear of the platform's text areas?

Decide for each shot: pick (use as is), fix (an edit can correct it, M02), or redo (generate again with a changed prompt or reference). Know what the grade can fix later: small color and saturation changes are cheap in the grade. Wrong light direction, wrong identity, and wrong composition are not.

The animatic

An animatic is the storyboard on a timeline. Each chosen frame stays on screen for the planned duration. A slow move (push, pull, or pan) on the still shows the intended camera move. Add temporary sound: a synthetic voice for dialogue and narration, temp music, and the key sound effects.

Watch it 3 times, with one question each time:

  1. Does the story work? Can a new viewer follow it?
  2. Is the timing right? Where does it drag? Where is it too fast to read?
  3. What is missing? A reaction shot, an insert, a sound?

Fix the plan now: cut, re-time, add a shot, or change a beat. Each change costs minutes. The same change after video generation costs every take of the changed shots. Then generate motion only for approved frames (C05).

Tool walkthrough

Run the storyboard script

The reference solution starter/solutions/C04-M04/storyboard.py uses the open path: workflow 02 from the C11 starter kit (two references) through the ComfyUI API. Plan first with --dry-run:

python storyboard.py shots.json --refs refs/ --look look.json --out storyboard/ --options 3 --dry-run

It prints the jobs and the full prompt of the first job, and writes plan.json and review.csv. Read the prompt. Check the reference roles and the order. Then run without --dry-run against your ComfyUI server. To use a hosted image API instead, replace the backend call with the API call from M01. Keep the prompt builder.

Build the animatic

python starter/tools/animatic.py shots.json --frames storyboard/ --out animatic.mp4 --audio temp_mix.wav --size 1080x1920

Each shot needs id and dur. Optional: move (push, pull, pan_left, pan_right, hold), frame (a file name), and label. Without frame, the script uses <id>_chosen.*, then the first <id>_* file. A shot with no frame becomes a grey card with "[NO FRAME]", so gaps are visible. Labels show the shot ID and duration at the bottom, so reviewers can name shots in notes.

Make the temp mix in any audio tool, or with a synthetic voice: on macOS, say -o vo.aiff "...", then ffmpeg -i vo.aiff vo.wav.

Watch

  • ShotDeck — reference frames searchable by color and lightCollect 10–20 reference frames for your look bible. Note the color, the contrast, and the light direction of each.
  • StudioBinder — What is an animatic?Read the definition and look at the examples. Note how simple the moves are.

Worked example

Look bible for "The Camera" (60 s, vertical, from C02·M05):

Rule Value
Palette Teal-grey base #3E5A5E; skin warm; one accent: practical amber #D9922E; nothing else above 30 % saturation
Night interiors Cold top light; one warm practical in frame; faces 1.5 stops under the practical
Morning (payoff) Soft window light, warmer; the only shots with daylight
Texture 35 mm grain, soft halation on practicals
Lens CU/MCU 85 mm look, shallow; WS 28 mm look
Camera Locked or slow push only; handheld only in the turn (35–48 s)
Do not lens flares; pure white backgrounds; teal-and-orange look

Look suffix: "muted teal and amber palette, 35 mm film grain, soft halation, deep blacks, motivated practical light".

Storyboard run: 14 shots × 3 options = 42 frames. Open model on a rented 48 GB GPU: about 3 s per image, 4 minutes in total including uploads. Review result: 9 picks, 3 fixes (a hand, the photo content, a second lamp), 2 redos (S10 was day light instead of night; S12 broke screen direction).

Animatic: 60 s with a synthetic voice and temp music. We built it with animatic.py in under 10 s. Two problems were found on the second viewing:

  1. Shots S04–S06 (the setup) drag: 12 s for one idea. Cut S05; extend S06 by 1 s.
  2. The turn (S11, the blank print) has no reaction. Add S11b: ECU, her eyes, 1.5 s. The plan changes cost 20 minutes. Without the animatic, S05 would have cost about 8 video takes.

Lab

Deliverable: C04/M04/ with the look bible, look.json, the storyboard folder, review.csv, the animatic MP4, and plan_changes.md.

  1. Write the look bible for your story (C02·M05): the rules table, 10 reference frames with one line each, and the do-not rules. Every rule must be checkable.
  2. Write look.json with the suffix, the aspect ratio, and the do-not rules.
  3. Write or adapt the storyboard script. Generate 3 options per shot from your shot list and references. Log every option.
  4. Fill in review.csv for every option. Decide pick, fix, or redo for each shot. Do the fixes and redos.
  5. Build a 30–60 s animatic with the chosen frames, durations, moves, and temp audio.
  6. Watch it 3 times with the 3 questions. Write plan_changes.md: each change, the reason, and the shots it affects. Update the shot list and rebuild the animatic.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Look bible with hex values, checkable rules, and do-not rules.
  • [ ] Storyboard made by a script; every option in the prompt log.
  • [ ] review.csv complete, with decisions.
  • [ ] Animatic version 1 and version 2, and plan_changes.md.

Self-check quiz

1. Which look-bible rule can a reviewer check?

A rule is useful when two people would give the same pass/fail answer. Use numbers and named colors.

2. Your look bible has the do-not rule 'no lens flares'. Why is 'avoid lens flares' a bad thing to add to the prompt?

Text encoders do not reliably understand negation. Name what you want in the prompt. Check what you do not want in review.

3. Why does code add one fixed look suffix to every prompt, instead of a new description per shot?

Paraphrase is a source of drift. A fixed string is a constant in the system.

4. How many key-frame options per shot are useful in review?

One gives no choice. Many give review overload and cost. 2–4 options with different seeds usually contain a good one.

5. In the animatic, shots 4–6 feel slow. What is the cheapest correct action?

The animatic exists to find story and timing problems before motion. A cut now saves every take of that shot.

6. A key frame is 10 % too saturated against the look bible, and everything else is right. What do you do?

Know what the grade can fix. Saturation and small color shifts are cheap later. Wrong light direction, identity, or composition are not.

7. What must each row of the review sheet have?

The sheet is the record of decisions. The fix and redo notes become the next round of work.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong look bible fits on one page and can be checked: "one saturated color per frame", "faces 1.5 stops under the practical", "85 mm look for close-ups". It has no adjectives without numbers.

review.csv (extract):

shot,option,file,story,continuity,identity,look_bible,no lens flares,no pure white backgrounds,decision,note
S07,a,S07_a.png,4,4,5,4,ok,ok,pick,grade: saturation -10%
S07,b,S07_b.png,4,3,4,4,ok,ok,,
S10,a,S10_a.png,3,2,4,2,ok,ok,redo,day light in a night scene; add "night, window black" to light
S12,b,S12_b.png,4,1,5,4,ok,ok,redo,screen direction flipped (she faces left); see plan.png
S09,c,S09_c.png,5,4,4,3,FLARE,ok,fix,mask-remove flare on lamp

plan_changes.md:

Change Reason (from the animatic) Shots affected Saved
Cut S05 Setup drags: 12 s for one idea S05 removed; S06 +1 s About 8 video takes
Add S11b (ECU eyes, 1.5 s) The turn has no reaction New shot —
S14 from 4 s to 3 s Payoff is clear earlier S14 1 s of generation per take

The summary states the effect on the budget: "The animatic removed 1 shot and shortened 1. That is about 20 % fewer generated seconds in C05."

Program · Level 2

C05 Video Generation: Directing the Model

90 h · Prerequisites: C01, C02, C04

M01M02M03M04M05M06

About this course

This is the core craft of the program. You learn to direct a video model like a crew: a clear plan, exact instructions, references, and a review of every take.

Current tools (as of 2026-10): Kling 3.0 / 3.0 Omni, Seedance 2.5, Veo 3.1 + Flow, Gemini Omni Flash, Runway Gen-4.5 + Aleph, Luma Ray3; open: Wan 2.7, LTX-2.5, HunyuanVideo 1.5. Note: the Sora 2 API was removed on 2026-09-24.

Starter tools for this course (in tools/ of the starter kit):

Tool Use
takes.py Take log, selects with in/out points, caps, and cost per usable second (M01, M06)
join_check.py Measures loops and chained joins: jump ratio and color shift (M02, M03)
identity_score.py + drift_plot.py Identity per shot and the drift trend of a sequence (M03)
stems.py Splits native audio into dialogue and background stems (M04)
clip_diff.py Measures an edited clip against its source, frame by frame (M05)

Open-model workflows for image-to-video, first/last frame, and control video are in comfyui/ (C11 explains them).

Course outcomes

  1. Choose the right generation mode for each shot (T2V, I2V, R2V, V2V, edit).
  2. Write video prompts that control camera, motion, and timing.
  3. Use first/last frames, camera control, and motion references for exact shots.
  4. Keep characters, products, and places consistent across multi-shot sequences.
  5. Use native audio and dialogue generation, and know its limits.
  6. Edit existing video with AI editing models.
  7. Plan coverage and budgets with cost per usable second.

C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M01 Generation modes and when to use each

Study time: 12 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, video-to-video, and instruction editing, and what each mode fixes.
  2. Choose a mode for a shot from its requirements, with a decision table.
  3. Run the same shots in 3 modes and compare control, quality, and cost per usable second.
  4. Run a generation session with a take log, and calculate cost per usable second by mode and model.

Key words

text-to-video image-to-video reference-to-video video-to-video cost per usable second

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 01. Generation modes and when to use each. After this module, you can: 1. Explain text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video, video-to-video, and instruction editing, and what each mode fixes. 2. Choose a mode for a shot from its requirements, with a decision table. 3. Run the same shots in 3 modes and compare control, quality, and cost per usable second. 4. Run a generation session with a take log, and calculate cost per usable second by mode and model. There are five main modes. Text-to-video starts from a prompt only; it is fast to try but gives the least control. Image-to-video starts from a key frame; it fixes composition and identity. Reference-to-video uses several reference images, videos, or audio clips; it keeps identity without fixing the first frame. Video-to-video transforms existing footage and keeps its motion. Instruction editing changes one thing in an existing clip. In professional work, image-to-video and reference-to-video are the default modes. Measure every mode by cost per usable second, not by cost per generated second.

Learn

What a mode is

A mode is the set of inputs that you give the video model. Each input fixes some decisions and leaves the others to the model. The more you fix, the more control you have, and usually the more work you did before the generation. Choose the mode by asking: what must be exact in this shot?

The five modes

  1. Text-to-video (T2V). Input: a prompt only. The model chooses everything that you do not say: the face, the room, the framing, the light. It is fast to try. It is the weakest mode for planned shots, because identity and composition change in every take.
  2. Image-to-video (I2V). Input: a key frame and a motion prompt. The key frame becomes frame 1, so composition, identity, light, and look are fixed (C04). The prompt adds the motion. Some models also take a last frame (M02). This is the most common professional mode.
  3. Reference-to-video (R2V). Input: several references (character, product, place, style; in some models also video and audio) and a prompt. The model makes a new composition with those elements. It keeps identity without a fixed first frame. Use it when you need the same cast in many new framings.
  4. Video-to-video (V2V). Input: a source video, a prompt, and often a control signal (depth, pose, or edges). The source gives motion and timing. The prompt and references give the new look. Use it for a real performance, an exact action, or a rough 3D animation that you want to look real.
  5. Instruction editing. Input: an existing clip and one instruction. The model changes one thing (remove, add, relight, restyle) and keeps the rest (M05).

What each mode fixes

Mode Identity Composition Motion Look
T2V model model model prompt
I2V key frame key frame prompt key frame
R2V references model prompt references + prompt
V2V references + prompt source source prompt + references
Edit source source source source, except the one change

Read the table as a design tool. If identity and composition must both be exact, only I2V fixes both. If motion must be exact, only V2V fixes it.

Choose the mode

Requirement of the shot Mode
Composition approved as a still I2V
Same cast in many new framings R2V
A real performance or an exact motion V2V
One defect in a good clip Instruction edit
A fast idea, a texture, or abstract B-roll T2V

The professional default

  1. Explore ideas with images or T2V. It is cheap.
  2. Approve key frames (C04).
  3. Generate motion with I2V, or with R2V for coverage of the same scene.
  4. Fix defects with edits. This order gives the most control for the least money. Each step fixes decisions before the next, more expensive step.

Measure by cost per usable second

A video model costs money per generated second. But you pay for every take, and the edit uses only the good parts of the good takes. So the number that matters is:

cost per usable second = total cost of all takes / usable seconds in the selects
                       = price per generated second / usable share

A model at US$0.05/s with 15 % usable seconds costs US$0.33 per usable second. A model at US$0.12/s with 50 % costs US$0.24. The "cheap" model is more expensive. Usable share changes with the mode and the shot type, so measure it per mode and per shot type.

Takes and selects

Treat each generation as a take, as on a set. Name it by shot and number: S07_t03. Review each take and record a decision: select, maybe, or reject. For a select, record the usable part with in and out points, and a note ("hand flicker after 4.1 s"). The editor uses the selects. The budget uses the usable seconds. starter/tools/takes.py keeps this log and computes the report.

Tool walkthrough

Mode names in current products (as of 2026-10)

Products use their own names for the same modes:

  • Google Veo 3.1 / Flow: "Frames to Video" is I2V with first and last frame; "Ingredients" is R2V; "Extend" continues a clip.
  • Kling 3.0 / 3.0 Omni: I2V with start and end frames; Omni accepts references; multi-shot blocks (M03).
  • Seedance 2.5: up to 50 references (images, audio, 3D white models, style); region editing.
  • Runway Gen-4.5 + Aleph: generation plus editing of existing clips.
  • Open (ComfyUI): the C11 starter kit has I2V (03, 06), first/last frame (04, 08), and V2V with control (05).

Map every new product to the five modes. Then you can compare it with what you use now.

Log a session

python starter/tools/takes.py budget S07 --target 4 --cap 3.00
python starter/tools/takes.py add S07 --model kling-3.0 --mode i2v --dur 6 --cost 0.60 --file takes/S07_t01.mp4
python starter/tools/takes.py review S07_t01 select --in 0.4 --out 4.1 --note "hand flicker after 4.1 s"
python starter/tools/takes.py report

The report gives the select rate, the usable share, and US$ per usable second for each model, and the coverage and cap status for each shot.

Watch

  • ComfyUI blog — Wan 2.6 Reference-to-Video in ComfyUIAn example of reference-to-video with motion and style from reference clips.

Worked example

Shot S07 (Mara reads the photo, 4 s needed, planned in C04):

Take Mode Result Usable
S07_t01 T2V Wrong face, nice light 0 s
S07_t02 T2V Wrong face, wrong room 0 s
S07_t03 R2V (CHAR-MARA + LOC-LOCKER) Good face; wider than planned 2.5 s (usable as an alternative angle)
S07_t04 I2V from KF-S07-v3 Exact composition and face; push-in works; hand flicker after 4.1 s 3.7 s (0.4–4.1 s)

We entered these 4 takes (6 s each, US$0.60 each) into takes.py. The report:

model                    takes select rate usable %      US$ US$/usable s
hosted-A                     4         50%      26%     2.40         0.39
shot     takes usable s target     US$     cap  status
S07          4      6.2    4.0    2.40     3.0  covered

The 2 T2V takes cost US$1.20 and gave nothing. For planned shots like this one, start with I2V. Keep T2V for B-roll.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M01/ with 12 or more clips, the take log (takes/), and a mode report.

  1. Choose 4 shots from your storyboard (C04·M04). Set a target and a cap for each with takes.py budget.
  2. Generate each shot in T2V, I2V (from the approved key frame), and R2V (from your reference library).
  3. For one shot, make a V2V version from a phone video that you record of yourself.
  4. For one good clip, do one instruction edit.
  5. Review every take in takes.py: decision, in and out points, note.
  6. Run the report. Write a mode table: usable share and cost per usable second for each mode, with one sentence on when you will use each mode.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 12+ clips, each in the take log and the prompt log.
  • [ ] Every select has in and out points.
  • [ ] Mode table with numbers from the report.
  • [ ] One V2V clip and one edit.

Self-check quiz

1. A client approved a key frame. Which mode keeps it exactly as the first frame?

I2V starts from that exact image. The model never denoises the first frame (C11·M02 shows the mechanism).

2. You need the same 3 actors in 20 new shots with different framings. Which mode is best?

R2V keeps identity while the model composes each new shot. With I2V you would need 20 approved key frames first.

3. You filmed a rough phone video of a friend doing the action. You want a sci-fi version. Which mode?

V2V keeps the real motion and timing; the prompt and references set the new look.

4. The shot is perfect, but a car in the background is red; it must be white. Which mode?

An edit changes one element and keeps the rest. A new generation risks everything that was already right.

5. Model X costs US$0.05 per generated second and gives 15 % usable seconds. Model Y costs US$0.12 and gives 50 %. Which is cheaper per usable second?

Cost per usable second = price per second / usable share. 0.05 / 0.15 = 0.33. 0.12 / 0.50 = 0.24. The 'cheap' model is more expensive here.

6. In your test, T2V has a 10 % usable rate for planned shots and 60 % for abstract B-roll. What do you conclude?

A mode is good or bad for a job. T2V is good when you do not need exact control.

7. Why log takes with in and out points instead of 'usable: yes/no'?

The edit uses parts of takes. Usable seconds per dollar is the number that plans the next session.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong mode table from 4 planned shots looks like this:

Mode Takes Usable share US$ per usable second Use it for
T2V 8 9 % 1.11 B-roll and textures only
I2V 8 52 % 0.19 Every planned shot with an approved key frame
R2V 8 34 % 0.29 Coverage: new angles of the same scene
V2V 2 70 % 0.14 Exact actions that I can perform myself
Edit 2 1 of 2 succeeded — One-element fixes (M05)

The text explains the numbers:

  1. "T2V failed on identity in 7 of 8 takes. It is the most expensive mode per usable second for planned shots."
  2. "I2V wasted the least. Most rejects had hand or eye problems after 4 s, so I plan I2V shots at 4–5 s."
  3. "V2V had the highest usable share. The motion came from my phone video, so the model only had to change the look. Faces drifted at high strength; strength 0.6 was the best value."

The take log has notes that the editor can use: in and out points for every select, and the reason for every reject.
