C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M02 Camera, motion, and first/last-frame control

Study time: 16 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Write motion prompts that state subject motion, camera motion, timing, and what stays still.
  2. Use first and last frames to make transitions, reveals, loops, and product turns.
  3. Use camera-control settings, motion references, and 3D layouts when words are not exact enough.
  4. Measure joins and loops with a jump ratio and a color shift, and fix the common motion defects.

Key words

first/last frame motion control camera control morphing temporal consistency

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 02. Camera, motion, and first/last-frame control. After this module, you can: 1. Write motion prompts that state subject motion, camera motion, timing, and what stays still. 2. Use first and last frames to make transitions, reveals, loops, and product turns. 3. Use camera-control settings, motion references, and 3D layouts when words are not exact enough. 4. Measure joins and loops with a jump ratio and a color shift, and fix the common motion defects. A video prompt must describe three motions: what the subject does, what the camera does, and when. Keep one main action and one camera move per clip, and say what does not move. First and last frames give exact start and end states, so you can make transitions, reveals, and loops. Camera-control settings, motion references, and 3D layouts are more exact than words. The common defects are morphing, sliding feet, extra limbs, flicker, and drift. Measure joins instead of guessing, and fix defects with shorter clips, simpler motion, stronger references, or another mode.

Learn

Three motions in every prompt

A video prompt must describe motion. There are three kinds:

  1. Subject motion: what moves, how, and how fast. "She slowly lifts the photo to eye level."
  2. Camera motion: one move, its direction, and its speed (C02·M02). "Very slow push-in."
  3. Timing: when things happen. For clips of 8 s or more, write beats: "0–3 s she reads; 3–5 s she looks up; 5–8 s she turns to the locker."

Also say what does not move: "locked-off camera", "the people in the background are still", "her hands stay on the photo". A model fills every gap with its own default motion. Saying what stays still removes random drift.

One action, one move

Each generated clip should have one main action and one camera move. Several actions and a complex move in 5 s are the most common cause of morphing and broken anatomy. If the story needs several actions, plan several shots and cut between them (C02·M04). Editing is cheaper than fighting the model.

Speed words

Models tend toward a slow, dreamy speed. If you need real-time motion, say it: "real-time speed", "quick", "she snaps the locker shut". Give timing beats for longer clips. If the result is still slow, plan to speed up the clip in the edit by up to about 20 %; more than that makes motion look wrong.

First and last frames

With first/last-frame control you give the start and the end. The model makes the motion between them. Uses:

  • Transitions and match cuts: the last frame of shot A and the first frame of shot B share a composition, so the cut matches.
  • Reveals: the first frame is dark, the last frame is lit.
  • Loops: the first frame is the last frame.
  • Product turns: a front view to a side view.

The two frames must be reachable with natural motion in the clip time. A large change in 3 s forces a morph. Bring the frames closer (same lens, smaller move), or make the clip longer.

When words are not enough

Words are a weak control for camera paths. Use, in this order:

  1. Camera-control settings of the model (pan, tilt, zoom, orbit, speed), when it has them.
  2. A motion reference: a video that has the motion you want (a real dolly move, a dance, a walk). R2V and V2V modes accept it.
  3. A 3D layout: block the scene in 3D, render the camera path as a depth or edge video, and use it as control (C07·M03, C11 starter workflow 05). If you have only words, describe what the move does in the image. A dolly makes parallax: "the foreground lamp passes the frame from left to right; the window behind her moves less".

Common defects and fixes

Defect Cause Fix
Morphing (a face or an object changes) Too much motion; weak identity Shorter clip; one action; references; I2V from a key frame
Sliding feet, floating Weak physics of contact Follow camera; framing without feet; motion reference
Extra fingers or limbs Fast hand action Slower action; hide the hands; an insert shot
Flicker Unstable fine detail Fewer fine textures; deflicker in post (C09)
Camera ignores the instruction Conflicting words One move only; camera settings; motion reference
Slow-motion feel Model default "real-time speed"; timing beats; speed up in the edit
Drift (color or identity changes over the clip) Long clip; weak anchor Shorter clip; first/last frame; re-anchor (M03)

Measure joins

A join that must not be seen (a loop, a chained clip, a first/last-frame transition) can fail in two ways:

  1. Motion jump: the image changes more across the join than between normal neighbor frames.
  2. Color shift: the motion continues, but the color or brightness jumps.

starter/tools/join_check.py measures both. It reads small grey frames near the join. It compares the change across the join (step_join) with the median change between neighbor frames inside the clips (step_inside). The jump ratio is step_join / step_inside. About 1 is seamless. Above 3 is a visible jump. It also reports the mean RGB change across the join. Use it on every loop and every chained join. Your eyes miss small jumps on a laptop screen. Viewers on a large screen do not.

Tool walkthrough

Camera settings in current products (as of 2026-10)

  • Kling 3.0: per-shot camera moves in multi-shot mode; start and end frames; motion control.
  • Veo 3.1 / Flow: first and last frames ("Frames to Video"); camera words work well; Extend for continuation.
  • Seedance 2.5: 3D white-model references for camera and layout.
  • Open (ComfyUI): starter workflow 04_flf2v_wan22_14b (first and last frame), 05_v2v_control_wan22_5b (control video for exact camera paths), 08_flf2v_ltx25.

A first/last-frame run with the starter kit

python starter/solutions/C11-M04/comfy_run.py \
  --workflow starter/comfyui/workflows/04_flf2v_wan22_14b.json \
  --map starter/comfyui/workflows/04_flf2v_wan22_14b.map.json \
  --upload first_frame=KF-S07-v3.png --upload last_frame=KF-S07-photo-ecu.png \
  --set prompt="Very slow push-in into the photo in her hands. Locked focus on the photo. Real-time speed." \
  --set seed=7

Check a join or a loop

python starter/tools/join_check.py --loop loop_bg.mp4
python starter/tools/join_check.py S07_t04.mp4 S08_t02.mp4

Watch

  • Kling 3.0 — Zhihu overview: multi-shot, motion control, native audio (Chinese)Note the per-shot settings: duration, shot size, camera move.
  • ComfyUI docs — Wan 2.2 workflows, including first/last frameRead the first/last-frame section. You can run it with starter workflow 04.

Worked example

Calibrate the join check. We made a 4 s clip with a slow push-in on a portrait photo and cut it at frame 48 (2026-10-04):

Join Jump ratio Color shift (R, G, B) Result
Frame 47 → 48 of the same push (continuous) 1.32 (0.1, 0.1, 0.0) SEAMLESS
The same, but the second half warmed (red +6 %, blue −6 %) 1.51 (+6.2, 0.1, −7.4) COLOR SHIFT
8 frames removed at the join 6.31 (2.6, 2.3, 2.1) VISIBLE JUMP
A cut to a different shot 20.90 (21.1, 20.4, 22.6) VISIBLE JUMP

Two lessons. First, a jump of only 8 frames gives a ratio above 6, so the check is sensitive. Second, the warm join passes the motion test and fails only on color. This is the typical failure of chained generations.

Transition through the photo (locker room S07 → hospital roof at dawn S08):

  1. Last frame of S07: ECU of the printed photo, filling the frame (an image edit of the key frame).
  2. First frame of S08: the same composition, but now it is the real roof (image edit: "turn the photo into a real wide view of the roof, same composition").
  3. S07 with first/last frame: start = MCU key frame, end = photo ECU; "very slow push-in into the photo".
  4. S08 with I2V: start = roof frame; "camera slowly pulls back; dawn wind in her coat".
  5. Cut at the matching frame. join_check.py S07.mp4 S08.mp4 gives a high ratio, because the content changes on purpose. For a match cut, check by eye that the composition holds across the cut. Use the tool for joins that must be invisible.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M02/ with 5 clips, join reports, and a defect log.

  1. Make one first/last-frame transition between two of your shots.
  2. Make one seamless loop (a background or a product turn). Check it with join_check.py --loop until it passes.
  3. Make one shot with camera-control settings, a motion reference, or a control video.
  4. Make one 8–10 s shot with timing beats.
  5. Make one V2V shot with your own recorded motion as the reference.
  6. Chain two clips (last frame → first frame). Check the join. If it fails on color, fix the anchor frame and check again.
  7. Log every defect: take, defect, cause, fix, result.

Result checklist

  • [ ] A loop that passes join_check.py (report saved).
  • [ ] A chained join with its report before and after the fix.
  • [ ] Defect log with at least 6 entries; each fix is a specific change.
  • [ ] All takes in the take log.

Self-check quiz

1. Your prompt is 'She turns around, walks to the window, opens it, and the camera orbits her.' The result morphs. What is the first fix?

Several actions plus a complex camera move in one short clip is the most common cause of morphing. Simplify, then cut.

2. You want a match cut from the photo in her hand to the real roof. How do you use first and last frames?

The two frames share a composition, so the cut matches. Each shot only has to reach or leave that frame.

3. A first/last-frame clip of 3 s morphs between the two frames. What is the likely cause?

The model must find a physical motion between the frames. A large change in a short time forces a morph.

4. The join check of a loop gives jump ratio 1.3 and color shift (+6, 0, −7). What do you see when it plays, and what do you do?

The ratio measures motion continuity. The shift measures color. Both must pass.

5. The model ignores 'slow dolly left' and makes a zoom. What do you try first?

Settings and references are more exact than words. If you only have words, describe what a dolly does in the image: parallax.

6. Feet slide on the floor in a walking shot. Which change is most likely to help?

Foot contact is a known weakness. Hide it with framing, give real motion as a reference, or let the camera move with the subject.

7. Why write 'locked-off camera, background people are still' in a dialogue shot?

A model fills gaps with its own defaults. State the non-motion too.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Defect log (shape of a strong answer):

Take Defect Cause Fix Result
S04_t02 Face morphs at 5 s 8 s clip, 3 actions Split into S04a (look) and S04b (walk); 4 s each ✓
S04b_t01 Feet slide Wide shot, floor visible MS framing, follow camera ✓
S09_t03 Camera zooms instead of dolly Word conflict "push in, dolly left" Removed "push in"; added parallax description ✓ on try 2
S11_t01 Slow-motion feel Model default "real-time speed" + beats; sped up 12 % in edit ✓
LOOP_t02 Jump at loop First ≠ last frame Generated with first = last frame ratio 1.4, ✓
S07→S08 chain COLOR SHIFT (+5, 0, −6) Warm drift in S07 Color-matched the anchor frame to KF-S07 ratio 1.2, shift < 2, ✓

The summary names the main rule that the log shows: "Most defects came from too much in one clip. After I split actions into separate shots, the reject rate fell from 60 % to 30 %."

The loop report and the chain reports (before and after) are saved as JSON next to the clips. The V2V shot shows the phone reference and the result side by side.

C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M03 Multi-shot sequences and consistency

Study time: 16 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Plan and generate multi-shot blocks with native multi-shot features.
  2. Keep character, wardrobe, product, and location consistent across 10 or more shots with the consistency stack.
  3. Join blocks and extend shots without visible seams, and check each join.
  4. Measure identity drift across a sequence, tell drift from single rejects, and decide when to train a LoRA.

Key words

multi-shot consistency scene extension identity drift

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 03. Multi-shot sequences and consistency. After this module, you can: 1. Plan and generate multi-shot blocks with native multi-shot features. 2. Keep character, wardrobe, product, and location consistent across 10 or more shots with the consistency stack. 3. Join blocks and extend shots without visible seams, and check each join. 4. Measure identity drift across a sequence, tell drift from single rejects, and decide when to train a LoRA. Current top models can generate several connected shots in one generation, with a consistent cast and place. For longer sequences you combine methods: fixed descriptors, a reference library, native multi-shot blocks, first and last frames at joins, short extensions, and a panorama anchor for places. Consistency inside one generation is high; drift appears at the joins between generations and over long chains. Measure identity per shot and look at the trend of the passing shots. A falling trend is drift; a single low shot is a reject. If drift stays high across many shots, train a LoRA.

Learn

Why consistency is hard

Each generation starts from noise. The model keeps a character the same only when the inputs carry the character: references, descriptors, and the first frame. Inside one generation, the model attends across all its frames at once, so a face stays the same. Across two generations, nothing is shared except what you give. That is why drift appears at joins and grows over long chains.

Native multi-shot blocks

Current top models can make several connected shots in one generation. You give a shot list for the block: for each shot the duration, the shot size, the camera move, and the content. The model makes the cuts. Because the shots share one generation, the cast, the place, and the light stay consistent.

Use multi-shot blocks for short scenes of 2–6 shots in one place. Plan the block exactly as in a shot list (C03·M02). The model will not invent good coverage for you.

Longer sequences: the consistency stack

For sequences of 1–10 minutes, combine methods. Use them from the top of the stack down. Each one adds cost:

  1. Fixed descriptors in every prompt, word for word (C04·M03).
  2. References for every recurring element: characters, products, places (C04·M03).
  3. I2V from approved key frames for the important shots (M01).
  4. Native multi-shot blocks for short scenes.
  5. First and last frames at hard joins between blocks (M02).
  6. Short extensions for long continuous takes.
  7. A panorama anchor for places, so walls and windows stay in place.
  8. A LoRA for the cast and products when the scale is large (C14).

Joins between blocks

When you chain blocks, two methods are common:

  • Last frame → first frame. The next block starts from the last frame of the previous block. The join is smooth, but errors are copied forward: a small color drift or a slightly wrong face becomes the new start.
  • Fresh references each block. Each block starts from the original references and an approved key frame. The join needs a cut, an insert, or a first/last frame, but errors do not add up.

For long sequences, use fresh references at least every 2–3 blocks. Check each smooth join with join_check.py (M02).

Extensions

An extension continues a clip from its last frames. The look holds well. The action can wander, because the model has no plan for the story beyond your prompt. Rules: keep each extension short, give it one specific action, and prefer a cut to coverage over a long extension.

Measure drift

Score identity for every shot of the sequence, in order. Use identity_score.py (the same face-embedding scorer as in C11·M03) with your character references. Then plot the median score per shot with drift_plot.py.

Read the plot in two ways:

  • Single rejects: one shot is low, and the others are flat. That shot failed. Regenerate it.
  • Drift: the passing shots fall in a trend along the sequence. The method adds error. Re-anchor with fresh references, or train a LoRA.

The tool reports the trend of the passing shots only, so that one failed shot does not look like a drift. Scores do not cover everything. Check wardrobe details, products, and the place by eye with a scorecard (C04·M03).

Continuity at cuts

At every cut between generated shots, check:

  • eyeline and screen direction (the 180° rule, C02·M04);
  • light direction and color;
  • prop positions and states (the photo in which hand, the locker open or closed);
  • wardrobe details. Generated shots do not know their neighbors. A cutaway (insert, reaction) hides a join when continuity fails, and it is cheap to make.

Tool walkthrough

Native multi-shot (as of 2026-10)

  • Kling 3.0: up to 6 shots per generation; each shot 3–15 s with its own shot size, camera move, and content; voice lock from a reference.
  • Seedance 2.5: up to 30 s in one take as connected shots; up to 50 references.
  • LTX-2.5 (open): native multishot.
  • Veo 3.1 + Flow: Scene Builder joins clips; Extend continues a clip.

A multi-shot block prompt has one line per shot, for example:

Shot 1 (4 s, wide two-shot, locked): Mara and Leo at a small café table, night, rain on the window.
Shot 2 (3 s, over-the-shoulder on Leo, slow push): Leo slides the photo across the table.
Shot 3 (3 s, MCU Mara, locked): Mara looks at the photo, then up at Leo.
Same characters as the references in all shots. Same light: warm practical lamp, cold window.

Score the sequence

python starter/tools/identity_score.py --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/02_34.png \
  seq/S01.mp4 seq/S02.mp4 seq/S03.mp4 ... --json drift.json
python starter/tools/drift_plot.py drift.json --out drift.png

Watch

  • Bilibili — Seedance real-person short-drama workflow: multi-subject consistency (Chinese)Watch the consistency part: reference sets per character and micro-expression control.
  • Google — Flow help center: Scene Builder and ExtendRead how one product joins and extends clips. Note the limits it states.

Worked example

Test of the drift tools (2026-10-04, public-domain portraits). We scored 5 clips against a reference photo of one person: 4 clips of the same person and 1 clip of a different person.

PASS   median 0.632  A.mp4
PASS   median 0.610  B.mp4
PASS   median 0.609  Bwarm.mp4
PASS   median 0.624  push.mp4
REJECT median 0.145  C.mp4
5 shots; median range 0.14–0.63
trend of passing shots: -0.025 per 10 shots (all shots: -0.960)
REJECTS: single shots fail, but there is no trend. Regenerate those shots.

With all shots, the slope is −0.96 per 10 shots, which looks like strong drift. Without the reject, the trend is flat. The correct action is to regenerate clip C, not to train a LoRA.

Scene: 6 shots, 40 s, café dialogue (Mara and Leo):

  1. Block 1, native multi-shot: wide two-shot, OTS on Leo, OTS on Mara, with voice lock for both. Faces, café layout, and light are consistent.
  2. Block 2: the last frame of shot 3 as the first frame of shot 4, plus the same references. Leo's jacket color shifts slightly. Fix: an instruction edit (M05).
  3. Scorecard after the fix: face 5, 5, 5, 4, 4, 5; wardrobe 5, 5, 5, 4, 5, 5.
  4. Decision: no LoRA for this scene. For the 20-episode series, train LoRAs for both characters.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M03/ with a 45–60 s sequence of 8–12 shots, drift.json, drift.png, a scorecard, and notes.

  1. Use your story and reference library.
  2. Generate at least one native multi-shot block of 3 or more shots. If your model has no multi-shot mode, make the block from I2V shots with the same references.
  3. Join blocks with first/last frames, matching cuts, or fresh references. Check each smooth join with join_check.py.
  4. Use one short extension.
  5. Score identity for every shot. Make the drift plot. Fill in the scorecard for wardrobe, product, and place.
  6. Edit the sequence. List each continuity problem, and how you fixed or hid it.
  7. Write the LoRA decision for this piece and for a 20-episode version, with numbers.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 45–60 s sequence exported.
  • [ ] Drift plot, with each low shot explained (reject or drift).
  • [ ] Join reports for every smooth join.
  • [ ] Problem/fix list and the LoRA decision.

Self-check quiz

1. Inside one multi-shot generation, faces stay the same. Between two generations, the jacket color changes. Why?

Consistency inside a block comes from shared attention across its shots. Joins between blocks depend on your references and anchors.

2. Your drift plot: 11 shots between 0.58 and 0.63, one shot at 0.21. The trend of the passing shots is flat. What is it?

Drift is a trend. One low shot with a flat trend is a failed take. The fix is cheap: regenerate it.

3. The median identity falls from 0.62 in shot 1 to 0.48 in shot 12 of a chained sequence. What is the best fix?

Chaining from the last frame copies errors forward. Fresh references every block stop the error from adding up.

4. A scene extension continues a good 5 s clip to 12 s. The look holds, but the action wanders. What is the rule?

An extension keeps the look from the last frames but has no plan for the story. Give it a clear action, and keep it short.

5. When is a native multi-shot block the right tool?

Multi-shot blocks are strongest for short connected scenes. Long sequences still need joins.

6. Your piece is 60 s with 2 characters. Face scores are ≥ 4 in 11 of 12 shots after edits. The client now orders a 20-episode series. What is the decision?

The LoRA decision depends on the scale. A LoRA costs training and evaluation once and saves edits in every later shot.

7. Which check do you do at every cut between generated shots?

Continuity errors are what viewers notice. Generated shots do not know the shots next to them.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission shows the data and a clear reading of it.

Drift summary: "12 shots. Medians 0.52–0.66, one reject (S09, profile view, 0.31; regenerated: 0.55). Trend of passing shots: −0.08 per 10 shots. The trend comes from block 3, which started from the last frame of block 2. After I re-anchored block 3 with the original references, the trend became −0.01."

Continuity list:

Cut Problem Fix
S03 → S04 Photo in the left hand, then the right hand Instruction edit on S04 (mirror the hand pose)
S06 → S07 Window light from the left, then from the right Regenerated S07 with the location panorama as reference
S10 → S11 Leo's glasses missing Inserted reaction S10b to hide the join; S11 regenerated with the glasses close-up reference

LoRA decision: "For this 60 s piece: no LoRA. After 3 edits, face ≥ 4 in all shots. For 20 episodes (about 600 shots): train LoRAs for Mara and Leo. At my reject rate, references only would need about 150 extra takes for identity; a LoRA costs about US$15 and one day of evaluation (C14)."

C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M04 Native audio and dialogue in video models

Study time: 12 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Write an audio block in every video prompt - dialogue, effects, ambience, and music - with timing.
  2. Keep a character's voice consistent with voice references, and know the limits.
  3. Decide for each sound type whether to keep, replace, or layer native audio.
  4. Split native audio into dialogue and background stems, and judge the quality of the split.

Key words

native audio dialogue voice lock ambience audio-to-video

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 04. Native audio and dialogue in video models. After this module, you can: 1. Write an audio block in every video prompt - dialogue, effects, ambience, and music - with timing. 2. Keep a character's voice consistent with voice references, and know the limits. 3. Decide for each sound type whether to keep, replace, or layer native audio. 4. Split native audio into dialogue and background stems, and judge the quality of the split. Many current video models generate sound with the picture. Write dialogue in quotes with the speaker name, add sound effects and ambience, and say if there is music. Voice references keep a character's voice the same across shots. Native audio gives excellent sync for lips, footsteps, and impacts. Its weaknesses are voice drift between clips, generic music, and one mixed track. Professional work often keeps the native sync sounds and ambience, and replaces or layers dialogue and music in post. Source separation splits the mixed track into stems.

Learn

Joint audio-video generation

Some video models generate the sound and the picture together, in one model. The model learns from videos with sound, so it learns that a door makes a sound when it closes, and that lips move with speech. This gives very good sync for effects and lip movement. It also means that the audio is one mixed track, made again in every generation.

The audio block

Add an audio block to every prompt, even when you want silence. Name each layer:

  • Dialogue: speaker, delivery, and the exact words in quotes. MARA (quietly, surprised): "It's raining… in here?"
  • Sound effects: the actions that make sound. "Paper rustles; a locker door clicks shut."
  • Ambience: the place. "Distant hospital monitor beeps, air-conditioning hum."
  • Music: "no music" is the default for edited work. Or describe it.

Add timing for longer clips: "at 3 s she speaks". If you say nothing about audio, the model decides, and it often adds music.

Voice consistency

Without a reference, the model invents a voice from your description in each generation. A series character then has several voices. Methods, from strongest to weakest:

  1. Replace the dialogue with one fixed voice (a designed or cloned voice with consent, C06·M01). Then use lip sync or audio-to-video so the picture follows that voice (C11·M03).
  2. A voice reference in the generation. Some models take a reference clip and keep its voice and tone.
  3. The same voice description in every prompt. Expect drift. For one-off lines, native dialogue is often fine and has the best lip sync.

Audio-to-video

Some models take an audio track as input and make the picture follow it: lips follow a recorded line, motion follows music beats. This is the mode for a fixed voice (method 1 above) and for music videos.

Keep, replace, or layer

Decide for each layer, not for the whole track:

  • Keep sync effects and ambience. They are hard to place by hand, and native audio gets the timing right.
  • Replace recurring voices (consistency), brand voice-over (approved script and voice), and music (it must continue across cuts, follow the edit, and have a clear license).
  • Layer when native effects are thin: keep the native sound for timing, and add a stronger designed effect on top (C10·M01).

Split the mixed track into stems

Native audio arrives as one track. Source separation estimates the parts. A two-stem model gives "vocals" (dialogue) and "no vocals" (everything else). A four-stem model splits music further.

How to judge a split:

  • By ear: listen to each stem alone, on headphones. Typical artifacts: a thin or watery voice, music residue in pauses, and effects that leak into the dialogue stem (a cough, a laugh).
  • By measurement in a test: mix a voice and a background yourself, separate the mix, and compare each estimate with its original. The common measure is SI-SDR (scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio) in dB. Higher is better. You can measure it only when you have the originals, so it is a test of the tool, not a check of each clip.

Use stems inside a mix. A separated dialogue stem is not a clean studio recording. When a line must stand alone (a trailer, a voice-over), replace it.

Tool walkthrough

Native audio in current models (as of 2026-10)

  • Kling 3.0: native audio; voice and tone from a reference video, kept for new dialogue; supports Chinese dialects.
  • Veo 3.1: native 48 kHz audio with dialogue and effects.
  • Seedance 2.5: native audio; audio references.
  • LTX-2.5 (open): joint audio and video; starter workflow 06_i2v_ltx25. LTX-2.3 image + audio → video: starter workflow 07_lipsync_ia2v_ltx23.

Split stems

pip install demucs
python starter/tools/stems.py S07_t04.mp4 --out stems/
# -> stems/S07_t04_dialogue.wav, stems/S07_t04_background.wav
python starter/tools/stems.py S07_t04.mp4 --out stems/ --four   # vocals, drums, bass, other

The tool extracts the audio with ffmpeg and runs Demucs (MIT license). It runs on CPU. A GPU makes it faster.

Extract audio only

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vn -c:a pcm_s24le clip.wav

Watch

  • Google DeepMind — Veo model page (native audio examples)Listen to the examples with dialogue and effects. Note what sounds generic.
  • Demucs — open-source music and voice separation (README)Read the usage section and the note on two-stem separation.

Worked example

Separation test (2026-10-04, Demucs htdemucs, two stems, CPU). We mixed a synthetic voice line (5.9 s) with a synthetic music bed (three tones with tremolo and pink noise). Then we separated the mix and compared each stem with its original:

Estimate SI-SDR against the original
The mix, used as "dialogue" 16.4 dB
Demucs dialogue stem 25.7 dB (+9.3 dB)
The mix, used as "background" −16.5 dB
Demucs background stem 8.9 dB (+25.4 dB)

The separation took about 3 s for 5.9 s of audio on a laptop CPU (12 s including model load). The background stem gains most, because in the mix it is much quieter than the voice. Real native audio is harder than this test: effects overlap the voice, and the room adds reverb. Listen to every stem.

Shot S07 with native audio:

  • Audio block: MARA (whisper, surprised): "That's my locker." | SFX: paper rustle at 1 s | AMB: hospital beeps, AC hum | music: none.
  • Take 1: good lip sync; the voice is too young compared with S03.
  • Take 2, with a voice reference from S03: the voice matches; one beep is too loud.
  • Post: split stems; lower the beep in the background stem; keep the paper sound; keep the dialogue.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M04/ with 4 clips with native audio, their stems, a separation test, and a decision table.

  1. Generate 2 dialogue shots of the same character, without and then with a voice reference. Compare the voices.
  2. Generate 1 action shot with sync effects (steps, a door, an impact).
  3. Generate 1 shot from an audio track (audio-to-video), if one of your models supports it. Otherwise prepare a recorded line for C11·M03.
  4. Split stems for 2 clips with stems.py. Listen to each stem and write the artifacts that you hear.
  5. Run a separation test: mix your own voice recording with a music bed, separate it, and compute SI-SDR against the originals (use the script in the model answer).
  6. Fill in a decision table for each clip: keep, replace, or layer, for dialogue, effects, ambience, and music, with a reason.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Voice comparison with and without a reference.
  • [ ] Stems as WAV files, with listening notes.
  • [ ] Separation test with SI-SDR numbers.
  • [ ] Decision table with a reason for each cell.

Self-check quiz

1. How do you write a line of dialogue in a video prompt so that the right character says it?

Name, delivery, and quotes make it clear who speaks, how, and exactly what.

2. Mara speaks in 6 shots made in 6 generations, without a voice reference. What do you expect?

Without a reference, the voice is generated again each time. Use a voice reference, or replace dialogue with one fixed voice (C06).

3. Which part of native audio do you usually keep?

Sync effects are hard to make by hand and native audio gets their timing right. Music and recurring voices need control and licenses.

4. Why do most edited projects replace native music?

Music must flow across the cut and follow the edit. Use one music track for the scene (C06·M03, C10).

5. You split native audio into stems. The dialogue stem sounds a little thin, and there is faint music in the pauses. Is this a failure?

Separation estimates the sources. A stem is good for a mix. It is not a clean studio recording.

6. In a separation test, the voice estimate improves from 16.4 dB to 25.7 dB SI-SDR. What does SI-SDR measure?

SI-SDR compares an estimate with the original source. You can measure it only when you have the original, for example in a test that you mix yourself.

7. When is audio-to-video the right mode?

With audio-to-video the audio is fixed and the picture follows it. This is how C11·M03 makes lip-synced dialogue with a fixed voice.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

SI-SDR script used for the test:

import numpy as np, subprocess
def load(p):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", p, "-f", "f32le", "-ac", "1", "-ar", "44100", "-"],
                         capture_output=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)
def si_sdr(est, ref):
    n = min(len(est), len(ref)); est, ref = est[:n], ref[:n]
    target = np.dot(est, ref) / np.dot(ref, ref) * ref
    return 10 * np.log10(np.sum(target ** 2) / np.sum((est - target) ** 2))
print(si_sdr(load("stems/mix_dialogue.wav"), load("my_voice.wav")))

Decision table (shape of a strong answer):

Clip Dialogue Effects Ambience Music
S03 (Mara, first line) Replace: fixed voice for the series; lip sync in C11·M03 Keep: the locker click is exactly on the frame Keep Replace: one cue for the scene
S07 (Mara whisper) Keep: one-off line; the native lip sync is better than any dub Keep paper; lower one beep in the stem Keep None
S09 (running) — Layer: native steps for timing + a designed impact Keep Replace
Ad end card Replace: approved brand voice-over — — Licensed track

The listening notes are specific: "S07 dialogue stem: slight 'underwater' sound on the 's' sounds; one beep leaks into the stem at 2.1 s. Usable under the room tone in the mix." The voice comparison states the result: "Without a reference, S03 and S07 sound like two different women. With the reference, the pitch and accent match."

C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M05 Editing video with AI models

Study time: 14 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Use instruction-based video editing to remove, add, replace, relight, and restyle, with one change per run.
  2. Use region editing and conversational editing, and control drift across turns.
  3. Measure an edit frame by frame against the source, inside and outside the edit region.
  4. Decide between an AI edit and classic compositing for each job, with time and quality data.

Key words

video editing model region editing relight restyle conversational editing

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 05. Editing video with AI models. After this module, you can: 1. Use instruction-based video editing to remove, add, replace, relight, and restyle, with one change per run. 2. Use region editing and conversational editing, and control drift across turns. 3. Measure an edit frame by frame against the source, inside and outside the edit region. 4. Decide between an AI edit and classic compositing for each job, with time and quality data. Video editing models change an existing clip from an instruction. They can remove an object, add an element, change wardrobe, relight a scene, or change the style, and they keep the rest of the clip, mostly. Some models edit only a marked region; some edit by conversation. They are strong on generated and real footage, and they still fail on small text, exact logos, and long clips. Measure each edit against the source, frame by frame, outside and inside the edit region. Use AI edits for organic changes, and compositing for anything that must be exact.

Learn

What an edit model does

A video edit model takes a source clip and an instruction. It makes a new clip that follows the instruction and keeps the rest of the source. Inside, it usually encodes the source into latents and uses them as strong conditioning, while it generates the clip again. So "keep the rest" is a strong preference, not a guarantee. Every pixel of the output is new. That is why measurement matters.

Types of edits and reliability

Edit Reliability (as of 2026-10) Why
Color or material change (jacket, car) High Shape and motion stay; only appearance changes
Remove a simple object High The model fills in a plausible background
Day to night, relight Medium–high The whole frame changes, and shadows must agree
Restyle (live action to animation, painting) Medium–high Motion is kept; style is global
Add a new object with motion Medium The object must move and interact correctly
Change text, logos, exact product details Low Exact pixels are needed; the model draws plausible shapes
Long clips (more than 10 s) Medium–low Consistency over many frames; windowed processing

Method

  1. One change per run. Name what must stay: "Change the rider's helmet to matte white. Keep the rider, the bike, the bridge, and the light unchanged."
  2. Order the changes from local to global: object changes and removals first, relight and restyle last. A relight changes every pixel, so later edits would have to match it.
  3. Use a region (a mask or a box) if the model supports it. It is a hard limit, not a request.
  4. Run 2–3 tries. Edits vary like generations.
  5. Measure against the source (below).
  6. Fall back to compositing after two failures (C09·M03).

Conversational editing

Some models edit by conversation: each instruction applies to the last result. It is fast for exploration. But each turn regenerates the clip, and small losses add up: detail softens, colors move, faces change a little. Keep a version history, compare each version with the source, and return to the best version when quality drops.

Measure the edit

Play the source and the edit side by side, at full resolution, on a large screen. Check faces, hands, edges, and the light. Then measure:

  • Inside the region: did the change happen? The mean difference should be large.
  • Outside the region: did anything else change? The mean difference should be near the re-encode noise, and the signed color shift should be near 0.
  • Over time: in which frames? An edit can be clean in the first second and drift later.

starter/tools/clip_diff.py samples frames from both clips and reports these numbers per frame, with the worst frame. A small global color shift is easy to miss in one clip and easy to see when the edited shot cuts against its neighbors.

AI edit or compositing

AI edits are fast, and they handle light, shadows, and reflections well, because the model redraws the scene. Compositing (roto, tracking, paint, keying) is slower, and it is exact and controllable. Rule:

  • AI edit first for organic changes: wardrobe, removal of simple objects, relight, restyle.
  • Compositing for brand assets, text, logos, faces of real people, and anything that a client will check pixel by pixel.
  • Hybrid: an AI relight, plus the exact logo composited back from the source with a tracked mask.

For a batch, calculate both paths: AI edit time × all shots + compositing time × failed shots, against compositing for all shots.

Tool walkthrough

Edit models (as of 2026-10)

  • Runway Aleph 2.0 (also inside Adobe Firefly): remove, add, relight, change angle, restyle.
  • Gemini Omni Flash: conversational edits; each turn keeps characters and physics; SynthID watermark on outputs.
  • Kling 3.0 Omni, Seedance 2.5: region editing.
  • Wan 2.7 instruction edit (open weights, Apache 2.0): local editing on your own GPU.
  • Luma Ray3 Modify: restyles actor footage and keeps the performance.

Measure an edit

python starter/tools/clip_diff.py source.mp4 edited.mp4 --box 600,300,900,700 --csv per_frame.csv

The box is the area that may change, in source pixels (x0, y0, x1, y1). Find it by opening one frame in an image viewer. The result is PASS or FAIL, the worst frame, and the mean color shift. Open per_frame.csv to see when the drift starts.

Watch

  • Adobe Help — generate and edit videos with Runway models in FireflyLook at the types of edits and the stated limits.
  • The Next Web — Gemini Omni Flash: conversational video generation and editingNote how each turn keeps characters, and what the article says about watermarks.

Worked example

Calibrate the clip check (2026-10-04, a 4 s clip, 480 × 600, 12 sampled frames; the box is the edit area):

Edited clip Worst outside mean Mean shift (R, G, B) Inside mean Result
Re-encode only (H.264, CRF 23) 1.48 (0.1, 0.0, 0.1) 1.24 PASS
A local change inside the box 1.48 (0.1, 0.0, 0.1) 36.96 PASS
The same local change + a warm shift of 3 % 3.49 (+2.8, −0.2, −3.8) 38.79 FAIL in all 12 frames

The warm shift is small: 3 %. The mean difference outside (3.49) stays under the limit of 4.0. Only the signed channel shift catches it.

Ad shot: a rider on a bridge, generated, 6 s. Client notes: (1) a white helmet; (2) remove a second cyclist in the background; (3) golden hour.

  1. Edit 1: "Change the rider's helmet to matte white; keep everything else." First try. clip_diff PASS.
  2. Edit 2: "Remove the cyclist in the background on the left." The first try left a shadow; the second try is clean. PASS.
  3. Edit 3: "Relight to golden hour, low warm sun from the right." The look is right, but the bottle logo became soft. Fix: composite the logo back from the source with a tracked mask, and grade it warmer (C09·M03). 25 minutes of compositing.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M05/ with 6 edits (before and after), clip_diff reports, a reliability table, and an AI-versus-compositing comparison.

  1. Choose 2 generated clips and 1 real clip that you filmed.
  2. Do 6 edits across types: a color change, a removal, a relight, a restyle, an addition, and a text or logo change.
  3. Use at least 2 different edit models, one of them open if you have a GPU.
  4. Measure every edit with clip_diff.py. Save the reports.
  5. Record the tries, the result, the defects, and the time for each edit.
  6. For the failed text or logo edit, fix it with a classic method (mask, track, composite). Record the time. Compare quality and time with the AI attempts.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 6 before/after pairs, each with a clip_diff report.
  • [ ] Reliability table by edit type and model.
  • [ ] One AI-versus-compositing comparison with times.
  • [ ] A rule for your future projects, based on your data.

Self-check quiz

1. A client wants three changes in one shot: a white helmet, no background cyclist, and golden-hour light. How do you run the edits?

One change per run is followed more exactly. A relight changes the whole frame, so do it last; otherwise later edits must match the new light.

2. After a relight edit, the bottle logo is soft. What is the right fix?

Edit models redraw the frame. For brand assets, take the exact pixels from the source (C09·M03).

3. The frame-by-frame check shows outside-region shifts of +2.8 red and −3.8 blue in every frame, for an edit that should only change a jacket. What happened?

A small global shift is easy to miss on one clip and easy to see at the cut. Use a region edit, or match the grade back to the source (C09·M02).

4. Which edit type is least reliable with current models?

Text and exact logos need exact pixels. Models draw plausible shapes, not exact ones.

5. In conversational editing, quality drops after 5 turns. Why, and what do you do?

Like image edit chains (C04·M02), video edit chains drift. Keep a version history.

6. You must remove a boom microphone from 40 shots of real footage for a client deadline. Each AI edit takes 3 minutes and works in 70 % of cases. A compositor needs 20 minutes per shot. What is a good plan?

AI first: 40 × 3 min = 2 h, plus 12 failures × 20 min = 4 h. All compositing: 13 h. Measure each edit before you accept it.

7. Why are long clips (more than 10 s) harder for edit models?

Edit the shortest clip that the edit needs. Cut long takes into the parts that the edit uses.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Reliability table (shape of a strong answer):

Edit Model A tries / result Model B tries / result Outside drift Time
Jacket color 1 / ✓ 1 / ✓ none 3 min
Remove a cyclist 2 / ✓ 1 / shadow left none 6 min
Relight to night (real footage) 1 / ✓ 2 / ✓ whole frame (expected) 5 min
Restyle to animation (real footage) 1 / ✓ 1 / ✓, faces changed expected 4 min
Add a dog walking past 3 / legs wrong 2 / ✓ +1.9 red in frames 40–72 12 min
Change the shop sign text 3 / ✗ 3 / ✗ — 15 min, then compositing 30 min ✓

The conclusion is a rule with evidence: "AI edits for organic changes: 5 of 5 succeeded in 1–2 tries. Text: 0 of 6 AI tries. Compositing took 30 minutes and is exact. For client logos and text, I go straight to compositing. I measure every AI edit, because the dog edit shifted the color of 33 frames and I did not see it on my laptop."

C05 · Video Generation: Directing the Model

C05·M06 Coverage, selects, and budgets

Study time: 20 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Plan coverage for generated scenes so that the editor has choices - masters, singles, reactions, inserts, cutaways.
  2. Run a generation session like a shoot, with takes, selects, in and out points, and a gap list.
  3. Route shots to models by cost per usable second, from your own measured data.
  4. Build a budget with caps per shot, track it during sessions, and change the approach when a shot hits its cap.

Key words

coverage selects routing budget cost per usable second

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C05, module 06. Coverage, selects, and budgets. After this module, you can: 1. Plan coverage for generated scenes so that the editor has choices - masters, singles, reactions, inserts, cutaways. 2. Run a generation session like a shoot, with takes, selects, in and out points, and a gap list. 3. Route shots to models by cost per usable second, from your own measured data. 4. Build a budget with caps per shot, track it during sessions, and change the approach when a shot hits its cap. A real shoot films each moment from several angles, called coverage. An AI production must plan coverage on purpose, because a model makes only what you ask. Treat each generation as a take: review takes, mark selects with in and out points, and write notes, like a script supervisor. Route each shot type to the model with the best measured cost per usable second for it. Set a budget and a cap per shot, and track them during each session. When a shot hits its cap, change the approach instead of generating more takes. Stop when the edit has enough material.

Learn

Coverage

On a film set, each moment is filmed from several angles. This is coverage. The editor needs it: to choose the best performance, to control rhythm, and to cut around mistakes. A video model makes only what you ask. So in an AI production, coverage must be planned on purpose.

For each scene, plan:

  • a master (wide) of the whole action;
  • singles or over-the-shoulder shots for each speaker;
  • reactions: listening faces, 1–2 s each;
  • inserts: hands, objects, details;
  • cutaways: the place, the weather, a detail of the room;
  • an alternative angle for the key moment.

Reactions and inserts are the most useful coverage. They are short and cheap. They let the editor change the rhythm, hide a join between generations, and cut around a defect in another shot (a hand flicker at 4 s).

Takes and selects

Run a session like a shoot. Each generation is a take, named by shot: S07_t03. Review the takes of a shot together, in a grid. For each take record:

  • a decision: select, maybe, or reject;
  • for a select, the usable part (in and out points);
  • a note: "hand flicker after 4.1 s", "best eyeline", "face drift". The selects bin goes to the editor with the trims. This is the job of the script supervisor on a set. In this program it is your job, and takes.py keeps the log.

Routing

Different shot types have different best models. Make a routing table from your own data (the mode table of M01, your eval set from C01·M07):

Shot type Model class Mode Reason
Hero product Premium hosted I2V + product references Highest usable rate for logos
Dialogue Joint audio-video R2V + voice reference Lip sync
Wide B-roll Open model on a rented GPU T2V Lowest cost per usable second
Inserts Fast model I2V Short and simple

Update the table after every project. Models change monthly.

The budget

Set a budget per shot before the session:

shot budget = target usable seconds × cost per usable second (for this shot type) × 1.5

The safety factor (about 1.5) covers bad luck and client notes. Set the cap of the shot to this budget. Track actual spend per shot during the session.

When a shot reaches its cap, stop. More takes of the same method rarely help. Change the approach:

  1. another mode (I2V from a fixed key frame instead of R2V);
  2. a simpler action, or a shorter clip;
  3. another model;
  4. another shot that tells the same beat (a reaction instead of the action).

Sessions and gap lists

A project has several sessions. Each session ends with a rough edit of the selects and a gap list: what the edit still needs. "No reaction of Leo at the key line." "The OTS on Mara has the wrong eyeline." The gap list is the shot list of the next session. This keeps generation focused on what the edit needs. Stop when every beat has good material, with one alternative for the key moments.

Reported numbers

Creators report very low costs, for example US$2–4 per short ad made with an LLM, an image model, and a video model. Short-drama producers in China report about ¥200 per finished minute with end-to-end tools. These are claims. They often leave out failed takes, subscriptions, edits, music, and time. Use your own tracker for your quotes.

Tool walkthrough

A session with takes.py

# before the session: targets and caps from the formula
python starter/tools/takes.py budget S07 --target 4 --cap 3.00
python starter/tools/takes.py budget S07r --target 1.5 --cap 0.40     # a reaction

# during the session: one line per take
python starter/tools/takes.py add S07 --model kling-3.0 --mode i2v --dur 6 --cost 0.60 --file takes/S07_t01.mp4

# review
python starter/tools/takes.py review S07_t01 select --in 0.4 --out 4.1 --note "hand flicker after 4.1 s"

# after the session
python starter/tools/takes.py report      # cost per usable second per model; coverage and cap per shot
python starter/tools/takes.py selects > selects.csv    # for the editor

The report marks each shot as covered, GAP <seconds>, or OVER CAP. Copy the gaps into the gap list.

Selects into the edit

selects.csv has the file, the in point, and the out point of each select. In C08·M02 you turn this list into a timeline automatically (OTIO). For now, import the files into your editor and set the in and out points by hand.

Watch

  • Wikipedia — Master shot and coverageRead how a master shot and closer coverage work together.
  • X — How a creator makes AI UGC ads for US$2–4 (Claude + GPT Image 2 + Seedance 2)A claim about cost. Note what is counted and what is not (time, failed takes).

Worked example

Scene: café dialogue, 40 s, 9 planned shots + 6 coverage shots.

Measured cost per usable second from the M01 mode table: dialogue (joint audio, R2V) US$0.20; reactions and inserts (fast model, I2V) US$0.13.

Shot group Target usable s Cost per usable s × 1.5 Cap
9 dialogue shots 25 0.20 US$7.50
6 coverage shots 20 0.13 US$3.90
Total US$11.40

Session 1: 31 takes, US$8.20, 13 selects. The rough edit gives the gap list:

  1. No reaction of Leo at the key line (S05).
  2. The OTS on Mara (S06) has the wrong eyeline: she looks camera-left; she must look camera-right.
  3. S08 reached its cap (US$1.50) with no select: Mara's hand morphs when she pushes the photo.

Changes: for S08, a new approach: an insert of the photo sliding (hands only, I2V) plus a reaction. For S06, a new key frame with the eyeline fixed (C04·M02), then I2V.

Session 2: 6 takes, US$1.60. All gaps closed. Total US$9.80, under the cap of US$11.40. The usable share by model is written back into the routing table.

Lab

Deliverable: C05/M06/ with the coverage plan, the routing table, the budget, the take log, the selects, two gap lists, a 60 s scene, and a report.

  1. Plan coverage for a 60 s scene of your story: a master, singles, 3 reactions, 3 inserts, 2 cutaways.
  2. Write the routing table from your M01 data and your eval set.
  3. Set targets and caps for every shot with the formula.
  4. Run session 1. Log every take. Review every take. Make a rough edit from the selects. Write the gap list.
  5. Run session 2 from the gap list only. Respect the caps: when a shot reaches its cap, change the approach and write the change.
  6. Edit the 60 s scene from selects only.
  7. Report: planned versus actual cost per shot and in total; usable share per model; which caps were reached and what you changed. Update the routing table.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Coverage plan with reactions, inserts, and cutaways.
  • [ ] Take log with in and out points and notes for every take.
  • [ ] Two gap lists.
  • [ ] 60 s edit.
  • [ ] Planned-versus-actual report and an updated routing table.

Self-check quiz

1. Why are reaction shots and inserts the most useful coverage in an AI production?

A 1.5 s reaction costs little and solves many problems in the edit. Plan them in every scene.

2. A shot has used its US$3 cap with no usable take. What do you do?

A cap is a signal that the method does not work for this shot. More takes of the same method rarely help.

3. Hero dialogue: Model A US$0.10/s with 50 % usable; Model B US$0.25/s with 80 % usable. Which is cheaper per usable second?

Cost per usable second = price / usable share. A: 0.10 / 0.5 = 0.20. B: 0.25 / 0.8 = 0.31. B may still be the right choice if the shot is hard and time matters; decide with both numbers.

4. How do you set the budget for a shot?

The formula uses your measured data per shot type. The safety factor covers bad luck and notes from the client.

5. After session 1, the editor says: 'I cannot cut from the wide to Mara's close-up; the eyeline is wrong, and I have no reaction from Leo.' What is this list called, and what happens to it?

Sessions end with a gap list from the edit. The next session makes only what the edit needs.

6. A creator claims US$2–4 per finished ad. What must you check before you use this number in a quote?

Reported numbers are claims. Your quote must use your own measured numbers.

7. When do you stop generating?

The edit is the goal. Extra takes beyond what the edit needs are waste.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong report is short and uses numbers:

Planned Actual
Total cost US$14.20 (caps) US$11.65
Takes — 47
Usable seconds in selects 60 74 (14 s of alternatives)
Usable share, hosted dialogue model 50 % (from M01) 44 %
Usable share, fast model (reactions, inserts) 30 % 41 %

"Two shots reached their caps. S08 (hand pushes the photo) failed 4 times on the hand; I replaced it with an insert and a reaction, which cost US$0.45 and cut better. S12 (wide with rain) failed on the rain physics; I switched to the open model with a control video from a 3D layout (C07·M03) on the second session."

"Reactions and inserts were 25 % of the takes and 9 % of the cost, and they are in 11 of the 22 cuts of the final edit. They solved every continuity problem at the joins."

The updated routing table moves reactions and inserts to the fast model for the next project, and keeps hero dialogue on the hosted model despite its lower usable share, because its lip sync was the best.

Program · Level 2

C06 Audio Generation: Voice, Music, Sound

M01M02M03M04

About this course

Sound is half of the experience. AI now makes voices, music, and effects at production quality. This course teaches you to use these tools well and legally. C10 then teaches you to mix the result.

Current tools (as of 2026-10): ElevenLabs (TTS, cloning, dubbing, music v2.5, avatars), HeyGen, Synthesia, Suno v6; open: IndexTTS-2, CosyVoice 3, Qwen3-TTS; Demucs for stems.

C06 · Audio Generation: Voice, Music, Sound

C06·M01 Synthetic voice - design, direction, cloning

Study time: 14 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Choose a TTS model by quality, languages, latency, license, and duration control, with a small listening test.
  2. Direct a synthetic voice with context, tags, punctuation, and reference audio, and assemble clean takes.
  3. Fit lines to time slots, and measure the fit.
  4. Clone a voice only with documented consent, and store the consent record.
  5. Make a consistent 2-minute voice-over and store the voice settings in the character bible.

Key words

TTS voice clone consent duration control voice design

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C06, module 01. Synthetic voice - design, direction, cloning. After this module, you can: 1. Choose a TTS model by quality, languages, latency, license, and duration control, with a small listening test. 2. Direct a synthetic voice with context, tags, punctuation, and reference audio, and assemble clean takes. 3. Fit lines to time slots, and measure the fit. 4. Clone a voice only with documented consent, and store the consent record. 5. Make a consistent 2-minute voice-over and store the voice settings in the character bible. Text-to-speech models now sound human. Choose a model by quality, languages, speed, license, and control, and test it on your own lines. Direct the voice like an actor: give context, emotion, pace, and pauses, with text tags or a reference recording. Many projects need each line to fit a time slot, so measure the speech length against the slot. A cloned voice needs documented consent from the person. Store one voice ID and its settings per character, and use them in every line.

Learn

How modern TTS works

A current text-to-speech model takes text (and often a voice reference or a voice ID) and produces audio. Many current models work like language models: they turn the text into tokens, predict audio tokens (a compressed code of sound), and decode the tokens into a waveform. Others use diffusion or flow matching on audio features. For you, two consequences matter:

  1. The model can take acting directions as text, because text is its input.
  2. Each generation is a new take. The same line gives a slightly different delivery each time, like an actor.

Choose a model

Choose by your requirements, then test:

Requirement What to check
Quality and emotion Blind listening test on your own lines
Languages and accents Native listeners for each language
Duration control Can it target a length? (dubbing, C06·M02)
Latency Streaming output for live or interactive use
Privacy Can it run on your own machine? Where does the text go?
License Commercial use of outputs; voice cloning terms; open-model license

A fair test: generate the same 10 lines of your own script with each model. Mix the order. Rate each take blind for naturalness, pronunciation, and emotion (1–5). Count errors: wrong words, wrong stress, artifacts.

Direct the voice

Direct a synthetic voice like an actor:

  • Context: who speaks, to whom, why, and where. "A tired nurse, whispering at night in an empty locker room."
  • Tags: many models accept delivery tags such as [whispers], [laughs], [pause]. Use them sparingly.
  • Punctuation: a comma is a short pause, a full stop a longer one. An ellipsis (…) makes hesitation. A question mark raises the pitch at the end.
  • Reference read: some models copy the delivery of a reference recording (a "read" by you or by a voice actor).
  • Takes: generate 2–3 takes of each line. Pick the best. Join takes in an audio editor (DAW) at breaths or pauses.

Fit lines to time

In video, a line often has a slot: the time between two cuts, or the time that a mouth moves on screen. Measure the fit. Speech length is the audio length without the silence at the start and the end. Compare it with the slot:

  • More than about 10 % longer: generate a faster take, use duration control, or shorten the text.
  • More than about 25 % shorter: add a word, or slow the pace.
  • Speed changes in post: up to about 10 % sound natural. More sounds wrong. starter/tools/fit_check.py measures every line of a script against its slot and reports the speaking rate in characters per second. You use the same tool for dubbing (M02) and localization (C15·M02).

Library, designed, and cloned voices

  • Library voice: a vendor voice. You may use it under the vendor's terms.
  • Designed voice: made from a text description ("warm, low, 40s, slight rasp"). No real person behind it.
  • Cloned voice: copied from a real person's recording (from about 10 s to several minutes of audio). It needs that person's documented consent. Store who consented, the scope, the time, the revocation terms, and the signature. Many vendors also require a verification step in which the person reads a text. The starter kit has a template (templates/voice_consent.md); a lawyer must check it for client work (C16·M02).

Consistency across a project

Store one voice ID and its exact settings per character in the character bible (C04·M03): the model, the voice ID, the settings (for example stability and style values), and one reference line. Use them for every line. If the model version changes, test the voice again before you continue a series.

Tool walkthrough

Hosted and open voices (as of 2026-10)

  • Hosted: ElevenLabs (TTS, voice design, cloning with verification, dubbing). Other hosted TTS services are in the landscape page.
  • Open: IndexTTS-2 and 2.5 (duration control and emotion control), CosyVoice 3 (0.5B, about 4 GB VRAM, Apache 2.0), Qwen3-TTS (check its license). Fish Audio S2 weights are for research only.

Measure the fit of a voice-over

# slots.json: one line per entry with start, end (from the edit), and text
python starter/tools/fit_check.py slots.json --audio-dir vo/

Name each audio file by the line ID (vo/L01.wav). The tool ignores silence at the start and the end.

A quick local voice for tests

For timing tests before you pay for TTS, any system voice works. On macOS: say -v Samantha -o vo/L01.aiff "Every photo showed tomorrow." Do not use test voices in deliveries.

Watch

  • ElevenLabs — Text to Speech docs (models, voice settings, tags)Read the voice settings and the expressive tags section.
  • IndexTTS-2 (open source) — GitHubLook at the duration control and emotion control examples.

Worked example

Fit test (2026-10-04, system voices, slots set from an English read):

Line Slot English speech Fit Spanish speech Fit
L01 "Every photo showed tomorrow." 1.49 s 1.56 s +5 % ✓ 2.35 s +58 % ✗
L02 "Except mine." 0.85 s 0.89 s +5 % ✓ 1.15 s +35 % ✗
L03 "I took this photo an hour ago…" 2.81 s 2.96 s +5 % ✓ 7.32 s +160 % ✗

The Spanish L03 was a long, literal translation with extra words. The tool reports "cut about 31 characters". The fix is not a faster voice. It is a shorter translation that keeps the meaning: this is the job of M02.

Mara's voice-over, 2 minutes:

  1. Voice design: "woman, early 30s, calm, slightly husky, tired, warm". Three candidates; candidate 2 chosen in a blind test (naturalness 4.4 / 5).
  2. Line: "Every photo showed tomorrow… [pause] except mine." Take 3 chosen.
  3. Settings stored in refs/CHAR-MARA/sheet.json: model, voice ID, stability 0.45, style 0.3, one reference line.
  4. All 24 lines pass fit_check.py after 3 re-takes with a faster pace.

Lab

Deliverable: C06/M01/ with voice tests, a 2-minute voice-over, a fit report, and a consent record.

  1. Design 3 candidate voices for one character. Rate them blind on 5 lines. Choose one with reasons.
  2. Write slots.json for a 2-minute voice-over from your animatic (C04·M04): one entry per line with the slot from the picture.
  3. Generate the voice-over with direction. Run fit_check.py. Re-take lines that do not fit. Assemble one clean track at 48 kHz.
  4. Generate the same 30 s with one open TTS model, locally or on a rented GPU. Compare blind with the hosted take.
  5. Fill in the consent template for your own voice. Clone your own voice. Compare it with the designed voice.
  6. Store the voice ID and settings in your character bible. Log every kept take in the prompt log.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 2-minute voice-over WAV at 48 kHz; all lines pass fit_check.py.
  • [ ] Blind rating sheet for 3 candidate voices and for hosted versus open.
  • [ ] A filled consent record for your own voice clone.
  • [ ] Voice ID and settings in the character bible.

Self-check quiz

1. A line must fit a 2.8 s slot in the picture. The take is 3.4 s of speech. What are your options, in order?

Speech sped up more than about 10 % sounds unnatural. Direct the pace first, then edit the words. Duration control in some models targets a length directly.

2. Which input helps a TTS model most to deliver a whispered, tired line?

Models use the context and tags as acting notes. Punctuation also shapes pauses and pitch.

3. A client asks you to clone the voice of their CEO from a conference video. The CEO is not in the email thread. What do you do?

A voice clone needs the person's consent. A public video is not consent. Many vendors also require voice verification (C16·M02).

4. Why store a voice ID and the exact settings per character?

Voice consistency is like visual consistency: a fixed reference, used every time.

5. Your Spanish dub lines are 35–160 % longer than the English slots. What does this tell you?

Text expands in translation. Give the translator a character limit per line from the slot length and the speaking rate (C06·M02).

6. When does an open TTS model win over a hosted one?

Hosted models often lead on emotional range. Open models are close on clean narration and win on privacy and cost.

7. How do you compare two TTS models fairly?

Vendor demos are chosen examples. Your lines, rated blind, predict your project.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Blind rating sheet (shape of a strong answer):

Voice Naturalness Pronunciation errors (5 lines) Fits the character Notes
A (designed, hosted) 4.4 0 5 Warm, slightly husky
B (library, hosted) 4.1 0 3 Too bright for a night-shift nurse
C (open model, local) 3.8 1 ("locker" stress) 4 Clean; less range in the whisper

"Chosen: A. The open model C is close on calm narration and loses on whispers. I will use C for internal drafts and A for delivery."

Fit report: "24 lines. First pass: 19 fit, 4 too long, 1 too short. Fixes: 3 faster takes, 1 text edit ('I took this photo an hour ago' → 'I took this an hour ago'; approved by the writer), 1 slower take. Final: 24 of 24 fit; mean speaking rate 14.2 characters per second."

The consent record names the scope ("my voice, this course project, online video, until 2027-06-30"), the revocation terms, and the vendor where the clone is stored. The rights log has a line that points to it.

C06 · Audio Generation: Voice, Music, Sound

C06·M02 Lip sync, avatars, and dubbing

Study time: 12 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Lip-sync generated or real faces to new dialogue, and know when lip sync fails.
  2. Make a talking-avatar video from a script, with consent and a clear disclosure.
  3. Run a dubbing pipeline - transcribe, adapt, voice, fit, lip sync, review - with files at each step.
  4. Check dubbing quality with measurements (fit, transcript errors) and a human review.

Key words

lip sync avatar dubbing localization

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C06, module 02. Lip sync, avatars, and dubbing. After this module, you can: 1. Lip-sync generated or real faces to new dialogue, and know when lip sync fails. 2. Make a talking-avatar video from a script, with consent and a clear disclosure. 3. Run a dubbing pipeline - transcribe, adapt, voice, fit, lip sync, review - with files at each step. 4. Check dubbing quality with measurements (fit, transcript errors) and a human review. Lip-sync models change the mouth movement of a face to match new audio. Avatar tools make a talking person from a script. Dubbing tools translate speech, keep the speaker's voice, and re-sync the lips. A dubbing pipeline has clear steps: transcribe with word timestamps, adapt the translation to the time slots, voice it, check the fit, lip-sync the speaker shots, and review. Measure what you can: transcript errors, line fit, and lip sync on frontal shots. A fluent human must review meaning and tone.

Learn

Lip sync

A lip-sync model takes a video and an audio track and changes the mouth region so that it matches the audio. It works best when:

  • the face is frontal or three-quarter, and large enough in the frame;
  • the light is good, and nothing covers the mouth (hands, a microphone, a cup);
  • the head does not turn fast. It fails at profiles, at fast head turns, and with teeth or tongue detail at high resolution. Joint audio-video models (C05·M04) and audio-to-video models (C11·M03) already make synced lips. Use separate lip sync for new lines in existing shots, and for dubbing.

Apply lip sync only where the mouth is readable. Wide shots, B-roll, and the backs of heads need none. Each lip-synced shot is a chance for an artifact, so check every one at full size.

Avatars

An avatar tool makes a talking person from a script and a voice: a presenter for training, explainers, or localized product videos. Two rules:

  1. Consent for any real person whose face or voice the avatar uses (C16·M02).
  2. Disclosure: the video and its description say that the presenter is AI-generated (C16·M03).

The dubbing pipeline

Build dubbing as a pipeline with a file at each step. Then you can check and repeat each step:

  1. Separate the voice from music and effects (stems, C05·M04). You get a voice stem and an M&E stem.
  2. Transcribe the voice stem with word timestamps. Separate speakers. Fix names and terms.
  3. Adapt the translation. Keep the meaning and fit the time. Each line has a slot (start and end) from the transcript. Give the translator a character limit for each line: slot length × the speaking rate of the target voice, minus a margin. Keep a glossary of names and product terms.
  4. Voice the lines: a cloned voice of the speaker (with consent), or a chosen TTS voice. Use duration control if the model has it.
  5. Check the fit of each line against its slot (M01). Re-take or re-adapt lines that do not fit.
  6. Lip-sync the speaker shots.
  7. Mix the new voice over the M&E stem (C10).
  8. Review: a fluent person checks meaning, tone, and naturalness. You check the fit, the lips, the voice, and the mix.

Transcription quality

Transcription models are very good on clean speech, and they fail in noise. Larger models are more robust. Two rules help most:

  • Transcribe the separated voice stem, not the full mix.
  • Give the model the names and terms in a prompt ("Mara, Leo, locker room"). Read every transcript. Names, numbers, and product terms are the most common errors. Words with low confidence are where to look first.

Why translation is adaptation

Most languages need more syllables than English for the same meaning. Spanish, German, and French lines are often 15–30 % longer. A word-for-word translation does not fit the slots. Ask for an adapted translation with a character limit per line. An LLM can do this well if you give it the limits, the context of the scene, and the glossary. A fluent human must still review it.

Measurable QC

Check Method Pass
Transcript Read it; correct names and terms No errors in names, numbers, terms
Fit fit_check.py per line ≤ 10 % longer, ≤ 25 % shorter
Meaning Fluent reviewer (back-translation as a first filter) No meaning errors
Tone Fluent reviewer Natural for the audience
Lips Watch every lip-synced shot at full size No visible mismatch on frontal shots
Voice Listen across the video Same voice for each speaker
Mix Dub over M&E; loudness check (C10·M02) M&E unchanged; loudness on target

Tool walkthrough

Transcribe with word timestamps

pip install faster-whisper
python starter/tools/stems.py demo.mp4 --out stems/
python starter/tools/transcribe.py stems/demo_dialogue.wav --model small --lang en \
  --prompt "Mara, Leo, locker room" --out tr/
# -> tr/demo_dialogue.json (segments, words), tr/demo_dialogue.srt, tr/demo_dialogue.slots.json

The slots.json file has one entry per line with its start and end. Add a text_target field with the translated line, then check the target voice with fit_check.py.

Adaptation prompt for an LLM

Translate each line into Spanish (Spain) for a dub. Keep the meaning and the tone (a tired nurse, quiet,
night). Each line has a character limit; never go over it. Use the glossary: "locker" = "taquilla".
Return JSON: [{"id": "L01", "text_target": "...", "chars": N}].
Lines: [{"id": "L01", "text": "Every photo showed tomorrow.", "max_chars": 21}, ...]

Tools (as of 2026-10)

  • Hosted dubbing and avatars: ElevenLabs (dubbing, Avatars), HeyGen (Avatar IV, lip-synced dubbing in 175+ languages), Synthesia.
  • Open: Whisper models (faster-whisper) for transcripts; IndexTTS-2 for duration-controlled voice; lip sync with LTX-2.3 audio-to-video (starter workflow 07) or community lip-sync models in ComfyUI.

Watch

  • HeyGen — Best AI dubbing tools 2026 (vendor comparison, read critically)Note the test criteria. Compare them with the QC checklist of this module.
  • Wav2Lip — research code of an early lip-sync modelLook at the examples. Modern tools are much better, but the idea is the same.

Worked example

Transcription test (2026-10-04, faster-whisper, CPU, int8). A synthetic voice line of 18 words, with speech-shaped noise added at 4 signal-to-noise ratios. Word error rate (WER):

Signal-to-noise ratio tiny base small
+10 dB 0 % 0 % 0 %
0 dB 15 % 25 % 0 %
−5 dB 100 % 115 % 30 %
−10 dB 100 % 100 % 100 %

On clean speech all sizes were perfect (0 %, also with a music bed under the voice). In noise, the small model was much more robust. Above 100 % means the model wrote more wrong words than the line had. Real dialogue has accents, overlaps, and room sound, so test on your own material.

Product demo, 90 s, English → Spanish, German, Japanese:

  1. Stems; transcript of the voice stem with word timestamps (small model). Two terms corrected by hand.
  2. Slot limits from the timing: 14 characters per second for the target voices, minus 10 %.
  3. LLM adaptation with the limits and the glossary. 3 of 24 Japanese lines over the limit → re-adapted.
  4. Voice: the presenter's cloned voice (consent on file), duration-controlled.
  5. fit_check.py: Spanish 24 of 24, German 22 of 24 (two re-takes), Japanese 24 of 24.
  6. Lip sync on 6 speaker shots; the B-roll needs none.
  7. Fluent review: German line 7 too formal ("Sie" → "du" for this brand); the product term in line 12 wrong → glossary fixed.

Lab

Deliverable: C06/M02/ with a 60 s video in 2 extra languages, the files of each pipeline step, and a QC report.

  1. Record or generate a 60 s talking video (you, or a person who consents).
  2. Separate the voice. Transcribe it with transcribe.py. Correct the transcript.
  3. Compute character limits per line. Adapt the translation to 2 languages, with a glossary.
  4. Voice the lines. Check each language with fit_check.py until all lines fit.
  5. Lip-sync the speaker shots. Mix the new voice over the M&E stem.
  6. Get a fluent review (a person; use back-translation only as a first filter).
  7. Fill in the QC table for both languages.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Every step has a file: stems, transcript JSON, adapted lines JSON, voice files, fit reports, final videos.
  • [ ] All lines fit in both languages.
  • [ ] QC table with the problems found and fixed.
  • [ ] Consent and disclosure recorded.

Self-check quiz

1. Which shots of a dubbed video need lip sync?

Lip sync costs time and can add artifacts. Apply it where the mouth is readable.

2. Your transcript of a noisy clip has many wrong words. What do you do first?

In the module test, at 0 dB signal-to-noise ratio the small model had 0 % word errors and the base model 25 %. Clean input and a larger model reduce errors.

3. A translated line is 58 % longer than its slot. What is the correct fix?

Dubbing translation is adaptation, not word-for-word translation. Give the translator (human or LLM) a character limit per line.

4. How do you compute a character limit for a dub line?

Example: a 2.8 s slot at 14 characters per second gives about 39 characters, so aim for 35.

5. Why do you dub over the voice stem only and keep the M&E (music and effects) track?

An M&E track is the standard delivery for dubbing (C10·M02). Without it, the dub would need a new mix of everything.

6. A back-translation by a second LLM says the Spanish dub is correct. Is the review done?

Machine checks are a filter. A fluent person decides whether it sounds natural and right for the audience.

7. You make a talking avatar of a real employee for a training video. What must you have?

Likeness and voice need consent (C16·M02). Viewers must know that the person is synthetic (C16·M03).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

QC report (shape of a strong answer):

Check Spanish German
Transcript 2 corrections (product name, "24 hours" heard as "20 hours") same transcript
Fit (fit_check.py) 21 of 24 first pass → 24 of 24 after 3 re-adaptations 19 of 24 → 24 of 24 (3 re-adaptations, 2 re-takes)
Meaning (fluent reviewer) 1 error: "taquilla" vs "casillero" (regional word; we chose Spain) 0 errors
Tone natural line 7 too formal → changed
Lips (6 shots) 5 good; 1 profile shot with a visible mismatch → recut to a reaction 6 good
Mix over M&E; −14 LUFS same

"Back-translation found 0 problems in German. The fluent reviewer found the formality problem and one unnatural phrase. Machine checks are a filter, not a review."

The folder has a file for each step, so a client change (a new product name) reruns only the steps from the transcript on.
