C06 · Audio Generation: Voice, Music, Sound

C06·M03 Music generation and licenses

Study time: 12 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Write a music brief with genre, tempo, key, mood, instruments, structure with times, and length.
  2. Edit generated music to the cut on bar lines, and land a picture hit on a strong beat.
  3. Read the license terms of every track, save a copy, and record them in the rights log.
  4. Choose between generated, library, and commissioned music for a job, with reasons.

Key words

music generation stems license tier tempo

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C06, module 03. Music generation and licenses. After this module, you can: 1. Write a music brief with genre, tempo, key, mood, instruments, structure with times, and length. 2. Edit generated music to the cut on bar lines, and land a picture hit on a strong beat. 3. Read the license terms of every track, save a copy, and record them in the rights log. 4. Choose between generated, library, and commissioned music for a job, with reasons. Music models make full songs or instrumentals from a prompt. Give genre, tempo, key, mood, instruments, structure with times, and length. Generate instrumentals for most video work, and get stems if you can, so you can edit and mix. Cut music on bar lines and land picture hits on strong beats; a bar grid from the tempo shows where. The license depends on the service and the plan, and it changes; save a copy of the terms with every download. For brand campaigns, library or commissioned music is often the safer choice.

Learn

The music brief

A music model follows a brief like a composer does. Write it with:

  • Genre and character. Describe the musical features: "indie electronic, plucked synth, warm bass". Do not name artists. Many services block artist names, and an output that sounds too close to a known song is a legal risk.
  • Tempo in BPM, for example 96 BPM. Tempo sets the bar length, so it sets where you can cut.
  • Key and mood: "D minor, tense, then hopeful".
  • Instruments: "felt piano, soft synth pad, light percussion, no vocals".
  • Structure with times: "0–8 s intro; 8–24 s build; hit at 24 s; 24–30 s resolve".
  • Length in seconds, and the type of ending: "clean ending on a held chord".

For most video work, ask for instrumentals. Vocals compete with dialogue, because they use the same frequency range, and lyrics add meaning that you did not plan.

Music time

To edit music you need its grid:

  • one beat = 60 / BPM seconds; at 112 BPM, 0.536 s;
  • one bar of 4/4 = 4 beats; at 112 BPM, 2.14 s; at 120 BPM, exactly 2.00 s;
  • the downbeat is beat 1 of a bar. Phrases usually last 4 or 8 bars.

A music edit sounds right when you cut on a bar line, ideally at the start of a phrase. A picture hit (a door, a cut, a title) feels right when it lands on a strong beat, within about 40 ms. starter/tools/bars.py makes the grid from the tempo and the first downbeat. It shows the nearest beat and bar for each picture event, and where to end the cue.

Beat detectors (in bars.py --detect) find the tempo well. They often choose the wrong downbeat, and sometimes half or double the tempo. Check by ear: tap along, and listen for beat 1.

Editing to the cut

  1. Place the cue so that the main hit lands on its picture event. Slip the music in time if needed.
  2. Cut out bars (or whole phrases) to shorten. Cut on bar lines, with a short crossfade (10–30 ms).
  3. For the end, use the music's own ending. Generate an "ending" variant if the cue has none.
  4. Use stems if you have them: lower the drums under dialogue; remove the lead instrument under voice-over.

Licenses

The license of a generated track depends on the service, the plan, and the date. Typical differences between plans: commercial use or not, streaming platforms or not, download limits, and credit requirements. Terms change often. For every track that you use:

  • save the audio, the prompt, the track ID, the plan, and the date;
  • save a PDF copy of the terms on that date;
  • add a line to the rights log (promptlog.py rights).

Choose a source

  • Generated: best fit to timing and mood, fast variants, low cost. The license depends on the plan and can change. There is a small risk of similarity to existing music.
  • Library (stock): clear, proven licenses and known quality. It fits less exactly, so it needs more editing.
  • Commissioned: a composer writes for the picture. The highest cost and full control. Common for brand campaigns. Many brand clients still require library or commissioned music. Social content and prototypes often use generated music.

Tool walkthrough

Services (as of 2026-10; check the current terms)

  • Suno v6 (2026-09-09): trained on licensed music (deals with WMG, BMG, Believe); downloads capped by plan.
  • ElevenLabs Music v2.5 (2026-09-11): licensed data (Merlin, Kobalt, Believe; UMG deal); the Starter plan is "commercial, no streaming"; higher plans are broader.

Make the grid and check hits

python starter/tools/bars.py --bpm 112 --sig 4/4 --offset 0.27 --length 30           # bar lines
python starter/tools/bars.py --bpm 112 --offset 0.27 --snap 6.0,20.1                 # picture events
python starter/tools/bars.py --bpm 112 --offset 0.27 --cut-to 30                     # where to end
pip install librosa
python starter/tools/bars.py --detect cue.wav --snap 6.0,20.1                        # estimate BPM and first beat

Log the track

python starter/tools/promptlog.py rights --id MUS-AD-CUE2 --source "music service, plan X, track 8f2c…" \
  --license "plan X terms 2026-10-04 (rights/terms/plan_x_2026-10-04.pdf)" --use "online ad, no broadcast" \
  --file music/cue2.wav

Watch

  • Best AI music models Sept 2026 — prices and rights (TeamDay)Read the license column for each plan.
  • Suno vs ElevenLabs Music 2026 — v6 vs v2.5, licensingNote the download caps and the streaming rights by plan.

Worked example

Detection test (2026-10-04, librosa). A 30 s test track with clicks at exactly 112 BPM; the first downbeat is at 0.270 s:

detected: 112.3 BPM, first beat at 0.824 s

The tempo is correct to 0.3 %. The first beat is wrong: 0.824 s is beat 2 (0.270 + 0.536 = 0.806 s). If you used the detected offset, every "bar line" would be one beat late. We set the offset by ear to 0.27 s. Then:

python bars.py --bpm 112 --offset 0.27 --snap 6.0,20.1
   event nearest beat  off ms nearest bar  off ms
   6.000        6.163    +163       6.699    +699  <- move the cut or the music
  20.100       20.091      -9      19.556    -544

The second event is 9 ms from a beat: it already feels right. The first is 163 ms early. A change before the first event moves both events, so it would break the second hit. Fix with two picture changes:

  1. Extend the shot before the first event by 4 frames (167 ms at 24 fps). Event 1 moves to 6.167 s: 4 ms from the beat. Event 2 moves to 20.267 s.
  2. Trim 4 frames from a shot between the two events. Event 2 moves back to 20.100 s: 9 ms from its beat. Check again with --snap after every change.

30 s ad cue: Prompt: "Instrumental, 112 BPM, upbeat indie electronic, plucked synth, claps, warm bass; 0–6 s sparse intro; 6–20 s build; 20 s drop on a big clap; 20–30 s full groove; clean ending at 30 s; no vocals." Three takes; take 2 chosen; stems downloaded; drums −6 dB under the voice-over. The cue ended at 31.3 s, so we cut one bar inside the groove (on a bar line, with a 20 ms crossfade). The rights-log line has the plan, the terms PDF, and the track ID.

Lab

Deliverable: C06/M03/ with 3 cues fitted to picture, bars.py reports, rights-log lines with terms copies, and a comparison.

  1. Write briefs for 3 cues of your project: tension, light, and ending.
  2. Generate each with 2 services (or 2 plans), 2–3 takes each.
  3. Find the tempo and the downbeat of each chosen cue (bars.py --detect, then check by ear).
  4. Edit each cue to your animatic or sequence: cut on bar lines, land one picture hit within 40 ms, end on the music's ending.
  5. Record the license details for each track, with a PDF of the terms.
  6. Compare one generated cue with one library cue for the same scene: fit, quality, license, cost, time.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 cues fitted to picture; one hit within 40 ms (show the --snap output).
  • [ ] Rights-log lines with terms PDFs.
  • [ ] Generated-versus-library comparison.

Self-check quiz

1. At 112 BPM in 4/4, how long is one bar?

One beat = 60 / BPM = 0.536 s. A 4/4 bar has 4 beats: 2.14 s.

2. A beat detector reports 112.3 BPM and a first beat at 0.82 s. The real downbeat is at 0.27 s. What happened?

Detectors find beats well and downbeats less well. They can also choose half or double tempo. Always check by ear.

3. A picture hit (a door slam) is at 6.00 s; the nearest strong beat is at 6.70 s. What do you do?

A hit that is more than about 40 ms off the beat feels wrong. Slip the music, edit it on a bar line, or trim the picture.

4. Why ask for 'instrumental, no vocals' for most video music?

Under speech, music must leave space. Vocals fill the same frequency range as the voice.

5. What do you save with every downloaded generated track?

Terms change. You must be able to show which terms applied when you made and used the track.

6. Your prompt says 'in the style of [famous band]'. What is the problem?

Describe tempo, instruments, harmony, and mood. Do not name artists. Check outputs for similarity to known songs.

7. A 30 s cue ends at 31.3 s, on a bar line. The picture ends at 30.0 s. What is a clean fix?

Music needs a real ending. Edit on bars so the last phrase lands at the end, or make an ending variant.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Fitting report (shape of a strong answer):

Cue BPM (detected / checked) Downbeat Picture hit Off after edit Edits
Tension (S01–S06) 84.1 / 84 0.42 s (detector chose beat 3) Photo reveal at 3.00 s +8 ms slipped −0.31 s
Light (S07–S12) 56 / 112 (detector halved it) 0.10 s Locker opens at 14.20 s −12 ms 2 bars cut at 18.4 s
Ending (S13–S14) 70 / 70 0.00 s Rain starts at 52.80 s +21 ms ending variant generated

"The detector halved the tempo of the light cue (56 instead of 112). I found it by ear: the claps were on every 'beat'."

Comparison:

Generated Library
Fit to the cut Exact structure from the brief Needed 3 edits
Time to final 40 min (6 takes + edit) 70 min (search + edit)
Cost Plan fee US$49 single-use license
License Plan terms, no broadcast Broadcast allowed
Choice for this film Generated (online only) Would use for a TV version

C06 · Audio Generation: Voice, Music, Sound

C06·M04 Sound effects, ambience, separation, and cleanup

Study time: 12 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Generate sound effects and ambience from text and from video, with prompts that name source, action, material, space, and distance.
  2. Make seamless ambience loops, and measure the loop point.
  3. Clean noisy dialogue at the least strength that works, and compare classic denoising with AI voice isolation by measurement and by ear.
  4. Build a sound library with IDs, metadata, and licenses that pipelines can search.

Key words

sound effects ambience stem separation noise reduction

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C06, module 04. Sound effects, ambience, separation, and cleanup. After this module, you can: 1. Generate sound effects and ambience from text and from video, with prompts that name source, action, material, space, and distance. 2. Make seamless ambience loops, and measure the loop point. 3. Clean noisy dialogue at the least strength that works, and compare classic denoising with AI voice isolation by measurement and by ear. 4. Build a sound library with IDs, metadata, and licenses that pipelines can search. Sound-effect models make effects and ambience from text, and some make them from the video itself, in sync. Name the source, the action, the material, the space, and the distance. Ambience beds must loop without a step or a click. Stem-separation and voice-isolation models split a mix into voice and the rest; they now clean noisy dialogue much better than classic spectral noise reduction. Use the least strength that works, compare with the original, and keep some room sound. Store every sound with an ID, metadata, and its license.

Learn

What effects and ambience do

Sound effects are the sounds of actions: a door, steps, paper, a cup. Ambience is the sound of a place: rain, traffic, a hospital air system, a café. Ambience runs under a whole scene and tells the viewer where they are. Effects make actions feel real and land the edit (C10·M01).

Prompt effects like a sound designer

A sound depends on five things. Name all five:

  1. Source: a heavy wooden door; a metal locker door.
  2. Action: slams; creaks open slowly; clicks shut.
  3. Material: wood, metal, glass, gravel, linoleum.
  4. Space: a small tiled bathroom; a large stone hall; outdoors.
  5. Distance: close to the microphone; across the room; far away. "Cinematic", "epic", and "high quality" carry no information. Generate 3–4 takes. The material and the distance usually need 2–3 prompt changes.

Some models make sound from the video itself (video-to-audio). They place effects on events in the clip: steps when the feet touch the floor. Check the sync at the frame level. Step through the clip one frame at a time at each impact. The sound should start on the frame where the contact happens, or one frame later. A sound that starts before the contact is easy to notice, even when it is only one or two frames early.

Ambience beds

Generate ambience long: 60–120 s. Say what must not be in it: "no voices, no music". Viewers notice when a bed repeats in a short loop.

A bed that plays under a long scene must loop. A loop point joins the end of the file to the start. If the level or the texture differs, the listener hears a step or a click every cycle. Fix: crossfade the last seconds into the first seconds with equal-power curves (one fades out, the other fades in, so the loudness stays even). Then check the loop point. starter/tools/loop_audio.py does both.

Separation

Source-separation models split a mix into parts: voice and the rest (two stems), or voice, drums, bass, and other (four stems). Uses:

  • take the voice out of a native-audio clip (C05·M04);
  • remove music from a clip that you must re-score;
  • reuse the ambience of a clip.

Cleanup: classic and AI

Noisy dialogue has two kinds of tools:

  • Classic spectral noise reduction estimates the noise spectrum and subtracts it. It needs a correct noise estimate. It works on steady noise (hum, hiss, air conditioning). Too much strength makes the voice "watery".
  • AI voice isolation and separation models learned what voices sound like. They remove changing noise too (traffic, babble, music). They can remove breaths and room sound, and make a voice sound pasted onto the scene.

Rules for both:

  1. Measure the noise first, in a pause: its level and its type.
  2. Use the least strength that works. Try 3 strengths and listen.
  3. A/B every result with the original, on headphones and on a small speaker.
  4. Keep a little room sound. Mix room tone back under a fully isolated voice.

The sound library

Store every sound you keep:

sfx/
  DOOR-LOCKER-SLAM-01.wav
  DOOR-LOCKER-SLAM-01.json   {"tags": ["door", "metal", "slam", "small room", "close"],
                              "origin": "generated: model X, prompt '...'", "license": "...", "date": "2026-10-04"}

Tags follow the five prompt parts, so you can search "metal, close, small room". Add a rights-log line for every sound that you did not make yourself (C16).

Tool walkthrough

Effects tools (as of 2026-10)

  • Hosted: ElevenLabs sound effects (text to effect); some video models add synced effects natively (C05·M04).
  • Open separation: Demucs (MIT) through starter/tools/stems.py.
  • Cleanup: iZotope RX, Adobe Podcast, DaVinci Resolve Voice Isolation (hosted or desktop); ffmpeg afftdn for classic denoising in scripts.

Make and check a loop

python starter/tools/loop_audio.py rain_90s.wav --out rain_loop.wav --xfade 2.0
python starter/tools/loop_audio.py rain_loop.wav --check

Classic denoise in a script

Measure the noise level in a pause first (for example with ffmpeg -i in.wav -af astats -f null - on a cut of the pause). Then set the noise floor (nf) to that level:

ffmpeg -i noisy.wav -af "afftdn=nr=12:nf=-21" clean_nr12.wav

AI isolation

python starter/tools/stems.py noisy_line.wav --out iso/     # iso/noisy_line_dialogue.wav

Watch

  • ElevenLabs — sound effects docsRead the prompt tips for effects.
  • Demucs — GitHub (music source separation)Read the usage section; you run it in the lab.

Worked example

Loop test (2026-10-04). A 20 s ambience bed (pink noise with a slow level change and a low hum):

File Level step at the loop point Ratio to normal steps Click Result
Raw file, end → start 5.35 dB 3.66 no AUDIBLE JOIN
After a 2 s equal-power crossfade 2.96 dB 2.07 no SEAMLESS

Cleanup test (2026-10-04). A synthetic voice line with steady broadband noise at 5 dB signal-to-noise ratio. SI-SDR against the clean voice (higher is better), and the noise level in the pause before the line:

Method SI-SDR Noise in the pause
Noisy input 4.2 dB −20.9 dBFS
Classic denoise, noise floor set wrong (−40 dB) 4.3 dB −21.0 dBFS (no effect)
Classic denoise, floor −21 dB, 6 dB reduction 7.3 dB −24.6 dBFS
Same, 12 dB reduction 8.5 dB −26.2 dBFS
Same, 24 dB reduction 9.1 dB −27.1 dBFS
Same, 40 dB reduction 9.1 dB −27.2 dBFS
AI separation (Demucs, voice stem) 14.9 dB −54.7 dBFS

Three lessons:

  1. A wrong noise estimate makes a classic reducer do nothing. Measure the noise first.
  2. Above 24 dB of reduction there was no gain. More strength only adds artifacts.
  3. The AI model was much better here: 5.8 dB more than the best classic setting, and an almost silent pause. Listen anyway: the pause is now unnaturally silent, so add room tone in the mix.

Lab

Deliverable: C06/M04/ with before/after audio, a cleanup table, 2 loops with reports, and 10 library entries.

  1. Take 2 native-audio clips (or recordings with noise). Separate the stems.
  2. Clean one noisy voice with a classic reducer at 3 strengths (measure the noise floor first) and with AI isolation. Measure each result (SI-SDR if you have a clean reference; otherwise the noise in a pause) and listen. Choose one, and explain why.
  3. Generate 6 effects and 2 ambience beds for your scene. Use the five prompt parts. Write how many takes each needed.
  4. Make both beds loop with loop_audio.py. Save the check reports.
  5. Add 10 entries to your sound library with JSON metadata and rights-log lines.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Cleanup table with measurements and a listening note for each version.
  • [ ] 6 effects and 2 loops, with loop reports that pass.
  • [ ] 10 library entries with tags, origin, and license.

Self-check quiz

1. Which prompt gives the most useful door sound?

Source, action, material, space, and distance decide how a sound sounds. 'Cinematic' and 'high quality' carry no information.

2. An ambience loop has a soft 'step' in level every 90 s. What is the cause and the fix?

A loop point joins the end to the start. Any difference in level or texture is heard every cycle. In the module test, the step fell from 5.4 dB to 3.0 dB after a 2 s crossfade.

3. You set a classic noise reducer to remove 40 dB of noise, but the output is unchanged. What is a likely cause?

In the module test, a floor of −40 dB gave no change on noise at −21 dBFS. With the floor at −21 dB, the reducer worked.

4. Classic denoising at 24 dB and at 40 dB gave the same measured result. Which do you use?

Use the least strength that works. Extra strength adds artifacts without benefit.

5. On the same noisy line, classic denoising reached 9.1 dB SI-SDR and an AI voice-isolation model reached 14.9 dB. What else must you check before you use the AI result?

Numbers say how close to the clean voice. Ears say whether it sounds natural in the scene.

6. Why keep a little room sound under cleaned dialogue?

Every place has a sound. Dialogue edits need a continuous room tone under them (C10·M01).

7. What does each sound-library entry need?

Pipelines search by tags. C16 needs the origin and the license.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Cleanup choice (shape of a strong answer): "Noise in the pause: −32 dBFS, mostly air conditioning (steady). Classic denoise at 6 / 12 / 18 dB: the 12 dB version removes the hum and keeps the voice natural; 18 dB starts to sound watery on 's' sounds. AI isolation: the cleanest, but her breaths are gone and the voice sounds dry against the room. Choice: classic 12 dB for this steady noise. For the café scene (babble and music), AI isolation plus room tone at −42 dBFS."

Effects log:

Sound Takes What changed between takes
Locker door click 3 "metal locker" + "small tiled room" fixed the material and the space
Photo paper rustle 2 "close to the microphone"
Rain on a window, inside 4 "heard from inside, through glass" removed the outdoor splash

The two loop reports show SEAMLESS. The library entries use the same tag vocabulary, so grep -l '"metal"' sfx/*.json finds every metal sound.

Program · Level 2

C07 World Models, 3D, and Virtual Production

40 h · Prerequisites: C01, C05

M01M02M03

About this course

Video models guess space. 3D tools know space. When you combine them, you get exact camera control and stable locations. World models such as Genie 3 and Marble now generate whole 3D or interactive worlds. This course shows how to use them in production today.

Starter tool: tools/whitebox.py in the starter kit builds a white box from a JSON layout and renders depth, edge, and clay videos with a real lens (M03). It runs with Blender's Python module (pip install bpy, Python 3.11) without opening Blender. On 2026-10-04 it rendered 48 frames of all three passes at 640 × 352 in 25 s on a laptop CPU.

Course outcomes

  1. Explain meshes, NeRFs, and Gaussian splats, and when each is useful.
  2. Generate explorable 3D worlds and use them as sets and previs.
  3. Use 3D layout to control camera paths for video models exactly.
  4. Use a real-time engine for previs and virtual production.

Modules

  1. C07·M01 3D representations - mesh, NeRF, Gaussian splats 10 h
  2. C07·M02 Generated worlds and interactive world models 10 h
  3. C07·M03 3D layout for exact camera, and real-time engines 20 h

C07 · World Models, 3D, and Virtual Production

C07·M01 3D representations - mesh, NeRF, Gaussian splats

Study time: 10 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain meshes, NeRFs, and Gaussian splats - what each stores, how it renders, and what it is good for.
  2. Estimate the size of a splat scene from its number of Gaussians.
  3. Capture a real place as a Gaussian splat with a phone, and clean it.
  4. Render exact camera moves through a splat, and use them to control a video model.

Key words

mesh NeRF Gaussian splatting photogrammetry

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C07, module 01. 3D representations - mesh, NeRF, Gaussian splats. After this module, you can: 1. Explain meshes, NeRFs, and Gaussian splats - what each stores, how it renders, and what it is good for. 2. Estimate the size of a splat scene from its number of Gaussians. 3. Capture a real place as a Gaussian splat with a phone, and clean it. 4. Render exact camera moves through a splat, and use them to control a video model. A mesh is a surface of triangles with textures; it is the standard of games and VFX. A NeRF is a neural network that stores how a scene looks from every direction. A Gaussian splat stores a scene as millions of small, colored, semi-transparent ellipsoids; it renders in real time and looks photographic. You can capture a real place with a phone and get a splat in an hour. In AI-native video, a splat gives the real layout and the exact camera move, and the video model adds light, people, and life.

Learn

Why 3D in an AI-native course

A video model guesses space from 2D training data. It does not know that the window is 1.2 m to the left of the door, or that the camera moved 0.8 m. A 3D representation knows. When you combine them, the 3D scene fixes the layout and the camera path, and the video model adds light, people, and life. This course shows three ways to store a 3D scene, and in M02 and M03 how to make them and use them.

Mesh

A mesh is a surface made of triangles. Each triangle has texture coordinates (UVs) into images that give color and other material values. Every game engine, 3D application, and VFX tool uses meshes.

  • Strong: editing, animation, physics, relighting, exact geometry.
  • Weak: photoreal results need much work: modeling, textures, materials, and lights.

NeRF

A NeRF (neural radiance field) is a small neural network. You give it a 3D point and a view direction. It returns a color and a density. To render a pixel, you sample many points along the camera ray and combine them. NeRFs gave very good new views of captured scenes.

  • Strong: view synthesis quality.
  • Weak: slow rendering (many network calls per pixel), hard editing. NeRFs were the step before splats. You will see them in papers and some tools.

Gaussian splat

A Gaussian splat scene is a set of millions of small 3D Gaussians: soft, semi-transparent ellipsoids. Each Gaussian stores:

  • a position (3 numbers);
  • a size in three directions (3 numbers) and a rotation (4 numbers, a quaternion);
  • an opacity (1 number);
  • a color that changes with the view angle, stored as spherical-harmonic coefficients (up to 16 coefficients × 3 colors = 48 numbers). That is about 59 numbers per Gaussian. To render, the GPU sorts the Gaussians by depth and blends them onto the screen. This runs in real time, even in a web browser.

A capture tool makes the splat by optimization: it starts from points that it found in the photos, then adjusts all Gaussians until renders from the photo positions match the photos. Because the colors come from the photos, a splat looks photographic. It also stores the captured light, so you cannot easily relight it.

Size estimate: 1.8 million Gaussians × 59 numbers × 4 bytes ≈ 425 MB as an uncompressed .ply file. Compressed formats (for example .spz or .sog) are several times smaller. Use the estimate to plan storage and web delivery.

Capture a real place

  1. Choose a static scene. Avoid moving people, strong reflections, glass, and plain white walls (they have no detail to match).
  2. Lock exposure, focus, and white balance on the phone. Changing exposure gives inconsistent colors.
  3. Move slowly around and through the space. Cover it from many positions and at 2–3 heights. Overlap each view with the last one. 60–200 photos, or a 1–2 minute video.
  4. Process with a capture app or an open tool.
  5. Clean: delete "floaters" (stray blobs, often near windows and at the edges) and crop the scene.

Use splats in production

  • Virtual location scout: walk through the place on a screen before you generate or shoot.
  • Camera planning: try moves interactively, because the splat renders in real time.
  • Exact plates: render a camera move along a path, at a real focal length.
  • Video conditioning: use the render as the first frame (I2V), as the source of V2V, or as a location reference (C05·M01).

The video model hides many splat faults (soft areas, small floaters) when it redraws the frames at medium strength.

Tool walkthrough

Capture and edit (as of 2026-10)

  • Phone capture apps process on the phone or in the cloud and export .ply or .spz. Check the export format and the license of the output before you choose one.
  • Open pipeline: Nerfstudio (splatfacto) on a rented GPU. Steps: ns-process-data video --data capture.mp4 --output-dir data/, then ns-train splatfacto --data data/, then export the splat.
  • Editing: a splat editor in the browser (for example SuperSplat) to delete floaters, crop, and set the orientation.

Render a camera move

Most splat viewers and editors can record a camera path. For exact moves, set two key positions and a focal length, and render at 24 fps at your working size (for example 1280 × 704). Name the file by shot: S08_splat_dolly.mp4.

Into the video model

  • I2V: the first frame of the render, plus a prompt for light and people.
  • V2V with control: depth or edges of the render as the control video (C11 starter workflow 05), plus a reference image for the look.

Watch

  • 3D Gaussian Splatting — project page (INRIA)Watch the video on the page. Note the real-time rendering and the soft areas.
  • Radiance Fields — news site for splats and NeRFsRead 3 recent articles about splats in film and video production.

Worked example

Café capture (a shape that you can follow):

  1. Phone video, 2 minutes, exposure and focus locked, two passes at 1.0 m and 1.6 m height.
  2. Processing gives a splat with 1.8 million Gaussians (about 425 MB as .ply, about 60 MB compressed).
  3. Cleaning: about 30 floaters near the window deleted; the street outside cropped.
  4. Camera path: a slow dolly along the counter, 6 s, 35 mm lens look, 1.4 m height.
  5. V2V with the render as the source and the prompt "same camera move, morning light, a barista works at the espresso machine".

Result: the counter, the window, and the camera path match the real café exactly. The model added the barista and the morning light. A text-to-video shot with the same description invented a different café with a different layout in each take.

Lab

Deliverable: C07/M01/ with a splat, 2 rendered moves, a video-model shot, and a comparison.

  1. Capture one real space (a room, a corridor, a shop with permission) as a splat. Write your capture settings and path.
  2. Count the Gaussians. Estimate the file size with the formula. Compare with the real file size.
  3. Clean the splat. Write what you deleted and why.
  4. Render 2 camera moves at real focal lengths (one dolly, one pan or crane).
  5. Use one render as the first frame (I2V) or as the source (V2V) for a video model.
  6. Generate a text-to-video shot from a written description of the same space. Compare layout, camera, and look.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Splat file and a viewer screenshot.
  • [ ] Size estimate versus real size.
  • [ ] 2 rendered moves with their lens and speed written down.
  • [ ] Video-model result and the T2V comparison.

Self-check quiz

1. Which representation do you choose for a set that a 3D artist must edit and animate (doors that open, a car that drives)?

Meshes are made of editable surfaces with materials, so every engine can animate and light them. Splats and NeRFs are hard to edit.

2. Why does a splat look photographic with no lighting setup?

A splat stores the appearance that the camera saw, including light and reflections. That is also why you cannot easily relight it.

3. A splat has 1.8 million Gaussians with full view-dependent color (about 59 numbers each, 32-bit). About how large is the file?

1.8 M × 59 numbers × 4 bytes ≈ 425 MB. Compressed formats make it several times smaller.

4. Your capture has 'floaters' (fog-like blobs) near the windows. What causes them, and what do you do?

Glass, mirrors, and thin coverage confuse the reconstruction. Clean the scene, and plan the capture path.

5. What is the most important rule while you film a capture?

Reconstruction needs sharp, consistent views of a static scene from many positions.

6. Why render a camera move through a splat and use it in a video model, instead of only describing the move in a prompt?

Words are a weak control for space and camera paths (C05·M02). A render is exact.

7. You want a splat of your kitchen for a shot. A NeRF method gives a slightly better still image but renders at 1 frame per second. Which do you use for an interactive camera planning session?

Interactive planning needs real time. Quality differences are small after the video model pass.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Capture notes (shape of a strong answer): "Kitchen, 3.5 × 4 m. iPhone video, 1 min 40 s, exposure and focus locked. Two loops: one at chest height, one at 1.8 m looking down. Result: 1.2 M Gaussians; formula 1.2 M × 59 × 4 B = 283 MB; real .ply 290 MB (header and extra fields). Cleaning: deleted floaters in front of the oven glass and the window; cropped the garden."

Comparison:

Splat render → I2V Text-to-video
Layout Real kitchen, window left of the fridge Different kitchen in each take
Camera Exact 0.8 m dolly, 35 mm look A random slow push-in
Look Real light + the prompted evening light Generic
Faults Soft area under the table (thin capture) —

"The splat fixed what words could not: the layout and the camera move. The soft area under the table disappeared at medium V2V strength. For the next capture, I will add a low pass at 0.5 m."

C07 · World Models, 3D, and Virtual Production

C07·M02 Generated worlds and interactive world models

Study time: 10 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain what a world model is, and how interactive world streams and 3D world generators differ from video models.
  2. Generate a 3D world from text or an image, and use it as a fixed set for many shots.
  3. Plan shots in a generated world (positions, lenses, moves) and turn them into video-model shots.
  4. Test the current limits of a world model - resolution, coherence over time and distance, scale, editing - and plan around them.

Key words

world model generated world previs interactive video

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C07, module 02. Generated worlds and interactive world models. After this module, you can: 1. Explain what a world model is, and how interactive world streams and 3D world generators differ from video models. 2. Generate a 3D world from text or an image, and use it as a fixed set for many shots. 3. Plan shots in a generated world (positions, lenses, moves) and turn them into video-model shots. 4. Test the current limits of a world model - resolution, coherence over time and distance, scale, editing - and plan around them. A video model makes a fixed clip. A world model makes a space that you can move through. Interactive world models generate a video stream in real time that reacts to your input, but only for a limited time. 3D world generators make a scene from text or an image that you can export, often as a Gaussian splat, and use like a captured set. In production, a generated world is the fixed truth for layout and camera across many shots, and the video model adds detail and life. Test the limits before you plan a project around them.

Learn

What "world model" means

In research, a world model is a model that predicts what happens next in an environment, given an action. In media production the term covers two kinds of tools:

  1. Interactive world streams. The model generates the next frames from the frames before and your input (move forward, turn left, open the door). The output is a video stream that follows your actions in real time.
  2. 3D world generators. The model makes a 3D scene from text, an image, a panorama, or a video. You export the scene, often as a Gaussian splat (M01), and use it like a captured set.

A normal video model makes a fixed clip from a prompt. It has no action input, and it does not export a space.

Interactive streams: strengths and limits

An interactive model must make each frame fast, and it can keep only a limited memory of what it showed before. So:

  • Coherence is limited in time and distance. If you walk away and come back, things can change.
  • Resolution and detail are lower than top video models.
  • Control is through actions, not through exact camera parameters. Use interactive streams for exploration and pitches: a director walks through an idea, and you record the views that work.

3D world generators: strengths and limits

An exported 3D world is static. Every render shows the same layout. That makes it a good set:

  • Strengths: one consistent place for many shots; exact camera moves (render them like a splat capture, M01); fast variants of a location.
  • Limits: soft or blurry far areas; seams; wrong scale (a chair as tall as a door); weak moving characters; limited editing.

How to use a generated world in production

  1. Design the location: generate 3–5 variants from your look bible (C04·M04). Choose one. Freeze it as the location reference (C04·M03).
  2. Check the scale against a known object: a door is about 2.0 m high, a table about 0.75 m, a step about 0.18 m.
  3. Plan shots: place the camera positions, choose real focal lengths, and record the moves (C02·M02).
  4. Render each move at your working size and frame rate.
  5. Generate the final shots with I2V or V2V, using the renders. Add the characters and the life with the video model and your references.
  6. Keep the world file and the renders with the project. Every later shot in the same place starts from them.

Plan around the limits

  • Blurry backgrounds: shallow depth of field, or point the camera toward the detailed area.
  • Seams: avoid camera paths that cross them; let the video model redraw at medium strength.
  • Scale: fix it in the world before you plan lenses, or scale the camera height and speed to match.
  • Short coherence (interactive): record short clips; do not plan a long continuous shot.

Tool walkthrough

Current world models (as of 2026-10)

  • Genie 3 (Google DeepMind): interactive world stream; available to Google AI Ultra users via Project Genie since January 2026; about 720p at 24 fps, with about 60 s of coherence.
  • Marble (World Labs): 3D world generator from text, an image, a panorama, or a video; exports Gaussian splats (a full version of about 2 M splats, or a light version of about 500 k). Reports say Sony Pictures used it for virtual-production previs.
  • NVIDIA Cosmos: world models mainly for robotics and simulation; useful for physics-aware synthetic video.

A world-to-shot pipeline

  1. Concept frame from your image model (C04), in the look of the bible.
  2. World generator → export the splat.
  3. Open it in a splat viewer or editor (M01). Check the scale with a door or a table.
  4. Record moves at 24 fps with real focal lengths.
  5. Video model: I2V from the first frame of each render, or V2V with a depth or edge control from the render (C11 starter workflow 05).

Watch

  • Google DeepMind — Genie 3Watch the demo clips. Note how the world reacts to input, and where it starts to change.
  • World Labs — MarbleLook at the examples and the export options (splats).

Worked example

Sci-fi short: an abandoned greenhouse on Mars, 9 shots.

  1. Concept frame from the image model: "abandoned greenhouse dome on Mars, broken glass panels, dead plants, red dust, low sun".
  2. The world generator made a splat world (light version) in a few minutes. Scale check: the door was 2.9 m high. We scaled the world to 69 % so the door is 2.0 m.
  3. In the viewer: 6 camera positions, 3 moves (a slow push through the door, 28 mm; a pan across the dead plants, 50 mm; a crane-up to the broken roof, 24 mm).
  4. Renders at 1280 × 704, 24 fps. The far end of the dome was blurry, so the pan uses a shallow depth of field and the near plants.
  5. I2V and V2V with the renders: added drifting dust, the astronaut (character references), and the light change.
  6. Result: all 9 shots share one set. The broken panel above the door is in the same place in every shot.

Lab

Deliverable: C07/M02/ with a generated world, a scale check, 3 renders, 3 final shots, and a limits report.

  1. Generate a world for the main location of your story with any 3D world generator. If you have access to an interactive world model, also record a 30–60 s exploration.
  2. Check the scale against a known object. Fix it, or write the factor.
  3. Plan 3 shots in the world: position, focal length, move, duration. Record the 3 moves.
  4. Make 3 final shots with a video model from the renders.
  5. Test the limits: one long move (does the world hold?), one view of the far background (detail?), and in an interactive model, a return to a place after 60 s (does it stay the same?).
  6. Write the limits that you hit and how you worked around them.

Result checklist

  • [ ] World file or viewer link, and the scale check.
  • [ ] 3 renders and 3 final shots, with lens and move written down.
  • [ ] Limits report with a workaround for each limit.

Self-check quiz

1. What is the main difference between a video model and an interactive world model?

The world model is conditioned on actions at every step. That makes it interactive, and also limits how long it stays coherent.

2. You need the same set in 9 shots with different angles. Which tool fits best?

An exported 3D scene is static and stable. Every render shows the same layout.

3. In an interactive world, you walk away from a fountain and come back after 60 s. The fountain is now a statue. What is this limit called, and how do you plan around it?

Interactive models keep a limited memory. Use them to explore and pitch, not as the source of truth for a set.

4. A generated world looks right, but a chair is as tall as the door. Why does it matter for shots?

Generated worlds can have wrong scale. A reference object fixes your estimate of every distance and lens choice.

5. Why do you add characters with the video model and not in the generated 3D world?

Use each model for its strength: the world for space and camera, the video model for people and motion.

6. Which is a strong use of an interactive world stream in a project?

Interaction sells an idea and helps choose shots. Final shots come from stable sources.

7. The far background of a generated world is blurry. How can you hide it in shots?

Plan around the limit: lens and composition choices, plus the video model's redraw.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Limits report (shape of a strong answer):

Test Result Workaround
Scale Door 2.6 m → scaled to 77 % Scale before planning lenses
Long move (8 s through the room) Seam visible at 5 s on the right wall Shortened to 4 s; cut to a reverse angle
Far background Soft beyond about 6 m 50 mm with shallow depth of field; camera toward the near props
Interactive return after 60 s The fountain became a different shape Used the interactive model only for the scouting video

"The world was the truth for layout and camera. The video model added the people and the dust. In 3 final shots, the window and the broken lamp are in the same places. A text-to-video version of shot 2 put the window on the other side of the room."

C07 · World Models, 3D, and Virtual Production

C07·M03 3D layout for exact camera, and real-time engines

Study time: 20 h · Level 2

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Block out a scene in 3D (a white box) at real scale, with a camera at real focal length and speed.
  2. Calculate the field of view and the frame width from focal length, sensor size, and distance.
  3. Render depth, edge, and clay passes, and use them as control videos for video models.
  4. Use a real-time engine for previs, and explain LED-volume virtual production and where AI fits.

Key words

white box previs virtual production depth control Unreal Engine

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C07, module 03. 3D layout for exact camera, and real-time engines. After this module, you can: 1. Block out a scene in 3D (a white box) at real scale, with a camera at real focal length and speed. 2. Calculate the field of view and the frame width from focal length, sensor size, and distance. 3. Render depth, edge, and clay passes, and use them as control videos for video models. 4. Use a real-time engine for previs, and explain LED-volume virtual production and where AI fits. A white box is a simple 3D block-out of a scene: grey boxes for walls and furniture, simple mannequins for people, all at real scale. With it you control the exact camera path, lens, and timing. Render the white box as depth, edges, or clay shading, and use those renders as the control video of a video model. Then the camera move and the layout are exact, and the model adds the look. Real-time engines do the same job interactively and are the base of LED-volume virtual production.

Learn

The white box

A white box (also: block-out, layout, grey box) is a simple 3D model of a scene. Walls, doors, windows, and furniture are boxes. People are simple mannequins at their real height. Nothing has texture. The white box answers the questions that words cannot: where things stand, how far the camera is, and how the camera moves.

Rules:

  • Real scale in meters. A door is about 2.0 m high and 0.9 m wide. A person is 1.6–1.9 m. A table is 0.75 m high.
  • People face somewhere. Add a marker (a small nose block) that shows the facing direction. This makes eyelines and the 180° rule visible (C02·M04).
  • Start from the top-view plan of the environment sheet (C04·M03).

Camera math

A camera in 3D uses the same optics as a real camera. Two formulas let you plan shots:

horizontal field of view = 2 × atan(sensor width / (2 × focal length))
frame width at distance d = d × sensor width / focal length

On a full-frame sensor (36 mm wide):

Focal length Field of view Frame width at 2.4 m
24 mm 73.7° 3.60 m
35 mm 54.4° 2.47 m
50 mm 39.6° 1.73 m
85 mm 23.9° 1.02 m

So a close-up of a face (about 0.4 m of frame height) at 2.4 m needs a long lens, or the camera must come closer. The white box makes these choices visible before you generate.

Move the camera at real speed. A slow push-in is about 0.1–0.3 m/s. A walking-speed dolly is about 1.2 m/s.

Render passes as control

Render the white box along the camera path as several passes. Each pass is a control signal (C11·M02):

  • Depth: every pixel's distance from the camera, as a grey value (near = white). It fixes the 3D layout and the camera move. It is the strongest layout control.
  • Edges: the outlines of objects, found where depth changes. It fixes shapes and silhouettes.
  • Clay: grey, softly lit shading. Use it as a V2V source at high strength, or as a layout reference.
  • Pose: the skeleton of animated mannequins, for pose control.

Feed the pass as the control video of a video model, with references for the look and the characters. The camera move and the layout then follow the plan exactly. The model adds materials, light, and people.

Thin objects (poles, cables, chair legs) are small in a depth map and easy to lose inside the model, which works at a lower resolution. Make important thin objects thicker in the white box, or add the edge pass.

Real-time engines

A real-time engine renders 3D at interactive speed. It is the standard tool for previs and virtual production. AI fits in at several points:

  • generated textures, skies, and backgrounds;
  • splats from captures (M01) or world generators (M02), imported as sets;
  • previs renders made final-looking with video models (animatics with the final look);
  • generated plates for LED walls.

LED volumes in short

An LED volume is a large curved LED wall (and often a ceiling). The engine shows a 3D world on it. The camera is tracked, and the engine renders the world with the correct perspective for the camera position and lens, so the wall looks like a real place from the camera. The wall also lights the actors. Final pixels are captured in camera. AI speeds up building the worlds for the wall.

Tool walkthrough

A white box from a JSON layout (open, scripted)

starter/tools/whitebox.py builds a room, boxes, and mannequins from a JSON layout, animates a camera with a real lens, and renders depth, edges, and clay videos. It uses Blender's Python module, so it runs without opening Blender:

pip install bpy opencv-python-headless numpy     # bpy needs Python 3.11
python starter/tools/whitebox.py layout.json --out wb/S07/ --res 640x352
# -> wb/S07/depth.mp4, edges.mp4, clay.mp4, first_frame_clay.png

layout.json (meters; z is up):

{"fps": 24, "seconds": 2,
 "room": {"w": 6, "d": 4, "h": 2.7, "door": {"wall": "back", "x": 1.0, "w": 0.9, "h": 2.0},
          "window": {"wall": "left", "y": 1.0, "w": 1.2, "h": 1.0, "sill": 0.9}},
 "boxes": [{"name": "lockers", "pos": [-1.5, 3.5, 0], "size": [2.4, 0.5, 1.9]},
           {"name": "bench", "pos": [0, 1.6, 0], "size": [1.8, 0.4, 0.45]}],
 "people": [{"name": "MARA", "pos": [0.3, 2.2, 0], "height": 1.68, "facing": 180}],
 "camera": {"lens_mm": 35, "sensor_mm": 36,
            "from": {"pos": [0.2, -0.2, 1.5], "look": [0.3, 2.2, 1.4]},
            "to":   {"pos": [0.25, 0.8, 1.5], "look": [0.3, 2.2, 1.5]}}}

Then use depth.mp4 or edges.mp4 as control_video in starter workflow 05_v2v_control_wan22_5b, with a start frame from your references as ref_image.

Blender and Unreal by hand

  • Blender: add a camera (Add → Camera), set the focal length in the camera properties, set two keyframes on its location (press I over the field), and add a Track To constraint to an Empty for the look target. Render the depth pass from the View Layer passes (Z or Mist).
  • Unreal Engine: a Cine Camera Actor with a real lens and sensor; Sequencer for the camera move; Movie Render Queue for passes.

Watch

  • Unreal Engine — virtual production hubLook at the LED-volume and previs case studies.
  • Blender — official getting-started tutorialsDo the navigation and camera animation lessons (about 1 hour).

Worked example

Push-in on Mara in the locker room (2026-10-04). The layout above: a 6 × 4 × 2.7 m room, lockers, a bench, a door, a window, and a 1.68 m mannequin facing the camera. The camera pushes in from 2.4 m to 1.4 m in 2 s, with a 35 mm lens.

  • Frame width at the start: 2.4 × 36 / 35 = 2.47 m (a medium-wide shot). At the end: 1.4 × 36 / 35 = 1.44 m (a medium shot).
  • The speed is 0.5 m/s, a slightly fast push for a quiet moment. For the final shot we used 4 s (0.25 m/s).
  • whitebox.py rendered 48 frames of depth, edges, and clay at 640 × 352 in 25 s on a laptop CPU.

What the passes showed before any generation:

  1. Her head touches the edge of the dark door opening behind her, so the silhouette of her head merges with the door frame. We moved the camera 0.3 m to the left.
  2. The bench is out of frame for the whole move: at 1.5 m camera height, the lower edge of the frame is 0.7–1.1 m above the floor at her distance (vertical field of view 31.6° at this aspect ratio), and the bench top is at 0.45 m. If the story needs the bench (she sits down), lower the camera or start further back.

The depth video then became the control video of workflow 05, with the approved key frame KF-S07-v3 as the reference image.

Lab

Deliverable: C07/M03/ with a layout file, render passes, 2 final shots, a 20 s previs, and a lens plan.

  1. Write the layout of one location of your story at real scale (from your top-view plan). Include the people and their facing.
  2. Plan 2 camera moves. For each, write the focal length, the distance, the frame width (with the formula), and the speed in m/s.
  3. Render depth, edges, and clay for both moves (with whitebox.py, Blender, or Unreal).
  4. Fix what the passes show (merges, objects out of frame, wrong scale), and render again.
  5. Make 2 final shots with a video model controlled by the depth or edge pass.
  6. Make a 20 s previs from the clay renders with temp sound, and use it to approve the timing.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Layout file and lens plan with calculated frame widths.
  • [ ] Render passes, before and after one fix.
  • [ ] 2 controlled shots that match the planned moves (show plan and result side by side).
  • [ ] 20 s previs.

Self-check quiz

1. On a full-frame sensor (36 mm wide), what is the horizontal field of view of a 35 mm lens?

FOV = 2 × atan(36 / (2 × 35)) ≈ 54.4°. An 85 mm lens gives about 23.9°.

2. The camera is 2.4 m from an actress, with a 35 mm lens on a 36 mm sensor. How wide is the frame at her distance?

Frame width = distance × sensor width / focal length. 2.4 × 36 / 35 ≈ 2.47 m. That is a medium-wide shot, not a close-up.

3. Why must a white box be at real scale?

A white box is a measurement tool. Wrong scale gives wrong framing and wrong motion.

4. Which render pass gives a video model the strongest control of layout and camera?

Depth fixes space. Edges fix outlines. A clay render is useful as a V2V source or reference.

5. The video model ignores a thin pole in the depth video. Why, and what do you do?

Control maps are low resolution inside the model. Make important thin objects bigger, or add edges.

6. In an LED volume, why does the camera need tracking?

The LED wall is a window into a 3D world. Without tracking, the parallax is wrong.

7. Where does AI fit into LED-volume virtual production today?

AI makes worlds and previs faster. The volume still captures real actors and real light in camera.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Lens plan (shape of a strong answer):

Shot Lens Distance Frame width Move Speed
S07 push-in 35 mm 2.4 → 1.4 m 2.47 → 1.44 m dolly in 0.25 m/s
S09 profile 85 mm 3.0 m 1.27 m locked —

"The S09 plan showed that 85 mm at 3.0 m gives 1.27 m of frame width: a medium close-up. The room is 4 m deep, so the camera fits. At 50 mm the lockers behind her would be in frame and compete with her face."

Fix log: "Pass v1: her head merged with the edge of the door. Moved the camera 0.3 m left (v2). Pass v1 of S09: the thin coat hooks disappeared in the depth map; made them 3 cm thick and added the edge pass."

The controlled shots match the planned moves within a few frames. The previs shows that S07 needs 4 s, not 2 s, so the shot list was updated before any paid generation.

About this course

The edit is where a video becomes a story. In 2026, agents can do much of the mechanical work: organize, assemble, trim, version, and render. You stay the editor: you decide rhythm, emotion, and story. C08 · Agentic Editing

C08·M01 NLE concepts for engineers

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain media, clips, bins, timelines, tracks, and edits, and the difference between source and record time.
  2. Use timecode and frame rates correctly, and find frame-rate problems before the edit.
  3. Exchange timelines with OpenTimelineIO, EDL, FCPXML, and AAF, and know what each format loses.
  4. Build a timeline from code (selects to timeline), and check a round trip with a diff.
  5. Do a first edit in an NLE - import, cut, trim, J and L cuts, export.

Key words

NLE timeline timecode EDL OpenTimelineIO proxy

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C08, module 01. NLE concepts for engineers. After this module, you can: 1. Explain media, clips, bins, timelines, tracks, and edits, and the difference between source and record time. 2. Use timecode and frame rates correctly, and find frame-rate problems before the edit. 3. Exchange timelines with OpenTimelineIO, EDL, FCPXML, and AAF, and know what each format loses. 4. Build a timeline from code (selects to timeline), and check a round trip with a diff. 5. Do a first edit in an NLE - import, cut, trim, J and L cuts, export. An NLE (non-linear editor) never changes your media files. A timeline is a list of references: each edit points to a part of a media file (source in and out) and places it at a time on a track (record in and out). Timecode addresses frames, so the frame rate must be known and consistent. Timelines move between tools as exchange files: OpenTimelineIO is an open model with a Python API, and adapters write EDL, FCPXML, and other formats. Each format keeps some information and loses some, so check every round trip with a diff.

Learn

Non-linear editing

An NLE never changes your media files. It keeps a project: a database of references and decisions. This is why you can try ten versions of a cut in one afternoon, and why a timeline file is small.

The core objects

  • Media: files on disk (video, audio, images). Never changed by the edit.
  • Clip: a reference to a media file, with metadata: scene, shot, take, tags, notes.
  • Bin: a folder of clips in the project.
  • Timeline (also: sequence): tracks in time. Video tracks stack: V1 is at the bottom, and a higher track covers the tracks below. Audio tracks mix together.
  • Edit: a clip placed on a track. It has two time ranges:
  • source in and out: which part of the media file it uses;
  • record in and out: where it sits on the timeline.

Every exchange format stores these two ranges for each edit. If you understand them, you can build, read, and change timelines in code.

Timecode and frame rate

Timecode HH:MM:SS:FF addresses a frame: hours, minutes, seconds, frames. It means nothing without the frame rate. Common rates: 23.976, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 50, 60. The timeline has one rate.

Generated clips come at many rates: 16, 24, 25, or 30 fps, depending on the model. Find mismatches before you edit, and conform those clips (C09·M04): interpolate frames, or change the speed if the motion allows it. A 25 fps clip on a 24 fps timeline either drops a frame every second (stutter) or plays 4 % slower.

29.97 and 23.976 rates use drop-frame or non-drop-frame timecode. Do not mix them in one project.

Basic edits

  • Cut: one shot ends and the next starts.
  • Trim: move the in or the out point of an edit.
  • Ripple trim: a trim that moves everything after the edit, so no gap appears.
  • Roll: move a cut point between two edits; one gets longer, the other shorter.
  • J-cut and L-cut: the audio and the picture of a cut change at different times. In a J-cut, the sound of the next shot starts first. In an L-cut, the sound of the last shot continues under the next picture. They make dialogue cuts feel natural (C02·M04).

Exchange formats

Format Keeps Loses (typical)
EDL (CMX 3600) One video track: cuts, source and record times, reel names, short comments Other tracks, effects, long names; comments become upper case
FCPXML Tracks, clips, ranges, markers, many effects Some effects between applications
AAF Video and audio tracks between editing and audio systems Depends on the tools
OTIO An open model of tracks, clips, gaps, markers, and metadata, with a Python API Effects are application-specific

OpenTimelineIO (OTIO) is the key tool for engineers. It reads and writes many formats through adapters. You can build a timeline in Python, write it as FCPXML for the editors that read it, or as an EDL for any system.

Round trips and diffs

When a timeline goes to another tool and back, some information can be lost. Check every round trip with a diff: compare the clips, their ranges, their order, and their markers, track by track. The same diff is how you review an agent's changes (M03).

Proxies

Generated masters can be large: 4K, 10-bit, high bitrate. Make proxies: small copies with the same name and timecode (for example 1080p H.264 or ProRes Proxy). Edit with the proxies. Relink to the masters for color and delivery (C09).

Tool walkthrough

Your first edit in DaVinci Resolve (free version)

  1. Project: open the Project Manager → New Project. In Project Settings, set the timeline frame rate (24) and resolution before you import anything. You cannot change the frame rate of a timeline later.
  2. Import: on the Media page, drag your takes into the Media Pool. Make a bin per scene.
  3. Timeline: on the Edit page, right-click in the Media Pool → Timelines → Create New Timeline.
  4. Cut: open a take in the source viewer, set in (I) and out (O), and press F9 (insert) or F10 (overwrite) to put it on the timeline.
  5. Trim: press T for the trim tool; drag the edit points. Press A to return to selection.
  6. J and L cuts: unlink audio from video (the link button, or Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+L), then drag the audio edit point before or after the picture cut.
  7. Export a timeline: File → Export → Timeline (FCPXML, EDL, OTIO, AAF).
  8. Render: on the Deliver page, choose a preset (for example H.264 1080p), add to the queue, render. Other NLEs use the same ideas with other keys. The landscape page lists the current tools.

Build a timeline from selects

pip install opentimelineio otio-cmx3600-adapter otio-fcpx-xml-adapter
python starter/tools/takes.py selects > selects.csv            # from C05·M06
python starter/tools/selects_to_otio.py selects.csv --order shots.json --rate 24 \
  --out S01_rough.otio --edl --fcpxml

shots.json gives the shot order and the planned durations. Shots without a select become labeled gaps (GAP S03), so holes are visible. The script warns about frame-rate mismatches. Import the FCPXML (or OTIO) into your NLE.

Diff two versions

python starter/tools/otio_diff.py S01_rough.otio S01_rough_from_nle.fcpxml

Watch

  • OpenTimelineIO — documentationRead 'Quickstart' and 'Architecture'.
  • Blackmagic — DaVinci Resolve training (free official books and videos)Download the beginner's guide; do the editing chapters (about 3 hours).

Worked example

Selects to timeline, and three round trips (2026-10-04, OTIO 0.18.1). Three selects and a 4-shot order (S03 has no select):

{"timeline": "S01_rough", "shots": 4, "seconds": 10.0, "gaps": ["S03"],
 "files": ["rough.otio", "rough.edl", "rough.fcpxml"]}

The EDL (extract):

001  S01t01mp V     C        00:00:00:00 00:00:03:00 00:00:00:00 00:00:03:00
* FROM CLIP NAME:  S01_t01
* LOC: 00:00:00:00 RED     BEST EYELINE
002  S02t01mp V     C        00:00:00:10 00:00:02:22 00:00:03:00 00:00:05:12
003  S04t01mp V     C        00:00:00:12 00:00:03:12 00:00:07:00 00:00:10:00

Read event 002: source in 00:00:00:10 (the select starts 0.4 s into the file, rounded to frame 10), record in 00:00:03:00. Event 003 starts at 00:00:07:00, after the 1.5 s gap of S03.

otio_diff.py on the round trips:

  • OTIO → EDL: the audio track is gone ("an EDL has one video track only"), and the marker notes changed to upper case ("best eyeline" → "BEST EYELINE"). Cuts and ranges are the same.
  • OTIO → FCPXML: 0 changes.
  • A simulated agent edit (trim S02 by 0.5 s, rename S04, add a marker): the diff lists exactly these 3 changes.

In a second test, the script warned: P01 is 25.000 fps, timeline is 24.0 fps: conform it. The clip came from a source at 25 fps. Without the warning, it would have stuttered in the edit.

Lab

Deliverable: C08/M01/ with your timeline script (or the starter script), the exported timelines, an NLE screenshot, and a round-trip report.

  1. Do the first-edit steps in your NLE with 6 takes: cut, trim, one J-cut, one L-cut, render.
  2. Export your selects from takes.py. Build a timeline with V1 and A1 in shot order, with planned durations.
  3. Export OTIO, FCPXML, and EDL. Import one into your NLE. Take a screenshot.
  4. Change 2 edits in the NLE (a trim and a reorder). Export the timeline. Diff it against the original with otio_diff.py.
  5. Do the EDL round trip. Write what the format lost.
  6. Check the frame rate of every take. Conform any mismatch (or list it for C09).

Result checklist

  • [ ] A rendered first edit with a J-cut and an L-cut.
  • [ ] Timeline built by code; imported in the NLE.
  • [ ] Diff report that shows exactly your 2 changes.
  • [ ] List of what the EDL lost; frame-rate check done.

Self-check quiz

1. You delete a clip from the timeline. What happens to the media file on disk?

An NLE is non-destructive. Edits are references with in and out points.

2. An edit has source in 00:00:01:12 and record in 00:00:10:00 at 24 fps. What do the two times mean?

Source time is inside the media. Record time is on the timeline. Every exchange format stores both.

3. Your selects come from three models at 16, 24, and 25 fps. The timeline is 24 fps. What do you do before you edit?

Mixed frame rates cause stutter, repeated frames, or wrong durations. The starter timeline script warns about each mismatch.

4. You export a timeline as an EDL and import it again. The audio track is gone and the marker notes are now in capital letters. Is the exporter broken?

EDL is old and universal, and it is limited. Know what each format keeps.

5. Why name clips on the timeline by take ID (S07_t04) instead of the file name?

IDs connect the edit to the prompt log and the take log (C05·M06, C16).

6. What is an L-cut?

In a J-cut, the sound of B starts before its picture. In an L-cut, the sound of A continues under B. Both make cuts feel natural (C02·M04).

7. Why edit with proxies?

A proxy is a low-resolution copy with the same timecode and name. Finish from the masters.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Round-trip report (shape of a strong answer):

Round trip Changes found Expected?
OTIO → Resolve (FCPXML) → back trim S04 −8 frames; S06 and S07 swapped Yes: my 2 edits
OTIO → EDL → back audio track missing; notes upper case; long clip names cut to 8 characters in the reel field Known EDL limits
OTIO → FCPXML → back (no edit) none —

"Rule for this project: FCPXML between the script and Resolve; EDL only for a system that needs it, and never as the master."

Frame-rate check: "14 takes at 24 fps, 3 at 16 fps (the open model), 1 at 30 fps. The 16 fps takes go to frame interpolation (C09·M04) before the fine cut. The 30 fps take is a 1 s insert: I slowed it to 24 fps (80 % speed); the motion still looks natural."

The script uses take IDs as clip names, puts the take note into a marker, and makes a labeled gap for every shot without a select.

C08 · Agentic Editing

C08·M02 Transcript-based and script-based assembly

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Edit talking content by editing a transcript, and keep natural pauses.
  2. Assemble a first cut automatically from the shot list and the selects.
  3. Use an LLM for a paper edit of long material, and validate every quote against the transcript.
  4. Judge the machine cut, and improve rhythm, hook, and coverage in the editor's pass.

Key words

paper edit assembly transcript editing rough cut

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C08, module 02. Transcript-based and script-based assembly. After this module, you can: 1. Edit talking content by editing a transcript, and keep natural pauses. 2. Assemble a first cut automatically from the shot list and the selects. 3. Use an LLM for a paper edit of long material, and validate every quote against the transcript. 4. Judge the machine cut, and improve rhythm, hook, and coverage in the editor's pass. In transcript editing, the words are the timeline: delete text and you delete media. In an AI production you also have the script, the shot list, and the selects, so a script can build the first assembly. For long interviews, an LLM can make a paper edit: it chooses and orders quotes for a story. LLMs also invent words and join sentences from different places, so every quote must be found exactly in the transcript before it becomes an edit. The machine cut is a start. The editor's pass makes the rhythm, the hook, and the emotion.

Learn

Transcript editing

A transcript editor shows the words of the media, with each word linked to its time. When you delete text, the editor deletes that media. When you move a sentence, it moves the media. Many NLEs now have a transcript panel, and some tools are built around it.

Rules:

  • Remove fillers ("um", "you know") when they distract. Do not remove all of them; people sound unnatural without them.
  • Keep breaths and short pauses. A cut with no pause sounds rushed.
  • Check every cut by ear. A cut in the middle of a word or a breath is audible.
  • Look at the picture too: a text cut can make a jump cut in the face. Hide it with B-roll or a cutaway.

Script-based assembly

In an AI production you already have:

  • the script and the shot list with shot IDs and planned durations (C03·M02);
  • the selects with in and out points (C05·M06);
  • the native audio, or the replaced dialogue (C05·M04, C06). So a script can build the first assembly in shot order with the planned durations (M01: selects_to_otio.py). The assembly shows the story at once, with gaps where shots are missing. Watch the assembly before you fix any shot. Many problems are story problems, not shot problems: a beat that is not needed, a missing reaction, or an order that hides the turn. Fixing those first saves work on shots that you would cut later.

LLM paper edit

For long material (interviews, conversations, events), a paper edit is a list of quotes in story order. An LLM can make a first paper edit from transcripts in seconds:

  1. Transcribe each file with word timestamps and speakers (C06·M02).
  2. Prompt the LLM with: the story goal, the audience, the target length, the transcripts with file IDs, and strict rules: "quote exactly, never change a word, do not join sentences from different places, return JSON: file, quote, reason".
  3. Validate each quote (below).
  4. Build selects from the valid quotes, then the timeline.
  5. Fill gaps by hand: choose a quote yourself, or ask the LLM again with the reject reasons.

Validation is mandatory

LLMs make three typical errors in paper edits:

  • Invented words: a quote that nobody said.
  • Merged quotes: two sentences from different places joined into one. It changes what the person said.
  • Paraphrase: "picture" instead of "photo". There is no media for the new word.

A validator accepts a quote only if its words are an exact, contiguous sequence in the named transcript (after you ignore case and punctuation). Then the times of the first and the last word give the in and out points. Rejected quotes go back to you with the reason. starter/tools/papercut.py does this and writes a selects file for the timeline script.

When a merged quote is right for the story, make it an edit that viewers can see (a cut to B-roll or a reaction between the two parts), and keep the meaning of what the person said.

The editor's pass

Watch the assembly once without stopping. Note where you lose interest. Then:

  • Pacing: tighten or open pauses; remove repeated ideas.
  • Hook: move the strongest moment into the first seconds if the start is weak.
  • Coverage: add reactions and inserts (C05·M06); they control rhythm.
  • J and L cuts at dialogue cuts (M01).
  • B-roll on words: cut to the image on the word that it illustrates. Use the word timestamps.
  • Music: temp music and the energy curve (C06·M03).

Tool walkthrough

Paper-edit prompt (any LLM)

You are the story editor. Goal: a 90 s brand story for city cyclists: problem → turning point → result.
Use only the transcripts below. Rules:
1. Quote exactly. Never change, add, or remove a word inside a quote.
2. Never join text from different places into one quote. Make two quotes instead.
3. Return JSON only: [{"id": "P01", "file": "<file id>", "quote": "<exact words>", "reason": "<story role>"}]
4. Total spoken length about 100 s (the editor will cut to 90 s).
Transcripts: {"interview_a": "<text>", "interview_b": "<text>"}

Validate and build

python starter/tools/transcribe.py interview_a.mp4 --model small --out tr/        # C06·M02
python starter/tools/papercut.py edit.json --transcripts tr/ --out pc_selects.csv
python starter/tools/selects_to_otio.py pc_selects.csv --rate 24 --out papercut.otio --fcpxml

In the NLE

Import the FCPXML. Put B-roll on V2 above the interview. Use the transcript panel of your NLE for the fine pass, if it has one.

Watch

  • Descript — edit video by editing text (help center)Look at text-based editing and filler-word removal.
  • TechCrunch — Adobe adds its AI assistant to Premiere (first cut, storyboard to video)Note which tasks the assistant does and which remain with the editor.

Worked example

Validator test (2026-10-04). A transcript (faster-whisper, word timestamps) of the line "That's my locker. It is raining in here. I took this photo an hour ago, and now it is real." A paper edit with 4 segments, written like typical LLM output:

ID Quote Validator
P01 "I took this photo an hour ago," Valid: 2.19–4.03 s
P02 "That's my locker. It is raining in here." Valid: 0.00–2.13 s
P03 "It is raining, and now it is real." REJECT: not found as spoken (3 of 8 words match in a row) — a merged quote
P04 "I took this picture an hour ago." REJECT: not found as spoken (3 of 7 words match in a row) — a paraphrase

The two valid segments became selects (with a 0.15 s pad) and a timeline. The timeline script also warned that the clip was 25 fps on a 24 fps timeline.

Brand story: 3 interviews (45 min) → 90 s:

  1. Transcripts with speakers.
  2. LLM paper edit: 11 segments, 104 s; story: problem → turning point → result.
  3. Validation: 2 rejects. Segment 6 merged two sentences from minutes 4 and 31. Segment 9 changed "bike lane" to "cycle path". Both replaced by hand.
  4. Timeline built; B-roll from tagged selects placed on keywords.
  5. Editor's pass: cut to 90 s, added 3 reactions, moved the strongest quote to the opening.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/papercut/ with transcripts, the LLM prompt and output, the validator report, the machine cut, your final cut, and a change list.

  1. Get 20–40 minutes of interview material: record conversations with consent, or use public-domain or CC-licensed interviews (record the license in the rights log).
  2. Transcribe with word timestamps.
  3. Write the paper-edit prompt. Run it. Save the JSON.
  4. Validate with papercut.py (or your own validator). Fix or replace every reject. Build the timeline.
  5. Do your editor's pass in the NLE.
  6. Compare the machine cut and your cut. List 10 changes and the reason for each.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Validator report with at least one reject that you found and fixed.
  • [ ] Machine cut and final cut exported.
  • [ ] 10 changes with reasons.
  • [ ] Rights-log lines for the interview material.

Self-check quiz

1. In a transcript editor you delete all the 'um's and every pause. The result sounds wrong. Why?

Remove fillers that distract. Keep the breaths and pauses that carry rhythm and meaning.

2. An LLM returns the quote 'It is raining, and now it is real.' The speaker said 'It is raining in here.' and, 3 seconds later, '…and now it is real.' What is this, and what does the validator do?

A merged quote changes what the person said. In documentary and brand work this is not acceptable, unless the cut is visible and the meaning is kept. Choose by hand.

3. The LLM writes 'I took this picture an hour ago.' The speaker said 'photo'. Why must you reject it?

A paper edit must point to real words in the media. A paraphrase has no media.

4. What must the LLM paper-edit prompt contain?

Give the goal, the constraints, and the output format. The validator then checks the most dangerous failure: invented words.

5. How do you find the in and out times of a valid quote?

Word timestamps (from transcription, C06·M02) make paper edits exact.

6. A machine assembly from the shot list is coherent but feels flat. What does the editor usually change?

The machine follows the plan. The editor follows the feeling: rhythm and emphasis.

7. Why put B-roll on words, not on fixed time intervals?

Cut to the image when the word is said, or just before it.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Validator summary (shape of a strong answer): "The LLM returned 14 segments. 11 valid. 3 rejects: 1 merged quote (minutes 3 and 22), 1 paraphrase ('started' for 'began'), 1 quote from the wrong file. After a second prompt with the reject reasons, 2 of 3 were replaced by valid quotes; I chose the third by hand."

Change list (extract):

# Change Reason
1 Moved P07 ("I almost quit") to the start The machine cut started with context; the hook was at 40 s
2 Removed P03 It repeats P02
3 Added a 1.5 s reaction after P07 The line needs a beat to land
4 J-cut into P09 (0.4 s) The cut felt abrupt
5 B-roll of the bike lane on the word "lane" Shows what she says
…

"The machine cut was coherent, with even pacing and no reactions. Most of my changes were about rhythm and the hook. The validator caught 3 problems that I would not have heard in a fast review, because the merged quote sounded natural."
