C08 · Agentic Editing

C08·M03 Agents in the NLE through MCP

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Connect an AI assistant to an NLE through MCP, a built-in assistant, a bridge, or your own scripting wrapper.
  2. Delegate organization, conform checks, markers, versions, and renders, with clear permissions per task.
  3. Review every agent session with a timeline diff and a check of the agent's own log.
  4. Write and test repeatable agent recipes for your team.

Key words

MCP agent recipe conform plan-approve-act-review

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C08, module 03. Agents in the NLE through MCP. After this module, you can: 1. Connect an AI assistant to an NLE through MCP, a built-in assistant, a bridge, or your own scripting wrapper. 2. Delegate organization, conform checks, markers, versions, and renders, with clear permissions per task. 3. Review every agent session with a timeline diff and a check of the agent's own log. 4. Write and test repeatable agent recipes for your team. Current NLEs can be operated by AI agents: some have a native MCP server or a built-in assistant, others work through bridges or scripting APIs. Agents are good at mechanical work: organizing bins, renaming, conform checks, markers, cut-downs by rules, and render queues. You keep story, rhythm, performance, music, and approval. Run every session as plan, approve, act, review. Work on a duplicate, ask the agent to log every change, and compare its log with a diff of the timeline before and after. Save tested instructions as recipes.

Learn

How an agent reaches the NLE

An agent is an LLM that can call tools (C03·M04). To edit, it needs tools that read and change the NLE project. There are four ways to give it these tools:

  1. A native MCP server in the NLE: the NLE offers tools (list clips, add markers, rename, render) to any MCP client (C03·M05).
  2. A built-in assistant inside the NLE: the vendor's own agent, with its own set of actions.
  3. A bridge: a separate application that connects MCP clients to one or more NLEs.
  4. Your own MCP server around the NLE's scripting API: you choose a few safe tools and their limits (C12·M03).

Good tasks for agents

Agents are fast and exact at mechanical, rule-based work:

  • Organize: bins by scene, rename clips from metadata, add metadata from the shot list.
  • Markers: shots shorter than N frames, flash frames, gaps, offline media, frame-rate mismatches.
  • Conform checks: frame rate, resolution, and color space of every clip (read-only).
  • Versions by rules: a 15 s cut-down from marked shots of the 30 s; 9:16 timelines (M04).
  • Renders: queue several formats; check delivery specs (C09·M04, C10·M02).

Keep for the editor

Story, rhythm, the choice of performance, the music, and the final approval. These need judgment about feeling and meaning. An agent can propose; you decide.

Plan, approve, act, review

Run every session in this cycle:

  1. Plan: the agent lists the steps it will take. Read them.
  2. Approve: accept, change, or remove steps.
  3. Act: the agent works on a duplicate timeline, never on the original.
  4. Log: the agent writes every change as a structured record (type, clip, old value, new value) and adds a marker at each change.
  5. Review: export the timeline before and after, diff them with code (M01), and compare the diff with the agent's log.

The log check finds two kinds of problems:

  • Unreported changes: the diff shows a change that the log does not mention. These are the dangerous ones.
  • Not done: the log claims a change that the diff does not show. starter/tools/agent_review.py does this comparison.

Permissions

Give each task the least power that it needs, like any API design:

  • A conform check needs read access and markers. It must not move clips.
  • A rename task needs rename only.
  • A render task must not change the timeline. Write the permissions into the recipe. If your MCP server or bridge supports it, give the agent only the tools of that task.

Recipes

A recipe is a tested instruction that your team can reuse. It has:

  • the task, with placeholders (timeline name, frame rate);
  • the allowed actions, and explicit "do not change" rules;
  • the format of the agent's report (JSON);
  • how to check it (the diff and the log check). Test each recipe on two different timelines. If the results differ in kind, the recipe is ambiguous: make it more precise. The starter kit has three recipe templates in templates/recipes/.

Tool walkthrough

Connection options (as of 2026-10)

  • DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.1: native MCP server. Assistants can organize timelines, rename, grade, apply LUTs, add markers, render, and check delivery specs. Works with MCP clients such as Claude Desktop and Claude Code.
  • Adobe Premiere 26.x: Firefly AI Assistant inside the app (bins, renames, markers, first cut, storyboard to video). An MCP server is reported.
  • Bridges: Jumper (local MCP for Premiere, Resolve, Final Cut, Avid), EditAssist.
  • Scripting APIs: Resolve has a Python and Lua API (also in the free version, with limits); Premiere has UXP scripting.

A read-only conform check with the Resolve Python API

This sketch uses the Resolve scripting API (see the README in Resolve's Developer folder). We did not run it for this release, because it needs a Resolve installation. Wrap it as an MCP tool in C12·M03.

import DaVinciResolveScript as dvr
resolve = dvr.scriptapp("Resolve")
project = resolve.GetProjectManager().GetCurrentProject()
tl = project.GetCurrentTimeline()
target_fps = float(project.GetSetting("timelineFrameRate"))
report = []
for item in tl.GetItemListInTrack("video", 1):
    mp = item.GetMediaPoolItem()
    fps = float(mp.GetClipProperty("FPS") or 0)
    if abs(fps - target_fps) > 0.01:
        frame = item.GetStart() - tl.GetStartFrame()
        tl.AddMarker(frame, "Red", f"FPS {fps:g}", item.GetName(), 1)  # frame is relative to the timeline start
        report.append({"type": "markers", "clip": item.GetName(), "problem": f"FPS {fps:g}"})
print(report)

Review a session

python starter/tools/otio_diff.py before.otio after.otio --json diff.json
python starter/tools/agent_review.py --log agent_log.json --diff diff.json

Watch

  • DaVinci Resolve 21.1 MCP — Y.M.CinemaRead the list of actions.
  • Broadcast Now — Adobe rolls out AI agent on PremiereNote which project-panel and timeline tasks it can do.

Worked example

Review test (2026-10-04). A timeline with 3 clips. A simulated agent session renamed S04, trimmed S02, and added a marker on S01. Two agent logs were checked against the measured diff:

Agent log agent_review.py result
Lists all 3 changes MATCH
Lists the rename and the marker, and a relink of S03 that it did not do; forgets the trim UNREPORTED change: trimmed S02_t01; NOT DONE: relinked S03_t01

The second case is the typical failure: the agent did something extra and claimed something it did not do. Only a check against the real timeline finds it.

Session on a 30 s ad (Resolve Studio 21.1 via MCP, with an MCP client):

  1. "Duplicate timeline 'Ad v5' as 'Ad v5 agent'." ✓
  2. Recipe conform-check with fps 24 → 3 clips at 30 fps marked red. Diff: 3 markers only ✓.
  3. Recipe rename-from-metadata → 18 clips renamed; 2 clips without metadata marked "NO METADATA" ✓.
  4. Recipe multi-format-render with "YT_16x9" and "Reels_9x16" → both rendered; the 9:16 file at −12.8 LUFS flagged (target −14 ± 1).
  5. The editor reviews the markers, conforms the 30 fps clips (C09·M04), fixes the mix (C10·M02), and runs the render recipe again.

Lab

Deliverable: C08/M03/ with a session log, before and after timelines, a diff report, an agent_review.py result, and 3 tested recipes.

  1. Connect an agent to your NLE: a native MCP server, a built-in assistant, a bridge, or your own scripting wrapper.
  2. Run a 6-step session on a duplicate of your C05 sequence, with plan and approval for each step.
  3. Ask the agent to log every change as JSON and to add a marker at each change.
  4. Export the timeline before and after. Run otio_diff.py and agent_review.py. Explain every unreported change.
  5. Adapt the 3 recipe templates (conform check, rename, multi-format render) to your NLE. Test each one on two different timelines.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Session log with plan, approvals, and actions.
  • [ ] Diff report and an agent_review.py result (MATCH, or each problem explained).
  • [ ] 3 recipes, each tested twice, with the results.

Self-check quiz

1. Which task do you give to an agent, and which do you keep?

Agents are fast and exact at mechanical checks. Story and feeling are the editor's decisions.

2. Why does the agent work on a duplicate timeline?

A duplicate is the cheapest safety net, safer than undo across many steps.

3. The agent says: 'I renamed 18 clips.' The diff shows 18 renames and 2 trims. What do you do?

Unreported changes are the dangerous ones. A review that compares the log and the diff finds them.

4. What makes a good agent recipe?

A recipe is like a function: inputs, allowed side effects, output, and a test.

5. You test a recipe on a second timeline, and the result is different from the first run. What does this tell you?

A recipe is ready when it gives the same kind of result on different material.

6. Your NLE has no native MCP server. What are your options?

A scripting API plus a small MCP server gives an agent exactly the tools that you choose.

7. Why add markers where the agent changed something?

Markers make the agent's work visible inside the editor's normal workflow.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Review (shape of a strong answer): "Step 5 (rename) also trimmed 2 clips by 1 frame. The agent did not report it. Cause: it used 'replace clip' instead of 'rename' for 2 clips with a long name. Fix: the recipe now says 'Use the rename action only. Never replace a clip.' On the second run: MATCH."

Recipe test table:

Recipe Timeline A Timeline B Same kind of result? Change to the recipe
Conform check 3 markers, 0 other changes 0 markers (all 24 fps), 0 changes Yes —
Rename from metadata 18 renamed, 2 "NO METADATA" 9 renamed Yes —
Multi-format render 2 files, 1 loudness fail 2 files, both pass Yes Added "report, do not fix" after the agent tried to change the mix in run 1

"Agents saved about 25 minutes per version on mechanical work. The review step takes 3 minutes and found one real problem in 6 sessions."

C08 · Agentic Editing

C08·M04 Long-to-short and multi-format versions

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Find the best standalone short moments in long content with transcripts, signals, and an LLM ranking.
  2. Reframe 16:9 to 9:16 with face tracking, and find the shots where tracking fails.
  3. Make cut-downs (60/30/15/6 s) from one master, each with its own hook and ending.
  4. Burn captions in social and sentence styles inside platform safe zones, and deliver SRT and VTT files.

Key words

reframe cut-down safe zone captions highlight detection

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C08, module 04. Long-to-short and multi-format versions. After this module, you can: 1. Find the best standalone short moments in long content with transcripts, signals, and an LLM ranking. 2. Reframe 16:9 to 9:16 with face tracking, and find the shots where tracking fails. 3. Make cut-downs (60/30/15/6 s) from one master, each with its own hook and ending. 4. Burn captions in social and sentence styles inside platform safe zones, and deliver SRT and VTT files. One master edit becomes many versions: shorter cut-downs, other aspect ratios, and clips from long content. A highlight finder uses the transcript and signals to propose moments, and an LLM ranks them by standalone value. Reframing moves a vertical crop window with the main face; it fails on two-shots, fast moves, and text, so the report must list these. For AI shots, a vertical version made natively from the key frame is often better than a crop. Each cut-down needs its own hook and end. Captions must stay inside the safe zones of each platform.

Learn

One master, many versions

Most projects deliver more than one file: a 60 s master, 30, 15, and 6 s cut-downs, vertical and square versions, and short clips from long content. Plan the versions in the edit. Mark which shots belong to which version. Then most of the work can be automated, and the agent recipes of M03 can render and check every file.

Highlights from long content

For podcasts, streams, webinars, and interviews:

  1. Transcribe with word timestamps and speakers (C06·M02).
  2. Signals: audio energy, laughter, speaker changes, and (optionally) a vision model that tags moments.
  3. Candidates: sentences or exchanges of 15–60 s.
  4. Rank with an LLM by standalone value: does the clip make sense without context? Is there a hook in the first 2 s? Does it end on a point, not in the middle of a thought?
  5. Validate the quotes against the transcript (M02) and check the top picks yourself.

Reframe

A vertical crop of a 16:9 frame keeps only 32 % of its width (9:16 of the height). Tracking moves the crop window with the main subject, usually the largest face. Smoothing makes the move calm, with some lag.

Reframing fails in typical places:

  • Two-shots: two people at the left and the right of the frame do not fit in one vertical crop.
  • Fast moves: the crop lags or moves nervously.
  • Text and logos: the crop cuts them off.
  • Composition: a shot composed for 16:9 often has the subject at a third of the frame, with the space on the other side for a reason (eyeline, C02·M01).

So the reframe step must report where it fails. Then the editor decides for each problem shot:

  • cut between two singles instead of a two-shot;
  • set manual crop keyframes;
  • for AI shots: generate a native vertical version from the same key frame and references (C04·M02). This is often the best fix, because the frame is composed for vertical.

Cut-downs

A cut-down is a new edit made from the same material. Each version needs its own hook in the first second or two, and its own ending. Do not cut the end off a long version. A typical plan:

  • 30 s: hook, 3 build shots, payoff.
  • 15 s: hook, the core action, payoff.
  • 6 s: one strong action and the logo or the end line.

Captions

  • Transcribe and correct names and terms (C06·M02).
  • Social style (Reels, TikTok, Shorts): 1–3 words at a time, large, high contrast, near the center. End a caption group at a full stop or comma, so a group does not run across a sentence.
  • Sentence style (YouTube, accessibility): 1–2 lines of up to about 42 characters. Deliver SRT or VTT files too, so the platform can show captions that viewers switch on.
  • Safe zones: vertical platforms cover parts of the frame with their interface: the top, a bottom area with the caption and the buttons, and a column on the right. Keep captions and important picture content out of these areas. The zones differ by platform and change; use each platform's current template.

Tool walkthrough

Reframe with a report

pip install opencv-python numpy
python starter/tools/reframe.py master_16x9.mp4 --out master_9x16.mp4 --aspect 9:16 --smooth 0.85 --report reframe.json

The report lists two_faces_cut_s (time spans where several faces do not fit), face_outside_s (the main face partly outside the crop), and max_speed_px_s. Check each span by eye. Smart reframe features in NLEs do the same job with more options; check the same failure types.

Captions inside safe zones

python starter/tools/captions.py master_9x16.mp4 --transcript tr/master.json --preview zones.png
python starter/tools/captions.py master_9x16.mp4 --transcript tr/master.json --out master_9x16_capt.mp4 --style words --n 3
python starter/tools/captions.py master_16x9.mp4 --transcript tr/master.json --out master_16x9_capt.mp4 --style sentence \
  --top 0.05 --bottom 0.08 --right 0.05

The preview shows the frame with the unsafe areas in red. The default margins (top 14 %, bottom 22 %, right 12 %) are example values. Set them from each platform's current template. The tool also writes .srt and .vtt files, and works with every ffmpeg build (it draws text with Pillow).

Render all versions

Use the multi-format-render recipe (M03) with an agent, or a script that calls ffmpeg for each version and runs the spec checks (C09·M04, C10·M02).

Watch

  • CapCut — help center (long video to shorts, auto-reframe, auto-captions)Look at the auto-reframe and long-to-shorts features.
  • DaVinci Resolve — training (Smart Reframe in the editing guide)Find Smart Reframe in the editing guide.

Worked example

Reframe test (2026-10-04, 1280 × 720 → 404 × 720 crop):

Clip Two faces cut Main face outside Max crop speed
One person moving left to right at 200 px/s none none 216 px/s
Two people, static, at the left and the right 0.00–1.96 s (the whole clip) none 0 px/s

The first version of the tool started the crop at the center and jumped to the face (984 px/s in the first frame). Now it starts on the first face. The two-shot cannot be fixed by tracking: it needs an editorial decision.

Caption test: a 5 s line in 9:16 at 1080 × 1920. The first version of the word grouping made "in here. I" (across a sentence end). With groups that end at punctuation: "That's my locker." | "It is raining" | "in here." | "I took this" | "photo an hour" | "ago," | "and now it" | "is real." — 8 captions, all inside the safe zone.

Master 60 s ad (16:9) → versions:

  • 30 s: hook + 3 build shots + payoff. 15 s: hook + product action + payoff. 6 s: product close-up + logo.
  • 9:16 of each: 7 of 12 shots reframed well; 3 shots (two-shots and a wide with text) regenerated natively vertical from their key frames; 2 shots re-cropped by hand.
  • Captions: word style for Reels and TikTok; sentence style and SRT for YouTube.
  • The multi-format-render recipe rendered 8 files and checked them; 1 loudness fail fixed.

Lab

Deliverable: C08/M04/ with 8 versions from one master, the reframe reports, caption previews, and a review sheet.

  1. Take your best 60 s piece (or edit one from your C05 material).
  2. Plan the 30, 15, and 6 s versions on paper: shots, hook, end. Edit them.
  3. Make 9:16 versions with reframe.py (or your NLE's reframe). Read the reports. Fix each problem shot: singles, manual keyframes, or native vertical generation.
  4. Add captions in two styles. Make a safe-zone preview for each vertical platform that you deliver to.
  5. Render all versions with a recipe or a script, and run the spec checks.
  6. Fill in the review sheet: shot, problem, fix, result.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 8 files rendered and spec-checked.
  • [ ] Reframe reports, with every flagged span reviewed.
  • [ ] Caption previews inside the safe zones; SRT and VTT for the horizontal version.
  • [ ] Review sheet.

Self-check quiz

1. A 16:9 two-shot (two people talking, at the left and the right of the frame) is reframed to 9:16. What happens, and what is the fix?

In the module test, the reframe report flagged the two-shot for its whole length. Two-shots need an editorial decision.

2. Why is a native vertical version often better than a crop for AI shots?

A 9:16 crop of a 16:9 frame keeps only 32 % of its width. A native generation uses the full vertical frame (C04·M02).

3. How do you make the 15 s version of a 30 s ad?

A cut-down is a new edit with the same parts, not a truncation.

4. A highlight finder proposes 20 clips from a 1-hour podcast. How does an LLM rank them usefully?

A short clip must work for a viewer who has seen nothing else. Rank by that, and check the top picks yourself.

5. Why does the reframe report give the maximum crop speed?

Smoothing trades lag for calm. Check the fast parts by eye.

6. Your burned-in captions sit at 85 % of the frame height. On the phone they are behind the app's caption and buttons. What is the rule?

Each platform covers parts of the frame with its interface. Use its current safe-zone template.

7. Social captions show 1–3 words. Why should a caption group end at a full stop or comma?

Group words by meaning: end a caption at punctuation, then start the next one.

Review sheet (shape of a strong answer):

Shot Problem (report) Fix Result
S02 two-shot café two_faces_cut 0–3.2 s Cut to OTS singles S02a/S02b (already in coverage) ✓
S05 wide with the shop sign sign cut off (seen by eye) Native 9:16 from the key frame, sign in the upper third ✓

"Cut-downs: the 15 s needed a new hook (the cold test at 0 s instead of the dawn ride). The 6 s works only with the product close-up and the logo; we cut the dialogue."

The summary names the main rule: "Reframing worked for singles. Every two-shot and every shot with text needed a decision. For the next project, I plan a vertical key frame for those shots in C04."

C09 · AI Finishing: Image

C09·M01 Color science essentials

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain color space, gamut, transfer function, white point, and range, and read them from a file.
  2. Explain bit depth and chroma subsampling, and why 8-bit 4:2:0 sources need a 10-bit intermediate for grading.
  3. Set up a color-managed project for mixed sources (generated, phone HDR, stock), and tag every source.
  4. Tag delivery files correctly, and prove it with a check.
  5. Explain SDR and HDR delivery basics, and when not to deliver HDR.

Key words

color space gamut transfer function bit depth chroma subsampling ACES

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C09, module 01. Color science essentials. After this module, you can: 1. Explain color space, gamut, transfer function, white point, and range, and read them from a file. 2. Explain bit depth and chroma subsampling, and why 8-bit 4:2:0 sources need a 10-bit intermediate for grading. 3. Set up a color-managed project for mixed sources (generated, phone HDR, stock), and tag every source. 4. Tag delivery files correctly, and prove it with a check. 5. Explain SDR and HDR delivery basics, and when not to deliver HDR. A color space has four parts: primaries (which colors exist), white point, transfer function (how values map to light), and encoding (range, bit depth, subsampling). A video file carries tags for them; a missing or wrong tag makes players guess, and a guess changes how the picture looks. Generated clips are usually 8-bit 4:2:0 with Rec.709-like color: fine to watch, weak to grade, so convert them once to a 10-bit intermediate. A color-managed project converts every tagged source into one working space and makes the delivery with one output transform.

Learn

Why color science matters in AI-native video

A film made from generated shots mixes sources from several models, plus phone clips, stock, and graphics. Each source has its own color encoding. If the encodings are not known and managed, the same grade looks different on each shot, and the delivery looks different on each screen. Color science is the set of facts that makes all of this predictable.

The four parts of a color space

  1. Primaries and gamut: the red, green, and blue that the system uses, and so the range of colors it can show. Rec.709 (HD video, sRGB-like) is the smallest common gamut. DCI-P3 is larger. Rec.2020 is larger again.
  2. White point: the color of "white". Video uses D65.
  3. Transfer function: how code values map to light. SDR video uses the Rec.709 / BT.1886 gamma. HDR uses PQ (absolute brightness, up to 10,000 nits) or HLG (relative, compatible with SDR screens). Cameras record log curves to keep more range for grading.
  4. Encoding: how the values are stored. This includes range, bit depth, and chroma subsampling (below).

Range

  • Video (limited) range: luma from 16 to 235 in 8-bit. Values below 16 are "blacker than black", above 235 "whiter than white". This is the normal range for video files.
  • Full range: 0 to 255. Normal for images (JPEG, PNG) and some cameras. When a full-range image becomes video without a range conversion, its blacks and whites fall outside the legal range. Players may clip them, and the image looks harsher.

Bit depth and chroma subsampling

  • 8-bit: 256 steps per channel. A grade stretches the values, and a smooth gradient (a sky, a wall) shows bands.
  • 10-bit: 1,024 steps. The standard for grading and HDR.
  • 4:4:4: full color resolution. 4:2:2: half the horizontal color resolution. 4:2:0: a quarter (half in each direction). Detail is in the luma, so 4:2:0 looks fine, but color keys and strong color grades show the loss. Most generated clips arrive as 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 or H.265: good to watch, weak to grade. Convert each clip once to a 10-bit 4:2:2 intermediate (for example ProRes 422 HQ or DNxHR HQX) before finishing. This adds no detail, but the grade loses less.

File tags

A video file stores tags for the primaries, the transfer, the matrix (how RGB becomes Y′CbCr), and the range. Players use them to show the picture. If a tag is missing, the player guesses, and different players guess differently. Check the tags of every source and every delivery. Tag what you deliver, and prove it with a check (C09·M04).

Color management

A color-managed project works in three steps:

  1. Input: tag each source with its real color space (for example "Rec.709" for most generated clips, "Rec.2100 HLG" for a phone's HDR clips).
  2. Working space: the software converts every source into one large working space (for example a wide-gamut log space, or ACES with ACEScct). You grade there.
  3. Output: one output transform makes the delivery (Rec.709 SDR; HDR if you deliver it). With this setup, shots from different sources start from comparable contrast and color.

Generated sources

Most models output Rec.709-like or sRGB-like 8-bit video. Some report 10-bit or HDR output. Read the model card and tag accordingly. If the card says nothing, test: generate a clip with a known grey and color patch in the prompt, and look at it on the scopes.

HDR basics

HDR10 is Rec.2020 primaries + PQ transfer + 10-bit + static metadata. You can only judge an HDR grade on an HDR reference display. Without one, deliver SDR.

Tool walkthrough

Read the tags and the scopes

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -show_entries \
  stream=pix_fmt,color_range,color_space,color_primaries,color_transfer -of compact clip.mp4
python starter/tools/scopes.py clip.mp4 --at 2.0 --out scopes.png      # waveform, vectorscope, histogram + numbers

Make a 10-bit intermediate

ffmpeg -i gen.mp4 -c:v prores_ks -profile:v 3 -pix_fmt yuv422p10le -c:a pcm_s24le gen_hq.mov

Tag a delivery so that the tags stick

ffmpeg -i master.mov -vf "setparams=color_primaries=bt709:color_trc=bt709:colorspace=bt709:range=tv" \
  -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -ar 48000 web.mp4
python starter/tools/spec_check.py web.mp4 --spec starter/specs/web_1080p.json

Color management in DaVinci Resolve (as of 2026-10)

Project Settings → Color Management: set the color science to "DaVinci YRGB Color Managed", the working space to DaVinci Wide Gamut / Intermediate, and the output to Rec.709 Gamma 2.4 (or Rec.709-A for web viewing on Macs; follow the client spec). Then, in the Media Pool, right-click clips → Input Color Space, and set each source correctly.

Watch

  • Cullen Kelly — color management fundamentals (YouTube channel)Choose one video on color management; note the working space and the output transform.
  • ACES — Academy Color Encoding System (official site)Read the 'What is ACES' introduction.

Worked example

Tagging test (2026-10-04, ffmpeg 9.0.2, an untagged H.264 source):

Method primaries transfer matrix range
Output options -color_primaries bt709 -color_trc bt709 -colorspace bt709 -color_range tv unknown unknown bt709 tv
setparams filter on the frames bt709 bt709 bt709 tv
h264_metadata bitstream filter bt709 bt709 bt709 tv

The output options alone did not tag the primaries and the transfer. spec_check.py found it. Only a check shows this; the picture looks the same on your screen.

Range test: a full-range JPEG portrait put into an H.264 video without a range conversion. scopes.py on one frame: luma minimum 0, maximum 255, 5.1 % of the pixels at or below 16, and 9.9 % at or above 235. A legal web master must keep these within the video range.

Mixed project: 20 generated clips (H.264 8-bit, Rec.709), 6 phone clips (HLG HDR), 4 stock clips (Rec.709 ProRes).

  1. Generated clips to ProRes 422 HQ 10-bit.
  2. Color management: wide-gamut working space; output Rec.709 Gamma 2.4.
  3. Input tags: generated and stock Rec.709; phone Rec.2100 HLG.
  4. Result: the phone clips no longer look washed out; all sources start from comparable contrast.

Lab

Deliverable: C09/M01/ with a source table, scope images, a color-management screenshot, and a tagged delivery with its check.

  1. Collect 10 clips: 6 generated (from at least 2 models), 2 phone clips (one HDR if your phone records HDR), and 2 stock clips.
  2. Read the tags of each with ffprobe. Fill in a source table: codec, bit depth, subsampling, primaries, transfer, matrix, range, and what the model card says.
  3. Make scopes for one frame of each with scopes.py. Note any values outside the video range.
  4. Make 10-bit intermediates of the generated clips.
  5. Set up a color-managed project. Tag each source. Take before and after screenshots of the phone HDR clip.
  6. Export one tagged delivery. Prove the tags with spec_check.py.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Source table for 10 clips.
  • [ ] Scope images with notes on range problems.
  • [ ] Color-management setup with input tags; before/after of the HDR clip.
  • [ ] A delivery that passes the tag checks.

Self-check quiz

1. A file has no color tags. One player shows it with richer blacks than another. Why?

Tags tell the player how to show the values. Tag every delivery, and check the tags (C09·M04).

2. You export with the output options primaries=bt709 and transfer=bt709 from an untagged source, and the check still shows 'unknown' for both. What is a reliable fix in ffmpeg?

In the module test (ffmpeg 9), the output options alone wrote only the matrix and range tags. The setparams filter wrote all four.

3. A JPEG (full range, 0–255) becomes a frame of an H.264 video in video range (16–235) without conversion. What do the scopes show?

In the module test, 5 % of the pixels were at or below 16 and 10 % at or above 235 in the converted frame. Convert the range explicitly.

4. Why convert 8-bit 4:2:0 generated clips to a 10-bit 4:2:2 intermediate before grading?

The intermediate does not add detail, but the grade does not lose more on the way.

5. Your project mixes generated clips (Rec.709), phone clips (HLG HDR), and stock (Rec.709). The phone clips look washed out on the timeline. What is wrong?

HLG shown as Rec.709 looks flat and grey. Color management with the right input tags fixes it.

6. You have no HDR monitor. The client asks for an HDR master. What do you do?

HDR highlights and blacks cannot be judged on an SDR screen. An HDR grade needs an HDR reference display.

7. What does a model card tell you that you need for color management?

Some models output Rec.709-like 8-bit video, some 10-bit or HDR. Read the card; do not assume.

C09 · AI Finishing: Image

C09·M02 Grading with scopes and matching shots

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Read the waveform, the RGB parade, and the vectorscope, and connect each to what you see.
  2. Do a primary correction - levels, white balance, exposure - with scopes, in a fixed order.
  3. Match shots from different models to a hero shot, with a measured color difference before and after.
  4. Build the project look from the look bible as a separate layer, and apply it consistently.
  5. Use secondaries for skin, sky, and brand colors, and check brand colors against their reference values.

Key words

scopes waveform vectorscope shot matching LUT delta E

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C09, module 02. Grading with scopes and matching shots. After this module, you can: 1. Read the waveform, the RGB parade, and the vectorscope, and connect each to what you see. 2. Do a primary correction - levels, white balance, exposure - with scopes, in a fixed order. 3. Match shots from different models to a hero shot, with a measured color difference before and after. 4. Build the project look from the look bible as a separate layer, and apply it consistently. 5. Use secondaries for skin, sky, and brand colors, and check brand colors against their reference values. Grading starts with measurement. The waveform shows brightness across the frame, the parade shows each color channel, and the vectorscope shows hue and saturation. Correct each shot first (levels, white balance, exposure), then match all shots of a scene to a hero shot, then apply one look to all of them. A statistical color match can produce a 3D LUT as a starting point; measure the result on the applied file, and check skin and blacks by eye. Generated shots differ by model in contrast, saturation, sharpness, and grain; remove model looks before you add the project look.

Learn

Scopes

Your eyes adapt to every picture, so they are bad at judging color and brightness alone. Scopes measure:

  • Waveform: the brightness of each column of the frame, from left to right. Low = dark, high = bright. In 8-bit video range, black is near 16 and white near 235 (the scale is often shown as 0–100 %).
  • RGB parade: the waveform for each channel, side by side. A neutral grey or white object has equal levels in R, G, and B. A higher red means a warm cast.
  • Vectorscope: hue as the angle, saturation as the distance from the center. Grey is in the center. Skin of all people sits near the skin-tone line (about the 11 o'clock direction); a skin trace far from it shows a cast.
  • Histogram: how many pixels have each brightness. Pixels piled at the ends are clipped.

Correct each shot

Use a fixed order:

  1. Levels: set the black level (the darkest real black near 16, without crushing large areas) and the white level (below 235).
  2. White balance: find something that should be neutral (a wall, a white shirt, grey concrete). Balance the parade there.
  3. Exposure: set the midtones for the subject. For faces, a common target is skin in the upper middle of the waveform.

Match shots to a hero

In each scene, choose a hero shot: the most important and best-looking shot. Match every other shot to it:

  • the same black level and white level;
  • the same position of skin on the vectorscope;
  • a similar contrast and saturation;
  • the same color of key objects (the raincoat, the product).

A statistical match can give a starting point: it moves the mean and the spread of each channel of the shot (in a perceptual color space, Lab) toward the hero shot. The result can be stored as a 3D LUT (.cube) and loaded in any grading tool. It matches overall balance and contrast. It does not know what is skin or sky. Finish by hand with scopes.

Measure a match

The color difference ΔE (Delta E) is the distance between two colors in Lab. Below about 2, most people do not see a difference between two shots at a cut. Above about 5, a cut shows a jump. Measure on the applied, encoded file, not on the tool's prediction.

The look

The look comes from the look bible (C04·M04): a contrast curve, palette shifts (for example warm highlights and cool shadows), saturation, and texture. Build it as one shared layer (a node, a group, or an adjustment layer) after the per-shot correction and match. Then every shot gets exactly the same look. A LUT can store a look; keep the per-shot corrections outside the LUT.

Secondaries

A secondary adjusts one part of the picture: a color range (qualifier) or a mask. Typical uses:

  • skin (a little less saturation, hue toward the skin line);
  • sky (more blue, less brightness);
  • the product: match its color to the brand value. Measure it: sample the product, compute ΔE against the reference, and stay inside the client's tolerance.

Generated-shot specifics

  • Model looks: some models add their own "cinematic" grade. Neutralize it first.
  • Contrast and saturation differ by model. The correction step removes most of it.
  • Sharpness: match it with a slight blur or sharpening, so shots from different models cut together.
  • Grain: remove the model's grain (or noise) where it differs, then add one project grain to all shots.

Tool walkthrough

Scopes from the command line

python starter/tools/scopes.py S08.mp4 --at 1.5 --out S08_scopes.png

A match LUT

python starter/tools/match_color.py --src S08.mp4 --ref S07_hero.mp4 --out S08_to_S07.cube
ffmpeg -i S08.mp4 -vf lut3d=S08_to_S07.cube -c:v prores_ks -profile:v 3 S08_matched.mov
python starter/tools/match_color.py --src S08_matched.mov --ref S07_hero.mp4 --out check.cube   # read "delta_e_mean_before"

Load the .cube in your grading tool as a starting node, at reduced strength if needed (--strength 0.7).

In DaVinci Resolve (as of 2026-10)

  • Scopes: Workspace → Video Scopes; choose waveform, parade, vectorscope.
  • Per-shot correction in the first nodes; a shared look with a Group (pre-clip and post-clip nodes) or an adjustment clip.
  • Shot match: right-click a clip in the clip strip → Shot Match to This Clip. A LUT: right-click a node → LUT → choose the .cube.

Watch

  • Blackmagic — The Colorist Guide to DaVinci Resolve (free official book)Do the chapters on primaries, scopes, and shot matching.
  • Mixing Light — articles on scopesRead one article on reading the vectorscope.

Worked example

Match test (2026-10-04). A reference shot (a portrait) and a version made warm and dark on purpose (red ×1.12, blue ×0.82, brightness −0.06, contrast 0.85). match_color.py on one frame of each:

"delta_e_mean_before": 14.61,   L mean 43.1 → ref 47.9,  b mean 14.4 → ref 0.6

After applying the 33-point LUT with ffmpeg and encoding to H.264, a new measurement of the matched clip against the reference gave ΔE 0.92. The tool's internal prediction was 0.0; the LUT interpolation and the encode added the rest. 0.92 is below what viewers see at a cut.

One defect: the LUT maps pure black to (0, 0, 0.07), a slight blue lift. Fix: a correction node after the LUT that sets the blacks neutral on the parade.

Scene of 6 shots from 3 models:

  1. Hero: S03 (model A).
  2. S01 (model B): lifted blacks → lower the lift; cyan cast → balance on the parade.
  3. S05 (model C): skin too saturated → −15 %; hue rotated toward the skin line.
  4. Shared look node: warm highlights, cool shadows, 35 mm grain.
  5. Product secondary: the camera body orange measured at ΔE 3.4 from #E8662A → adjusted to ΔE 1.6.

Lab

Deliverable: C09/M02/ with a graded scene of 6–8 shots, before/after scopes, a match table with ΔE values, and the look as a LUT.

  1. Choose a scene with shots from at least 2 models. Choose the hero shot.
  2. Correct each shot in the fixed order. Save scope images before and after for 2 shots.
  3. Match each shot to the hero. Use match_color.py for a starting LUT on at least 2 shots. Measure ΔE on the applied files.
  4. Build the look from your look bible as one shared layer. Export it as a LUT.
  5. Do one skin secondary and one product or key-color secondary. Measure the key color against its reference value.
  6. Export the scene. Watch it at full screen. Note any cut where you still see a jump, and fix it.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Graded scene exported.
  • [ ] Before/after scopes for 2 shots.
  • [ ] Match table with ΔE before and after (measured on the applied files).
  • [ ] Look LUT; key color within tolerance.

Self-check quiz

1. On the RGB parade, a white wall shows red higher than green and blue. What does the shot look like, and what do you adjust?

A neutral object has equal channels. Balance on something that should be neutral.

2. Why do you correct and match before you add the look?

Correct, match, then look. In a layer structure, the look node is shared and comes after the per-shot nodes.

3. A color match moves the mean color difference from ΔE 14.6 to a predicted 0.0. After you apply the LUT and encode, you measure ΔE 0.9. Is something wrong?

Always measure the applied file. A difference below about 2 is hard to see at a cut.

4. The match LUT made the blacks slightly blue. Why can a statistical match do this, and what do you do?

A statistical match is a starting point, not a grade. Finish with scopes.

5. Where does skin sit on the vectorscope?

Skin hue is similar for all people; brightness and saturation differ. A skin trace far off the line shows a color cast.

6. A model added its own 'cinematic' teal-and-orange grade to a shot. What do you do first?

Two looks on top of each other give a third look that you did not design.

7. How do you check that the product orange matches the brand color #E8662A?

Brand colors are numbers. Measure them.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Match table (shape of a strong answer):

Shot Model ΔE to hero before After LUT (strength 0.8) After hand finish Note
S01 B 9.8 2.4 1.1 blacks re-neutralized after the LUT
S02 A 3.1 — 1.3 correction only
S05 C 12.6 3.0 1.7 skin hue rotated 4° by hand
S06 C 11.9 2.7 1.4

"The LUT got each shot most of the way. The hand finish was needed for the blacks (a blue lift at full strength) and for skin. The cut S04 → S05 still showed a jump in sharpness, not in color: model C is softer. I added a slight sharpening to S05 and S06."

Key color: "Raincoat olive in S01–S06: ΔE 1.2–2.1 against the reference value from the character sheet."

C09 · AI Finishing: Image

C09·M03 AI masks, relighting, cleanup, and compositing

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Make AI masks and roto for people and objects, and refine edges (hair, motion blur).
  2. Remove objects and defects from shots, and check edges, shadows, and flicker.
  3. Relight shots with AI, and integrate generated elements into plates (levels, color, light, blur, grain).
  4. Restore exact brand elements - track an area, composite the source pixels back, and grade the patch to the shot.
  5. Measure a fix (sharpness, difference to the source) instead of judging it only by eye.

Key words

roto matte compositing relight planar tracking

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C09, module 03. AI masks, relighting, cleanup, and compositing. After this module, you can: 1. Make AI masks and roto for people and objects, and refine edges (hair, motion blur). 2. Remove objects and defects from shots, and check edges, shadows, and flicker. 3. Relight shots with AI, and integrate generated elements into plates (levels, color, light, blur, grain). 4. Restore exact brand elements - track an area, composite the source pixels back, and grade the patch to the shot. 5. Measure a fix (sharpness, difference to the source) instead of judging it only by eye. AI masks follow a person or an object through a shot from one click, and give a matte for grading, cleanup, or compositing. Video inpainting removes objects and repairs short defects. AI relight changes the light on faces and simple scenes. Compositing joins layers; integration makes them belong together: matching black levels, color, light direction, blur, grain, and shadows. When generation or an AI edit changes an exact element such as a logo, track the area and composite the exact source pixels back, then grade the patch to the shot.

Learn

Mattes and masks

A matte (or alpha) says, for each pixel, how much of a layer is visible: 1 = fully, 0 = not, values between for soft edges (hair, motion blur, smoke). A mask in grading limits a correction to an area. Making a matte frame by frame by hand is called roto (rotoscoping), and it is slow.

AI masks changed this. You click or draw a box on the subject in one frame. A segmentation model finds the object and follows it through the shot. Then you refine:

  1. Check the edges at 100 % in playback, not on a still.
  2. Hair and motion blur: use the tool's edge or detail mode, or soften the edge.
  3. Fix the frames where the mask jumps (occlusions, fast turns) with an extra click on that frame.

Cleanup

Video inpainting removes objects and repairs short defects: a wrong hand for 8 frames, a boom microphone, a sign. The model fills the area from the frames around it and from what it learned. Check:

  • edges of the filled area at 100 %;
  • effects of the removed object: its shadow, its reflection, light it blocked;
  • flicker: the filled area must be stable over time;
  • the measurement: outside the area, nothing may change (clip_diff.py, C05·M05).

Relighting

AI relight tools change the light on faces and simple scenes: add a key from the left, make it warmer, add a rim. Use them to match a shot to its scene or to the look bible. They redraw the frame, so small exact details (text, logos) can soften. Check those areas after each relight.

Compositing and integration

Compositing joins layers: a plate (the background), elements, and mattes. Integration makes the layers belong together. Match, in this order:

  1. Black level and contrast: the darkest areas of the element must not be blacker than the plate's.
  2. Color: the white balance and the color of the light.
  3. Light direction: the bright side of the element faces the plate's light.
  4. Sharpness and motion blur: the same focus and the same blur for the same motion.
  5. Grain: the same grain on all layers.
  6. Atmosphere: haze increases with distance.
  7. Contact: a shadow where the element touches a surface.

Exact brand elements

Generation and AI edits draw plausible shapes, not exact ones. When a logo, a product label, or text must be exact:

  1. Track the area. A point or area tracker follows position. A planar tracker follows position, scale, rotation, and perspective on a flat surface.
  2. Composite the exact pixels: the real logo file (corner-pinned to the track), or the area from the source clip if the source had it right.
  3. Feather the edge of the patch.
  4. Grade the patch to the shot: after a relight, the source pixels have the old light, so match their color to the area around them.
  5. Add the same blur and grain as the shot.
  6. Measure: the difference between the patch area and the source should be near the encode noise (before grading), and the sharpness in the area should match the source.

Tool walkthrough

Restore a soft logo from the source (scripted)

python starter/tools/patch_restore.py --src source.mp4 --edit relit.mp4 --box 226,336,274,384 \
  --out relit_fixed.mp4 --feather 6 --grade

--box is the logo area in the first frame (find it on a still with a grid). The tool tracks the area through the source by template matching, composites the source pixels onto the edit with a feathered edge, and with --grade shifts the patch color to match the edit around it. Both clips must have the same size and length. For perspective moves, use a planar tracker in your compositing tool.

Tools (as of 2026-10)

  • AI masks: DaVinci Resolve Magic Mask, After Effects Roto Brush, Nuke and Fusion AI roto, SAM 2-based tools.
  • Cleanup: Resolve object removal, After Effects content-aware fill, Runway Aleph and other edit models (C05·M05).
  • Relight: Resolve Relight, Aleph relight.
  • Planar tracking and corner pins: Mocha, the Resolve planar tracker, Nuke.

Measure sharpness

import cv2
g = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread("frame.png"), cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)[y0:y1, x0:x1]
print(cv2.Laplacian(g, cv2.CV_64F).var())   # higher = sharper; compare the same area in source and fix

Watch

  • Meta — SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos (GitHub, with demo links)Look at the video demos of masks that follow objects.
  • Foundry — Nuke learning (free tutorials)Do one introduction to compositing tutorial.

Worked example

Logo restore test (2026-10-04). Source: a 4 s clip in which a portrait moves 200 px/s across the frame. "AI edit": the same clip warmed (red ×1.08, blue ×0.9) and softened (blur σ 6), standing in for a relight that softened detail. The task: restore the NASA logo on the suit.

Measurement Result
Track from (226, 336) to (1016, 336) in 96 frames; largest step 10 px per frame; matches the 200 px/s motion
Sharpness in the logo area at 3.5 s, edit 11.9 (Laplacian variance)
Sharpness in the logo area, after restore 1,642.7
Patch vs source, ungraded mean difference 4.5 (encode noise and the feathered edge)

By eye, the ungraded patch was a visibly cooler square on the warm edit. With --grade, the patch took the warmth of the area around it and the square disappeared (its difference to the source rose to 15.9, as expected, because it is now warmer).

Street shot, 5 s: (1) a wrong logo on a bus; (2) a deformed hand in the foreground for 8 frames; (3) the scene must be warmer.

  1. Planar-track the bus side; corner-pin the correct logo file; add motion blur and grain.
  2. AI-mask the hand; inpaint the 8 frames; check 3 times at 100 % in playback.
  3. Relight warmer from the left to match the scene; check the logo again after the relight. Time: about 35 minutes. Regeneration had failed 4 times on the logo.

Lab

Deliverable: C09/M03/ with 3 fixed shots, before/after files, and a fix log with measurements.

  1. Mask and grade: AI-mask a person in one shot. Grade the background separately (darker, cooler). Check the edge in playback.
  2. Cleanup: remove one object or defect from a shot (with its shadow or reflection). Measure the outside area with clip_diff.py.
  3. Integrate: composite one generated element (a bird, a sign, a vehicle) into a plate. Match the 7 integration points. Show the layers before and after integration.
  4. Restore: make an AI relight or restyle of a shot with a logo or text. Restore the exact element (patch_restore.py or a planar track and corner pin). Grade the patch. Measure sharpness and difference.
  5. Write a fix log: shot, problem, method, measurement, time.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 fixed shots with before/after.
  • [ ] Integration shown step by step.
  • [ ] Restore measured: track, sharpness, difference.
  • [ ] Fix log with times.

Self-check quiz

1. An AI mask of a person looks clean on one frame, but the hair edge flickers in playback. What do you do?

Masks are judged in motion. Edges that change from frame to frame show as flicker.

2. After an object removal, the object's shadow is still on the floor. What is the rule?

Viewers notice a shadow without a cause. Removal includes the object's effects on the scene.

3. You composite a generated bird into a real sky plate. It looks pasted on. What do you check, in order?

Integration means matching every property that the camera gave the plate.

4. An AI relight made the shot golden-hour and softened the bottle logo. What is the exact fix?

The relight is good; only the logo needs the exact pixels. In the module test, sharpness in the logo area went from 11.9 to 1,642.7 (Laplacian variance).

5. The restored, ungraded patch shows a visible cool square on a warm relit shot. Why, and what is the fix?

A patch must look like the shot around it, not like the source. Grade it.

6. When do you use a planar tracker instead of a point tracker?

A corner pin on a planar track keeps a logo glued to a surface in perspective.

7. How do you prove that a restored logo is exact?

A number is evidence for a client: the patch matches the source within encode noise.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Fix log (shape of a strong answer):

Shot Problem Method Measurement Time
S04 Background too bright for the night look AI mask on Mara; −0.8 stop and cooler on the background Edge flicker at the hair on 5 frames → edge softened 2 px 12 min
S09 Cyclist in the background Video inpainting + shadow removal clip_diff outside the box: PASS, worst outside mean 1.6 9 min

"The most useful habit was to measure the area outside every fix. The inpaint in S09 was clean by eye but changed 2 % of the frame on the first try; the second try with a smaller mask passed."

C09 · AI Finishing: Image

C09·M04 Upscale, interpolation, repair, delivery, and QC

Study time: 15 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Upscale generated video and check faces, text, textures, and stability over time.
  2. Conform frame rates by interpolation, and measure the motion cadence and the frame count of the result.
  3. Repair typical generated-video artifacts - flicker, warping at the end of a clip, soft frames, black and frozen frames.
  4. Encode deliverables to platform and client specifications with correct tags.
  5. Run automated QC on every deliverable, and fix every failure before delivery.

Key words

upscaling frame interpolation deliverables QC cadence

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C09, module 04. Upscale, interpolation, repair, delivery, and QC. After this module, you can: 1. Upscale generated video and check faces, text, textures, and stability over time. 2. Conform frame rates by interpolation, and measure the motion cadence and the frame count of the result. 3. Repair typical generated-video artifacts - flicker, warping at the end of a clip, soft frames, black and frozen frames. 4. Encode deliverables to platform and client specifications with correct tags. 5. Run automated QC on every deliverable, and fix every failure before delivery. Generated clips often need more resolution, another frame rate, and repairs. Video upscalers add detail and can invent it; check faces, text, and stability. A frame-rate conform by repeated frames makes judder; blending makes ghosts; motion interpolation makes even motion with edge artifacts, and can change the frame count. Measure the cadence and the length after every conform. Encode each delivery to its spec with correct color tags, and run an automated QC on every file: format, color tags, loudness, black and frozen frames.

Learn

Upscaling

Video models often output 720p or 1080p. Deliveries ask for 1080p or 4K. Two kinds of upscalers:

  • Non-generative (for example lanczos scaling, classic super-resolution): sharper enlargement, no new content. Safe for text and faces of real people. Looks softer.
  • Generative / AI video upscalers: add detail with a trained model. Look sharper. They can invent detail: plastic skin, wrong letters, repeated textures, and detail that changes from frame to frame (shimmer).

Rules:

  1. Upscale only the shots that need it.
  2. Check faces, text, repeated textures (brick, leaves), and stability in playback.
  3. Lower the strength when faces look artificial.
  4. Upscale before the final grade, or test both orders on one shot: the upscaler can change contrast and noise.

Frame-rate conform

Generated clips arrive at 16, 24, 25, or 30 fps. The timeline has one rate (C08·M01). Three ways to convert, for example 16 → 24 fps:

  • Repeat frames: some frames are shown twice. The motion stutters (judder).
  • Blend frames: new frames mix their neighbors. The motion is smoother, but moving edges show double images (ghosting).
  • Motion interpolation: new frames are computed from the estimated motion between frames. The motion is even. Artifacts appear at edges, at occlusions (a hand that passes in front of a face), and in fast motion.

Measure after every conform:

  • Cadence: the size of the change between neighbor frames. Even motion has similar steps. Repeated frames show as steps near zero. starter/tools/cadence.py reports the share of repeated frames and the spread of the steps.
  • Frame count and duration: some tools drop or add frames at the start or end. Compare with the timeline.
  • By eye: moving edges for ghosts and warps.

For cinema-style work, keep 24 fps and conform other rates to it. Do not interpolate 24 fps material to 60 fps for a "smooth" look unless the client asks for it.

Repairs for generated video

Artifact Repair
Flicker in texture or light Deflicker or temporal denoise; check that it does not smear motion
Warping at the end of a clip Trim to the clean part; use coverage (C05·M06)
Soft frames in the middle Light sharpening, or replace from neighbor frames
One bad object for a few frames Cleanup (M03)
Black or frozen frames at the end Trim; QC finds them

Encoding deliverables

A delivery spec says the container, codec, size, frame rate, pixel format, color tags, bitrate limits, audio format, and loudness. Examples:

  • Web master: MP4, H.264, 1920 × 1080 (or 3840 × 2160 with H.265), the project frame rate, yuv420p, Rec.709 tags, AAC 48 kHz stereo, about −14 LUFS integrated, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP.
  • Vertical social: 1080 × 1920, the same codecs, the platform's duration limit.
  • Archive: ProRes 422 HQ master and WAV stems (C10·M02). The client's spec always overrides these examples.

Encoding facts for H.264: CRF sets quality (lower = better; 16–20 is high quality for masters, 20–23 for web), and the preset sets speed against compression efficiency. Tag the color with the setparams filter, so that all four tags are written (M01).

Automated QC

Run the same checks on every file, every time:

  • format: container, codec, size, frame rate, pixel format, duration;
  • color tags: primaries, transfer, matrix, range;
  • audio: codec, sample rate, channels, integrated loudness, true peak;
  • picture faults: black frames and frozen pictures. starter/tools/spec_check.py reads a spec JSON and runs all of these with ffprobe and ffmpeg. It prints PASS or FAIL with the fix for each failure. Deliver only files that pass, or document an exception that the client approved.

Tool walkthrough

Conform and measure

ffmpeg -i gen16.mp4 -vf "minterpolate=fps=24:mi_mode=mci:mc_mode=aobmc:me_mode=bidir:vsbmc=1" -c:v prores_ks -profile:v 3 gen24.mov
python starter/tools/cadence.py gen24.mov
ffprobe -v error -count_frames -select_streams v:0 -show_entries stream=nb_read_frames -of csv=p=0 gen24.mov

Dedicated interpolation tools (RIFE-type models, Topaz, Resolve Optical Flow / Speed Warp) usually give fewer artifacts than ffmpeg's minterpolate. Use the same measurements for all of them.

Encode and check

ffmpeg -i master.mov -vf "setparams=color_primaries=bt709:color_trc=bt709:colorspace=bt709:range=tv" \
  -c:v libx264 -preset slow -crf 18 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 web_1080p.mp4
python starter/tools/spec_check.py web_1080p.mp4 --spec starter/specs/web_1080p.json --json qc_web.json

The starter specs (web_1080p.json, reels_9x16.json, broadcast_ebu_r128.json) are examples. Copy one and change it to the client's spec.

Watch

  • Topaz Labs — video upscaling and frame interpolation (docs)Read the model descriptions for upscaling and interpolation.
  • FFmpeg — H.264 encoding guide (trac wiki)Read the CRF and preset sections.

Worked example

Conform test (2026-10-04). A 24 fps clip with even motion (a portrait moving at 200 px/s) was reduced to 16 fps (as a stand-in for a 16 fps model output), then conformed back to 24 fps in 3 ways:

Clip Repeated frames Step spread (lower = more even) Frames
Original 24 fps 0 % 0.07 96
16 fps source 0 % 0.22 (uneven: made by dropping frames) 64
16 → 24, repeat frames 33.7 % 0.76 96
16 → 24, blend frames 0 % 0.22 96
16 → 24, motion interpolation (minterpolate, mci) 0 % 0.19 94

Repeating frames gave the clear judder pattern. Blending looked even in the numbers but showed ghosts by eye. Motion interpolation gave the most even motion, and it lost 2 frames: the clip became 83 ms shorter. Pad or trim it to the timeline length before you replace the shot.

QC test with spec_check.py and the web spec:

  • An untagged export with a mix at −16.2 LUFS: FAIL on 4 color tags and loudness ("adjust the mix by +2.2 LU").
  • The same export tagged with setparams and normalized: PASS, 19 of 19 checks.
  • A file with 1 s of black at 4 s and a frozen 2 s tail: FAIL on black frames (4.00–5.04 s) and frozen picture (4.00 s for 1.04 s; 5.21 s for 2.04 s).

Lab

Deliverable: C09/M04/ with the conformed and repaired shots, cadence reports, the deliverables, the QC reports, and a delivery log.

  1. Take 3 clips at a frame rate other than your timeline's. Conform each in 2 ways. Run cadence.py and check the frame count. Choose a method per clip, with a reason.
  2. Upscale 2 hero shots. Compare a generative and a non-generative method on faces and text at 200 % zoom.
  3. Repair 2 artifacts (flicker, a warp at the end, a soft frame).
  4. Write the spec JSON for 3 deliverables (a web master, a vertical social version, and one spec of your choice).
  5. Encode the 3 deliverables from your C09 timeline. Run spec_check.py on each. Fix every failure and run it again.
  6. Write the delivery log: file, spec, QC result, fixes, date.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Cadence reports and frame counts for 3 conformed clips; a method chosen for each.
  • [ ] Upscale comparison with notes.
  • [ ] 3 deliverables that pass QC (reports saved).
  • [ ] Delivery log.

Self-check quiz

1. A 16 fps generated clip is conformed to 24 fps by repeating frames. What do viewers see, and what does a cadence check show?

In the module test: 33.7 % repeated frames and an uneven step size (spread 0.76, against 0.07 for native 24 fps).

2. Frame blending gives 0 % repeated frames. Why is it still a weak conform for motion?

Numbers and eyes check different things. Look at moving edges in playback.

3. After motion interpolation, the clip has 94 frames instead of 96. Why does it matter?

Conform tools can drop or add frames at the start or end. Check the length against the timeline.

4. A generative upscaler makes a face look like plastic. What do you change?

Generative upscalers draw new detail. On faces, too much looks artificial.

5. QC reports a 1.5 s frozen picture at the end of a clip. What is the typical cause in AI-native work?

Generated clips sometimes end with frozen or black frames. QC finds them before the client does.

6. Your QC passes 17 of 19 checks on a delivery. What do you do?

A spec is a contract. Every failure is fixed or approved in writing.

7. Why upscale before the final grade (or test both orders)?

Finish in an order where each step can correct the step before. Test on one shot.

Go deeper

  • FFmpeg filters — ebur128, blackdetect, freezedetect, minterpolate
  • EBU R 128 — loudness normalization and permitted maximum level (EBU tech page)

Program · Level 3

C10 AI Finishing: Sound

40 h · Prerequisites: C06

M01M02

About this course

A good mix makes generated video feel real. This course takes your dialogue, effects, ambience, and music from C06 and finishes them. Tools: Fairlight (in Resolve), Pro Tools, Reaper, Audition; iZotope RX; ffmpeg ebur128 for checks.

Starter tools for this course (in the starter kit):

Tool Use
tools/roomtone.py Fills dropouts in dialogue with room tone; refuses TTS "tone" that is really speech (M01)
tools/stems.py, tools/loop_audio.py Voice/background separation and seamless ambience loops (from C06)
tools/normalize.py Two-pass loudness normalization to a target, with a before/after report (M02)
tools/null_test.py Proves that stems add up to the mix; tells latency from mix-bus processing (M02)
tools/spec_check.py Loudness and true peak in the delivery QC (M02)

Course outcomes

  1. Edit and clean dialogue, and build sound design from generated and recorded elements.
  2. Mix to platform loudness targets with correct peak levels.
  3. Deliver stems, M&E mixes, and captions to specification.

Modules

  1. C10·M01 Dialogue edit and sound design 14 h

C10 · AI Finishing: Sound

C10·M01 Dialogue edit and sound design

Study time: 14 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Set up a standard session layout with dialogue, music, and effects tracks routed to buses that become stems.
  2. Edit dialogue - clicks, breaths, joins, level matching - and fill dropouts with room tone.
  3. Build four layers of sound design - ambience, Foley, hard effects, and design.
  4. Make shots from different generations sound like one space, with one ambience and one reverb.
  5. Use a DAW for the first time - import, edit, fade, route, automate, bounce.

Key words

dialogue edit room tone Foley sound design bus

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C10, module 01. Dialogue edit and sound design. After this module, you can: 1. Set up a standard session layout with dialogue, music, and effects tracks routed to buses that become stems. 2. Edit dialogue - clicks, breaths, joins, level matching - and fill dropouts with room tone. 3. Build four layers of sound design - ambience, Foley, hard effects, and design. 4. Make shots from different generations sound like one space, with one ambience and one reverb. 5. Use a DAW for the first time - import, edit, fade, route, automate, bounce. Sound finishing starts with order: one session layout, with dialogue (DX), music (MX), and effects (FX) on their own tracks and buses, because the buses become the stems. The dialogue edit removes distractions, smooths joins, matches levels, and fills every dropout with room tone. Sound design adds four layers: ambience for the space, Foley for human actions, hard effects, and design sounds for emotion. Generated shots each bring their own room sound; one ambience bed and one reverb make them one place.

Learn

Why sound finishing

Viewers forgive a weak image sooner than weak sound. In AI-native work, the sound comes from many sources: native audio of several generations, TTS or cloned voices, generated music and effects, and some recordings. Each has its own level, tone, and room. Sound finishing makes them one soundtrack.

The session layout

Use the same layout in every project:

  • DX: one track per character, plus a room-tone track.
  • FX: tracks for ambience, Foley, hard effects, and design sounds.
  • MX: music cues.
  • Buses: route all DX tracks to a DX bus, all FX tracks to an FX bus, all MX tracks to an MX bus. A bus is a submix: one fader and one set of processing for a group.
  • Mix bus: the three buses meet here. The DX, FX, and MX buses become the stems of the delivery (M02). Plan them from the start.

The dialogue edit

Goals: clear words, no distractions, and joins that nobody hears.

  • Clicks and mouth noise: remove them (a short cut or a de-click tool).
  • Breaths: remove loud or distracting breaths; keep the others. A voice with no breaths sounds machine-made.
  • Joins: short crossfades (5–20 ms) at every cut, so there are no clicks.
  • Levels: match the level of lines and takes, so the voice does not jump.
  • Tone and space: a generated line next to a recorded line often sounds brighter or closer. Match the EQ and the space.
  • Noise: clean only as much as needed (C06·M04).

Room tone

Every place has a sound: air, a fridge, distant traffic. This is room tone. When you cut dialogue, the room tone stops and starts with the cuts, and digital silence between lines sounds like a hole. Fill every gap with room tone, with short crossfades.

Generated and synthetic sources make this more important:

  • TTS and cloned voices have no room tone at all, only speech and digital silence.
  • Native audio of each generated shot has its own, different room tone. Get room tone from a recording of a real, similar place (30 s), from the quietest part of a native-audio clip of the scene, or from a generated ambience (C06·M04).

Four layers of sound design

  1. Ambience: the space and the time (night city, a hospital air system, rain on the window). It runs under the whole scene.
  2. Foley: human actions to picture: steps, cloth, hands, props. Generated clips often lack Foley or have weak Foley.
  3. Hard effects: distinct events: doors, lockers, cars, impacts.
  4. Design: sounds for emotion and transitions: whooshes, risers, low hits, tonal beds. Generate the missing layers (C06·M04), and keep their IDs in the sound library.

One space

Generated shots each carry their own reverb and background. Make them one place:

  1. Separate the dialogue from the native audio (stems, C05·M04), and reduce the native reverb if needed.
  2. Put one continuous ambience bed under the whole scene, across the cuts. Crossfade it slowly at scene changes.
  3. Send all dialogue of the scene to one reverb that fits the place (for example a small room, 0.6 s).
  4. Use J and L cuts for the ambience at scene changes (C02·M04): let the next place's sound start a little before its picture.

Tool walkthrough

Your first session in a DAW (DaVinci Resolve Fairlight, free)

  1. On the Fairlight page, import the picture (the edited timeline is already there if you edited in Resolve).
  2. Tracks: add tracks (right-click the track headers → Add Track): DX_MARA, DX_LEO, DX_ROOM, FX_AMB, FX_FOLEY, FX_HARD, FX_DESIGN, MX.
  3. Buses: in the Fairlight menu, open the bus setup (Bus Format in older versions); create DX, FX, and MX submix buses. Route each track to its bus in the mixer.
  4. Edit: cut clips with the blade (razor) tool; add fades by dragging the fade handles at the clip corners; crossfade by overlapping clips.
  5. Automation: turn on automation (the automation toolbar), choose "Volume", and draw level changes on the track.
  6. Bounce: Deliver page → Audio Only, or render stems with "Render each track / bus". Other DAWs (Pro Tools, Reaper, Logic) use the same ideas.

Fill dropouts with room tone (scripted)

python starter/tools/roomtone.py dx_mara.wav --tone room_tone.wav --out dx_mara_filled.wav

The tool finds stretches below −70 dBFS longer than 50 ms, fills them with looped room tone, and crossfades the joins. With --auto-tone it takes tone from the quietest non-silent part of the file, and it refuses if that part is speech (as in TTS files).

Generated Foley and effects

Use the five prompt parts of C06·M04 (source, action, material, space, distance). Place each effect on its frame: the sound starts on the frame of the contact.

Watch

  • Blackmagic — DaVinci Resolve training (Fairlight audio chapters)Do the Fairlight chapter on dialogue editing.
  • SoundWorks Collection — interviews with film sound designersWatch one sound-design interview. Note how sounds are layered.

Worked example

Room tone test (2026-10-04). Three TTS lines joined with digital silence (0.8 s, 1.1 s, 0.6 s gaps). Room tone: 5 s of pink noise at −62.5 dBFS (a stand-in for a quiet room).

roomtone.py dx_raw.wav --tone tone.wav   → {"gaps_found": 3, "gap_seconds": 2.55, "tone_level_dbfs": -62.5, "gaps_after": 0}
roomtone.py dx_raw.wav --auto-tone       → no room tone found: the quietest non-silent second is -15.0 dBFS (speech)

The second result is the lesson: a TTS file contains no room. The room must come from somewhere else.

Café scene, 6 generated shots with native audio:

  1. Separate the voice from each clip; light de-reverb on 2 clips that sounded like a hall.
  2. One café ambience bed for the whole scene (a generated 90 s loop, checked with loop_audio.py).
  3. Foley: cups and saucers generated and placed on the hand actions.
  4. One small room reverb (0.6 s) on both voices.
  5. Room tone from the quietest 2 s of shot 3, under all dialogue joins. Result: the 6 clips sound like one café.

Lab

Deliverable: C10/M01/ with a sound-designed scene (45–60 s), the session file, and a short sound report.

  1. Set up the standard layout with DX, FX, and MX buses.
  2. Edit the dialogue: clicks, distracting breaths, joins, levels. Fill every gap with room tone (roomtone.py or by hand).
  3. Build the 4 layers of sound design. Place Foley and hard effects on their frames.
  4. Unify the space: one ambience bed across the cuts and one dialogue reverb.
  5. Automate levels where needed (ambience under dialogue).
  6. Bounce a rough mix and the three bus stems (the final mix is in M02).
  7. Write the sound report: sources, what you generated, what you fixed.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Standard track layout with three buses.
  • [ ] No clicks, no dropouts, smooth joins (listen on headphones).
  • [ ] Four layers present; effects on their frames.
  • [ ] The scene sounds like one space.

Self-check quiz

1. Three TTS lines are joined with digital silence between them. On headphones the room 'disappears' at each gap. What is the fix?

Every place has a sound. Digital silence sounds like a hole. In the module test, 3 gaps (2.55 s) were filled and none were left.

2. The tool cannot find room tone in a TTS file: the quietest non-silent second is speech at −15 dBFS. Why?

Synthetic voices are 'dry'. You add the room in the mix.

3. Why route all dialogue tracks to one DX bus, all effects to an FX bus, and music to an MX bus?

Plan the stems at the start of the session, not at the end.

4. What is Foley?

Foley makes hands and bodies feel real. Generated clips often lack it or have weak versions of it.

5. Six generated shots each have their own reverb and background noise. The scene sounds like six places. What do you do?

One ambience and one reverb make one place. Crossfade the ambience across cuts.

6. You removed all breaths from a dialogue track. It sounds wrong. Why?

Edit for distraction, not for perfection.

7. A generated line sounds brighter and closer than the recorded lines around it. What do you match?

Lines match when level, tone, and space match.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong session is labeled and colored by group (DX blue, FX green, MX purple), and every track goes to its bus.

Sound report (shape of a strong answer):

Element Source Treatment
Mara dialogue Native audio of S03, S07; TTS in S09 (fixed voice) Stems; S09 TTS EQ'd darker (−3 dB at 6 kHz) and sent to the room reverb to match S07
Room tone Quietest 2.4 s of S07 native audio Filled 11 gaps
Ambience Generated "hospital night, air system, distant monitor" 90 s loop Loop checked: SEAMLESS
Foley Generated cloth and locker sounds; 2 recorded (photo paper) Placed on contact frames
Hard effects Generated locker door Layered with native click for timing
Design Low rumble on the turn (S11) Automated in over 2 s

"The TTS line in S09 was the most obvious problem: it was dry and bright next to the native lines. EQ, the room reverb, and room tone under it made it sit in the same room."

Go deeper

  • Holman — Sound for Film and Television (book)
  • FFmpeg filters — audio filters (afade, acrossfade, sidechaincompress)
