C10 · AI Finishing: Sound

C10·M02 Mix, loudness, and audio deliverables

Study time: 26 h · Level 3

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Mix with clear priorities - dialogue first - using EQ, compression, ducking, and panning, and check on several playback systems.
  2. Measure loudness (integrated LUFS, loudness range, true peak) and normalize to a target in two passes.
  3. Tune ducking with measurements - how much the music falls under speech and in pauses.
  4. Deliver a full mix, stems, and an M&E track, and prove with a null test that the stems add up to the mix.
  5. Add loudness and stem checks to automated QC.

Key words

LUFS true peak stem M&E null test ducking

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C10, module 02. Mix, loudness, and audio deliverables. After this module, you can: 1. Mix with clear priorities - dialogue first - using EQ, compression, ducking, and panning, and check on several playback systems. 2. Measure loudness (integrated LUFS, loudness range, true peak) and normalize to a target in two passes. 3. Tune ducking with measurements - how much the music falls under speech and in pauses. 4. Deliver a full mix, stems, and an M&E track, and prove with a null test that the stems add up to the mix. 5. Add loudness and stem checks to automated QC. A mix has one priority: the words are clear at all times; effects support the action, and music supports the emotion under the speech. Loudness is measured in LUFS over the whole program, plus the true peak. Platforms and broadcasters set targets, for example about −14 LUFS for streaming platforms and −23 LUFS for European broadcast, both with a true-peak maximum of about −1 dBTP. Normalize in two passes so one gain keeps the dynamics. Deliver the mix with stems and an M&E, and prove with a null test that the stems add up to the mix.

Learn

Mix priorities

  1. Dialogue is clear at all times.
  2. Effects support the action.
  3. Music supports the emotion, under the speech. Work at a fixed, calibrated listening level, so your sense of loudness stays the same. Check the mix on headphones, laptop speakers, and a phone. A phone speaker has almost no bass and shows whether the words are still clear.

Techniques

  • EQ: remove low rumble from dialogue (a high-pass filter at about 80 Hz). Make space for speech in the music (a small cut around 1–4 kHz under speech).
  • Compression: evens out the dialogue level, so quiet words are heard and loud words do not jump out.
  • Ducking (sidechain compression): the music falls when someone speaks. A compressor on the music listens to the dialogue (the sidechain) and lowers the music by a few dB. A good target is 6–10 dB under speech and almost no change in pauses. Too much ducking sounds like the music switches off.
  • Automation: draw level changes by hand where a rule does not work.
  • Panning: dialogue in the center; ambience wide; effects where their source is on screen.

Loudness

Loudness is perceived level. It is measured in LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale) with a standard method (ITU-R BS.1770) that weights frequencies like the ear and ignores silence.

  • Integrated loudness: over the whole program. This is the number that specs set.
  • Loudness range (LRA): how much the loudness changes in the program. Large values mean quiet parts are very quiet.
  • True peak (dBTP): the highest level of the reconstructed signal, including peaks between samples. Specs set a maximum (often −1 dBTP), because encoders and converters can clip above it.

Targets depend on the delivery (the diagram shows examples). Streaming platforms normalize to about −14 LUFS: a louder mix is turned down, a quieter one may be turned up. Broadcasters set strict values (−23 LUFS ± 0.5 LU in EBU R128). The client's spec decides.

Normalize in two passes

  1. Measure the program: integrated loudness, LRA, true peak.
  2. Apply one gain (linear mode) that moves the integrated loudness to the target. The dynamics stay the same.
  3. Measure again. If one gain would push the true peak over the limit, the normalizer must change the dynamics (dynamic mode). Better: put a true-peak limiter at the end of the mix bus, so the peaks are under control, and normalize again.

Deliverables

  • Full mix: stereo, and 5.1 or Atmos if the spec asks for it.
  • Stems: DX, MX, FX (and AMB or Foley if asked). Each full length, from the same start point.
  • M&E: music and effects with no dialogue, complete. If an effect was only in a dialogue recording (steps, a door in the native audio), re-create it on the effects, or the dubbed version loses it.
  • Captions: SRT or VTT (C08·M04).

Null test

Stems must add up to the mix. Sum the stems, subtract the mix, and measure what is left (the residual):

  • below about −60 dB relative to the mix: the stems null;
  • otherwise something differs. Two typical causes:
  • latency: the mix is shifted by a few milliseconds (a look-ahead limiter or a plugin without delay compensation). After alignment, the residual disappears;
  • mix-bus processing that is not on the stems (a limiter, a compressor, an EQ on the mix bus). After alignment, a residual remains. Print the stems through the same processing, or deliver the mix without it.

Automate the checks

Add loudness and true peak to the delivery spec (spec_check.py, C09·M04), and run the null test on every stem delivery. Fail the delivery if a check fails.

Tool walkthrough

Measure

ffmpeg -i mix.wav -af ebur128=peak=true -f null - 2>&1 | grep -E "I:|LRA:|Peak:"

Normalize in two passes

python starter/tools/normalize.py mix.wav --target -14 --tp -1 --out mix_web.wav
python starter/tools/normalize.py mix.wav --target -23 --tp -1 --out mix_broadcast.wav

Ducking with ffmpeg (or a sidechain compressor in your DAW)

ffmpeg -i music.wav -i dialogue.wav -filter_complex \
  "[0][1]sidechaincompress=threshold=0.05:ratio=3:attack=20:release=300:makeup=1[m]" -map "[m]" music_ducked.wav

In a DAW: put a compressor on the MX bus, set its sidechain input to the DX bus, and adjust the threshold and ratio while you watch the gain reduction meter.

Null test

python starter/tools/null_test.py --mix mix.wav --stems DX.wav MX.wav FX.wav

Watch

  • EBU R 128 — loudness recommendation (official page)Read the summary page.
  • Netflix — sound mix specifications (Partner Help Center)Search for 'sound mix specifications'; note the dialogue-gated measurement.

Worked example

Normalization test (2026-10-04, a 5.8 s mix of TTS dialogue, a music bed, and effects):

Integrated LRA True peak Mode
Before −16.6 LUFS 1.8 LU −5.2 dBTP —
Target −14 −13.9 LUFS 1.8 LU −2.5 dBTP linear
Target −23 −22.9 LUFS 1.8 LU −11.5 dBTP linear

Both results are within 0.1 LU of the target, and the loudness range did not change: one gain, no change to the dynamics.

Ducking test (the music bed under the same dialogue; the change in music level, measured in 50 ms blocks):

Sidechain settings Under speech In pauses
threshold 0.02, ratio 8 −18.1 dB −2.0 dB
threshold 0.05, ratio 4 −9.7 dB −0.4 dB
threshold 0.05, ratio 3 −8.6 dB −0.3 dB
threshold 0.1, ratio 2.5 −4.2 dB 0.0 dB

The first setting is too strong: the music almost switches off and does not fully recover in short pauses. Threshold 0.05 with ratio 3 is in the target range.

Null tests (stems DX, MX, FX and mixes made from them):

Mix Residual After alignment Diagnosis
Plain sum of the stems −219.4 dB — PASS
Sum delayed by 5 ms +0.7 dB −219.5 dB (offset 240 samples) latency
Sum through a look-ahead limiter −0.7 dB −5.9 dB mix-bus processing

Lab

Deliverable: C10/M02/ with the final mix in two loudness versions, the stems, an M&E, captions, a loudness report, a ducking table, a null-test report, and QC results.

  1. Mix your scene from M01 (or your best piece). Check it on headphones, laptop speakers, and a phone. Write what you changed after each check.
  2. Tune the ducking of the music under dialogue. Measure the music level under speech and in pauses for 3 settings. Choose one.
  3. Make a web version at −14 LUFS ± 1, true peak ≤ −1 dBTP, and a broadcast version at −23 LUFS ± 0.5. Use two-pass normalization.
  4. Bounce the DX, MX, and FX stems and an M&E. Check the dialogue stem for effects that must move to the M&E.
  5. Run the null test. Fix any residual (latency or mix-bus processing) until it passes.
  6. Make captions (SRT) and check them.
  7. Add loudness to your delivery spec and run spec_check.py on the final video.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Two loudness versions within tolerance (reports saved).
  • [ ] Ducking table with 3 settings and the choice.
  • [ ] Stems null with the mix (report saved); M&E complete.
  • [ ] QC passes on the final video.

Self-check quiz

1. What is the first priority of a mix?

If viewers cannot understand the words, nothing else works. Effects and music fit around the dialogue.

2. Integrated loudness is −16.6 LUFS; the target is −14. Why is a two-pass normalization better than a limiter that pushes it up?

In the module test, two-pass linear normalization moved −16.6 to −13.9 LUFS with the loudness range unchanged (1.8 LU).

3. Ducking lowers the music by 18 dB under speech. The mix feels like the music switches off. What do you change?

In the module test, threshold 0.02 / ratio 8 gave −18 dB; threshold 0.05 / ratio 3 gave −8.6 dB under speech and −0.3 dB in pauses.

4. What is an M&E track?

Effects that were only in the dialogue recording (steps, a door) must be added to the effects, or the dub loses them.

5. The stems do not null with the mix: residual −0.7 dB; after aligning by 240 samples it is still −5.9 dB. What is the cause?

An offset alone would null after alignment. A residual after alignment means the mix has processing that the stems do not.

6. The null test reports an offset of 240 samples and −219 dB after alignment. What happened?

A look-ahead limiter or a plugin added latency. Turn on delay compensation, or shift the mix.

7. Why check the mix on headphones, laptop speakers, and a phone?

A mix that works on a phone speaker works almost everywhere.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Report (shape of a strong answer):

"Playback checks: on the phone, the music hid Mara's whisper in S07 → music −2 dB in that scene and a 2 dB cut at 2.5 kHz in the MX bus under speech. On the laptop, the low rumble in S11 disappeared, which is fine: it is a design layer."

Check Web Broadcast
Integrated −14.1 LUFS −23.0 LUFS
True peak −1.6 dBTP −9.8 dBTP
LRA 6.2 LU 6.2 LU
Normalization linear linear

"Ducking: threshold 0.05 / ratio 3 → −8.4 dB under speech, −0.5 dB in pauses."

"Null test, first run: residual −0.8 dB, offset 240 samples, −6.1 dB after alignment. Cause: the limiter on the mix bus. Fix: limiter removed from the mix bus; a true-peak limiter on each stem bus instead. Second run: −74 dB, PASS."

"M&E: 2 effects were only in the native dialogue (the locker click in S03, steps in S09). Re-created on FX from the sound library. The M&E plays the whole scene with no gaps."

"QC: spec_check.py on the web video: PASS 19/19."

Go deeper

  • ITU-R BS.1770 — loudness measurement algorithm
  • FFmpeg loudnorm filter (two-pass normalization)
  • ATSC A/85 — techniques for establishing and maintaining audio loudness

Program · Level 4

C11 Node Pipelines (ComfyUI)

60 h · Prerequisites: C01, C04, C05 (C14 is not needed; you add a LoRA to the M03 pipeline later, in C14·M03)

M01M02M03M04

About this course

ComfyUI is the standard node-graph tool for open generative models. It gives you control of every step, it runs on your own hardware or in the cloud, and it has an HTTP API. In this course you use it as an engineer: you read graphs node by node, measure them, and run them from code.

Requirement: an NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB VRAM or more (32 GB recommended), or a rented cloud GPU. The LTX workflows (06–08) need about 44 GB of weights; they run best on 48–80 GB, so rent that size for a batch day. LTX-2.5 files are gated: log in to Hugging Face, accept the license, and set HF_TOKEN. You can do all client and test work (M04) on a laptop with a CPU-only ComfyUI.

Starter kit

Download the starter kit. The comfyui/ folder has:

File What it is

workflows/03_i2v_wan22_5b.json Image to video, 1280 × 704, 121 frames at 24 fps (M02)
workflows/04_flf2v_wan22_14b.json First and last frame to video, two-expert 14B model (M02)
workflows/05_v2v_control_wan22_5b.json Video to video with a control video and a reference image (M02)

All 8 workflows use core nodes only. We made them from the official ComfyUI templates (2026-10-04). We then checked them with the ComfyUI 0.38.0 server validation (commit f1072eb). We did not run them on a GPU for this release, so your first run is also a test. If a node changed in a newer ComfyUI version, the validator tells you which one.

The identity scorer (tools/identity_score.py) is in the starter tools; you first use it in C05·M03. Reference solutions are in solutions/ (C11-M01 Dockerfile, C11-M03 pipeline script, C11-M04 client and tests). Do each lab first, then compare.

License note: the lock file shows the license of each file. FLUX.2 klein 4B is Apache-2.0. The VAE file that the official klein template uses comes from the FLUX.2-dev repository (non-commercial license). LTX-2.3 and LTX-2.5 need a paid license for companies with annual revenue of US$10 million or more. Check before client work (C16·M01).

Course outcomes

  1. Install a pinned ComfyUI, manage model files with hashes and licenses, and explain how the server runs a graph.
  2. Build start-frame graphs with reference images, and video graphs for image-to-video, first/last frame, and control video.
  3. Predict time and memory from latent size and token count, and choose exploration and final settings from measurements.
  4. Build an end-to-end character pipeline with lip sync and an automatic identity check.
  5. Run ComfyUI headless through its API and through MCP, with tests, run logs, and reproducible versions.

C11 · Node Pipelines (ComfyUI)

C11·M01 ComfyUI graph model, install, and model management

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain how ComfyUI runs a graph - typed nodes, links, execution order, and the output cache.
  2. Read a current text-to-image graph node by node and say what each node does.
  3. Install a pinned ComfyUI version locally or in a container on a rented GPU.
  4. Download model files into the correct folders, check their hashes, and record their licenses in a lock file.
  5. Run a workflow from the UI and export it in UI format and API format.

Key words

ComfyUI node graph checkpoint custom node subgraph API format models.lock

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C11, module 01. ComfyUI graph model, install, and model management. After this module, you can: 1. Explain how ComfyUI runs a graph - typed nodes, links, execution order, and the output cache. 2. Read a current text-to-image graph node by node and say what each node does. 3. Install a pinned ComfyUI version locally or in a container on a rented GPU. 4. Download model files into the correct folders, check their hashes, and record their licenses in a lock file. 5. Run a workflow from the UI and export it in UI format and API format. ComfyUI is a graph executor for generative models. Each node does one job, for example load a model, encode a prompt, make noise, sample, decode, or save. Links carry typed data between nodes. When you run the graph, ComfyUI runs only the nodes whose inputs changed and takes the other results from its cache. Model files live in fixed folders by type. Pin the ComfyUI version, record each model file with its hash and license, and keep every workflow in Git. Custom nodes run code on your machine, so install only the nodes that you trust.

Learn

What ComfyUI is

ComfyUI is a graph executor for generative models. You build a directed graph of nodes. Each node is a Python class with typed inputs and typed outputs. The server sorts the graph and runs it on your GPU. The browser editor is only a client of that server.

You already know this pattern from build systems and data pipelines. A node is like a build target. A link is a dependency. The cache is like a build cache: a node runs again only when its inputs change.

Nodes, links, and types

Each input and each output has a type. A link can connect only an output to an input of the same type. These are the main types:

Type What it carries Example node that makes it
MODEL The diffusion model weights, with any LoRA applied Load Diffusion Model
CLIP The text encoder (the name is historical) Load CLIP
VAE The encoder and decoder between pixels and latents Load VAE
CONDITIONING Encoded prompt, plus any references or control CLIP Text Encode
LATENT The latent tensor that the sampler denoises Empty Latent Image
IMAGE Decoded frames as a batch of pixels VAE Decode, Load Image
NOISE, GUIDER, SAMPLER, SIGMAS The four parts of a custom sampling setup Random Noise, CFG Guider, KSampler Select, a scheduler

Widgets are the values that you type on a node, for example a seed or a file name. Most widgets can also become inputs. Then another node can drive them, for example one "Width" node that feeds both the latent size and the scheduler.

How a run works

  1. You click Run, or a client sends the graph to POST /prompt.
  2. The server checks the graph. It checks that each class exists, that each required input is set, that link types match, and that each file name exists.
  3. The server finds the output nodes (Save Image, Save Video, Preview) and walks back to find the nodes that they need. Nodes that no output needs do not run.
  4. For each node, the server compares the inputs with the cache. If the inputs did not change, it uses the cached output.
  5. The other nodes run in dependency order. The server sends progress messages on a WebSocket.

The cache explains a lot of behavior. If you change only the seed, the loaders and the text encoder do not run again. If you change only the file name prefix of the save node, only the save node runs. If the server restarts, the cache is empty and the first run loads all models again.

Two file formats

ComfyUI saves a workflow in two formats:

  • UI format (workflow.json): node positions, groups, notes, subgraphs, and the widget values as lists. The editor needs this format. Commit it so that people can open the graph.
  • API format (workflow_api.json): a flat map from node ID to class_type and named inputs. The server needs this format. Your code changes it and sends it (C11·M04).

A subgraph is a group of nodes that looks like one node in the editor. The official templates use subgraphs to hide detail. When you export in API format, the subgraph expands, and the inner nodes get IDs such as 77:65 (subgraph node 77, inner node 65).

Model folders

ComfyUI finds models by type in fixed folders under models/:

models/
  diffusion_models/      # DiT and UNet weights (FLUX.2, Wan, LTX transformer)
  checkpoints/           # all-in-one files (model + text encoder + VAE), for example the LTX-2.3 checkpoint
  text_encoders/         # umt5, Qwen, Gemma encoders
  vae/
  loras/
  latent_upscale_models/ # for example the LTX x2 spatial upscalers
  controlnet/  clip_vision/  upscale_models/

To share one model store between several installs or containers, use extra_model_paths.yaml or mount the store at models/. Do not copy models into a container image. Images become large and slow to deploy.

The lock file

A workflow is reproducible only if you can get the same model files again. Keep a models.lock.json file with one entry for each file:

"wan2.2_ti2v_5B_fp16.safetensors": {
  "directory": "diffusion_models",
  "url": "https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/Wan_2.2_ComfyUI_Repackaged/resolve/main/split_files/diffusion_models/wan2.2_ti2v_5B_fp16.safetensors",
  "bytes": 9999658824,
  "sha256": "456f901338bd...",
  "license": "apache-2.0",
  "checked": "2026-10-04"
}

The starter kit contains a complete lock file for all starter workflows (starter/comfyui/models.lock.json). download_models.py uses it and stops if a hash does not match.

Record the license of each file, not of the model family. Example from the starter kit: the first image model has a permissive license. But its official template loads a VAE file from a sibling repository that has a non-commercial license. The lock file shows this conflict at once. The worked example names the files.

Install options

  1. Local, NVIDIA GPU (Windows or Linux): the portable build, the desktop app, or a manual install with Python and a CUDA build of PyTorch.
  2. Container on a rented GPU: best for reproducible work. Pin the ComfyUI commit in the Dockerfile. Mount models, input, and output as volumes.
  3. Hosted ComfyUI: no setup, pay per use. Good for a first try. Check what you can export and which custom nodes are available.
  4. Apple silicon: many image models run. Most video models run much faster on CUDA. Use a rented GPU for C11 video labs.

Memory options

If a model does not fit in VRAM, ComfyUI can move parts of it to system RAM. This is slower but it works. Useful launch flags (as of ComfyUI 0.38, 2026-10):

  • --lowvram: split the model and offload more.
  • --reserve-vram 2: keep 2 GB free for other programs.
  • --cache-none: use less RAM and VRAM, but run every node every time.
  • --use-sage-attention: a faster attention kernel, if it is installed. Also choose smaller weight files: FP8 or 4-bit variants (C01·M06).

Custom nodes

A custom node is a Python package in custom_nodes/. It runs with the same rights as ComfyUI. It can read your files and your environment variables. Rules:

  • Use core nodes when they can do the job. All starter workflows use core nodes only.
  • Before you install a node pack, read its code and pin a commit.
  • Test new node packs in a separate container without secrets.
  • Record the commit of each node pack in your run log.

  • ComfyUI documentation — getting started and the interfaceRead 'Installation', 'Interface', and 'Workflow templates'. 20 minutes.

Worked example

Task: take apart the first starter graph, 01_t2i_flux2_klein_4b.json, node by node. This graph comes from the official FLUX.2 klein template. We kept the distilled branch (4 steps).

Node (ID) Class Key settings What it does
77:70 UNETLoader flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors Loads the 4B diffusion transformer (7.75 GB file)
77:71 CLIPLoader qwen_3_4b.safetensors, type flux2 Loads the text encoder, a 4B language model (8.04 GB)
77:72 VAELoader flux2-vae.safetensors Loads the VAE (0.34 GB)
76 PrimitiveStringMultiline the prompt text Holds the prompt, so one value can feed several nodes
77:74 CLIPTextEncode text from node 76 Turns the prompt into positive conditioning
77:76 ConditioningZeroOut Makes an empty negative. With CFG 1 the negative has no effect
77:68, 77:69 PrimitiveInt 1024, 1024 Width and height. They feed the latent and the scheduler
77:66 EmptyFlux2LatentImage 1024 × 1024, batch 1 Makes the empty latent canvas
77:73 RandomNoise seed Makes the start noise from the seed
77:62 Flux2Scheduler 4 steps Makes the noise levels (sigmas) for 4 steps at this size
77:61 KSamplerSelect euler Chooses the solver
77:63 CFGGuider CFG 1 Combines model, positive, and negative into a guider
77:64 SamplerCustomAdvanced Runs the denoising loop
77:65 VAEDecode Turns the latent into pixels
9 SaveImage prefix C11/t2i_klein Writes a PNG with the workflow in its metadata

Three points:

  1. The classic KSampler node does noise, guidance, solver, and schedule in one node. Current templates split them into four nodes. This lets you change one part, for example use a different schedule, and keep the others.
  2. The scheduler takes width and height. Flow-matching models shift the noise schedule with image size. One "Width" node feeds both places, so they cannot disagree.
  3. The total download for this graph is 16.1 GB. The 4B text encoder is bigger than the diffusion model.

Cache test. We ran a small graph three times on a ComfyUI 0.38.0 server (2026-10-04). First run: all nodes ran. Second run, same inputs: no node ran; all came from the cache. Third run, only the save prefix changed: only the save node ran.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/comfy/ with INSTALL.md, models.lock.json, 3 workflows (UI and API format), and runs.md.

  1. Install ComfyUI. Use a container on a rented GPU or a local NVIDIA GPU. Pin the version and write the commit in INSTALL.md.
  2. Download the models for 01_t2i_flux2_klein_4b and 03_i2v_wan22_5b with starter/comfyui/download_models.py. Check that the hashes pass.
  3. Run starter/comfyui/validate_workflow.py on both workflows against your server. Fix any problem that it reports.
  4. Open the official templates for both workflows in the editor. Run them. Save the UI format and export the API format into Git.
  5. Make one change of your own to the image graph, for example a second branch with a different seed and size. Save it as your third workflow.
  6. Do the cache test: run, run again unchanged, change the seed, change only the save prefix. Write which nodes ran each time and the time of each run in runs.md.
  7. Add a license field to each lock entry. Mark any file that you cannot use for commercial work.

Result checklist

  • [ ] INSTALL.md has the ComfyUI commit, the GPU, the driver, and the PyTorch version.
  • [ ] All hashes in the lock file pass.
  • [ ] 3 workflows in Git, each in UI and API format, each validated.
  • [ ] runs.md shows the cache test with times.
  • [ ] Each lock entry has a license, and you marked the restricted files.

Self-check quiz

1. You run a graph. Then you change only the seed and run it again. Which nodes run the second time?

ComfyUI caches each node output by its inputs. The loaders and the text encoder have the same inputs, so they come from the cache. The noise node and all nodes downstream of it run again.

2. A teammate sends you a workflow JSON. The first key is 'nodes' and each node has 'pos' and 'widgets_values'. What is it, and can you POST it to /prompt?

UI format stores the layout and widget lists for the editor. The server accepts only API format, which maps node IDs to class types and named inputs.

3. Your klein graph uses 'flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors' (Apache-2.0). The VAE file comes from the FLUX.2-dev repository. What do you record before client work?

Licenses attach to files and repositories, not to model families. A graph is only as free as its most restricted file. Check the VAE license or use a VAE file with a license that permits your use.

4. Text encoding takes 9 s on each run, but you never change the prompt. What does this tell you?

A node runs again only when one of its inputs changes. Find the changing input. A common cause is a server restart, which clears the cache, or a node that outputs a new value on every run.

5. A custom node pack promises a 3× speed-up. It has 40 GitHub stars and no releases. What is the safe procedure for a production machine?

Custom nodes are Python code with full access to the machine. Review the code, pin the version, and isolate the test. Many production pipelines use custom nodes, but they control them.

6. Your models are on a shared NAS at /mnt/models, and you run 3 ComfyUI containers. How do you avoid 3 copies of 60 GB?

ComfyUI reads model folders from its models directory or from extra paths in extra_model_paths.yaml. Keep models out of the image. Mount them read-only.

7. The distilled klein graph uses CFG 1 and 'ConditioningZeroOut' for the negative input. Why?

With CFG 1 the sampler uses only the positive prediction, so one model call per step is enough. This is part of why the distilled model is fast (C01·M06).

C11 · Node Pipelines (ComfyUI)

C11·M02 Image and video graphs with control

Study time: 16 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Build a start-frame graph that uses two reference images, and explain how reference latents reach the model.
  2. Run image-to-video, first/last-frame, and control-video graphs with open models, and explain each conditioning node.
  3. Calculate latent size and token count from width, height, and frame count, and use it to predict cost.
  4. Chain clips into a longer sequence and control drift.
  5. Log time and peak VRAM for each run and choose exploration and final settings from the data.

Key words

ControlNet IP-Adapter first/last frame tiled decode reference latent MoE frame count rule

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C11, module 02. Image and video graphs with control. After this module, you can: 1. Build a start-frame graph that uses two reference images, and explain how reference latents reach the model. 2. Run image-to-video, first/last-frame, and control-video graphs with open models, and explain each conditioning node. 3. Calculate latent size and token count from width, height, and frame count, and use it to predict cost. 4. Chain clips into a longer sequence and control drift. 5. Log time and peak VRAM for each run and choose exploration and final settings from the data. Control enters the graph in three places. References and start frames enter as latents attached to the conditioning or placed into the latent. Control videos (depth, pose, edges) enter as extra conditioning frames. LoRAs change the model itself. Video graphs add frame count and frame rate, and each model has a frame count rule, for example 4n+1 for Wan. The latent size sets the number of tokens, and the token count sets time and memory. Long shots are chains of clips: the last frame of one clip is the first frame of the next. Log time and peak VRAM for every run.

Learn

Three ways to add control

A video model makes a clip from noise. Everything that you add to steer it enters the graph in one of three ways:

  1. Into the latent. The VAE encodes a start frame, a last frame, or a reference. The graph writes it into the latent or attaches it. A noise mask tells the sampler which parts to keep. This gives the strongest control. The first frame of an image-to-video clip is your key frame because it is never denoised.
  2. Into the conditioning. The prompt, reference latents, and control signals (depth, pose, edges) are attached to the CONDITIONING data. The model reads them at every step through attention. Strength and step range set how much they push.
  3. Into the model. A LoRA changes the model weights. Use it for identity or style that references cannot hold (C14).

Older graphs use separate adapter models for references (IP-Adapter) and structure (ControlNet). Current open models often accept references and control natively. The starter workflows use the native nodes. The ideas are the same.

Reference images (start frames)

A reference-image graph makes a start frame from two or more images, for example a character and a place. For each reference:

  • a scale node brings it to about 1 megapixel;
  • the VAE encodes it into a latent;
  • a reference node attaches that latent to the conditioning. The reference nodes are chained, so the conditioning carries all references. The prompt then says what to do with them: "the woman from image 1 in the place from image 2". The output size often comes from the first reference.

Video settings and the frame count rule

A video VAE compresses time as well as space. This gives each model a frame count rule. If the VAE puts 4 frames into one latent frame, the valid counts are 4n + 1: the first frame is encoded alone, then groups of 4. Examples: 81, 97, 121. If the VAE puts 8 frames into one latent frame, the rule is 8n + 1.

If you enter a wrong count, the node rounds it down or the editor refuses it. Width and height have a step too, for example 16 or 32 pixels, because the VAE and the patch size divide the image into blocks. The Tool walkthrough lists the rules for the starter models.

From settings to cost

The sampler works on tokens. Each token is a small patch of the latent. You can calculate the token count:

def tokens(width, height, frames, t_comp, s_comp, patch=2):
    lat_t = (frames - 1) // t_comp + 1
    return lat_t * (height // (s_comp * patch)) * (width // (s_comp * patch))

tokens(1280, 704, 121, 4, 16)   # Wan 2.2 5B  -> 31 * 22 * 40 = 27,280 tokens
tokens(640, 640, 81, 4, 8)      # Wan 14B FLF -> 21 * 40 * 40 = 33,600 tokens

Attention compares each token with every other token. So time grows faster than the token count. Double the width and the height, and the token count grows 4 ×, but attention work grows about 16 ×. This is why you explore at low size and render finals only for chosen takes.

Long shots

A model makes one clip of 5–20 s. For longer shots:

  • Chain: use the last frame of clip N as the first frame of clip N+1. Keep the prompt, LoRAs, and settings. Change only the action text.
  • First and last frame: when you know where the shot must end, give both frames.
  • Extension nodes: some models continue a clip from its last latent frames. This keeps motion better than one still frame.

Chained clips drift. Each VAE round trip shifts color and detail a little. Fix this:

  1. Every 2–3 clips, color-match the anchor frame to the approved key frame before you use it.
  2. Keep identity conditioning (reference, LoRA) in every clip.
  3. Hide joins with a cut or a cross-fade when the story allows it (C02·M04).
  4. Do the final match in grading.

Performance log

Record each run in one line: workflow hash, model files, width, height, frames, steps, seed, time, peak VRAM, and result (usable or not). Read peak VRAM with nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv -lms 500 in a second terminal, or from the ComfyUI /system_stats endpoint.

Ways to make a run faster, in the order to try them:

  1. Lower the size for exploration. Keep the seed and the prompt.
  2. Use step-distilled LoRAs or distilled models (4–8 steps) for exploration.
  3. Use FP8 weights. Use a faster attention kernel if it is installed.
  4. Use tiled VAE decode (VAEDecodeTiled) if the decode at the end runs out of memory.
  5. Rent a bigger GPU only after steps 1–4.

Tool walkthrough

Frame count rules of the starter models

Model family VAE compression (time × height × width) Frame count rule Example
Wan 2.2 5B 4 × 16 × 16, 48 channels 4n + 1 121 frames = 5 s at 24 fps
Wan 2.1 / 2.2 14B 4 × 8 × 8, 16 channels 4n + 1 81 frames = 5 s at 16 fps
LTX-2.3 / 2.5 8 × 32 × 32, 128 channels 8n + 1 121 frames at 24 fps

The reference graph (02)

02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b follows the pattern above with these nodes: ImageScaleToTotalPixels (about 1 megapixel), VAEEncode, and two chained ReferenceLatent nodes. GetImageSize takes the output size from the first reference.

The four video graphs in the starter kit

03 — Image to video (Wan 2.2 5B). Wan22ImageToVideoLatent encodes the start frame into latent frame 1. It sets the noise mask to 0 there. ModelSamplingSD3 with shift 8 moves the noise schedule toward high noise, which flow-matching video models need at this size. KSampler: 20 steps, CFG 5, uni_pc. CreateVideo at 24 fps, then SaveVideo. The official template ships with the start image bypassed (text to video). The starter version connects it.

04 — First and last frame (Wan 2.2 14B). The 14B model is a mixture of two experts (MoE). The high-noise expert decides layout and motion. The low-noise expert adds detail. The graph has two UNETLoader nodes and two KSamplerAdvanced nodes:

  • Sampler 1: high-noise expert, steps 0–10 of 20, adds noise, returns the latent with leftover noise.
  • Sampler 2: low-noise expert, steps 10–20, adds no noise, finishes. WanFirstLastFrameToVideo puts both frames into the latent. The model must find a motion that connects them. The template also contains 4-step "lightx2v" LoRAs, bypassed. Turn them on for exploration: 4 steps (2 + 2) and CFG 1, at some cost in motion quality.

05 — Control video (Wan 2.2 5B Fun Control). LoadVideo → GetVideoComponents gives the frames of a control video. Wan22FunControlToVideo takes the control frames and a reference image. The control video must already be a control signal: depth, pose, or edges. Make it from your own footage with a preprocessor node (for example the core Canny node for edges) or from a 3D layout render (C07·M03).

06 — Image to video with audio (LTX-2.5). LTX-2.5 makes video and audio together. The graph loads the parts separately: the distilled transformer (INT8), a video VAE, an audio VAE, and the text encoder. ResolutionSelector chooses width and height from an aspect ratio and a megapixel value. The graph runs in two stages:

  • Stage 1 samples at half size with a long list of noise levels (ManualSigmas).
  • LTXVLatentUpsampler doubles the latent size.
  • Stage 2 refines detail with a short list of noise levels. LTXVImgToVideoInplace places the start image in both stages. LTXVConcatAVLatent and LTXVSeparateAVLatent join and split the video and audio latents around each sampler. LTXVDualCFGGuider has separate guidance values for video and audio.

Watch

  • ComfyUI docs — Wan 2.2 video workflows (official)Read the 5B and 14B sections. Note which files go in which folder.
  • Wan 2.2 — official repository (model card and efficiency notes)Read the TI2V-5B section: 720p at 24 fps, and the stated GPU requirements.
  • Lightricks — LTX-2.5 model card (gated: log in to read the files)Read the frame and size rules and the two-stage (upscaler) pipeline.

Worked example

Task: plan VRAM and time for the four video graphs before you rent a GPU.

Step 1: add up the weight files from models.lock.json:

Workflow Large files Sum of weights
03 Wan 5B I2V model 10.0 GB (FP16) + text encoder 6.7 GB (FP8) + VAE 1.4 GB 18.1 GB
04 Wan 14B FLF2V 2 experts × 14.3 GB (FP8) + text encoder 6.7 GB + VAE 0.25 GB 35.6 GB on disk; about 21 GB in VRAM at one time
05 Wan 5B control 10.0 + 6.7 + 1.4 GB 18.1 GB
06 LTX-2.5 I2V transformer 21.5 GB (INT8) + text encoder 15.4 GB (INT8) + 2 VAEs 1.8 GB + upscaler 1.0 GB + prompt-enhance LLM 5.2 GB (optional) 44.9 GB

Step 2: compare with the GPU. The text encoder runs once, at the start. ComfyUI can move it out of VRAM before sampling. The two Wan 14B experts run one after the other, so only one must be in VRAM. Activations come on top of weights.

Step 3: decide:

  • 24 GB GPU: 03 and 05 run. The Wan team states that the 5B model makes a 5 s 720p clip on a 24 GB GPU in under 9 minutes. The ComfyUI docs state that the 5B model fits in 8 GB with ComfyUI offloading, more slowly. 04 runs with offloading, slowly.
  • 32 GB GPU: 03, 04, 05 run well. 06 runs with offloading of the text encoder.
  • 48–80 GB GPU: all four run without offloading. Rent one for a batch day of 06 renders.

Step 4: the token check for 03: 27,280 tokens. For an exploration pass at 640 × 352, the token count is 31 × 11 × 20 = 6,820. That is 4 × fewer tokens, and attention work falls about 16 ×.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/comfy/graphs/ with 4 workflows, perf.csv, and a 15 s chained sequence.

  1. Start frame. Run 02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b with your character sheet image (C04·M03) and a location image. Make 3 start frames for 3 shots of your storyboard.
  2. Image to video. Run 03_i2v_wan22_5b from each start frame. Write the motion prompt from your shot list (C02·M06).
  3. First and last frame. Run 04_flf2v_wan22_14b between two of your key frames. Run it once at 20 steps and once with the 4-step LoRAs on.
  4. Control. Record 5 s of yourself doing the action on a phone. Make an edge control video with the Canny node (or a depth video). Run 05_v2v_control_wan22_5b with a start frame as the reference.
  5. Chain. Make a 15 s sequence from three 5 s clips. Re-anchor the color before clip 3.
  6. Measure. Run graphs 03 and 04 at 2 sizes. Write each run in perf.csv: workflow, size, frames, steps, seed, seconds, peak VRAM, usable (yes/no).
  7. Decide. Write 5 lines: your exploration settings and your final settings, with the numbers.

Validate each workflow with validate_workflow.py before you commit it.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 4 workflows in Git, UI and API format, validated.
  • [ ] perf.csv with at least 8 runs, including peak VRAM.
  • [ ] The 15 s sequence, with a note on where you re-anchored and why.
  • [ ] A settings decision that uses the numbers.

Self-check quiz

1. You set a Wan 2.2 graph to 120 frames at 24 fps. What happens, and what do you set instead?

The Wan VAE compresses 4 frames into one latent frame after the first frame. So valid counts are 4n+1: 81, 97, 121. The editor widget steps by 4 for this reason.

2. How does Wan22ImageToVideoLatent make the video start on your exact key frame?

The node writes the encoded image into the latent and masks it. The sampler denoises only the masked-in (value 1) frames. This is why the first frame matches your key frame.

3. A shot at 1280 × 704, 121 frames takes 8 minutes. You need a version at 1920 × 1056, same length. About how much longer will sampling take?

Width and height each grow 1.5 ×, so tokens grow 2.25 ×. Attention compares every token with every other token, so that part grows about 5 ×. Expect 2.5–4 × in practice, and more VRAM. Test at low size, then upscale (C09·M04).

4. In the Wan 2.2 14B first/last-frame graph, why are there two models and two samplers?

The first KSamplerAdvanced runs steps 0–10 with the high-noise expert and returns the latent with leftover noise. The second runs steps 10–20 with the low-noise expert. Only one expert needs to be in VRAM at a time.

5. Your 15 s sequence is three 5 s clips chained by last frame → first frame. The colors get warmer in each clip. What is the best fix?

Each VAE encode/decode round trip shifts color a little, and the error adds up. Correct the anchor frame before each clip, and do the last match in grading (C09·M02).

6. You add a depth control video to an image-to-video shot. The camera path now matches your 3D layout, but the actress's face changes. What do you try first?

Control fixes structure, not identity. Identity comes from references and LoRAs. When control is strong in late steps, it can also fight fine detail.

7. The LTX-2.5 image-to-video template samples at half size and then uses a latent upscaler. Why?

Stage 1 makes motion and layout cheaply. The x2 latent upscaler doubles the size. Stage 2 refines detail with few steps. This multi-stage pattern is common in current video models.

8. You log runs. Exploration at 640 × 352 takes 70 s; final settings at 1280 × 704 take 8 min. You need 40 usable shots and expect 1 in 3 takes to be usable. What is a sensible plan?

Low-size takes predict the final composition and motion well when seed and prompt stay the same. You pay the full price only for chosen takes. Check that this holds for your model with 5 test pairs first.

04_flf2v_wan22_14b,640,640,81,20,8,391,24.6,no (morph between frames)
04_flf2v_wan22_14b,640,640,81,4,8,85,24.6,no (morph between frames)

Decision note:

  1. Low-size takes predict the final take: the same 2 seeds were usable and unusable at both sizes.
  2. Explore 03 at 640 × 352 (about 74 s). Render finals at 1280 × 704 (about 410 s) only for chosen seeds.
  3. For 04, the 4-step LoRAs cut time 4.5 × with stiffer motion. Use them to find seeds. Use 20 steps for finals.
  4. Morphs in first/last-frame shots come from frames that are too different. Bring the two key frames closer (same lens, smaller move).
  5. Peak VRAM stayed under 25 GB, so a 32 GB GPU is enough for this course. Rent 80 GB only for batch days of LTX renders.

Chain note: "Clip 2 ended 150 K warmer than the key frame (measured on a white wall area). I color-matched frame 120 of clip 2 to KF-S07-v3 before it became the first frame of clip 3. The join is on a head turn, so a cut hides it."

C11 · Node Pipelines (ComfyUI)

C11·M03 End-to-end character pipeline

Study time: 16 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Build a pipeline from character references and a script line to a lip-synced dialogue shot.
  2. Measure identity automatically with face embeddings, and set a reject threshold from your own data.
  3. Retry failed takes automatically and keep a report of every try.
  4. Package the pipeline with named inputs, a README, and a lock file, so another person can run it in 30 minutes.

Key words

character pipeline identity score lip sync subgraph cosine similarity

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C11, module 03. End-to-end character pipeline. After this module, you can: 1. Build a pipeline from character references and a script line to a lip-synced dialogue shot. 2. Measure identity automatically with face embeddings, and set a reject threshold from your own data. 3. Retry failed takes automatically and keep a report of every try. 4. Package the pipeline with named inputs, a README, and a lock file, so another person can run it in 30 minutes. A character pipeline turns a script line into a finished shot with the same character every time. The stages are: references, a start frame made from the references and the shot prompt, image-to-video with the spoken line as audio input, and an identity check. A face embedding model turns each face into a vector. Cosine similarity with the reference vector gives the identity score. Set the reject threshold from takes that you judged by eye. On a reject, the pipeline tries the next seed. A LoRA makes identity stronger; you add it in C14 and measure the gain.

Learn

What the pipeline must do

A series needs the same character in every shot. The face, the hair, the clothes, and the voice must not drift. You cannot check every frame by eye at scale. So the pipeline has two jobs: make the shot, and measure whether the shot is on-model.

The stages:

  1. References. The character sheet from C04·M03: front, 3/4, and side views, on plain light. One place image per location.
  2. Start frame. A reference-image graph puts the character into the place, with the shot size, angle, and light from the shot list.
  3. Line audio. The spoken line in the character's fixed voice (C06·M01). Record consent for any cloned voice (C16·M02).
  4. Video with lip sync. An image-and-audio-to-video model animates the start frame. It moves the mouth to the audio.
  5. Identity score. A face embedding model compares the faces in the video with the references.
  6. Decision. PASS goes to the edit. REJECT tries the next seed. After N tries, a person looks at the report.

The starter kit has the workflows for stages 2 and 4 (02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b, 07_lipsync_ia2v_ltx23), the scorer (identity_score.py), and a script that chains them (character_shot.py).

References versus LoRA

References put identity into each generation through the conditioning. They need no training. They are weaker at angles and expressions that the references do not show.

A character LoRA puts identity into the model weights (C14). It holds identity at more angles. It costs a dataset, a training run, and an evaluation.

Build the pipeline with references first. In C14·M03 you add your LoRA to the same pipeline and measure the change in identity score. Then you know what the LoRA is worth for your character.

How the identity score works

  1. Detect the face in a frame. The detector gives a box and 5 landmarks (eyes, nose, mouth corners).
  2. Align the face. Rotate and scale it so that the landmarks are in standard positions. Crop it.
  3. Embed the face. A recognition network turns the crop into a vector (128 numbers for SFace). Faces of the same person give vectors that point in similar directions.
  4. Compare with cosine similarity: score = dot(a, b) / (|a| × |b|). 1.0 means the same direction. Values near 0 mean unrelated faces.

Do this for frames sampled across the clip. Compare each frame with the mean of the normalized reference vectors. Report:

  • median score: is the take mostly on-model?
  • minimum score and its frame: where is the worst moment?
  • face rate: in how many sampled frames was a face found? A low rate means the face is turned away, covered, or broken.

Set the threshold from data

A threshold is a decision rule. Calibrate it like any classifier threshold:

  1. Generate 20–30 takes of your character, including some that drift.
  2. Label each take by eye: on-model or off-model.
  3. Score all takes.
  4. Choose the threshold that separates the two groups with the fewest errors.
  5. Prefer false rejects to false passes. A false reject costs one more take. A false pass reaches the client.

Recalibrate when you change the model, the style, or the character.

Retries and the report

When a take fails, the cheapest fix is often a new seed. The pipeline tries seed, seed+1, and seed+2. It writes a report with every try: seed, start frame, video, scores, worst frame, and result. A person reads the report only when all tries fail. Usually the report then shows a pattern, for example "always fails at the profile view". That pattern tells you what to fix in the input.

Packaging

Another person (or an agent, C12) must run the pipeline without opening the graphs:

  • Named inputs. Each workflow has a map file (*.map.json): prompt, seed, start_image, line_audio. Code uses names, not node IDs.
  • One entry point. character_shot.py --shot S07.json --char-ref ... --place-ref ... --line ....
  • Requirements. The README states the GPU memory, the model files (with the lock file), and the ComfyUI version.
  • Example inputs. One shot file, one reference set, one line audio file, and the expected report.

In the ComfyUI editor you can also group the nodes of one stage into a subgraph with named inputs. This helps people who work in the editor. The API export expands it again.

Watch

  • OpenCV — face detection (YuNet) and face recognition (SFace) tutorialRead how detection, alignment, and the cosine score work. The starter scorer uses these two models.
  • The Daring Creatives — Mickmumpitz publishes the workflow file with every videoRead how a creator structures and shares character workflows.
  • Lightricks — LTX-2.3 model card (audio-to-video input)Read what the model does with an input audio track.

Worked example

Calibration on real faces. We tested the starter scorer on public-domain NASA portraits (2026-10-04, OpenCV YuNet + SFace, CPU):

Input (reference: Neil Armstrong, 1964 portrait) Median Minimum Result at 0.45
Armstrong, a different photo, as a 3 s push-in video 0.668 0.650 PASS
Armstrong, the same different photo, as a still 0.676 0.676 PASS
Buzz Aldrin (a different person), still 0.135 0.135 REJECT
3 s video: 1.5 s Armstrong, then 1.5 s Aldrin 0.345 0.111 (frame 43) REJECT

Two facts come from this test:

  1. Same person, different photos: about 0.67. Different person: about 0.14. There is a wide gap. OpenCV states 0.363 as its "same person" cosine threshold for SFace on real photos.
  2. The mixed clip fails, and the report names frame 43, inside the second half. The minimum and its frame show where the drift is.

One shot through the pipeline. Shot S07: @MARA: "That's my locker." Medium close-up, 85 mm look, night, locker room.

python character_shot.py --shot shots/S07.json \
  --char-ref refs/CHAR-MARA_front.png --char-ref refs/CHAR-MARA_34.png \
  --place-ref refs/LOC-LOCKER.png --line audio/S07_mara.wav --out shots/S07/

The script runs the start-frame workflow (seed 1000), then the lip-sync workflow with the line audio, then the scorer. A typical run (illustrative numbers): the first try fails, median 0.41, worst frame at a head turn. The second try (seed 1001) passes: median 0.58, face rate 100 %. The report keeps both tries.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/character/ with the packaged pipeline, a calibration report, 5 dialogue shots, and an identity report.

  1. Inputs. Use your character sheet (C04·M03) and two locations. Make 5 line audio files in the character's fixed voice (C06·M01). Write 5 shot files from your shot list.
  2. Run the stages by hand. Run 02_ref_edit_flux2_klein_4b, then 07_lipsync_ia2v_ltx23, for one shot, with comfy_run.py. Check the outputs.
  3. Calibrate the scorer. Make 20 takes or more. Label each take by eye. Score them with identity_score.py. Choose your threshold and write why in calibration.md, with a table.
  4. Automate. Chain the stages with retries. Use your own script, or read and run starter/solutions/C11-M03/character_shot.py.
  5. Produce. Make the 5 dialogue shots in at least 3 shot sizes. Keep every report.
  6. Package. Write the README: requirements, model files and licenses, one command, expected output. Ask another student (or a fresh container) to run it from the README. Time it.
  7. Prepare C14. Write down the 2 shots where identity was weakest. In C14·M03 you will rerun them with a LoRA.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 5 shots, each with a report (all tries).
  • [ ] calibration.md with 20+ labeled takes and the chosen threshold.
  • [ ] README that another person followed in under 30 minutes.
  • [ ] Rejection rate and its main cause.
  • [ ] Two "weak" shots chosen for the C14 comparison.

Self-check quiz

1. Your identity scorer gives 0.67 for two real photos of the same person and 0.14 for a different person. A generated take scores median 0.52, minimum 0.20. What do you check first?

The median says the take is mostly on-model. The minimum says that some frames are not. Look at the worst frame that the report names. If the drift is on screen for more than a few frames, reject or cut around it.

2. Why does the pipeline compare against the mean of several reference embeddings, not one?

A single reference also encodes its pose and lighting. Averaging several normalized embeddings reduces that bias.

3. How do you choose the reject threshold?

Generated faces, lighting, and styles change the score range. A threshold is a decision rule that you calibrate on labeled examples, like any classifier threshold.

4. When do you use a separate lip-sync stage instead of letting a joint audio-video model invent the voice?

If the model invents the voice, it changes between shots. A fixed voice from C06 gives series consistency. The video model then follows the audio.

5. The pipeline rejects 4 of 5 takes for one shot, always at a profile view. What is the best change?

The failure has a cause: the references do not show that angle. Fix the input. Do not move the threshold to hide a real problem.

6. Which face embedding model can you use in a client pipeline without a licensing problem?

Some popular face-analysis packages have permissive code but non-commercial pretrained weights. The license of the weights decides.

7. Another student runs your packaged pipeline and gets a different start frame from the same seed. What is the most likely cause?

Same inputs and same versions give the same or nearly the same output. The run log (C11·M04) shows which version differs.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

calibration.md (shape of a strong answer):

Group Takes Median score range
On-model (by eye) 17 0.49–0.71
Off-model (by eye) 7 0.18–0.47

"Overlap is between 0.47 and 0.49 (2 takes). We choose 0.48. Error check: 0 false passes, 1 false reject (a take with a hand over the mouth). Rule: also reject if face rate < 80 %."

  out/S01..S05/report.json

C11 · Node Pipelines (ComfyUI)

C11·M04 Headless ComfyUI - API, MCP, and versioning

Study time: 16 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Run API-format workflows through the HTTP and WebSocket API, with uploads, progress, errors, and downloads.
  2. Set workflow inputs by name through a map file, and validate a workflow before you queue it.
  3. Write automated tests for a ComfyUI client that run on a CPU-only server.
  4. Connect an agent to ComfyUI through an MCP server, with limits on what the agent can run.
  5. Pin and log the versions that make a run reproducible, and reproduce an earlier output from the log.

Key words

headless API format WebSocket Comfy MCP reproducibility

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C11, module 04. Headless ComfyUI - API, MCP, and versioning. After this module, you can: 1. Run API-format workflows through the HTTP and WebSocket API, with uploads, progress, errors, and downloads. 2. Set workflow inputs by name through a map file, and validate a workflow before you queue it. 3. Write automated tests for a ComfyUI client that run on a CPU-only server. 4. Connect an agent to ComfyUI through an MCP server, with limits on what the agent can run. 5. Pin and log the versions that make a run reproducible, and reproduce an earlier output from the log. ComfyUI runs as an HTTP server. You send an API-format workflow to POST /prompt and get a prompt_id. The WebSocket sends progress, errors, and a final message. GET /history gives the output file names, and GET /view downloads them. Keep a map file from input names to node inputs, so code never depends on node IDs. Validate the workflow first. Test the client on a CPU server with a workflow that needs no models. Agents use ComfyUI through MCP servers; give them packaged workflows with strict inputs. Log the workflow hash, model hashes, node versions, ComfyUI version, seed, and GPU for each run.

Learn

ComfyUI as a service

The editor in the browser is one client of the ComfyUI server. Your code can be another client. Then ComfyUI becomes a generation service: your pipeline sends jobs, follows them, and collects files. This is the base for agents (C12), serving (C13), and scale (C15).

The routes that a client needs

Route Use
POST /upload/image Upload an input file (images, and also audio and video files). Returns name and subfolder.
POST /prompt Queue a job: {"prompt": <api workflow>, "client_id": <uuid>}. Returns prompt_id, or HTTP 400 with node_errors.
GET /ws?clientId=<uuid> WebSocket with progress and status messages for your client ID.
GET /history/<prompt_id> Status and output file names of a finished job.
GET /view?filename=..&subfolder=..&type=output Download one output file.
GET /system_stats ComfyUI version, PyTorch version, devices, VRAM. Put these in the run log.
GET /object_info All node classes and their inputs. The validator uses it.
POST /interrupt, POST /queue Stop the running job; clear the queue.

The WebSocket messages

Filter every message by your prompt_id. Other clients can use the same server.

  • execution_start: the job started.
  • execution_cached: these nodes come from the cache.
  • executing with a node ID: this node runs now.
  • progress: step value of max for the running sampler.
  • executing with node: null: the job is done.
  • execution_error: a node failed. The message has the node ID, the class, and the exception text.
  • execution_interrupted: someone stopped the job. Binary messages are preview images. Skip them unless you show previews.

Set inputs by name

Do not edit workflow JSON with string replace. Load it as JSON, copy it, and set values. Keep a map file for each workflow:

{"prompt": "6.text", "start_image": "56.image", "seed": "3.seed", "frames": "55.length"}

Your code and your agents use the names on the left. When the workflow changes and node IDs move, you change only the map. Every starter workflow has a map file. Three rules:

  1. Never change the template file. Change a copy.
  2. If a map entry points to a link, not a value, stop with an error. The map does not fit this workflow version.
  3. Validate before you queue. validate_workflow.py checks classes, required inputs, link types, and file names against the server.

Errors that you must handle

Where Example Client action
Before the job Unknown input name, missing local file Exit with a clear message (exit code 2)
POST /prompt HTTP 400: value not in list, missing input, wrong type Show node_errors; exit 3
During the job execution_error: out of memory, missing model, bad file Show node and message; exit 4
No end A node hangs, the server crashes Total timeout; exit 5
Upload HTTP 413: file too large (default limit 100 MB) Raise --max-upload-size or use shared storage

Clear exit codes let a pipeline decide what to do: fix the input, retry, or call a person.

Test the client without a GPU

Most client code does not need a GPU. The server, validation, WebSocket, history, and downloads behave the same on CPU. So:

  • Start ComfyUI with --cpu in CI.
  • Use a workflow of core nodes that needs no models. The starter kit has test/00_smoke_cpu.json: LoadImage → ImageInvert → SaveImage.
  • Test the success path, the log fields, that the template file does not change, and each error path.
  • Test the real model workflows in a separate GPU job, for example once a night.

Agents and MCP

An agent can drive ComfyUI through an MCP server (C03·M05). Options as of 2026-10:

  • Comfy MCP (official, public beta): agents search and run workflows on Comfy Cloud.
  • Community MCP servers for a local ComfyUI: inspect graphs, queue jobs, manage models.
  • Your own MCP server (C12·M03): wrap your packaged workflows as tools.

Design agent tools with the least power that does the job. A tool generate_shot(shot_id, prompt, seed, duration_s) with ranges and a budget is safe to give an agent. A tool run_any_workflow(json) gives the agent every node, every size, and every file path on the server. Log every tool call with its inputs and cost.

Reproducibility

To reproduce an output you need the same inputs and the same versions:

  • workflow file hash (SHA-256 of the API JSON that you sent);
  • model file hashes (models.lock.json);
  • custom node commits (if any);
  • ComfyUI version and commit;
  • seed and all input values;
  • GPU, driver, and PyTorch version.

With all of these the same, output is the same or nearly the same. Small differences can come from GPU kernels that are not deterministic. If you need exact repeats, start ComfyUI with --deterministic. It is slower, and the ComfyUI help says that it does not guarantee exact repeats in all cases.

Watch

  • ComfyUI docs — server routes and WebSocket messagesRead /prompt, /history, /view, /upload/image, and the message types.
  • ComfyUI — example API scripts (script_examples)Compare websockets_api_example.py with the starter client.
  • GIGAZINE on X — Comfy MCP lets agents like Claude Code automate ComfyUI (Japanese)Short news. Note that Comfy MCP uses Comfy Cloud.

Worked example

A real run log line. We ran the smoke workflow with the starter client against a ComfyUI 0.38.0 server on CPU (2026-10-04):

python comfy_run.py --server http://127.0.0.1:8199 \
  --workflow workflows/test/00_smoke_cpu.json --map workflows/test/00_smoke_cpu.map.json \
  --upload image=smoke_in.png --out renders --log runs.jsonl

{"prompt_id": "2fa08d93-108b-4355-95f2-74607e199c06",
 "workflow_sha256": "e4a9ee2aa5b380095f5abf8f31be4a904a8b7507b7783fbf499a70d5e1ff5138",
 "inputs": {"image": "smoke_in.png"}, "seconds": 0.1,
 "outputs": ["renders/smoke_00001_.png"],
 "comfyui_version": "0.38.0", "pytorch_version": "2.14.1", "devices": ["cpu"]}

The error paths, on the same server:

Test Client output Exit code
--set promt=x (typo) unknown input 'promt'. Known: filename_prefix, image 2
--set image=does_not_exist.png HTTP 400 from /prompt with node_errors 3
Wan 5B workflow with an empty model file execution error in node 39 (VAELoader): Error while deserializing header 4

The test file test_comfy_run.py checks these cases. Result on the CPU server: 5 passed in 0.31 s.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/comfy_client/ with a CLI client, tests, an agent demo, and a reproduction report.

  1. Client. Write comfy_run.py --workflow X --map X.map.json --set name=value --upload name=file. It must upload files, follow the WebSocket, handle the 5 error cases in the table, download outputs, and append a log line.
  2. Validation. Call the validator (or your own checks) before you queue.
  3. Tests. Start ComfyUI with --cpu. Write tests with the smoke workflow: success, log fields, template unchanged, and each error path. Run them in CI (for example a GitHub Actions job).
  4. Real runs. Run 2 starter workflows on your GPU server through the client. Use the same log format.
  5. Agent. Connect an agent to ComfyUI through an MCP server. Expose one packaged workflow (for example generate_shot) with limited inputs. Ask the agent in natural language to make one shot. Save the transcript and the tool-call log.
  6. Reproduce. Pick one earlier GPU run from the log. Rerun it from the log only. Compare the two outputs (pixel difference or identity score). Write the result.

Try the lab yourself first. Then compare with starter/solutions/C11-M04/.

Result checklist

  • [ ] The client handles all 5 error cases with clear exit codes.
  • [ ] Tests pass on a CPU server in CI.
  • [ ] 2 GPU workflows ran through the client, with complete log lines.
  • [ ] Agent demo: transcript and tool-call log, with limited inputs.
  • [ ] Reproduction report with the measured difference.

Self-check quiz

1. POST /prompt returns HTTP 400 with 'value_not_in_list' for a LoadImage node. What happened, and what is the fix?

The server validates file names against its folders before it queues the job. Upload first. The response gives the name (and subfolder) to use.

2. Your client waits for the 'executing' message with node null. Which extra condition prevents a wrong 'done'?

A server can run jobs from several clients. Filter every message by prompt_id. Also handle execution_error and execution_interrupted, and set a total timeout.

3. A 2-minute control video upload fails with HTTP 413. What do you change?

The upload endpoint has a size limit. For large media, a shared volume is often better than HTTP uploads.

4. Why does the starter client refuse to set an input that is a link in the workflow?

A map entry must point to a widget value. If it points to a link, the map is wrong for this workflow version. Fail loudly.

5. How can CI test your ComfyUI client without a GPU and without model files?

The server, the validation, the WebSocket, the history, and the downloads are the same on CPU. Only the model nodes need a GPU. Test those in a separate, scheduled GPU job.

6. You give an agent an MCP tool that accepts any API-format workflow JSON. What is the risk, and what is better?

An agent tool is an API. Design it with the least power that does the job: a named workflow, a few inputs with ranges, a budget, and a log.

7. You rerun a logged job with the same workflow, seed, and models, and the output differs slightly. What is the most likely cause, and what do you do?

Same versions and same seed give near-identical output. Exact repeats can need deterministic kernels, which are slower. Record the GPU, driver, and PyTorch version for this reason.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission has this shape:

pipelines/comfy_client/
  comfy_run.py            # about 250 lines; no dependency except websocket-client (optional)
  test_comfy_run.py       # 5+ tests on a CPU server
  .github/workflows/ci.yml   # starts ComfyUI --cpu, runs pytest
  mcp/generate_shot.py    # MCP tool: shot_id, prompt (≤ 600 chars), seed, duration_s (2–8)
  agent_demo.md           # transcript + tool-call log
  REPRODUCE.md

REPRODUCE.md (example):

"Run 9c1e… (03_i2v_wan22_5b, seed 1001, 640 × 352) was rerun from its log on the same RTX 5090, same driver, ComfyUI 0.38.0. Mean absolute pixel difference: 0.4 / 255. Identity score of both: 0.612 and 0.611. Visually identical. Without --deterministic, small differences come from GPU attention kernels. With --deterministic, the difference was 0 and the run took 18 % longer. We keep the default and record the GPU in each log."

What makes this submission strong:

  1. Clear exit codes. A pipeline that calls the client can tell "fix your input" (2) from "the server rejected the graph" (3), "a node failed" (4), and "no answer" (5). Each needs a different action.
  2. The tests run without a GPU. CI starts ComfyUI with --cpu in about 20 s and runs the smoke workflow. GPU tests run once a night.
  3. The agent tool is narrow. The MCP tool accepts a shot ID, a prompt with a length limit, a seed, and a duration from 2 to 8 s. It rejects other values before it calls ComfyUI. Every call is logged with its cost.
  4. The reproduction is measured. The report gives a number (pixel difference and identity score), not "it looks the same", and it explains the cause of the difference.

The reference client and tests are in starter/solutions/C11-M04/. Compare your error handling with it, line by line.
