60 h · Prerequisites: C03, C11

M01M02M03M04

About this course

This course turns your tools into a production system. You build services that call many models, a media-tool MCP server, and a multi-agent studio with clear human approvals and automatic checks.

Starter code for this course (in pipeline/ of the starter kit; all tested on 2026-10-04):

File Use Tests
genqueue.py Job queue: idempotency keys, backoff with jitter, Retry-After, timeouts, dead letters, budget caps (M01) test_genqueue.py: 8 passed
mediakit.py Media functions: probe, intermediate, proxy, frame-accurate trim, concat with conform, loudness, contact sheet (M02) test_mediakit.py: 6 passed
studio_mcp.py MCP server (Python SDK 2.x) with a path sandbox, dry runs, approvals, budget guard, audit log (M03) test_studio_mcp.py: 6 passed over stdio
qc_gate.py Stage gates with PASS / FIX / REJECT and reasons (M04) checked on 4 test clips

Python packages: pip install "mcp>=2.3" pytest numpy opencv-python. The MCP SDK 2.x renamed FastMCP to MCPServer; tutorials that import mcp.server.fastmcp are for SDK 1.x.

Course outcomes

  1. Call model APIs reliably with async jobs, queues, retries, and webhooks.
  2. Use ffmpeg and Whisper as programmable pipeline stages.
  3. Build your own MCP server for a media tool.
  4. Design a multi-agent production system with human gates.
  5. Add automated quality gates to every stage.

Modules

  1. C12·M01 Model APIs - async jobs, queues, retries, webhooks 14 h
  2. C12·M02 ffmpeg, Whisper, and media utilities as pipeline stages 10 h
  3. C12·M03 Build your own MCP server for media 16 h
  4. C12·M04 Multi-agent production and automated quality gates 20 h

C12 · Orchestration and Agents

C12·M01 Model APIs - async jobs, queues, retries, webhooks

Study time: 14 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Call video, image, and audio model APIs that run as asynchronous jobs, and download results before they expire.
  2. Build a job queue with idempotency keys, retries with backoff and jitter, timeouts, and a dead-letter state.
  3. Enforce budgets per shot and in total before any job is sent.
  4. Receive results with webhooks or polling, and verify webhook signatures.
  5. Put vendors behind one interface, so a model change is a configuration change.

Key words

async job idempotency key exponential backoff webhook dead-letter queue

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C12, module 01. Model APIs - async jobs, queues, retries, webhooks. After this module, you can: 1. Call video, image, and audio model APIs that run as asynchronous jobs, and download results before they expire. 2. Build a job queue with idempotency keys, retries with backoff and jitter, timeouts, and a dead-letter state. 3. Enforce budgets per shot and in total before any job is sent. 4. Receive results with webhooks or polling, and verify webhook signatures. 5. Put vendors behind one interface, so a model change is a configuration change. Generation APIs are asynchronous: you submit a job, the vendor queues and runs it, and you collect the result later. A reliable pipeline needs a queue with idempotency keys (a retry never pays twice), retries with exponential backoff and jitter that respect Retry-After, timeouts, and a dead-letter state for jobs that need a person. Budgets must be checked before a job is sent. Webhooks deliver results efficiently; polling is simpler. One backend interface for all vendors turns a removed model into a configuration change.

Learn

Why generation APIs are asynchronous

A video generation takes from seconds to many minutes. An HTTP request cannot stay open that long. So generation APIs work as jobs:

  1. Submit: you send the model, the inputs, and often a webhook URL. You get a job ID at once.
  2. Run: the vendor queues and runs the job. States: queued → running → succeeded or failed.
  3. Result: you get output URLs, by webhook or by polling. Many URLs are temporary: download the files at once, and store them in your own storage.

What can go wrong

  • Rate limits (HTTP 429): too many requests. The response often has a Retry-After value.
  • Server errors (5xx) and network errors: temporary. Retry later.
  • Permanent errors: bad input, a content-policy refusal, an unknown model. Do not retry; fix the input.
  • Lost responses: the job was accepted, but you did not receive the ID. A naive retry pays twice.
  • Hanging jobs: no result after a long time.
  • Silent cost: every retry and every take costs money.

The queue

Put every generation into your own queue first. The queue is the single source of truth: which jobs exist, their state, their tries, and their cost. A worker takes due jobs, sends them, and updates them. A simple database table is enough for one studio. Larger systems use a queue service.

Reliability patterns

  • Idempotency key: a deterministic key for each logical job, for example S07.p2.g4 (shot S07, prompt version 2, generation 4). Submitting the same key again returns the same job. Some vendors also accept the key, so a repeated request does not start a second paid job.
  • Retries with exponential backoff and full jitter: after try n, wait a random time between 0 and min(cap, base × 2ⁿ). The randomness spreads retries, so many workers do not hit the API at the same moment. A Retry-After from the vendor is a minimum.
  • Timeouts: a job that runs longer than its timeout is checked and resubmitted (with the same key).
  • Dead-letter state: after the last try, the job stops and waits for a person. The person decides: fix the input, wait for the vendor, or switch the backend.

Budget guards

Check the budget before the job is sent: the estimate of this job, plus what the shot and the project have already spent, plus what is already queued. Refuse above the cap. A shot that reaches its cap needs a new approach, not more takes (C05·M06).

Webhooks and polling

  • Webhooks: the vendor calls your endpoint when the job finishes. Efficient, but you need a public HTTPS endpoint, and you must verify the vendor's signature on every call. Reject unsigned events and unknown job IDs.
  • Polling: your worker asks for the status every few seconds (5–15 s is enough for video). Simple, and works behind a firewall. Many pipelines use webhooks with polling as a fallback.

One interface for all backends

Write one interface:

class Backend(Protocol):
    def estimate(self, inputs: dict) -> float: ...    # US$
    def submit(self, inputs: dict) -> str: ...        # remote job id; raises TransientError / PermanentError
    def poll(self, remote_id: str) -> tuple[str, dict]: ...   # ("running" | "succeeded" | "failed", result)

Each vendor is one class. Your own node-graph server is one more (C11·M04). A routing config chooses the backend per shot type (C05·M06). When a vendor removes a model, you change one line of the config and re-test that shot type.

Tool walkthrough

The starter queue

cd starter/pipeline
python genqueue.py submit S07.p2.g4 --backend fake --inputs '{"prompt": "...", "seconds": 6}' --cap 3.0
python genqueue.py work --once            # or: python genqueue.py work  (loop every 5 s)
python genqueue.py status S07.p2.g4       # the job and its event history
python genqueue.py dead                   # jobs that need a person

genqueue.py uses SQLite (one file, no server). It has two backends: fake (for tests; the FAKE_PLAN variable sets outcomes such as 429,500,ok) and comfy (the C11 client). Add a vendor by writing a class with estimate, submit, and poll. Map HTTP 429 and 5xx to TransientError (with retry_after from the header) and 4xx input errors to PermanentError.

Run the tests: pytest -q test_genqueue.py.

Vendor APIs (as of 2026-10)

  • Aggregators: fal.ai and Replicate offer many models with one queue and webhook model.
  • Vendor APIs: model vendors offer their own job APIs (see the landscape page). Read each vendor's limits: concurrency, rate limits, output URL expiry, and webhook signing.

Watch

  • fal.ai — documentation (queue, webhooks, model APIs)Read the queue and webhook sections.
  • Replicate — documentation (predictions, webhooks)Compare its job model with fal's.

Worked example

Queue tests (2026-10-04, pytest -q test_genqueue.py, 8 passed in 0.03 s):

Test What it proves
success A job goes queued → sent → succeeded; cost logged (US$0.60 for 6 s)
idempotent submit The same key twice gives one job
Retry-After and backoff Plan 429,500,ok: the first wait is ≥ 2 s (Retry-After), then a backoff, then success after 3 tries
dead letter Plan 500 with 3 tries maximum: the job ends in dead after 3 tries
permanent error Plan bad: dead (permanent) at once, no retry
shot cap A second US$0.60 job on a shot with a US$1.00 cap is refused before it is sent
total cap The 9th job of US$0.60 is refused under a total cap of US$5.00
jitter Backoff waits stay within the cap and are all different

Routing config of a project:

hero_product: {backend: veo,   model: veo-3.1,   mode: i2v, cap_per_shot: 3.00}
dialogue:     {backend: kling, model: kling-3.0, mode: r2v, cap_per_shot: 2.00}
broll:        {backend: comfy, workflow: 03_i2v_wan22_5b.json, cap_per_shot: 0.50}

A job for S07 (dialogue): budget check ✓ → submit with key S07.p2.g4 → HTTP 429 with Retry-After 2 → wait 2.0 s → HTTP 500 → wait 3.1 s (backoff with jitter) → accepted → webhook "succeeded" (signature verified) → download → cost US$0.60 logged in the take log (C05·M06) and the prompt log.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/genqueue/ with your queue (or the starter queue extended), one real vendor backend, tests, and a routing config.

  1. Run the starter queue and its tests. Read the code.
  2. Write one real backend for a vendor or aggregator that you use: estimate, submit, poll. Map its errors to transient and permanent.
  3. Add a webhook receiver (a small HTTP server) that verifies the vendor's signature. Keep polling as a fallback.
  4. Write a routing config for your shot types and route 10 real shots through the queue.
  5. Write tests with the fake backend for: a lost response (submit twice with the same key), Retry-After, the dead-letter state, and both caps.
  6. Simulate a vendor outage (make your backend raise transient errors). Show the dead-letter list, then switch the routing for that shot type and finish the jobs.

Result checklist

  • [ ] One real backend; 10 real shots through the queue with costs logged.
  • [ ] Webhook signature verification (and a rejected forged request in a test).
  • [ ] Tests for idempotency, Retry-After, dead letters, and caps pass.
  • [ ] The outage drill: dead letters, routing change, jobs finished.

Self-check quiz

1. A network error happens after you send a job, before you receive its ID. You retry. How do you avoid paying for two generations?

An idempotency key (for example S07.p2.g4) makes a retry safe. The starter queue returns the existing job for a known key.

2. A vendor answers HTTP 429 with 'Retry-After: 2'. What does your worker do?

Retry-After is a minimum. Backoff with jitter spreads retries so many workers do not hit the API together.

3. Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?

Full jitter waits a random time between 0 and the backoff limit.

4. Where must the budget check happen?

A check after the job is a report, not a guard.

5. A job fails 5 times with HTTP 500. What happens to it?

A limit on tries protects money and makes problems visible.

6. Your webhook endpoint receives 'job succeeded' for a job ID you do not know. What is the rule?

A public endpoint can receive forged requests. Vendors sign webhooks; verify the signature and the job ID.

7. A vendor removed the model that all your dialogue shots used. With a backend interface and a routing config, what changes?

This is the point of the abstraction. The Sora 2 API removal (2026-09-24) stopped pipelines that called one vendor directly.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission has a backend of about 60 lines and tests that use the fake backend for every failure path. Its README states the vendor facts that the code depends on:

Vendor fact Value (from the docs, date) Where in the code
Rate limit 10 concurrent jobs worker concurrency = 8
Retry-After on 429 yes, seconds TransientError(retry_after=...)
Output URL expiry 1 hour download in the success handler
Webhook signature HMAC-SHA256 of the body, header X-Signature verify_webhook() + test with a forged body

"Outage drill: 6 dialogue jobs went to dead after 5 tries each in 4 min 10 s (backoff cap 60 s). I changed dialogue.backend from kling to comfy with workflow 07_lipsync_ia2v_ltx23 and resubmitted with new keys (.g5). All 6 finished. Total extra cost: US$0, because no failed try was charged."

Go deeper

  • OpenAI API deprecations page (Sora 2 / Videos API removal)
  • AWS Architecture Blog — Exponential backoff and jitter
  • Stripe — idempotent requests (a clear explanation of idempotency keys)

C12 · Orchestration and Agents

C12·M02 ffmpeg, Whisper, and media utilities as pipeline stages

Study time: 10 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Use ffmpeg in code for probe, transcode, trim, concat, audio, and analysis, and know which features depend on the build.
  2. Use Whisper-family models for transcripts with word timestamps as a pipeline stage.
  3. Write media functions that never overwrite inputs, return structured results, and raise clear errors.
  4. Test media functions with generated media in CI, without real footage.
  5. Store media with a metadata sidecar that connects to the prompt log and the rights log.

Key words

ffmpeg ffprobe sidecar metadata frame-accurate trim test media

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C12, module 02. ffmpeg, Whisper, and media utilities as pipeline stages. After this module, you can: 1. Use ffmpeg in code for probe, transcode, trim, concat, audio, and analysis, and know which features depend on the build. 2. Use Whisper-family models for transcripts with word timestamps as a pipeline stage. 3. Write media functions that never overwrite inputs, return structured results, and raise clear errors. 4. Test media functions with generated media in CI, without real footage. 5. Store media with a metadata sidecar that connects to the prompt log and the rights log. ffmpeg and ffprobe are the workhorses of every media pipeline: they read, convert, cut, join, and measure almost any file. Use them from code through small functions with one job each, which never overwrite inputs, return structured results, and raise errors with the ffmpeg message. Some filters depend on how ffmpeg was built, so test for them. Generated test media (test patterns and tones) let you test every function in CI. Transcription is a stage like any other. Every asset gets a metadata sidecar that links it to its prompt, its rights, and its tech data.

Learn

ffmpeg and ffprobe

ffprobe reads facts about a file: container, streams, codecs, size, frame rate, duration, color tags, audio format. ffmpeg reads inputs, applies filters, and writes outputs. Almost every pipeline stage in this program uses them. Learn four ideas:

  1. Inputs, filters, outputs. Options before -i apply to the input; options after it apply to the output.
  2. Filter graphs. -vf and -af for one stream; -filter_complex for several inputs and outputs, with labels like [0:v] and [v].
  3. Stream copy versus re-encode. -c copy copies the compressed data: very fast, no quality loss, but it can only cut at keyframes and cannot change anything. Re-encoding decodes and encodes: exact and flexible, and slower.
  4. The build. Some filters exist only if ffmpeg was built with a library: drawtext needs freetype, subtitles needs libass, some codecs need their libraries. Test for the filters you need (ffmpeg -filters) and have a fallback.

Common stages

  • Probe every input before you use it: fps, size, duration, audio, color tags.
  • Intermediate: convert generated clips once to a 10-bit intermediate for finishing (C09·M01).
  • Proxy: a small file with the same frame rate and length, for editing (C08·M01).
  • Trim: frame accurate. Decode and re-encode to an intermediate; put -ss and -to after -i.
  • Concat: the concat demuxer with stream copy works only for identical files. For real material (different sizes, rates, or audio), use the concat filter, and conform each clip first.
  • Audio: extract, resample to 48 kHz, measure loudness (C10·M02).
  • Review images: a contact sheet of frames for reviewers and for agents that can see images (M04).

Function design

  • One job per function: trim(src, t_in, t_out, dst), make_proxy(src, dst).
  • Never overwrite an input. Refuse to overwrite an existing output unless the caller says overwrite=True.
  • Structured results: return a dict with paths, durations, sizes, and warnings.
  • Clear errors: raise an exception that contains the ffmpeg error message.
  • Tests with generated media: testsrc2 (a moving test pattern) and sine (a tone) at known sizes, rates, and lengths. Assert frame counts and durations.

Encoding settings for each stage

Choose the encoding by the job of the file, not by habit:

  • Intermediates and selects (for finishing): an intra-frame, 10-bit codec such as ProRes 422 HQ, with 24-bit PCM audio. Every frame is a keyframe, so cuts are exact and decoding is fast. Files are large: Apple's target data rate for ProRes 422 HQ at 1080p and 24 fps is about 176 Mbit/s (about 1.3 GB per minute) for natural images; the real rate depends on the content (a synthetic test pattern encoded at 63 Mbit/s in our test).
  • Proxies (for editing): H.264 at a small size and a fast preset. Same frame rate and length as the source.
  • Deliveries (for viewers): H.264 or H.265 at the spec's size, with CRF or a bitrate from the spec, yuv420p, color tags set, AAC audio (C09·M04).
  • Archive: the master in the intermediate codec, plus the stems as WAV (C10·M02). Each re-encode with a lossy codec loses a little quality. Re-encode from the intermediate, never from a delivery file.

Transcription as a stage

A transcript with word timestamps feeds captions (C08·M04), paper edits (C08·M02), dubbing (C06·M02), and search. Run it on the dialogue stem (C05·M04) with names and terms in the prompt. Store the transcript JSON next to the media.

The asset sidecar

Every generated or processed file gets a sidecar JSON file with the same name:

assets/gen/S07/S07.p2.g4.mp4
assets/gen/S07/S07.p2.g4.json
  {"prompt_log_id": "S07.p2.g4", "model": "...", "seed": 1234, "cost_usd": 0.60,
   "rights": {"status": "own", "refs": ["CHAR-MARA", "LOC-LOCKER"]},
   "tech": {"fps": 24, "width": 1280, "height": 704, "duration": 6.04, "color": {...}}}

The sidecar connects the file to the prompt log (C04·M01), the rights log (C16), the take log (C05), and search. Write it in the same stage that writes the file.

Tool walkthrough

The starter media library

import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "starter/pipeline")
import mediakit as mk
info = mk.probe("takes/S07_t04.mp4")
mk.trim("takes/S07_t04.mp4", 0.4, 4.1, "selects/S07_t04.mov")
mk.concat(["selects/S06.mov", "selects/S07_t04.mov"], "assembly.mov", fps=24)
print(mk.loudness("assembly.mov"))
mk.contact_sheet("assembly.mov", "review/assembly_sheet.png")

Run its tests: pytest -q starter/pipeline/test_mediakit.py.

Check the build of ffmpeg

ffmpeg -version | head -1
ffmpeg -hide_banner -filters | grep -E " (drawtext|subtitles|lut3d|ebur128|minterpolate) "

Transcribe as a stage

starter/tools/transcribe.py (C06·M02) writes the transcript JSON, an SRT, and dub slots. Call it on the dialogue stem.

Watch

  • FFmpeg — documentationRead the main ffmpeg tool page and the pages of the filters you use.
  • WhisperX — GitHubRead about word-level timestamps and diarization.

Worked example

Media library tests (2026-10-04, pytest -q test_mediakit.py, 6 passed in 1.0 s):

Test Generated input Assertion
probe 640 × 360, 24 fps, 2 s, with a tone size, rate, duration, audio codec
frame-accurate trim 4 s clip; trim 1.0–2.5 s exactly 36 frames, 10-bit 4:2:2
no overwrite a proxy made twice the second call raises "exists"
concat with mixed inputs 640 × 360 at 24 fps with audio + 1280 × 720 at 30 fps without audio one 640 × 360 24 fps file of 2 s with audio
loudness and errors a 3 s tone; a clip without audio a value between −30 and 0 LUFS; "no audio" error
contact sheet a 3 s clip a PNG file

The build lesson: the test machine's ffmpeg 9.0.2 had no drawtext and no subtitles filter. Two starter tools (the animatic labels and the captions) first used them and failed. Both now draw text with Pillow and use overlay, which every build has. The same version also removed -vsync (use -fps_mode) and -filter_complex_script (use -/filter_complex). Pin and record the ffmpeg version in your pipeline README.

Selects to assembly as a script:

  1. For each select: trim() with 2-frame handles → selects/S07_t04.mov.
  2. concat() all selects with conform → assembly.mov.
  3. Transcribe the dialogue stem → SRT; correct terms with the glossary.
  4. loudness() and spec_check.py → report.
  5. A sidecar JSON for every output.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/mediakit/ with your media functions (or the starter library extended), tests, and a make_assembly.py script.

  1. Run the starter library and its tests. Read the code.
  2. Add 3 functions that your project needs, for example add_handles(), burn_logo(), make_vertical(). Each with a test on generated media.
  3. Write make_assembly.py: selects CSV → trimmed clips → assembly → transcript → loudness → QC report → sidecars.
  4. Run it on your C05 selects.
  5. Run the tests in CI (for example a GitHub Actions job with ffmpeg installed). Record the ffmpeg version.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 new functions, each with a test.
  • [ ] make_assembly.py runs end to end on real selects.
  • [ ] Every output has a sidecar JSON.
  • [ ] Tests pass in CI; the ffmpeg version is recorded.

Self-check quiz

1. Why is `-ss` after `-i` (with re-encoding) used for a frame-accurate trim?

Stream copy is fast but cuts at keyframes. For edits, decode and re-encode (to an intermediate). The starter trim test checks that 1.5 s gives exactly 36 frames at 24 fps.

2. Your script uses the `subtitles` filter. It works on your laptop and fails in CI with 'No such filter'. Why?

This course's test machine (ffmpeg 9.0.2) had neither drawtext nor subtitles. The starter caption tool draws text with Pillow and uses overlay.

3. Two clips have different sizes, frame rates, and one has no audio. Why does `-f concat -c copy` fail or give a broken file?

The starter concat() conforms each input, adds silence for clips without audio, and then joins them.

4. What must a media function return?

Structured results make stages composable and testable.

5. How do you test media functions without real footage?

Generated test media make tests fast, repeatable, and free of rights questions.

6. What goes into the sidecar JSON of a generated clip?

The sidecar connects the file to its history (C04 prompt log), its rights (C16), and search.

7. Why should a function refuse to overwrite an existing output by default?

Safe defaults matter most in automated pipelines and agent tools (M03).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong make_assembly.py is short, because the functions do the work:

for row in csv.DictReader(open("selects.csv")):
    out = mk.trim(row["file"], max(0, float(row["in"]) - 2/24), float(row["out"]) + 2/24, f"selects/{row['take']}.mov")
    write_sidecar(out["path"], prompt_log_id=row["take"], tech=out)
asm = mk.concat(sorted(glob("selects/*.mov"), key=shot_order), "assembly.mov", fps=24)
L = mk.loudness("assembly.mov")
report = {"assembly": asm, "loudness": L, "qc": run_spec_check("assembly.mov", "web_1080p")}

Its README states: "ffmpeg 9.0.2; filters used: scale, pad, fps, concat, ebur128, overlay (all in the default build)." The script never writes outside selects/, assembly.mov, and reports/, and it stops with a clear message if a select file is missing, instead of making a shorter assembly without telling anybody.

The three new functions each have a test with generated media: add_handles() (asserts 2 extra frames at each end, and no handles beyond the media), burn_logo() (asserts that the logo area changed and the rest did not, with clip_diff.py), and make_vertical() (asserts 1080 × 1920 and the same frame count). The CI log shows 9 tests passing in 2.4 s. The QC report of the first real run found 2 selects at 16 fps (from the probe() data that the script checks), which were conformed before the assembly.

C12 · Orchestration and Agents

C12·M03 Build your own MCP server for media

Study time: 16 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Design tools for agents - names, descriptions, schemas, short results, actionable errors.
  2. Implement an MCP server in Python (SDK 2.x) that wraps your media functions and your queue.
  3. Add a path sandbox, dry runs, confirmation for cost, budget guards, and an audit log.
  4. Test the server at the protocol level with an MCP client, including adversarial tests.
  5. Connect it to a real agent and check the audit log against what you asked for.

Key words

MCP server tool design sandbox audit log dry run

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C12, module 03. Build your own MCP server for media. After this module, you can: 1. Design tools for agents - names, descriptions, schemas, short results, actionable errors. 2. Implement an MCP server in Python (SDK 2.x) that wraps your media functions and your queue. 3. Add a path sandbox, dry runs, confirmation for cost, budget guards, and an audit log. 4. Test the server at the protocol level with an MCP client, including adversarial tests. 5. Connect it to a real agent and check the audit log against what you asked for. An MCP server gives agents tools. Design each tool like a small API: a clear verb-object name, a description that says when to use it and what it returns, strict typed inputs, short results with IDs, and errors that say what to do next. Wrap your tested media functions and your queue. Make side effects safe: paths only inside the project, no delete tools, dry runs by default, confirmation above a cost, budget caps in the queue, and an audit log of every call. Test the server through the real protocol, including requests that it must refuse.

Learn

What an MCP server is

The Model Context Protocol (C03·M05) connects an agent (the client side) with tools and data (the server side). An MCP server publishes:

  • tools: functions the agent can call, each with a name, a description, and an input schema;
  • resources: data the agent can read, each with a URI (for example studio://budget);
  • prompts: reusable instructions (optional). The agent's model reads the tool names, descriptions, and schemas, and decides which tool to call with which arguments. So tool design is interface design for a model.

Tool design

  • Name: a verb and an object: probe_media, queue_generation, job_status.
  • Description: what it does, when to use it, what it returns, and its limits. "Without confirm=True this is a dry run."
  • Inputs: strict types and ranges. Few parameters. Use enums for choices (a spec name, not a free path).
  • Results: short JSON with the facts and the IDs that the agent can pass to other tools. Do not return large blobs; return a path.
  • Errors: say what to do next. "Unknown spec 'web'; known: broadcast_ebu_r128, reels_9x16, web_1080p." An agent can recover from that error.
  • Granularity: one tool per meaningful action. Not one tool per ffmpeg flag, and not one tool that "does everything".

Safety

An agent tool is an attack surface and a cost risk. Design for the least power:

  1. Path sandbox: resolve every path, and refuse anything outside the project root (.., absolute paths, symbolic links outside).
  2. No delete tools. Write new files only; overwrite only in a work folder.
  3. Dry run by default for anything that costs money or changes state. A real run needs confirm=True.
  4. Human approval above a limit: above a cost, the tool needs evidence of a person's approval (an approval file, a ticket, a button in your UI). The agent cannot create it.
  5. Budget guards in the queue (M01), not only in the tool, so that every path to the queue is limited.
  6. Input limits: prompt length, duration range, number of shots per call.
  7. Audit log: every call, with its arguments and a result summary, including refusals.

Implementation (Python SDK 2.x)

The current Python SDK (2.3, as of 2026-10) uses MCPServer:

from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer
mcp = MCPServer("studio", instructions="Media studio tools. Always estimate before you queue.")

@mcp.tool()
def probe_media(path: str) -> dict:
    """Technical facts of a media file: duration, size, fps, codecs, color tags."""
    return mediakit.probe(safe(path))

@mcp.resource("studio://budget")
def budget() -> str:
    return json.dumps(budget_status())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")

The SDK builds the input schema from the type hints and the description from the docstring. Older tutorials use from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP (SDK 1.x). In SDK 2.x this import fails. Pin the SDK version in your requirements, and read the migration guide when you upgrade.

Testing

  1. Protocol tests in CI: start the server as a subprocess, connect with an MCP client over stdio, list the tools, call each tool with good and bad inputs, read the resources. Assert the results.
  2. Adversarial tests: paths outside the root, costs above the caps, prompts above the length limit, the same key twice. The server must refuse each one, and log it.
  3. Interactive: the MCP Inspector lists tools and lets you call them by hand.
  4. Agent tests: give a real agent 5 tasks. Compare the audit log with what you expected it to do.

When the agent chooses a wrong tool or wrong arguments, the first fix is usually the tool description, not the agent's prompt. Descriptions are read on every call, by every client.

Tool walkthrough

The starter studio server

starter/pipeline/studio_mcp.py publishes 6 tools and 1 resource: probe_media, qc_check, contact_sheet, estimate_generation, queue_generation, job_status, and studio://budget. It uses mediakit.py (M02), genqueue.py (M01), and spec_check.py (C09·M04).

pip install "mcp>=2.3" pytest
cd starter/pipeline
pytest -q test_studio_mcp.py                      # protocol tests over stdio
STUDIO_ROOT=~/ai-video-lab python studio_mcp.py   # run it for an MCP client

Connect it to an MCP client

Most MCP clients take a server definition with a command and environment variables, for example:

{"mcpServers": {"studio": {"command": "python", "args": ["/path/to/starter/pipeline/studio_mcp.py"],
  "env": {"STUDIO_ROOT": "/path/to/ai-video-lab", "STUDIO_BACKEND": "comfy", "CONFIRM_ABOVE_USD": "2.0", "SHOT_CAP_USD": "3.0"}}}}

Check your client's documentation for the file location and the format.

A protocol test (from the starter tests)

from mcp import Client, StdioServerParameters
params = StdioServerParameters(command=sys.executable, args=["studio_mcp.py"], env=env)
async with Client(params) as c:
    tools = await c.list_tools()
    r = await c.call_tool("probe_media", {"path": "../../etc/passwd"})
    print(json.loads(r.content[0].text))   # {"error": "path '../../etc/passwd' is outside the project root; refused"}
    # r.structured_content is None here: the tools return a plain dict, with no output schema.

  • MCP — build a server (official guide)Follow the Python path. Check the SDK version: SDK 2.x renamed FastMCP to MCPServer.
  • MCP Python SDK — GitHubRead the server examples and the v2 migration notes.

Worked example

Protocol tests of the starter server (2026-10-04, MCP Python SDK 2.3.0, pytest -q test_studio_mcp.py: 6 passed in 3.0 s):

Test Steps Result
tools listed list_tools the 6 expected tool names
sandbox probe ../../etc/passwd and /etc/passwd both refused: "outside the project root"
QC qc_check on a 640 × 360 clip with the web spec pass false; failure "width" with its fix
dry run → real → repeat → approval 6 s at US$0.10/s, approval limit US$1.00 dry run with estimate US$0.60; queued; same key → "existing job"; a 12 s job (US$1.20) → needs_confirmation
shot cap four 9 s jobs (US$0.90 each) with approval files, cap US$3.00 3 queued, the 4th refused with "cap US$3.00"
audit log a good and a refused call two lines, the second with the error

The first version of this module used the SDK 1.x API (FastMCP). During the build, pip install mcp gave version 2.3.0, and the old import failed. The protocol tests caught it at once. That is why they run in CI.

An agent session (an MCP client with the studio server and an NLE server, C08·M03): Task: "Make a 15 s cut-down of the café scene from the approved selects; generate one missing insert of the cup; QC it." Audit log: job_status(S03-INS2.p1.g1) → no job; estimate_generation(S03-INS2.p1.g1, 3) → US$0.30; queue_generation(..., confirm=false) → dry run; the agent asked the user, who agreed; queue_generation(..., confirm=true) → queued; job_status → succeeded; (cut-down on the NLE server); qc_check(cutdown.mp4, reels_9x16) → FAIL loudness −12.8 LUFS with the fix; the agent reported it and stopped, as the recipe says (C08·M03).

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/studio_mcp/ with your server (or the starter server extended), protocol tests, adversarial tests, an agent session, and the audit log.

  1. Run the starter server and its tests. Read the code.
  2. Add 2 tools for your pipeline, for example make_proxy and assemble_from_selects (from M02). Write their descriptions for an agent: when to use, what it returns, limits.
  3. Write protocol tests for the new tools, with good inputs and bad inputs.
  4. Write 4 adversarial tests: a path outside the root, a cost above the cap, a too-long prompt, and a repeated key. Each must be refused and logged.
  5. Connect the server to an agent. Give it 5 tasks. Compare its audit log with your expectations. Fix tool descriptions where the agent chose a wrong tool or wrong arguments.
  6. Pin the SDK version in requirements.txt, and run the tests in CI.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 2 new tools with agent-quality descriptions and protocol tests.
  • [ ] 4 adversarial tests that pass (refused and logged).
  • [ ] Agent session: 5 tasks and the audit log, with 1 or more description fixes explained.
  • [ ] Pinned SDK and CI.

Self-check quiz

1. Which tool description helps an agent most?

The description is the agent's documentation: what it does, when to use it, what it returns, and its limits.

2. The agent asks probe_media for '../../etc/passwd'. What must the server do?

A tool is an attack surface. In the starter server test, both '../../etc/passwd' and '/etc/passwd' were refused.

3. Why does queue_generation default to a dry run?

Expensive or irreversible actions need two steps. The person stays in control of money.

4. Where is the budget cap enforced: in the tool, or in the queue?

Guards belong where they cannot be bypassed. A prompt instruction is not a guard.

5. An MCP SDK upgrade breaks your server: 'No module named mcp.server.fastmcp'. What happened, and what do you do?

This happened while this module was written (SDK 2.3.0, 2026-10). Pin dependencies and run protocol tests in CI.

6. How do you test an MCP server so that the test proves what an agent will see?

Protocol tests catch schema, serialization, and transport problems that direct function calls miss.

7. What does each audit-log line need?

The audit log is how you review what an agent did, and the evidence when something goes wrong.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Description fix (shape of a strong answer): "In task 3 the agent called assemble_from_selects with a folder of all takes, not the selects. The old description said 'Assemble clips.' The new one says: 'Assemble the SELECTED takes of one scene in shot order from selects.csv (the output of takes.py selects). Do not pass a folder of takes. Returns the assembly path and its duration.' On the rerun the agent passed the CSV."

C12 · Orchestration and Agents

C12·M04 Multi-agent production and automated quality gates

Study time: 20 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Design a multi-agent studio - writer, director, generator, editor, reviewer - with clear input and output contracts.
  2. Write the orchestrator as code (a state machine), and use LLM agents inside its steps.
  3. Place human gates where creative, legal, and cost decisions happen.
  4. Add automated gates at every stage that return PASS, FIX, or REJECT with reasons.
  5. Measure the system - cost per finished minute, human minutes per finished minute, rejection rate per gate, lead time.

Key words

orchestrator quality gate human gate LLM judge pipeline metrics

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C12, module 04. Multi-agent production and automated quality gates. After this module, you can: 1. Design a multi-agent studio - writer, director, generator, editor, reviewer - with clear input and output contracts. 2. Write the orchestrator as code (a state machine), and use LLM agents inside its steps. 3. Place human gates where creative, legal, and cost decisions happen. 4. Add automated gates at every stage that return PASS, FIX, or REJECT with reasons. 5. Measure the system - cost per finished minute, human minutes per finished minute, rejection rate per gate, lead time. A multi-agent studio splits production into roles with contracts: the writer makes a tagged script, the director a shot list and prompts, the generator clips, the editor timelines, and the reviewer scores. The orchestrator is usually code: a state machine that moves each item through the stages, calls agents and tools, and stops at gates. Human gates sit at story, legal, cost, and final approval. Automated gates check every item and return PASS, FIX, or REJECT with reasons, so the system can fix or regenerate without a person. Measure the system, not only the film.

Learn

Roles and contracts

A multi-agent studio splits the work into roles. Each role has a contract: its input, its output (with a schema), and its tools.

Role Input Output Tools
Writer brief, bible treatment, tagged script LLM
Director script, references, look bible shot list (JSON), prompts, routing LLM, prompt adapters
Generator approved shots clips, prompt-log lines, sidecars queue (M01), node-graph server (C11)
Editor selects, script timeline, versions media functions (M02), NLE tools (C08)
Reviewer any output + rubric scores, defects, verdict gates, vision LLM, QC scripts

Contracts make agents replaceable. If the director agent changes model, the shot list must still pass the same schema.

The orchestrator

The orchestrator moves each item (a script, a shot, a cut) through states: drafted → approved → generating → generated → passed → edited → delivered. Write it as code: a state machine with a database (the queue of M01 is one). It calls agents and tools in each step, applies the gates, retries within limits, and stops at human gates. Code gives predictable states, retries, budgets, and an audit trail. Use an LLM as the orchestrator only for open-ended tasks where the steps are unknown.

Human gates

Place a person where decisions need judgment or responsibility:

  • Story and legal: the treatment and the script. Real people, brands, music, claims (C16).
  • Cost: spend above a limit (the approval step of M03).
  • Final cut: rhythm, emotion, the story as a whole.
  • Publication: the last check before the public sees it, including disclosure (C16·M03). Keep human gates few and fast: a clear summary, the evidence, and a yes/no. A person who must open ten files to decide will skip the check.

Automated gates

Every stage has a gate that returns one of three verdicts, with reasons:

  • PASS: move on.
  • FIX: a known, cheap fix exists (trim a frozen tail, conform the frame rate, normalize loudness). The orchestrator applies it and checks again.
  • REJECT: regenerate (wrong identity, too short, unusable). After N rejects, the item goes to a person.

Gates per stage:

  • Script and shot list: schema validation; durations add up; every tagged character has references.
  • Shot: frame rate, length, black and frozen frames, identity against the references (C11·M03), logo and text checks.
  • Timeline: no gaps, no flash frames, durations match the plan.
  • Delivery: the full spec: format, color tags, loudness, true peak, captions (C09·M04, C10·M02); provenance signing present (C16·M03).

LLM judges

A vision-capable LLM can score clips against a rubric ("Is the photo in her left hand? Is the room the locker room?"). Treat it as a classifier: give concrete questions, calibrate it on 20 or more items that you judged yourself, and use it next to the measurable gates, not instead of them.

Metrics of the system

  • Cost per finished minute (generation, compute, licenses).
  • Human minutes per finished minute, split by gate.
  • Rejection rate per gate (which stage wastes the most?).
  • Lead time from brief to delivery. Reported numbers from Chinese AI short-drama producers: about 2 hours of human time and about ¥200 per finished minute with end-to-end tools. These are claims; measure your own.

Tool walkthrough

The starter gate runner

cd starter/pipeline
python qc_gate.py --stage shot --item takes/S07_t04.mp4 --refs refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png refs/CHAR-MARA/02_34.png --json gate.json
python qc_gate.py --stage delivery --item out/film_web.mp4 --spec web_1080p

Exit codes: 0 = PASS, 1 = FIX, 2 = REJECT, so a shell or a workflow engine can branch on them. Edit GATES in the file for your project (allowed frame rates, identity threshold, black and freeze limits).

An orchestrator step (sketch)

for shot in db.items(state="generated"):
    verdict = run_gate("shot", shot.file, refs=shot.refs)       # qc_gate.py
    if verdict == "PASS":
        db.move(shot, "passed")
    elif verdict == "FIX" and shot.fix_tries < 2:
        apply_fixes(shot); shot.fix_tries += 1                  # trim, conform; then gate again
    elif shot.regen_tries < 3:
        genqueue.submit(f"{shot.id}.p{shot.prompt_v}.g{shot.gen + 1}", shot.backend, shot.inputs, cap=shot.cap)
        db.move(shot, "generating")
    else:
        db.move(shot, "needs_person")                           # with the gate reasons

  • Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research systemRead the lessons on orchestration, delegation, and evaluation.
  • X — Claude Code can run your creative team (thread/article)Read critically: which steps still need a human?

Worked example

Gate test (2026-10-04, qc_gate.py --stage shot with one reference photo):

Clip Verdict Reasons
A 4 s, 24 fps shot of the right person PASS —
The same shot with a 1.5 s frozen tail FIX frozen picture at 2.96 s for 1.54 s
The same shot at 16 fps FIX frame rate 16.0
A shot of a different person REJECT identity 0.145

The first version of the gate showed "no score" for every clip: it wrote the identity JSON to /dev/stdout inside a captured subprocess, which failed silently. The fix was to write to a temporary file. A gate that cannot measure must not pass: it returned REJECT, and the problem was visible at once.

"Weekly series" system for a product channel: 5 videos × 45 s per week.

  • Writer: 5 scripts from a topic list → human gate (15 min).
  • Director: shots and prompts → schema gate.
  • Generator: 60 shots → shot gates: 18 % rejected (11 shots), regenerated once; 2 to a person.
  • Editor: cuts and 3 versions each → delivery gates: 4 FIX (loudness), all fixed automatically.
  • Human final gate: 20 min for 5 videos. Week 1: US$38 generation, 2.5 h human time for 3.75 finished minutes: about 40 human minutes per finished minute.

Lab

Deliverable: pipelines/studio/ with an orchestrator, gates for every stage, a run of a real mini-project, and a metrics report.

  1. Define the contracts (input, output schema, tools) for 5 roles.
  2. Write the orchestrator as a state machine (a database table of items and states). Use the queue (M01) for generation and the gates (qc_gate.py, extended) for checks.
  3. Put human gates at the script, at spend above your limit, and at the final cut. Make each gate a short summary with a yes/no.
  4. Add one LLM-judge check with a rubric of 5 concrete questions. Calibrate it on 20 clips that you judged yourself; write its agreement rate.
  5. Run a mini-project end to end: 3 videos of 30–45 s from 3 briefs.
  6. Write the metrics report: cost per finished minute, human minutes per finished minute (by gate), rejection rate per gate, lead time.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Contracts and the state machine in code.
  • [ ] Gates with PASS/FIX/REJECT and limits on loops.
  • [ ] LLM judge with a calibration result.
  • [ ] 3 delivered videos and the metrics report.

Self-check quiz

1. Why is the orchestrator usually code, not an LLM?

Use LLM orchestration for open-ended tasks. Use code for a repeatable production line.

2. Where do human gates belong?

Too many gates and nothing moves; too few and the system publishes mistakes.

3. A shot gate returns FIX for a frozen 1.5 s tail. What does the orchestrator do?

FIX means a cheap, known fix exists. REJECT means regenerate. Only repeated failures go to a person.

4. A gate scores identity 0.145 against the character references. What is the verdict and the next step?

Identity is not fixable in post. Regenerate.

5. Why must every fix loop have a limit?

Limits protect money and surface real problems (C03·M03, C05·M06).

6. An LLM 'reviewer' scores clips 1–10 for quality. How do you make its score useful?

An LLM judge is a classifier. Calibrate it like one (C03·M03).

7. Which system metric shows that automation is working?

The goal is quality output with less human time and a known cost.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Metrics report (shape of a strong answer):

Metric Value
Finished minutes 2.1 (3 videos)
Generation and compute cost US$22.40 → US$10.67 per finished minute
Human time 84 min → 40 min per finished minute
Human time by gate script 25 min, cost approvals 4 min, final cut 40 min, "needs person" items 15 min
Rejection rate shot gate 21 % (identity 14 %, frozen tails 7 % → FIX), delivery gate 0 % REJECT, 2 FIX (loudness)
Lead time brief → delivery: 1 day 3 h

"LLM judge calibration: agreed with my judgment on 17 of 20 clips (85 %). The 3 disagreements were all 'photo in the wrong hand', which the judge missed. I keep it as a filter for the room and the wardrobe, and the hand check stays with the person at the final cut."

"The shot gate saved most time: 9 identity rejects were regenerated without me. The most expensive part was still the final cut (40 of 84 minutes), which is where it should be."

C13 · Infrastructure for Generative Video

C13·M01 GPU fundamentals for generative video

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, compute at low precision, and the software stack, and which one limits a workload.
  2. Explain why video diffusion is compute-bound and LLM decoding is bandwidth-bound, with the arithmetic.
  3. Predict whether a workflow fits on a GPU (weights, encoder offload, two-expert models, activation headroom).
  4. Compare CUDA, Apple Metal/MLX, and ROCm for this work, and choose a platform per workload.

Key words

VRAM memory bandwidth tensor cores compute-bound bandwidth-bound

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C13, module 01. GPU fundamentals for generative video. After this module, you can: 1. Explain VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, compute at low precision, and the software stack, and which one limits a workload. 2. Explain why video diffusion is compute-bound and LLM decoding is bandwidth-bound, with the arithmetic. 3. Predict whether a workflow fits on a GPU (weights, encoder offload, two-expert models, activation headroom). 4. Compare CUDA, Apple Metal/MLX, and ROCm for this work, and choose a platform per workload. Three hardware numbers decide most questions: VRAM capacity (does it fit), memory bandwidth (how fast weights can be read), and compute at low precision (how fast the matrix work runs). Video diffusion processes thousands of tokens per step with the same weights, so it is limited by compute. LLM decoding produces one token at a time and reads all weights for each token, so it is limited by bandwidth. Whether a workflow fits depends on what must be in VRAM during sampling; the text encoder can be offloaded, and two-expert models need one expert at a time.

Learn

Three numbers

  1. VRAM capacity (GB): the weights in use, the activations, and the working buffers must fit. If they do not, the run fails, or it becomes much slower because parts move between system RAM and the GPU.
  2. Memory bandwidth (GB/s): how fast data moves from VRAM to the compute units.
  3. Compute at low precision (TFLOPS): how fast the tensor cores do matrix work in BF16, FP8, or FP4. Lower precision is faster when the hardware supports it. A fourth factor is the software stack: drivers, kernels, and framework support. A fast GPU with weak kernels for your model is slow.

Compute-bound and bandwidth-bound

A useful mental model: for each byte of weights that the GPU reads, how much arithmetic does it do?

  • Video and image diffusion: each step processes the whole latent, thousands of tokens (C11·M02 computed 27,280 tokens for a 5 s clip). The same weights are used for all of them. So each weight read feeds a lot of arithmetic: the work is compute-bound. More low-precision compute gives faster steps.
  • LLM decoding: each step makes one new token, and must read all weights for it. Little arithmetic per byte: the work is bandwidth-bound. An upper bound: tokens per second ≤ bandwidth / weight bytes. An 18 GB model on a 1,792 GB/s GPU: at most about 100 tokens/s.
  • Training (LoRAs, C14) needs both, plus memory for gradients and optimizer states.

Will it fit?

Add up what must be in VRAM during sampling:

  • The diffusion model: all of it, while it samples. A two-expert model (high-noise and low-noise experts) needs only one expert at a time.
  • The VAE and small extras (upscalers, LoRAs).
  • Activation headroom: grows with resolution and frame count. Start with about 6 GB and measure (C11·M02).
  • The text encoder: it runs once, at the start. It can be offloaded to system RAM before sampling. A large encoder (a 12B language model) is often bigger than you expect. If it still does not fit: lower-precision weights (FP8, 4-bit), offloading of parts of the model (much slower), or a bigger GPU.

Load time

Weights must be read from storage at every cold start: load time = weight bytes / read speed. 45 GB loads in about 7 s from a fast PCIe 4.0 NVMe drive (about 6 GB/s), about 40 s from a 10 GbE NAS, and more than 2 minutes from a typical network volume. This matters for serving (M04).

Platforms

  • NVIDIA with CUDA: the default for generative video. New kernels and low-precision paths (FP8, FP4) appear here first. Consumer cards have 24–32 GB; professional cards up to 96 GB; data-center GPUs 80–141 GB or more, mostly rented.
  • Apple silicon (Metal, MLX, PyTorch MPS): large unified memory, quiet, and very good for editing, grading, and LLMs. Diffusion runs, but usually much more slowly, and video tools often arrive later.
  • AMD (ROCm): many PyTorch models run; check each model and kernel.
  • Unified-memory boxes (128 GB in a small computer): large capacity, lower bandwidth. Good for big models that would not fit elsewhere; slower per step.

Media engines

Hardware video encoders and decoders matter for editing and delivery, not for generation: H.264, H.265, and AV1 on most GPUs; ProRes on Apple silicon.

Tool walkthrough

Plan the fit and the load time

python starter/tools/gpu_plan.py 03_i2v_wan22_5b 04_flf2v_wan22_14b 06_i2v_ltx25
python starter/tools/gpu_plan.py --weights-gb 29.2 --encoder-gb 9.5 --headroom 8
python starter/tools/gpu_plan.py --llm-gb 18
python starter/tools/gpu_plan.py 06_i2v_ltx25 --gpu "My GPU:48:960"

The tool reads the file sizes from the starter models.lock.json. It uses vendor spec-sheet numbers for VRAM and bandwidth. Add your own GPU with --gpu name:vram_gb:bandwidth_gbs.

Measure on the real GPU

  • nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.used,memory.total,utilization.gpu --format=csv -lms 500 in a second terminal during a run.
  • ComfyUI's /system_stats endpoint for VRAM (C11·M04).
  • PyTorch: torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() after a run.

Platforms and numbers (as of 2026-10)

RTX 5090: 32 GB, 1,792 GB/s. RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell: 96 GB, 1,792 GB/s. H100 SXM: 80 GB, 3,350 GB/s. H200: 141 GB, 4,800 GB/s. DGX Spark: 128 GB unified, about 273 GB/s. Apple M5 Max and M5 Ultra: up to 128 and 512 GB unified memory (see the landscape page and the vendor's spec sheet for bandwidth).

Watch

  • NVIDIA — Blackwell architecture overviewNote FP4/FP8 support and the memory numbers.
  • RTX 5090 vs 128 GB unified memory: Strix Halo, DGX Spark, Mac Studio M5 (analysis)Read the trade-off: fast 32 GB against larger, slower memory.

Worked example

Fit plan for three starter workflows (gpu_plan.py, 6 GB headroom; 2026-10-04):

Workflow Weights In VRAM while sampling 24 GB (RTX 4090) 32 GB (RTX 5090) 96 GB
03 Wan 2.2 5B I2V 18.1 GB 11.4 GB fits with encoder offload fits fits
04 Wan 2.2 14B FLF2V 35.6 GB 14.5 GB (one expert) fits with encoder offload fits fits
06 LTX-2.5 I2V 44.9 GB 24.3 GB does not fit (needs about 30 GB) fits with encoder offload fits

Load times of all weights for workflow 06: about 7 s from PCIe 4.0 NVMe, 41 s from a 10 GbE NAS, 150 s from a typical network volume.

LLM decode bound for an 18 GB model: RTX 5090 at most about 100 tokens/s; H100 about 186; DGX Spark about 15. The unified-memory box can hold much larger LLMs, but it reads them slowly.

Question: LTX-2.5 (22B) on a Mac Studio with 128 GB, or a PC with an RTX 5090?

  • Capacity: 44.9 GB of weights. The Mac holds it all; the 5090 needs the text encoder offloaded.
  • Speed: diffusion is compute-bound, and the CUDA GPU has much more low-precision compute and the most mature kernels. Expect several times faster steps on the 5090.
  • Software: day-one workflow support targets CUDA.
  • Decision: the 5090 for generation; the Mac for editing, grading, and local LLMs.

Lab

Deliverable: C13/M01/ with a fit plan for your workflows, one measured run, and a platform decision.

  1. Run gpu_plan.py for the workflows that you use. Add the GPU that you have or rent.
  2. Run one workflow on a real GPU. Measure peak VRAM and the time per step. Compare with the plan. Explain the difference.
  3. Run a local LLM (any size that fits) and measure tokens per second. Compare with the bandwidth bound.
  4. Write a platform decision for your studio: which machine for generation, editing, grading, LLMs, and training, with the numbers.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Fit plan for your workflows.
  • [ ] One measured run: peak VRAM and time, against the plan.
  • [ ] LLM tokens/s against the bound.
  • [ ] A platform decision with reasons.

Self-check quiz

1. An LLM has 18 GB of weights. A GPU has 1,792 GB/s of memory bandwidth. What is the upper bound of its decode speed?

Decode speed ≤ bandwidth / bytes per token. Real speed is lower (other reads, overheads).

2. Why is video diffusion compute-bound?

Many tokens per weight read = high arithmetic intensity. That is where low-precision tensor cores give large gains.

3. A workflow has a 10 GB model, a 7 GB text encoder, and a 1.4 GB VAE. On a 24 GB GPU with 6 GB of activation headroom, does it fit?

The text encoder runs once at the start. Moving it to system RAM before sampling frees its VRAM.

4. A two-expert 14B video model has two 14.3 GB files. Why does it fit on a 32 GB GPU?

Mixture-of-experts models with sequential experts can swap them between the two sampling phases (C11·M02).

5. A Mac with 128 GB of unified memory and a PC with a 32 GB GPU: which is better for a 22B video model that fits in both?

Capacity decides whether it runs. Compute and software decide how fast.

6. A new FP4 kernel speeds up sampling 2×, but only on the newest GPU generation. What is the lesson for planning?

Low-precision formats help only when the hardware and the software path support them.

7. Why does the speed of the disk matter for a generation service?

Load time = bytes / read speed. It adds to every cold start (M04).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Plan versus measurement (shape of a strong answer):

Run Plan Measured Why the difference
03 Wan 5B, 1280 × 704, 121 frames, RTX 5090 fits; 11.4 GB weights + about 6 GB headroom peak 23.6 GB the activations at this size need about 12 GB, not 6
03 Wan 5B, 640 × 352 same peak 15.1 GB a quarter of the tokens: about 4 GB of activations
LLM 18 GB (Q8), RTX 5090 ≤ 100 tokens/s 71 tokens/s the KV cache and other reads add traffic

"Decision: an RTX 5090 workstation for exploration with the Wan 5B and 14B workflows. LTX-2.5 batches and LoRA training on a rented 80 GB GPU. Editing and grading on the existing Mac. I set the headroom for my sizes to 12 GB in all future plans."

C13 · Infrastructure for Generative Video

C13·M02 Workstation, storage, and network design

Study time: 10 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Specify a workstation for AI video by workload - generation, editing and grading, local LLMs, training.
  2. Calculate storage needs from data rates, durations, takes, models, and caches.
  3. Design storage tiers - NVMe for work, a NAS for shared media, object storage for archive - with tested backups.
  4. Size the network for shared editing and for moving models.

Key words

NVMe NAS RAID object storage 3-2-1 backup

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C13, module 02. Workstation, storage, and network design. After this module, you can: 1. Specify a workstation for AI video by workload - generation, editing and grading, local LLMs, training. 2. Calculate storage needs from data rates, durations, takes, models, and caches. 3. Design storage tiers - NVMe for work, a NAS for shared media, object storage for archive - with tested backups. 4. Size the network for shared editing and for moving models. A studio for AI video has two kinds of load: GPU work (generation and training) and media work (editing, grading, delivery). They need different machines or at least different priorities. Storage size is data rate times duration, for every copy: takes, intermediates, proxies, renders, and models. Plan three tiers: fast NVMe for active work, a NAS for shared media with snapshots, and object storage for the archive and the offsite copy. Follow 3-2-1 and test restores. The network must carry the media of every editor at once.

Learn

Two kinds of load

An AI video studio does two kinds of work:

  • GPU work: generation and training. It needs VRAM, low-precision compute, and fast storage for weights (M01).
  • Media work: editing, grading, sound, delivery. It needs a responsive editing machine, a color-accurate monitor, fast storage for intermediates, and hardware video decoding. One machine can do both for a solo creator. A team usually separates them: a generation box (or rented GPUs) and editing machines.

Workstation by workload

Workload Priority
Local video generation GPU VRAM 32 GB or more (96 GB on professional cards); 128 GB RAM for offloading; 4 TB+ NVMe
Editing and grading 4K A modern GPU or media engine; fast NVMe; a calibrated monitor
Local LLMs Large memory (VRAM or unified) and high bandwidth
LoRA training VRAM 24–96 GB; RAM 64–128 GB; fast NVMe for datasets

Storage math

Size = data rate × duration, for every copy you keep. Data rates (Apple's ProRes white paper, 23.976 fps):

Format 1920 × 1080 3840 × 2160
ProRes 422 Proxy 36 Mbit/s 145 Mbit/s (65 GB/h)
ProRes 422 HQ 176 Mbit/s (79 GB/h) 707 Mbit/s (318 GB/h)

Convert with: GB per hour = Mbit/s × 3,600 / 8 / 1,000. H.264 web deliveries are 5–20 Mbit/s. Generated takes from APIs are small H.264 or H.265 files (a few MB each), but there are many of them.

Plan for every stage of a project:

  • takes: all generations, not only the selects (C05·M06);
  • intermediates of the selects for finishing (C09·M01);
  • proxies for editing;
  • renders and deliveries in each version and format;
  • audio: stems and the M&E as WAV (C10·M02);
  • models and caches: 15–45 GB per workflow (C13·M01), plus versions.

Storage tiers

  1. NVMe (local): the active project, caches, and the models in use. Fastest.
  2. NAS (shared): media for the team. RAID 6 or ZFS RAIDZ2 survives two failed disks: usable capacity ≈ (disks − 2) × disk size. Snapshots protect against deletions.
  3. Object storage (S3-compatible): the archive and the offsite copy. Cheap per TB; lifecycle rules move old data to colder tiers (M05).

Backups

RAID is not a backup: a deletion, ransomware, or a fire affects all disks of the array. Follow 3-2-1: 3 copies, on 2 different types of media, 1 offsite. Example: the NAS, an object-storage copy (offsite), and an offline disk. Test a restore every quarter. Measure how long it takes, and write the time into the plan.

Network

Link About Enough for
1 GbE 110 MB/s proxies, one HD intermediate stream
10 GbE 1.1 GB/s a few editors on UHD ProRes HQ (about 88 MB/s each)
25 GbE and more 2.8 GB/s and more bigger teams, fast model copies
Add up the streams of all users at the same time, plus headroom for scrubbing and copies. Remote editors use proxies or a cloud file system (M05).

Tool walkthrough

A storage plan in a few lines

rates_mbps = {"ProRes HQ UHD": 707, "ProRes HQ HD": 176, "Proxy HD": 36, "H.264 web HD": 12}
def gb(mbps, seconds): return mbps * seconds / 8 / 1000
takes  = 2400 * 0.003                      # 2,400 takes x about 3 MB (API H.264)
inter  = gb(rates_mbps["ProRes HQ UHD"], 20 * 60 * 1.3)   # 20 finished min + 30 % handles, UHD
proxy  = gb(rates_mbps["Proxy HD"], 20 * 60 * 1.3)
deliv  = gb(rates_mbps["H.264 web HD"], 20 * 60 * 6)      # 6 versions
models = 4 * 40                            # 4 workflows x 40 GB
print(round(takes + inter + proxy + deliv + models))      # GB per month

Example builds (as of 2026-10)

  • Generation box: RTX 5090 (32 GB), 128 GB RAM, 2 × 4 TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe, a 1,200 W power supply, Linux.
  • Editing and LLM machine: Mac Studio M5 Max with 128 GB unified memory and external Thunderbolt NVMe.
  • NAS: 6 × 16 TB in RAID 6 (about 64 TB usable), 10 GbE, snapshots.

Watch

  • Puget Systems — hardware recommendations for video editing and AIRead their test-based recommendations.
  • Backblaze — the 3-2-1 backup strategyRead the rule and the examples.

Worked example

Two-person studio, 20 finished minutes per month, UHD finishing:

Item Calculation Per month
Takes 2,400 takes × about 3 MB 7 GB
Intermediates 26 min (20 + 30 % handles) × 318 GB/h 138 GB
Proxies 26 min × 65 GB/h (UHD Proxy) 28 GB
Deliveries 6 versions × 20 min at 12 Mbit/s 11 GB
Stems and M&E 20 min × 4 files × 48 kHz 24-bit stereo (about 1 GB/h each) 1.4 GB
Total media about 185 GB
Models 4 workflows × about 40 GB (one time, on NVMe) 160 GB

The intermediates are 75 % of the monthly media. Plan:

  • Generation box: RTX 5090, 128 GB RAM, 8 TB NVMe.
  • Editing: Mac Studio M5 Max.
  • NAS: 6 × 16 TB RAID 6, 10 GbE: enough for more than 20 years at this rate, so the limit is the backup, not the space.
  • Archive: one object-storage folder per project (about 0.2 TB), lifecycle to a cold tier after 90 days.
  • Backup: NAS snapshots, a nightly sync to object storage, and a quarterly offline disk. A restore test of one project per quarter.

Lab

Deliverable: C13/M02/ with a workstation specification, a storage plan with calculations, a backup plan, and a restore test.

  1. Write the workloads of your studio for the next year: finished minutes per month, finishing resolution, number of versions, team size.
  2. Specify the machines (or rented capacity) for each workload, with reasons from M01.
  3. Calculate the storage per month for every stage, with the data rates and your take counts. Add models and caches.
  4. Design the tiers and the network. Check the network with the streams of all users at once.
  5. Write the backup plan (3-2-1). Do one real restore of a project folder from your offsite copy. Measure the time.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Machine specification with reasons.
  • [ ] Storage calculation per stage.
  • [ ] Tiers, network check, and backup plan.
  • [ ] A measured restore test.

Self-check quiz

1. How much storage does one hour of UHD (3840 × 2160) ProRes 422 HQ at 24 fps need?

Size = data rate × duration. Apple's table gives 707 Mbit/s for UHD 24p ProRes 422 HQ, which is 318 GB per hour.

2. A NAS has 6 disks of 16 TB in RAID 6. What is the usable capacity, roughly?

RAID 6 survives two disk failures because two disks' worth of space holds parity: (6 − 2) × 16 = 64 TB.

3. Is RAID a backup?

RAID is availability. Backup is recovery. You need both.

4. What does 3-2-1 mean?

And test the restore. An untested backup is a hope.

5. Three editors work on the same project from a NAS with UHD ProRes 422 HQ (about 88 MB/s each). Is 1 GbE enough?

Add up the streams of all users at the same time, plus headroom for scrubbing and copies.

6. Why plan 2–4 TB of fast storage only for models and caches?

The starter workflows alone are 18–45 GB each (C13·M01).

7. Generated takes are small (a 5 s H.264 clip is a few MB). Why does an AI project still need a lot of storage?

Plan for every stage: takes, intermediates, proxies, renders, deliveries, stems, and the archive.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong plan shows the calculations, not only the result, and finds the real limit:

"Our intermediates at UHD are 318 GB per hour. 12 finished minutes per month with 30 % handles: 83 GB per month. Total media about 110 GB per month. Space is not the problem; the network is: 3 editors on UHD ProRes HQ need about 265 MB/s, so 1 GbE (110 MB/s) is not enough. Decision: 10 GbE switch and NICs, or HD proxies for the two remote editors."

"Restore test: one 180 GB project from object storage over our 500 Mbit/s line took 52 minutes (the calculation said 48). The offline disk took 9 minutes. For a deadline restore, we use the offline disk first."

C13 · Infrastructure for Generative Video

C13·M03 Cloud GPU - rental, serverless, and per-output APIs

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Compare GPU rental (24/7 and on demand), serverless GPU, per-output model APIs, and hosted apps.
  2. Calculate the monthly cost of a workload on each path, per usable second, with measured inputs.
  3. Find the break-even volume between owning a GPU and paying per use.
  4. Use spot capacity safely, and keep data and models close to the GPU.

Key words

GPU rental serverless GPU per-output API break-even spot instance

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C13, module 03. Cloud GPU - rental, serverless, and per-output APIs. After this module, you can: 1. Compare GPU rental (24/7 and on demand), serverless GPU, per-output model APIs, and hosted apps. 2. Calculate the monthly cost of a workload on each path, per usable second, with measured inputs. 3. Find the break-even volume between owning a GPU and paying per use. 4. Use spot capacity safely, and keep data and models close to the GPU. There are four ways to pay for generation compute: rent a GPU by the hour (always on, or on demand), run on serverless GPUs billed per second, pay a model API per output second, or own the hardware. Each fits a different workload. The comparison needs measured inputs - GPU seconds per clip and the usable share - and the result per usable second. Always-on rental is expensive unless the GPU is busy; owning wins only at high, steady volume. Spot capacity is cheap for jobs that can restart. Keep models and data in the same region as the GPU.

Learn

Four ways to pay

  1. GPU rental: a virtual machine or container with a GPU, billed per hour. - Always on (24/7): the GPU waits for work. You pay 730 hours a month. - On demand: you start it for a session and stop it after. You pay the hours it is on, plus start, stop, and idle time.
  2. Serverless GPU: your container runs only when a job arrives; you pay per GPU second, plus cold starts (loading the container and the weights). It scales to zero when idle.
  3. Per-output APIs: the provider runs the model; you pay per output second or per image. No operations work. This is also the only way to use closed models.
  4. Own hardware: you buy it. You pay the purchase (spread over its life), the power, the space, and your time. Hosted apps (subscriptions with credits) are a fifth option for people without a pipeline. They are hard to automate.

The cost model

For one month:

  • rental 24/7 = 730 h × price per hour
  • rental on demand = busy hours × overhead × price per hour
  • serverless = (busy hours + cold-start hours) × price per hour
  • per-output API = output seconds × price per output second
  • own = purchase / months of life + busy hours / relative speed × power × electricity price

Busy hours = clips × GPU seconds per clip / 3,600. Measure the GPU seconds per clip for your workflow and size on the GPU type you plan to use (C11·M02). Divide each result by the usable seconds (generated seconds × usable share from your take log, C05·M01). That is the cost of what the edit can use.

What the numbers usually show

  • Always-on rental is expensive unless the GPU is busy most of the time.
  • On-demand rental and serverless are close for batches. Serverless is simpler to scale; rental gives full control and no cold starts during a session.
  • Per-output APIs cost more per second at volume, and nothing in operations work. At low volume, they are often the right choice.
  • Owning wins at high, steady volume over years, if one machine has enough capacity.

Break-even of owning

Owning has a fixed monthly cost (the purchase spread over its life) and a small variable cost (power). Pay-as-you-go has only a variable cost. Owning wins above the volume where the saving per clip pays the fixed cost. The number leaves out your time, space, repairs, the capacity limit of one GPU, and the risk that next year's models need more VRAM. Treat it as a starting point.

Spot capacity

Spot (preemptible) instances are cheaper and can stop at any moment. Use them for jobs that can resume: LoRA training with checkpoints every few hundred steps (C14·M02), and batch generation through a queue with retries (C12·M01). Do not use them for live sessions with a client.

Data locality

Keep models and data in the same region as the GPU. Every cold start reads tens of GB of weights (C13·M01): across regions this is slow, and it costs egress fees. Bake weights into the container image, or use a network volume in the same region (M04).

Tool walkthrough

The cost model

python starter/tools/cost_model.py --clips 1200 --gpu-s 60 --out-s 5 --usable 0.4 \
  --rent-h 2.89 --serverless-h 3.95 --api-s 0.05 --own-price 4500 --own-power-w 650 --kwh 0.30 --own-speed 0.5

The defaults are example list prices from mid-2026. Replace every price with the current price of the provider that you would use, with its date.

Providers (as of 2026-10; list prices mid-2026, check current)

  • GPU rental: RunPod (H100 about US$2.89/h; A100 community from about US$0.69/h), Lambda, and the hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure; more expensive, with more enterprise features).
  • Serverless GPU: Modal (H100 about US$3.95/h base, billed per second; region and non-preemptible multipliers), RunPod Serverless, Replicate deployments.
  • Per-output APIs: fal.ai (some video models about US$0.05 per output second; images about US$0.03), Replicate (per-second GPU billing; H100 effective about US$5.49/h), and vendor APIs (about US$0.10 per output second for some closed video models).

Watch

  • Fal.ai vs RunPod — pricing and features compared (2026)Note per-hour against per-output pricing.
  • Scale-to-zero serverless GPUs: Modal vs RunPod vs ReplicateRead the cold-start and pricing trade-offs.

Worked example

Workload: 1,200 open-model clips per month (5 s each), 60 GPU seconds per clip on an H100-class GPU, usable share 40 %. Output of cost_model.py with the default example prices (2026-10-04):

Path US$ per month US$ per usable second
Rental on demand (×1.3 overhead) 75.14 0.031
Serverless (+ 60 cold starts of 30 s) 80.98 0.034
Own GPU (US$4,500 over 3 years, half the speed, 650 W) 132.80 0.055
Per-output API (US$0.05/s) 300.00 0.125
Rental 24/7 2,109.70 0.879

"Owning beats the cheapest pay-as-you-go path above about 2,228 clips per month." At 6,000 clips per month the order changes: own GPU US$164, on-demand rental US$376, serverless US$397, API US$1,500. The owned GPU then runs about 200 hours a month (27 % of the time), so one machine still has the capacity.

Decision for 1,200 clips per month: serverless for the open model (the team can maintain a container), the vendor API for 300 premium closed-model clips (300 × 5 s × US$0.10 = US$150), and no purchase until the volume is steady above about 2,500 clips per month.

Lab

Deliverable: C13/M03/ with measured inputs, a cost comparison for your workload, a break-even analysis, and a decision.

  1. Measure the GPU seconds per clip of one workflow at your production size, on a rented GPU of the type that you would use.
  2. Take your usable share from your take log (C05).
  3. Collect current prices for each path from real providers, with the date.
  4. Run the cost model for your monthly workload, and for 3 times that workload.
  5. Write the decision per shot type (open models, closed models, training), with the numbers and what the model leaves out.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Measured GPU seconds per clip, with the GPU type and settings.
  • [ ] Current prices with dates and sources.
  • [ ] The cost table for 1× and 3× the workload.
  • [ ] A decision with the limits of the model.

Self-check quiz

1. A workload needs 20 busy GPU hours per month. Why is a 24/7 rental the most expensive choice?

In the module example: about US$2,110 per month for 24/7 against US$75 on demand for the same work.

2. Why compare paths per USABLE second?

The usable share comes from your take log (C05·M01). It changes the ranking less than it changes the budget.

3. When does a per-output API win over serverless GPUs for an open model?

Your time is a cost. At 1,200 clips per month the API cost US$300 against about US$81 serverless, a difference that may or may not pay for the operations work.

4. The cost model says owning beats pay-as-you-go above about 2,230 clips per month. What is missing from that number?

Break-even is a starting point for a decision, not the decision.

5. What is a spot (preemptible) instance good for?

Spot capacity is cheaper and can stop at any time. Design the job to resume (C12·M01, C14·M02).

6. Your models are in one region and your rented GPUs in another. What happens?

Data locality matters for large weights (C13·M01 load times).

7. Which input to the cost model must you measure yourself?

Measure on the GPU type you will rent (C11·M02 perf.csv).
