C13 · Infrastructure for Generative Video

C13·M04 Serving open models - containers, cold starts, autoscaling

Study time: 14 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Package an open video model or a ComfyUI workflow as a container service with pinned versions and a health check.
  2. Break a cold start into its parts, and reduce each one (image, weights, warm-up).
  3. Autoscale on queue depth and the age of the oldest job, with a budget limit, and scale to zero.
  4. Monitor queue time, load time, run time, VRAM, errors, and cost per output second.
  5. Secure the service - authentication, no open UI ports, secrets, isolated custom code.

Key words

container cold start autoscaling scale to zero observability

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C13, module 04. Serving open models - containers, cold starts, autoscaling. After this module, you can: 1. Package an open video model or a ComfyUI workflow as a container service with pinned versions and a health check. 2. Break a cold start into its parts, and reduce each one (image, weights, warm-up). 3. Autoscale on queue depth and the age of the oldest job, with a budget limit, and scale to zero. 4. Monitor queue time, load time, run time, VRAM, errors, and cost per output second. 5. Secure the service - authentication, no open UI ports, secrets, isolated custom code. A model service is a container with pinned versions, the model weights, and a small API in front. A cold start is the sum of starting the container, starting the runtime, loading the weights, and the first slow run; measure each part. Reduce them with weights in the image or on a volume in the same region, smaller weight formats, and a warm pool when people wait. Scale on queue depth and the oldest job's age, with a maximum set by the budget, and scale to zero when idle. Monitor each job's timings and cost, and secure the service like any API.

Learn

Two shapes of a model service

  1. A node-graph server as a service: the graph server, your API-format workflows (C11), and a thin API in front that accepts named inputs, runs the workflow, and returns a file URL.
  2. A direct model server: the model's reference code or a library pipeline behind a small HTTP API or a serverless handler. Both need: pinned versions (server, custom code, weights, drivers), a health check, structured logs, and outputs written to object storage, not to the container's disk.

The parts of a cold start

A cold start is everything that happens before the first useful run on a new worker:

  1. Schedule a GPU and pull the image. Large images take longer, unless the platform caches them.
  2. Start the runtime: Python imports and the server. In our test, the graph server of the starter kit started in 5.2 s on CPU without models.
  3. Load the weights: bytes / read speed (C13·M01). 45 GB from a typical network volume takes about 150 s; from a local NVMe drive about 7 s.
  4. First run: kernel compilation and warm-up make the first run slower than the next ones. Measure each part (log a timestamp at each stage). Then reduce the largest part.

Reduce cold starts

  • Weights in the image: a large image, but no download at start, if the platform caches images near the GPU.
  • Weights on a volume in the same region (a network volume or a model cache).
  • Smaller weights: FP8 or 4-bit formats halve or quarter the bytes to load (C01·M06).
  • A warm pool: keep 1 or more workers warm in studio hours; scale to zero at night.
  • Batching: route jobs of the same workflow to the same workers, so the model stays loaded.

Autoscaling

Scale on the signals that users feel:

  • queue depth (jobs waiting) and the age of the oldest job (how long somebody waits);
  • a maximum number of workers from the budget and the provider's quota;
  • scale to zero after N minutes without jobs. A simple rule: workers = min(max_workers, ceil(queued jobs × run time per job / target wait time)).

Throughput

Faster attention kernels, compiled models, step-distilled variants (4–8 steps), resolution tiers (preview first, final for chosen takes), and, for very large models, splitting work across several GPUs.

Observability

Log for every job: queue time, load time (0 on a warm worker), run time, peak VRAM, output seconds, the result (success, or the error type), and the cost. Dashboards: p50 and p95 wait time, error rate by type, GPU utilization, and cost per output second.

Security

  • Authentication on the API; rate limits per client.
  • No public UI ports of the graph server; keep it on a private network behind your API.
  • Secrets in a secret manager, not in the image.
  • Custom nodes and model code run with full rights: review, pin, and isolate them (C11·M01).
  • Scan images for known vulnerabilities; update base images on a schedule.

Tool walkthrough

A container for the graph server

starter/solutions/C11-M01/Dockerfile pins the ComfyUI commit and installs PyTorch for CUDA 12.8 (or CPU for tests). Models are mounted, not built in. To bake weights into an image for a serverless platform, add a stage that runs download_models.py for one workflow, and check the image size against the platform's limit.

Log the parts of a start

import time, json
t0 = time.time()
# ... start the server, wait for /system_stats ...
t_server = time.time()
# ... queue a tiny warm-up job of the workflow, wait for it ...
t_warm = time.time()
print(json.dumps({"server_s": round(t_server - t0, 1), "load_and_warmup_s": round(t_warm - t_server, 1)}))

Plan the load time

python starter/tools/gpu_plan.py 06_i2v_ltx25      # load time of all weights per storage type

Platforms (as of 2026-10)

Serverless GPU platforms (Modal, RunPod Serverless, Replicate deployments) offer image caching, network volumes, warm pools ("min workers"), and scale to zero. Check each platform's image-size limit, volume speed, and cold-start features.

Watch

  • Modal — examples (ComfyUI and diffusion as a service)Find a ComfyUI or video-model example; note how the weights are cached.
  • RunPod — Serverless documentationRead about workers, cold starts, and network volumes.

Worked example

Cold start plan for workflow 06 (LTX-2.5 I2V, 44.9 GB of weights) on a serverless 80 GB GPU (a calculation; replace the numbers with your measurements):

Part Network volume (about 0.3 GB/s) Weights in a cached image / local NVMe (about 6 GB/s)
Schedule + image 15 s 25 s (bigger image)
Server start 5 s (measured on CPU: 5.2 s) 5 s
Load weights 150 s 7 s
First-run warm-up 20 s 20 s
Total cold start about 190 s about 57 s

A run of this workflow is about 60–120 s. With the volume, a cold start costs more than a run: for interactive work, keep 1 worker warm; for batches, put weights in the image.

Service "ltx25-i2v":

  • Image: CUDA base + PyTorch + the pinned graph server + workflow 06 + weights (one workflow per image).
  • Handler: input {image_url, prompt, seed, duration_s}; output: an MP4 in object storage and a signed URL.
  • Scaling: min workers 1 from 09:00 to 19:00, 0 at night; max 6; scale up when the oldest job waits more than 60 s.
  • Dashboard: wait time p95, load time (should be 0 on warm workers), run time, errors by type, cost per output second.

Lab

Deliverable: infra/model-service/ with a container, a deployed service, a cold-start report, a load test, and a dashboard.

  1. Package one workflow (or one model) as a container with pinned versions and a health check.
  2. Deploy it on a serverless GPU platform (or on a rented GPU with your own small API).
  3. Measure a cold start in its parts. Make one change that reduces the largest part, and measure again.
  4. Run a load test: 20 jobs in a burst. Record the scaling, the wait times, and the cost.
  5. Build a dashboard (or a report from the logs) with the per-job fields.
  6. Check the security: no open UI port, authentication on the API, secrets out of the image.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Container with pinned versions; a deployed endpoint.
  • [ ] Cold start in parts, before and after one change.
  • [ ] Load-test results (scaling, p95 wait, cost).
  • [ ] Dashboard or report; security checklist done.

Self-check quiz

1. A cold start takes 150 s. The container starts in 10 s, the server in 5 s, and the first run is 20 s slower than later runs. Where are the other 115 s, and what is the fix?

Load time = bytes / read speed (C13·M01). Measure each part before you optimize.

2. When do you keep a warm pool of at least 1 worker?

A warm worker costs money every hour; a cold start costs a person's time. Choose per time of day.

3. On which signal do you autoscale a generation service?

GPU jobs are long. Queue depth and waiting time tell you if users wait too long.

4. Why batch similar jobs on one worker?

Route jobs of the same workflow to the same workers.

5. Your ComfyUI server is reachable on a public IP, port 8188, without authentication. What is the risk?

A generation server is a powerful remote-execution service. Treat it like one.

6. Which per-job fields does the dashboard need?

With these you can find the slow part, the expensive part, and the failing part.

7. Why pin the versions of the server, the custom nodes, and the weights in the image?

Autoscaling starts new workers at any time. They must be identical (C11·M04).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Cold start report (shape of a strong answer):

Part Before (volume) After (weights in image)
Schedule + image pull 12 s 41 s (cached after the first pull: 9 s)
Server start 6 s 6 s
Load weights (18 GB, workflow 03) 64 s 4 s
First-run warm-up 18 s 18 s
Total 100 s 37 s (warm image cache)

"Load test: 20 jobs at once, max 4 workers. p95 wait 6 min 20 s, because each worker ran 5 jobs one after another. With max 8 workers: p95 wait 3 min 10 s, the same total cost (the jobs are the same; only the parallel time changes). The cost per output second was US$0.011 at 74 % GPU utilization."

"Security: the graph server listens only on the container's private network; the API needs a token; the outputs are private in object storage with 1-hour signed URLs."

C13 · Infrastructure for Generative Video

C13·M05 Cloud media services, cost control, and secure operations

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Use cloud services for review, shared storage, asset management, and delivery.
  2. Define a project's infrastructure as code, and destroy it after delivery.
  3. Control cost with budgets, alerts, tags, lifecycle rules, and generation caps.
  4. Report cost per finished minute by component.
  5. Protect client data, secrets, and model access with a written data rule per project.

Key words

infrastructure as code lifecycle rule budget alert least privilege data classification

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C13, module 05. Cloud media services, cost control, and secure operations. After this module, you can: 1. Use cloud services for review, shared storage, asset management, and delivery. 2. Define a project's infrastructure as code, and destroy it after delivery. 3. Control cost with budgets, alerts, tags, lifecycle rules, and generation caps. 4. Report cost per finished minute by component. 5. Protect client data, secrets, and model access with a written data rule per project. Cloud services carry the rest of the production: review with frame-accurate comments, shared storage for remote editors, object storage with signed links for clients, and a database of assets. Define each project's infrastructure as code, so that it can be built in minutes and destroyed after delivery. Control cost with budgets and alerts, tags on every resource, lifecycle rules for temporary data, and caps in the generation queue. Write a data rule for every project: which data may go to which vendor. Give every service only the rights it needs.

Learn

Cloud media services

  • Review and approval: reviewers comment on exact frames, compare versions, and approve. The comments go back into the editor's timeline in some tools.
  • Shared storage for remote editors: cloud file systems stream media on demand, so editors do not download whole projects; or a cloud NAS.
  • Object storage and delivery: buckets for masters and deliveries; signed URLs that expire for clients; a CDN for public delivery.
  • Asset management: a database of assets with their metadata. The sidecar JSON of C12·M02 is the start of it: prompt-log ID, rights, tech data, approvals.

Infrastructure as code

Define each project's resources in code: buckets with lifecycle rules, the queue, the workers or serverless functions, roles and policies, budgets and alerts, dashboards. Benefits:

  • the same environment in minutes for the next project;
  • changes are reviewed like code;
  • after delivery you destroy the compute, and nothing keeps costing money.

Cost control

  • Generation caps in the queue, per shot and per project (C12·M01). This is the first line: it refuses before money is spent.
  • Budgets and alerts per project (for example at 50 %, 80 %, and 100 %). This is the second line: it warns after money is spent.
  • Tags on every resource: project, client, environment, owner.
  • Lifecycle rules: delete temporary generations after 30 days; move archives to a cold tier after 90 days.
  • A monthly report: cost per finished minute by component (generation, compute, storage, licenses, review tools).

The review loop

Review is where most project time goes after generation. Make it fast and exact:

  • One link per version, with the version number in the file name and on screen (a small burned-in label on drafts).
  • Frame-accurate comments: a reviewer clicks a frame and writes the note there. Comments with timecodes can go back into the timeline as markers, where an agent or an editor works through them (C08·M03).
  • Clear states: draft, in review, changes requested, approved. Only approved versions go to delivery.
  • Expiring access: a signed link or a review project that closes after delivery.

Agents and vendors in the cloud

Agents (C12) and external vendors also need access, and each needs a boundary:

  • an agent's tools get the same least-privilege roles as a worker, and every call is logged;
  • a vendor gets only the files that the data rule allows, through a prefix or a signed URL, never the whole bucket;
  • revoke access when the project ends, in the same code that destroys the compute.

Data and security

  • A data rule per project: which files may go to which vendor. Client material (unreleased products, real people, contracts) often stays in your own storage and goes only to open models on your GPUs. Check each vendor's terms about training on your data (C16).
  • Least privilege: every service gets only the rights it needs. A worker reads its queue and the models and writes only to its output prefix.
  • Encryption at rest and in transit (usually default; check it).
  • Secrets in a secret manager; rotate keys; never in images or code.
  • Audit logs for people and agents (C12·M03).

Tool walkthrough

A lifecycle rule and a budget (Terraform, AWS example)

resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "project" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.project.id
  rule {
    id     = "temp-generations"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter { prefix = "gen/tmp/" }
    expiration { days = 30 }
  }
  rule {
    id     = "archive"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter { prefix = "archive/" }
    transition {
      days          = 90
      storage_class = "DEEP_ARCHIVE"
    }
  }
}

The same ideas exist on every cloud. Write the budget alert in the same code, with the project tag as its filter.

Cost per finished minute from your logs

python starter/tools/takes.py report                     # generation cost per model and shot (C05)
python starter/tools/promptlog.py cost --since 2026-10-01   # image and other generation costs (C04)
python starter/pipeline/genqueue.py status               # queued and spent jobs (C12)

Add the cloud bill per project tag, and divide by the finished minutes.

Services (as of 2026-10)

Review: Frame.io (Adobe), Blackmagic Cloud (Resolve). Shared storage: cloud file systems for media. Storage and delivery: S3-compatible object storage on any major cloud.

Watch

  • Frame.io — review and approval (help center)Look at frame-accurate comments and version stacks.
  • Terraform — getting startedOnly if you have not used infrastructure as code before.

Worked example

Project "Camera Ad Q4" (30 s ad, 6 versions):

  • Infrastructure as code creates: a bucket with two lifecycle rules (temporary generations deleted after 30 days; archive to a cold tier after 90), the queue and a serverless worker, a budget of US$400 with alerts at 50/80/100 %, and a review project.
  • Data rule: the client's product CAD files and photos stay in our bucket and are used only with open models on our serverless GPUs. Only generated backgrounds and public material go to external APIs.
  • Cost report:
Component US$
Generation (API takes, from takes.py report) 61.40
Serverless GPU (open-model takes and LoRA) 38.20
Storage and egress 4.10
Music license 49.00
Review tool (share of the month) 15.00
Total for 0.5 finished minutes (30 s master; versions are cut-downs) 167.70 → US$335 per finished minute
  • After delivery: the archive moved to a cold tier; the worker and the queue destroyed with terraform destroy; the bucket kept for the archive only.

Lab

Deliverable: infra/project/ with infrastructure as code, a data rule, a budget with alerts, a cost report, and a clean-up check.

  1. Write the infrastructure of one project as code: a bucket with lifecycle rules, the queue and a worker, roles with least privilege, a budget with alerts, and tags.
  2. Write the project's data rule: data classes, and which vendor may receive which class.
  3. Run a small production through it (your C12 mini-project).
  4. Make the cost report per component, and the cost per finished minute.
  5. After delivery, destroy the compute. Check (in the console or with the CLI) that no tagged compute resource remains.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Infrastructure as code with lifecycle rules, budget, and tags.
  • [ ] Data rule.
  • [ ] Cost report per component and per finished minute.
  • [ ] Clean-up check after delivery.

Self-check quiz

1. Why define a project's infrastructure as code?

Forgotten GPU workers and buckets are a common, silent cost.

2. What does a lifecycle rule do?

Storage is cheap per GB and expensive when nobody cleans it up.

3. Where must the generation budget be enforced?

Cloud alerts arrive after the money is spent. The queue refuses before.

4. A client's unreleased product photos must not go to any external model API. What is the practical rule?

Classify data per project. Check each vendor's terms on training with your data (C16).

5. How do you share a draft with a client securely?

Expiring, scoped links limit the damage if a link leaks.

6. Which tags belong on every cloud resource?

Without tags, you cannot report cost per project or find what to delete.

7. What is least privilege for a generation worker?

If the worker is compromised, the damage stays small.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong submission's data rule is a table that a teammate can follow without asking:

Data class Examples May go to
Client confidential product CAD, unreleased photos, contracts own bucket; open models on own or serverless GPUs only
Personal data faces and voices of real people, consent records own bucket; vendors only with consent and a data agreement
Generated, internal takes, drafts own bucket; external APIs allowed
Public press photos with license, public-domain material anywhere, with a rights-log line

C14 · Fine-Tuning and Self-Hosting

C14·M01 Datasets - collect, clean, caption, consent

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Collect 15–60 training images (or short clips) that cover angles, light, expressions, outfits, and places.
  2. Clean the data - duplicates, blur, size, watermarks - and crop consistently with aspect buckets.
  3. Write captions that describe what varies and leave the identity to the trigger word.
  4. Document the source and the consent or license of every item, and write a dataset card.
  5. Check a dataset automatically before you pay for training.

Key words

LoRA dataset trigger word caption dataset card

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C14, module 01. Datasets - collect, clean, caption, consent. After this module, you can: 1. Collect 15–60 training images (or short clips) that cover angles, light, expressions, outfits, and places. 2. Clean the data - duplicates, blur, size, watermarks - and crop consistently with aspect buckets. 3. Write captions that describe what varies and leave the identity to the trigger word. 4. Document the source and the consent or license of every item, and write a dataset card. 5. Check a dataset automatically before you pay for training. A LoRA learns what the dataset shows and what the captions do not explain. Collect images that vary in everything except the subject: angles, light, expressions, clothes, places. Remove duplicates and soft images, and keep the sizes high enough. Start every caption with the trigger word, describe everything that varies, and do not describe the identity features that the trigger should carry. Record the source and the consent or license of every item. A dataset check before training finds most problems in seconds; a bad dataset costs a training run.

Learn

What a LoRA learns

A LoRA (low-rank adapter) is a small set of extra weights added to a base model (C01·M06). Training adjusts only these weights, so that the model makes your subject when the prompt has the trigger word. The LoRA learns:

  • what is the same in all images (the subject, and anything else that never changes);
  • what the captions do not explain. Both rules decide how you build the dataset.

What to collect

  • Character: 20–40 images. Front, three-quarter, side, back; close-ups and full body; 5 or more expressions; 3 or more outfits; 3 or more light setups; plain and real backgrounds. Sources: your character sheet (C04·M03) and new scenes made from it, or photos of a real person who consents.
  • Product: 15–30 images. All sides, close-ups of the logo and materials, and the product in several contexts.
  • Style: 30–60 images with the style across many different subjects, so that the LoRA learns the style, not the subjects.
  • Video LoRAs: short clips (2–5 s) for a motion or a camera style. For identity, still images often generalize well to motion (practitioner reports).

Vary everything except the subject

If all images share a background, a light, or a lens, the LoRA learns it as part of the subject. New scenes then drift toward it. Vary the places, the light, the shot sizes, and the clothes. Keep only the subject constant.

Clean

  • Duplicates: near-identical images over-weight one view. Keep one.
  • Soft images: blurred or out-of-focus images teach softness.
  • Small images: below about 768–1024 px on the short side, detail is lost.
  • Artifacts and watermarks: extra fingers, warped features, text, logos. The LoRA learns them.
  • Wrong details: an image where the scar is on the wrong side teaches the wrong side.

Crop and buckets

Crop each image to the subject with a little space. Do not force everything to a square. Most trainers sort images into aspect-ratio buckets, so portraits, full bodies, and wide shots keep their framing.

Captions

Each image has a caption file with the same name. Rules:

  1. Trigger first: a rare token, for example mrx_mara.
  2. Describe what varies: clothes, place, light, shot size, action. "mrx_mara, wearing hospital scrubs, standing in a corridor, cold fluorescent light, medium shot."
  3. Do not describe the bound identity features (her bob, her scar) if you want the trigger to carry them. Words that explain a feature take it away from the trigger. Use a vision LLM to draft captions. Read and correct every one.

How many images

More is not always better. 20–40 good, varied images of a character usually beat 200 similar ones. Each new image should add something: an angle, a light, an outfit, an expression, a place. If a new image adds nothing, it only adds weight to what you already have.

Rights and the dataset card

Record the source and the license or consent of every item, with the date. For a real person, the consent record must cover training a likeness model (C16·M02). Write a dataset card: purpose, counts by type, sources, licenses and consent, known gaps or biases, and allowed uses. The model registry (M03) links to it.

Tool walkthrough

Folder layout

training/mara/
  01_front.png   01_front.txt     "mrx_mara, in an olive raincoat, plain grey studio, soft light, close-up"
  12_corridor.png 12_corridor.txt "mrx_mara, wearing hospital scrubs, hospital corridor at night, ..."
  rights.csv       file,source,license_or_consent,date
  CARD.md

Check before training

python starter/tools/dataset_check.py training/mara/ --trigger mrx_mara --bound "black bob,scar" --min-side 1024

It checks caption pairs, the trigger, size, blur, near duplicates (a perceptual hash), bound features in captions, and the rights lines.

Trainers (as of 2026-10)

musubi-tuner (kohya-ss) for Wan, HunyuanVideo, and FLUX.2; AI Toolkit (ostris); Diffusers training scripts; hosted LoRA trainers (for example fal). Each reads image + caption pairs; check its dataset config format.

Watch

  • musubi-tuner — dataset configuration docs (GitHub)Read the dataset config section (images and videos, buckets, captions).
  • Hugging Face — dataset cardsUse the structure for your own dataset card.

Worked example

Dataset check test (2026-10-04, public-domain portraits, trigger mrx_arm, bound feature "short brown hair"). Six planted problems in six images:

Planted problem Found as
a 480 × 600 copy PROBLEM: smaller than 768 px on the short side
a caption that starts with "a man…" PROBLEM: does not start with the trigger
an image without a caption PROBLEM: no caption file
an image without a rights line PROBLEM: no line in rights.csv
a blurred copy WARN: looks soft (sharpness 3 < 60)
"short brown hair" in a caption WARN: mentions the bound feature
a resaved copy of the front view WARN: near duplicates (0 of 64 bits differ)

The mirrored copy was not flagged as a duplicate. A mirror is a different image to the hash, but for a character with a scar on one side it is a wrong image. Check mirrors by eye.

Mara dataset: 32 images (24 from the sheet + 8 new scenes); outfits: raincoat 10, scrubs 12, casual 10; 6 places; 4 light setups. Captions by a vision LLM, then edited: the words "black bob" and "scar" removed from all captions. Trigger mrx_mara. Card: "Fictional character; all images generated by us (models listed in the prompt log); no real-person likeness; allowed uses: this series."

Lab

Deliverable: training/<subject>/ with images, captions, rights.csv, CARD.md, and a dataset-check report.

  1. Choose one subject: your main character (from your sheet) or a product that you own.
  2. Collect 20–40 images. Vary place, light, shot size, clothes, and expression.
  3. Clean them: remove duplicates, soft images, artifacts, and wrong details. Crop with buckets in mind.
  4. Write the captions: trigger first, describe what varies, leave the bound features out. Correct every LLM draft.
  5. Write rights.csv and CARD.md.
  6. Run dataset_check.py until there are no problems. Review every warning and write what you did about it.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 20–40 images with captions, varied in everything except the subject.
  • [ ] rights.csv complete; consent records for any real person.
  • [ ] CARD.md with purpose, counts, sources, gaps, and allowed uses.
  • [ ] Dataset check: 0 problems; each warning answered.

Self-check quiz

1. All 30 images of your character were made on the same grey background. What will the LoRA learn?

A LoRA learns what is constant in the data. Vary everything that should not belong to the subject.

2. Every caption says 'a woman with a short black bob'. What is the problem?

Caption what varies (clothes, place, light, shot). Leave the identity features to the trigger.

3. Three images are near duplicates of the front view. Why remove two of them?

Balance the views. The dataset check finds near duplicates with a perceptual hash.

4. Can you train a character LoRA on photos of a real person from social media?

A likeness model of a real person needs consent (C16·M02). Public is not the same as permitted.

5. Which images do you collect for a product LoRA?

Shape, logo, and materials must hold from every angle. Context images teach the model to place it.

6. Why use aspect-ratio buckets instead of cropping everything to a square?

Most trainers group images by aspect ratio into buckets. Keep the framing that your shots need.

7. What must the dataset card say?

The card is the documentation and the rights record of the model (C14·M03, C16).

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Dataset summary (shape of a strong answer):

Dimension Values (count)
View front 8, three-quarter 10, side 6, back 3, over-the-shoulder 5
Shot size close-up 9, medium 14, full body 9
Outfit raincoat 10, scrubs 12, casual 10
Place grey studio 6, locker room 7, corridor 6, street 5, café 4, kitchen 4
Light soft studio, fluorescent night, daylight window, warm practical

"The first check found 3 near duplicates of the front view (from re-generations) and 2 soft images. I removed them and made 3 new three-quarter views. The warnings for 'scar' in 4 captions: removed the word. One mirrored side view had the scar on the wrong side; I deleted it. Final: 32 images, 0 problems, 1 accepted warning (a short caption for a plain close-up, where little varies)."

The card states the gap: "No profile close-ups in daylight; expect weaker identity there." That gap is what M03's eval checks first.

C14 · Fine-Tuning and Self-Hosting

C14·M02 Train image and video LoRAs

Study time: 16 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain the main LoRA settings - rank, learning rate, steps, resolution, batch, precision - and what each changes.
  2. Train an image LoRA and a video LoRA on open models, locally or on rented GPUs, with checkpoints.
  3. Render fixed eval prompts at every checkpoint, and read the fidelity-flexibility curve.
  4. Choose a checkpoint by a rule with measurements, and log every experiment with its cost.

Key words

LoRA rank learning rate checkpoint overfitting sample grid

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C14, module 02. Train image and video LoRAs. After this module, you can: 1. Explain the main LoRA settings - rank, learning rate, steps, resolution, batch, precision - and what each changes. 2. Train an image LoRA and a video LoRA on open models, locally or on rented GPUs, with checkpoints. 3. Render fixed eval prompts at every checkpoint, and read the fidelity-flexibility curve. 4. Choose a checkpoint by a rule with measurements, and log every experiment with its cost. Training a LoRA adjusts a small set of extra weights until the base model makes your subject on the trigger word. Rank sets how much the LoRA can store, the learning rate how fast it changes, and the steps how long it trains. Save checkpoints often, and render the same eval prompts with the same seeds at each one. Identity rises with the steps; then flexibility falls and the subject starts to appear without the trigger. Choose the checkpoint where identity is strong, new prompts still work, and nothing leaks. Log the data version, settings, checkpoints, scores, and cost of every run.

Learn

What training does

Training shows the model your images with their captions, many times. At each step, the trainer measures how far the model's prediction is from the training image (the loss) and adjusts only the LoRA weights a little to reduce it (C01·M01). The base model stays frozen. After enough steps, the trigger word makes the subject.

The main settings

Setting What it changes Starting point: image LoRA (character) Video LoRA
Rank Capacity of the adapter; file size 16–32 16–64
Learning rate Size of each update 1e-4 (AdamW) 1e-4 to 2e-4
Steps Training length 1,500–3,000 2,000–5,000
Resolution Detail learned; VRAM; time about 1024 px, with buckets 480–720p, short clips
Batch size Images per step 1–4 1
Precision VRAM and speed BF16, or an FP8 base model FP8 base model, block swap if needed

These are starting points from practice, not rules. Change one setting at a time and compare checkpoints.

Overfitting and the checkpoint curve

As training goes on:

  1. Identity rises: the face, the hair, and the marks hold better.
  2. Then flexibility falls: the LoRA starts to copy training details (the same coat, the same room, the same expression), even when the prompt asks for something else.
  3. Leakage grows: the subject appears in prompts without the trigger, and other people start to look like it. So save a checkpoint every 250–500 steps, and choose one from the middle of the curve.

The eval set

Fix 6–12 prompts and their seeds before training:

  • in: like the training data (identity check);
  • out: new clothes, new places, new styles (flexibility check);

  • no trigger: the same kind of scene without the trigger (leakage check). Render all of them at every checkpoint. Score:

  • fidelity: the identity score on trigger prompts (face embeddings, C11·M03; for products, an image-similarity score);

  • leakage: the identity score on no-trigger prompts (should be low);
  • flexibility: prompt adherence on "out" prompts, scored 1–5 by you or by a calibrated LLM judge (C12·M04). Identity scores cannot see it.

Where to train

  • Local: a 24–96 GB GPU. Image LoRAs fit on 24 GB with FP8 base models; video LoRAs often need block swapping (moving parts of the model in and out of VRAM).
  • Rented GPU: a container with the trainer, the dataset and the output on persistent volumes, checkpoints on the volume. Spot capacity works if the trainer resumes from checkpoints (C13·M03).
  • Hosted trainers: upload the dataset, set a few parameters, receive the LoRA. Least control, no operations. Typical times (practitioner reports): an image LoRA in under 1 hour on one high-end GPU; a video LoRA in several hours.

The experiment log

For every run: the dataset version (and its check report), the base model and its hash, every setting, the checkpoints, the eval scores per checkpoint, the choice and its reason, the time, and the cost. A folder with a JSON file per run is enough; an experiment tracker adds charts.

Tool walkthrough

Trainers (as of 2026-10)

  • musubi-tuner (kohya-ss): Wan, HunyuanVideo, FLUX.2; FP8 base models; block swap for video.
  • AI Toolkit (ostris): FLUX-family image LoRAs and more.
  • Diffusers training scripts: a reference implementation.
  • Hosted trainers (for example fal's Wan 2.2 trainer). Read the trainer's current documentation for the config format and the recommended values for your base model. They change with each model release.

Render and score checkpoints

eval/
  prompts.json        [{"id": "in01", "kind": "in"}, {"id": "out01", "kind": "out"}, {"id": "nt01", "kind": "no_trigger"}]
  ckpt-1200/in01.png  ckpt-1200/out01.png  ...
  ckpt-1800/...
  flex.csv            checkpoint,prompt,score    (1–5 for "out" prompts)

Render the images with your LoRA loaded in the starter workflows (C11: add a LoRA loader after the model loader), or with the trainer's sample feature. Then:

python starter/tools/lora_eval.py eval/ --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/02_34.png --grid eval/grid.png

The grid has one row per checkpoint and one column per prompt.

Watch

  • fal — Wan 2.2 LoRA trainer (hosted training playground)See which parameters a hosted trainer exposes.
  • musubi-tuner — Wan / HunyuanVideo / FLUX.2 training docsRead the Wan training document; note the FP8 and block-swap options.

Worked example

Evaluator test (2026-10-04, synthetic checkpoints from public-domain portraits; reference: a photo of person A):

Checkpoint Fidelity Leakage Flex (from flex.csv) Pass
ckpt-0500 (identity mostly missing) 0.135 0.135 4.5 no
ckpt-1000 (identity on trigger prompts only) 0.676 0.135 4.0 yes
ckpt-1500 (person A in every image, also without the trigger) 0.676 0.676 2.5 no

"choose ckpt-1000 (highest flexibility among passing checkpoints)". The overfit checkpoint has the same fidelity as the right one; only the leakage and flexibility columns separate them.

Mara image LoRA: rank 32, learning rate 1e-4, 2,400 steps, 1024 buckets, 32 images; a rented 48 GB GPU, 38 minutes, about US$2. Checkpoints: 1,200 weak identity; 1,800 strong and flexible; 2,400 strong, but the raincoat in every image → choose 1,800. Mara video LoRA on Wan from the still images: rank 32, 3,000 steps, 3.5 h on an 80 GB GPU, about US$10–15. Identity holds in I2V and T2V with the trigger.

Lab

Deliverable: training/<subject>/runs/ with configs, logs, eval renders, grids, the evaluator output, chosen checkpoints, and costs.

  1. Write the eval set before training: 4 in, 4 out, 4 no-trigger prompts with fixed seeds.
  2. Train one image LoRA on your checked dataset (M01), with checkpoints every 300 steps.
  3. Train one video LoRA (or use a hosted trainer if you have no GPU).
  4. Render the eval set at every checkpoint. Score flexibility for the "out" prompts in flex.csv.
  5. Run lora_eval.py. Choose a checkpoint by its rule; write if you agree with it, and why.
  6. Log both runs: data version, settings, checkpoints, scores, choice, time, cost.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Two trained LoRAs with checkpoints.
  • [ ] Eval renders and a grid per run.
  • [ ] Evaluator table and the chosen checkpoint with a reason.
  • [ ] Experiment logs with costs.

Self-check quiz

1. Identity is weak at step 1,200, strong and flexible at 1,800, and at 2,400 the raincoat appears in every image, also in prompts for scrubs. Which checkpoint, and why?

This is the classic curve: identity rises, then flexibility falls. Choose before the fall.

2. Without the trigger word, half of the eval images show your character. What does it mean?

No-trigger prompts in the eval set measure leakage. A useful LoRA leaves other prompts alone.

3. What does a higher LoRA rank do?

Start at 16–32 for a character. Raise it only if fine details do not hold.

4. Why render the same prompts with the same seeds at every checkpoint?

Fixed seeds turn the checkpoint series into an experiment.

5. You train on a spot instance, and it stops at step 2,100 of 3,000. What makes this harmless?

Design training to resume (C13·M03).

6. Your identity score is high at every checkpoint, but images for 'in a café' still show the locker room. What does the score miss?

Measure fidelity, leakage, and flexibility. One number is not enough.

7. What must the experiment log of a run contain?

Without a log, you cannot repeat a good run or explain a bad one.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Run log (shape of a strong answer):

{"run": "mara-img-r32-lr1e4-v3", "dataset": "mara v3 (32 images, check: 0 problems)",
 "base": "flux-2-klein-base-4b.safetensors sha256 9c5fed22…", "rank": 32, "lr": 1e-4, "steps": 3000, "save_every": 300,
 "gpu": "rented 48 GB", "minutes": 44, "cost_usd": 2.35,
 "eval": {"ckpt-1500": {"fidelity": 0.52, "leakage": 0.14, "flex": 4.3},
          "ckpt-2100": {"fidelity": 0.61, "leakage": 0.17, "flex": 4.0},
          "ckpt-2700": {"fidelity": 0.64, "leakage": 0.41, "flex": 2.9}},
 "choice": "ckpt-2100", "reason": "passes fidelity >= 0.5 and leakage <= 0.3; best balance; 2700 leaks (Leo looks like Mara)"}

The log is short, but it answers every later question: which data, which base model, which settings, what it cost, and why this checkpoint.

The second run (the video LoRA) has the same fields. Its log also records the block-swap setting that made it fit in 48 GB, and one failed start: "step 0: out of memory at 720p with batch 2 → 480p, batch 1".

"The evaluator chose ckpt-1500 (highest flex). I chose ckpt-2100: its fidelity on the 'out' prompts was 0.58 against 0.44, and the profile shots in C11·M03 failed most often. I changed the rule for this character: fidelity on 'out' prompts ≥ 0.5." The disagreement is useful: it shows which number the project depends on, and the rule now says so.

C14 · Fine-Tuning and Self-Hosting

C14·M03 Evaluate, quantize, and serve adapted models

Study time: 22 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Evaluate a LoRA for fidelity, flexibility, leakage, and compatibility with other LoRAs and with the production workflows.
  2. Measure what the LoRA adds to the C11·M03 character pipeline, against references only.
  3. Combine several LoRAs and choose their strengths with tests.
  4. Serve LoRAs per request on a quantized base model, and keep a model registry with versions, hashes, evals, and rights.

Key words

LoRA evaluation leakage LoRA strength model registry adapter serving

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C14, module 03. Evaluate, quantize, and serve adapted models. After this module, you can: 1. Evaluate a LoRA for fidelity, flexibility, leakage, and compatibility with other LoRAs and with the production workflows. 2. Measure what the LoRA adds to the C11·M03 character pipeline, against references only. 3. Combine several LoRAs and choose their strengths with tests. 4. Serve LoRAs per request on a quantized base model, and keep a model registry with versions, hashes, evals, and rights. A LoRA is ready for production when it passes an eval set - fidelity, flexibility, and leakage - and when it improves the real pipeline. Measure the gain: run the weakest shots of the character pipeline again with the LoRA and compare identity scores and rejection rates. Combine LoRAs with tested strengths; two characters in one frame need regions or separate passes. Serve LoRAs per request on a quantized base model, and cache them. A registry records every adapter with its hash, base model, eval results, rights, and allowed uses.

Learn

Two levels of evaluation

  1. The eval set (M02): in, out, and no-trigger prompts at fixed seeds. It answers: does the LoRA hold identity, follow new prompts, and leave other prompts alone?
  2. The pipeline test: the real workflow, at the real sizes, angles, and lighting. It answers: does the LoRA make production better? Both are needed. A LoRA can pass the eval set and still fail at the angles that the story needs.

The pipeline test

In C11·M03 you chose the 2 shots where identity was weakest with references only. Now:

  1. Add a LoRA loader to the start-frame workflow (and, for a video LoRA, to the video workflow).
  2. Run the same shots with the same seeds and settings, with and without the LoRA.
  3. Compare: the median identity score, the minimum, the rejection rate over 5 tries, and the cost per accepted shot.
  4. Decide: use the LoRA for this character, for these shot types, at this strength.

Compatibility checks

  • Strength: test 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0. Identity LoRAs usually work at 0.8–1.0, style LoRAs at 0.4–0.7.
  • Combinations: a character LoRA with a style LoRA; two character LoRAs. Two identity LoRAs over the whole frame compete and mix faces. Use regional prompts or masks, or generate each character separately and composite them (C09·M03).
  • Base model version: a LoRA adapts specific weights of one base model. On another version, re-run the eval, or retrain.

Quantize and serve

  • The base model in FP8 or 4-bit (C01·M06) to fit the GPU and load faster.
  • LoRAs in BF16; they are small (tens to hundreds of MB).
  • The service (C13·M04) keeps the base model loaded, loads LoRAs on demand, caches the recent ones, and applies them per request with a strength: {"lora": "mara_v4", "strength": 0.9}.
  • Hosted alternative: some per-output APIs accept a LoRA URL per request.

When a LoRA is not worth it

A LoRA costs data work, training, evaluation, and maintenance (a new base model means a new LoRA). Use references only when:

  • the subject appears in few shots, or only from the front;
  • references already pass the identity gate in most tries (C12·M04);
  • the project is short and the base model may change soon. Train a LoRA when the subject appears in many shots, at many angles, over a long series, or when references fail at the angles the story needs.

Monitor in production

Keep the identity gate (C11·M03, C12·M04) on every shot, also with the LoRA. Watch the rejection rate per character per week. A rising rate means something changed: a new base model version, a new kind of shot, or a strength that is too low for a new workflow.

The registry

A registry is the source of truth for adapters. Each entry:

  • ID and version, the file hash;
  • the base model and its version;
  • a link to the dataset card (M01);
  • the eval results and the pipeline-test results;
  • rights and consent, with the consent record;
  • allowed uses (internal only, client X only, this series only);
  • an expiry date if the consent or license expires. The service reads the registry and refuses an adapter that is expired or not allowed for the project.

Tool walkthrough

Add a LoRA to a starter workflow

In the ComfyUI editor, add a LoraLoaderModelOnly node between UNETLoader and the next node that takes the MODEL, set the LoRA file and the strength, and export the API format again (C11·M01). Add the strength to the map file, for example "lora_strength": "<node id>.strength_model".

Measure with and without

python starter/solutions/C11-M03/character_shot.py --shot shots/S09.json --char-ref refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png \
  --char-ref refs/CHAR-MARA/03_side.png --place-ref refs/LOC-LOCKER/wide.png --line audio/S09.wav --out ab/S09_refs/
# then the same with the LoRA workflow (copy of 02 with the LoRA loader) -> ab/S09_lora/
python starter/tools/lora_eval.py eval/ --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/01_front.png --ref refs/CHAR-MARA/02_34.png

A registry entry

- id: mara_v4
  file: loras/mara_v4.safetensors
  sha256: 3f1c…
  base: flux-2-klein-base-4b.safetensors (sha256 9c5fed22…)
  dataset_card: training/mara/CARD.md
  eval: {fidelity: 0.61, fidelity_out: 0.58, leakage: 0.17, flex: 4.0, checkpoint: ckpt-2100}
  pipeline_test: {shots: [S07, S09], identity_median: [0.50, 0.62], reject_rate: [0.6, 0.2]}
  rights: {status: own, note: "fictional character, generated references"}
  allowed_uses: ["The Camera (series)"]
  strength: {single: 0.9, two_shot: 0.8}
  expires: null

Watch

  • Hugging Face — Diffusers: load and combine LoRAs (adapters)Read how to load several adapters and set their weights.
  • fal — LoRA inference for open video models (docs)Look at how hosted APIs accept LoRA URLs per request.

Worked example

Mara LoRA v3 → v4:

  • v3 eval: fidelity median 0.68 (threshold 0.6) ✓; flexibility 85 % of out prompts rated 4 or 5 ✓; leakage: 0 of 10 no-trigger prompts show Mara ✓; but 3 of 10 out prompts show the training locker room → retrain with more varied backgrounds (v4).
  • v4 eval: same scores; the locker room in 0 of 10.
  • Combined with Leo's LoRA: faces merge at 1.0 / 1.0 → regional prompts at 0.9 / 0.9 ✓.
  • Registry updated; the service loads v4.

Pipeline test on the weak shots of C11·M03 (S07 head turn, S09 profile; 5 tries each, the same seeds):

Shot References only: median / min / rejects With LoRA v4 (0.9): median / min / rejects
S07 (MCU, head turn) 0.58 / 0.41 / 2 of 5 0.63 / 0.55 / 0 of 5
S09 (profile MS) 0.50 / 0.31 / 3 of 5 0.62 / 0.49 / 1 of 5

(This table shows the shape of the result; your numbers come from your own runs.)

Decision: LoRA v4 at 0.9 for every Mara shot with a profile or a head turn; references only for frontal close-ups, where the gain was small.

Lab

Deliverable: training/eval/, ab/ (the pipeline test), infra/lora-service/ (or a hosted LoRA API setup), and registry.yaml.

  1. Run the full eval set on your LoRAs from M02 (lora_eval.py). Fix one problem that you find (retrain, more varied data, or a strength change) and evaluate again.
  2. Run the pipeline test: your 2 weakest shots from C11·M03, 5 tries each, with and without the LoRA. Compare the median, the minimum, the rejects, and the cost per accepted shot.
  3. Test 3 strengths, and one combination (with a style LoRA or a second character).
  4. Serve the LoRA per request (your service from C13·M04, or a hosted API that accepts LoRAs). Make 10 production shots through it.
  5. Write the registry entries for your LoRAs, including rights and allowed uses. Make the service refuse a LoRA that is not in the registry for the project.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Eval report and one documented fix.
  • [ ] Pipeline test with and without the LoRA, and a decision.
  • [ ] Strength and combination results.
  • [ ] 10 shots through the service; registry entries; the refusal works.

Self-check quiz

1. The LoRA passes the eval set. How do you know it is worth using in production?

The question is the gain in the real workflow, at the real angles and sizes.

2. Mara's LoRA at 1.0 and Leo's at 1.0 in one two-shot: their faces mix. What are the options?

Two identity LoRAs over the whole frame compete. Limit each to its region.

3. Why test strengths of 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0?

Typical: identity LoRAs 0.8–1.0, style LoRAs 0.4–0.7. Measure for yours.

4. A LoRA trained on one base model version is loaded on a newer version. What can happen?

A LoRA belongs to a base model and version. Record both in the registry.

5. How does a service apply different LoRAs per request without reloading the base model?

LoRAs are small. The base model is large. Load the large part once.

6. What must a registry entry contain?

The registry is the source of truth for what may be used where (C16).

7. The client's consent for a likeness LoRA expires on 2027-06-30. What does the pipeline do after that date?

Rights rules must be enforced in code, not only in a document.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Pipeline test summary (shape of a strong answer): "With the LoRA at 0.9, rejects on the 2 weak shots fell from 5 of 10 to 1 of 10. The cost per accepted shot fell from US$0.92 to US$0.66, so the LoRA (US$2.35 to train, 3 hours of my time for data and eval) pays back after about 9 weak shots. The series has about 40 such shots."

Strength Fidelity (out prompts) Leakage Flex
0.6 0.49 0.12 4.4
0.8 0.56 0.15 4.2
1.0 0.61 0.22 3.6

"0.9 for single shots; 0.8 with regional prompts for two-shots with Leo. The service read registry.yaml and refused leo_v1 for the client project 'Camera Ad Q4', because its allowed uses list only the series."

About this course

AI-native production is not only about one film. It makes 100 versions, 20 languages, and a weekly series possible. This course builds the systems for that, and connects them to what audiences actually watch.

File Use

localize.py Voice, fit check, mix over M&E, loudness, and captions per language (M02)

C15 · Video at Scale

C15·M01 Templates and data-driven variants

Study time: 14 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Design a video template with fixed and variable parts, and text slots with length limits.
  2. Generate variants from a data table, with validation of every row before any render or generation.
  3. Cache by input hash, so a re-run renders only what changed.
  4. Control quality at scale with automated gates on every file and human review of a sample.
  5. Design A/B variant sets that change one variable, and read the result with a significance test.

Key words

template variant input hash cache A/B test minimum detectable effect

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C15, module 01. Templates and data-driven variants. After this module, you can: 1. Design a video template with fixed and variable parts, and text slots with length limits. 2. Generate variants from a data table, with validation of every row before any render or generation. 3. Cache by input hash, so a re-run renders only what changed. 4. Control quality at scale with automated gates on every file and human review of a sample. 5. Design A/B variant sets that change one variable, and read the result with a significance test. A template fixes the structure, timing, look, and legal parts of a video, and leaves named slots for what changes: the hook, the product shot, the text lines, the voice, the language, the offer. A data table fills the slots, one row per variant. Validate every row first (columns, text lengths, files), cache outputs by a hash of their inputs, and gate every file. A/B tests compare variants that differ in one column, with a sample size planned before the test; most small differences in short tests are noise.

Learn

Why variants

AI-native production makes many versions cheap: one ad for 4 products, 3 hooks, and 6 languages is 72 videos. Without a system, 72 videos are 72 chances for a typo, a wrong logo, a cut-off line, or a missing disclosure. A template and a data table turn them into one design plus 72 rows of data.

Template design

Split the video into:

  • fixed parts: shot structure and timing, the look, the logo, legal text, the music bed, the end card;
  • variable slots: the hook shot, the product shot, text lines, the voice line, the background, the language, the offer, the call to action. Each text slot has a length limit from its layout (and from the safe zone, C08·M04). Each media slot has a naming rule, for example shots/hook_{hook_type}_{product_id}.mp4. Keep text as separate layers in the master; burned-in text cannot be localized (M02).

The data table

One row per variant: variant_id, product_id, audience, language, hook_type, offer_text, cta, voice_id, .... Validate every row before you spend anything:

  • every column that the template uses exists;
  • every text fits its slot limit (in its language);
  • every media file exists (or is queued for generation);
  • banned words and legal terms are checked against a list.

The pipeline

For each row:

  1. Generate the missing variable shots through the queue (C12·M01). Many rows share shots (the same product hook in 2 languages), so generate each unique shot once.
  2. Make the voice lines (C06·M01) and check their fit.
  3. Assemble the segments, burn the text, mix the voice over the music.
  4. Run the gates: spec, loudness, identity, logo, captions (C12·M04).
  5. Write a manifest line: variant ID, file, input hash, and the row.

Cache by input hash. Compute a hash of everything that goes into a file: the template, the row, and the input media. If a file with that hash exists, skip it. A re-run after a one-line change renders only the changed rows.

Generate each unique shot once

Count the unique inputs before you generate. 24 variants of 4 products × 3 hooks × 2 languages need only 12 hook shots, because the language changes the voice and the text, not the picture. A pipeline that generates per row pays twice for half of them.

Quality at scale

  • Automated gates on 100 % of the files.
  • People review every flagged file and a random sample (for example 5 %). Sampling finds the problems that no gate checks yet; add a gate for each new problem type.

A/B tests

An A/B test compares two variants that differ in one column (the hook type, or the voice, or the offer). Before the test, decide:

  1. the metric (CTR, 30-second retention, completion);
  2. the minimum effect worth acting on (for example +20 % relative);
  3. the sample size needed to detect it. Then run to that size and read the result with a significance test. With p ≥ 0.05 the honest result is "no difference found". Do not stop the test the first time it looks good; repeated checks raise false positives far above 5 %.

Sample sizes are larger than intuition suggests. At a 3 % click-through rate, detecting a +20 % change needs about 13,900 impressions per variant.

Tool walkthrough

Render variants

python starter/pipeline/variants.py template.json variants.csv --out variants/ --dry-run   # validate only
python starter/pipeline/variants.py template.json variants.csv --out variants/

The template format is in the script's help. Text is drawn with Pillow inside the default safe zone; voice is mixed over the music bed; outputs are named <variant_id>_<hash>.mp4 with a manifest.json. The script also reports which columns vary, and warns when a set changes more than one.

For large programs, code-based rendering frameworks (for example Remotion) or NLE templates with automation do the same job with more layout control.

Plan and read a test

python starter/pipeline/ab_report.py --plan --rate 0.03 --min-effect 0.2
python starter/pipeline/ab_report.py --a 120,4000 --b 152,4000

Watch

  • Meta — business help center (search 'dynamic creative')Note how the platform tests creative variants.
  • X — AI UGC ads workflow at US$2–4 each (practitioner article)Note which parts are templated.

Worked example

Variant test (2026-10-04): 5 rows (2 products × 2 hook types, plus one with a long offer line), a 3-segment vertical template (hook 2 s, product with offer text 3 s, end card with CTA 2 s), voice over a music bed.

5 variants; columns that vary: product_id, hook_type, offer_text
note: for an A/B test, change one column per test set; this set is a matrix, not a clean A/B test
PROBLEM v04: offer_text is 47 characters (limit 32): 'Ice cold for 24 hours and longer than you think'
rendered 4, from cache 0, rejected 1

The 4 valid variants rendered in 2.9 s (1080 × 1920, 7 s, H.264 + AAC). A second run: rendered 0, from cache 4.

Reading tests (ab_report.py; the numbers match statsmodels' z-test):

A B Relative p Result
120/4,000 (3.00 %) 152/4,000 (3.80 %) +27 % 0.048 a real difference, just
120/4,000 (3.00 %) 135/4,000 (3.38 %) +13 % 0.340 no difference found; 13,914 per variant needed for +20 %

Camera campaign: 4 products × 3 hooks × 2 languages = 24 variants. 12 unique hook shots and 8 voice lines generated (about US$40). 24 files rendered in 20 minutes; gates flagged 2 (a German line too long; an end card under the UI zone). The A/B test changed only the hook type, with 15,000 impressions per variant planned.

Lab

Deliverable: C15/M01/ with a template, a data table of 12 or more rows, the rendered variants, a manifest, gate reports, a sample-review note, and a test plan.

  1. Design a template for a 15–30 s piece of your project: fixed parts, slots, text limits, naming rules.
  2. Write a data table with 12 or more rows (at least 2 products or topics, 2 hooks, 2 languages).
  3. Validate with --dry-run. Fix every problem.
  4. Generate the missing shots through your queue; render all variants; run the gates on all files.
  5. Review every flagged file and a 10 % random sample. Write what the sample found that the gates did not.
  6. Plan one A/B test: the single variable, the metric, the minimum effect, the sample size. If you can, run it and read it with ab_report.py.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Template and data table; validation passes.
  • [ ] Variants rendered with a manifest; a re-run uses the cache.
  • [ ] Gate reports and the sample-review note.
  • [ ] A test plan with a calculated sample size (and a result, if run).

Self-check quiz

1. Which parts of an ad belong in the fixed part of the template?

Fixed parts carry brand and legal consistency. Variable parts are the things you want to test or localize.

2. A German offer line is 47 characters in a slot designed for 32. When should the pipeline find this?

Validation is free; a wasted render or a published cut-off line is not. In the module test, the row was rejected before rendering.

3. Why cache outputs by a hash of all their inputs?

In the module test, the second run rendered 0 and took all 4 valid variants from the cache.

4. Your variant set changes the product, the hook, and the offer at once. B wins. What did you learn?

A matrix of variants is fine for production. For a test, change one column.

5. A has 3.00 % CTR and B 3.38 % on 4,000 impressions each. Is B better?

Small differences on small samples are mostly noise. Plan the sample before the test.

6. What does a person review when 200 variants are rendered?

Gates on 100 %, people on a sample and the exceptions.

7. Why not stop an A/B test on the day it first shows p < 0.05?

Decide the metric, the minimum effect, and the sample size before the test.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Sample review (shape of a strong answer): "Gates passed 22 of 24 and flagged 2. The 10 % sample (3 files) found one problem that no gate checks: in v17 the offer text covers the product's logo. New gate: the text box must not overlap the logo box of the product shot (stored in the product sheet). Re-run: the gate flagged v17 and v18; I moved the text slot up for that product."

Test plan:

Item Value
Variable hook_type (result-first vs question) — everything else the same
Metric 3-second hold rate (viewers still watching at 3 s)
Base rate 42 % (last month)
Minimum effect +10 % relative
Sample size about 2,200 views per variant (ab_report.py --plan --rate 0.42 --min-effect 0.1)
Stop rule run until both variants have 2,200 views; no early stop

"Result: 46.7 % vs 42.3 % on 2,300 views each (+10 % relative, at the minimum effect): p = 0.002. Result-first hooks become the default for this series."

C15·M02 Localization pipeline at scale

Study time: 12 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Prepare a master for localization - M&E stem, clean transcript with slots, text layers, glossary, style guides.
  2. Automate translation, voice, fit check, mix over M&E, loudness, captions, and on-screen text per language.
  3. Route review by risk, and send lines that do not fit back to adaptation, not to a faster voice.
  4. Report cost, turnaround, and error rates per language.

Key words

localization M&E glossary style guide risk-based review

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C15, module 02. Localization pipeline at scale. After this module, you can: 1. Prepare a master for localization - M&E stem, clean transcript with slots, text layers, glossary, style guides. 2. Automate translation, voice, fit check, mix over M&E, loudness, captions, and on-screen text per language. 3. Route review by risk, and send lines that do not fit back to adaptation, not to a faster voice. 4. Report cost, turnaround, and error rates per language. Localization at scale is the dubbing pipeline of C06·M02 run for many languages at once. It starts with a master made for it: a complete M&E stem, a corrected transcript with time slots, text kept as separate layers, a glossary, and a style guide per language. Each language then runs the same automated steps: adapt the lines to their slots, voice them, check the fit, mix them over the M&E, normalize, add captions and on-screen text. Review effort follows risk: regulated claims get a full human review, social clips automated checks and a sample.

Learn

Localization starts in the master

A video that was not made for localization is expensive to localize. Make the master kit at the end of every project:

  • M&E stem: music and effects, complete, with no dialogue (C10·M02).
  • Transcript with slots: the corrected dialogue with start and end times per line (C06·M02).
  • Text layers: on-screen text as separate graphics, with a list of every text and its timecode.
  • Glossary: names, product terms, and phrases that must not be translated or must be translated one way.
  • Style guide per language: formality, units, date and number formats, brand names, caption rules.

The steps per language

  1. Adapt each line to its slot (C06·M02): a character limit from the slot length and the speaking rate of the target voice, the glossary, the style guide, and the scene context. An LLM can do it; a fluent person reviews it.
  2. Voice each line: a cloned voice with consent, or a chosen voice per language.
  3. Check the fit: up to about 10 % too long can be sped up; more must go back to step 1. A faster voice is the wrong fix.
  4. Mix every line at its slot start over the M&E.
  5. Normalize the mix to the delivery target (C10·M02).
  6. Lip sync the speaker shots where the mouth is readable (C06·M02).
  7. Captions in the language, timed to the slots, following the style guide.
  8. On-screen text: replace the text layers; re-render.
  9. Gates: spec, loudness, captions, and fit (C12·M04).

Review by risk

Risk Examples Review
High legal, medical, financial claims; safety; regulated markets fluent human, full review
Medium brand ads, product explainers fluent human spot check + automated checks
Low social clips, internal content automated checks + a back-translation sample

Lines that do not fit

A line that is too long for its slot has three fixes, in this order:

  1. Adapt the line again with the limit and the reason ("+70 % against a 3.0 s slot; at most 42 characters"). Most lines fit after one round.
  2. Open the slot: if the picture allows it, extend the shot or move the next line later in the edit (a small change in the master edit, applied to all languages).
  3. Split the line across a cut, if the speaker is off screen. A voice that is sped up by more than about 10 % sounds wrong in every language. Do not use it as a fix.

On-screen text and right-to-left languages

Text layers must be checked in every language: longer words (German), different scripts (Japanese, Chinese), and right-to-left layout (Arabic, Hebrew), which can also change the direction of graphics and lower-thirds. Plan the text boxes with room for about 30 % longer text.

Scale effects

At 10–20 languages, small errors repeat. Every error that review finds should become a rule: a glossary entry, a style-guide line, or a gate. Measure per language: cost, turnaround, errors found in review, and the re-work rate.

Tool walkthrough

The starter localization script

python starter/pipeline/localize.py --video master.mp4 --me me.wav --lines lines.json --langs es,de --out loc/

lines.json holds each line's slot and its adapted translations (from transcribe.py and your adaptation step). The default voice backend is the macOS system voices, for timing drafts only. For deliveries, use --tts cmd --tts-cmd '...' with your voice service. Per language the script writes the video, an SRT file, and report.json with the fit of every line and the loudness.

Tools (as of 2026-10)

Hosted dubbing (ElevenLabs, HeyGen, Rask, and others) does the whole chain in one product. Use the same QC on their output: fit, terms, tone, lips, loudness.

Watch

  • HeyGen vs ElevenLabs vs Rask vs Dubverse — dubbing compared (2026, vendor blog)Note the criteria; plan your own QC tests.
  • W3C — WebVTT captions formatReference for caption files.

Worked example

Localization test (2026-10-04): an 8 s master, an M&E stem, and 3 lines with adapted translations in Spanish and German. System voices; the run took 4.6 s for both languages.

Line Slot Spanish speech Fit German speech Fit
L01 "Every photo showed tomorrow." 1.8 s 1.68 s −7 % ✓ 1.97 s +10 % ✓ (sped up to fit)
L02 "Except mine." 1.0 s 0.86 s −14 % ✓ 0.84 s −16 % ✓
L03 "I took this photo an hour ago, and now it is real." 3.0 s 5.09 s +70 % ✗ 3.92 s +31 % ✗

Both versions: 2 of 3 lines fit; the mix over the M&E normalized to −14.0 LUFS (true peak −1.8 dBTP in Spanish, −1.0 in German); an 8.0 s MP4 with H.264 and AAC; captions in each language. The Spanish L03 had been translated with extra words ("…completamente real, aquí mismo, en esta habitación"); the report sends it back to adaptation with its slot.

Explainer (3 min) → 12 languages: about 2 hours of compute, about US$15–25 per language in API costs (example rates); 4 high-risk languages (regulated markets) with a full human review; turnaround 2 days instead of 3 weeks.

Lab

Deliverable: C15/M02/ with the master kit, 3 language versions, reports per language, and a pipeline report.

  1. Make the master kit for one finished piece: M&E (check it plays with no gaps), transcript slots, text layers and their list, glossary, style guides for 3 languages.
  2. Adapt the lines for 3 languages with slot limits. Review them (a fluent person for at least one language).
  3. Run the pipeline (the starter script or your own). Re-adapt every line that does not fit until all fit.
  4. Replace the on-screen text in every language.
  5. Assign a risk level and do the matching review. Record every error found.
  6. Report per language: cost, time, errors, re-work.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Master kit complete.
  • [ ] 3 language versions; all lines fit; loudness on target.
  • [ ] Review records by risk level.
  • [ ] Pipeline report per language.

Self-check quiz

1. Which master deliverable makes localization possible without a new mix of everything?

Effects that were only in the dialogue recording must be moved to the M&E before localization (C10·M02).

2. On-screen text was burned into the master. What does that cost in localization?

Plan for localization in the edit: text as graphics layers, with a list of text and timecodes.

3. The Spanish version of L03 is 70 % longer than its slot. The pipeline speeds lines up by at most 10 %. What happens to L03?

In the module test, L03 did not fit in Spanish (+70 %) or German (+31 %); both were listed for re-adaptation.

4. Which content needs a full review by a fluent human?

Review effort should follow the cost of an error.

5. What belongs in a style guide per language?

A style guide turns many small decisions into rules that translators and LLMs can follow.

6. Why measure the loudness of every language version?

In the module test, both versions were normalized to −14.0 LUFS after the voice was mixed over the M&E.

7. Which metric shows that the pipeline is getting better?

Track what review finds. Each recurring error becomes a glossary entry, a style-guide rule, or a gate.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Pipeline report (shape of a strong answer):

Language Risk Lines First fit After re-adaptation Review errors Cost Time
es-ES medium 24 21 24 1 (regional word) US$6.10 40 min
de-DE medium 24 19 24 2 (formality, a term) US$6.40 55 min
ja-JP high 24 22 24 3 (honorifics, a claim, a unit) US$7.20 + 2 h review 1 day

"Every error became a rule: 'taquilla' in the es-ES glossary; 'du' in the de-DE style guide; units in metric with the imperial value in brackets for ja-JP captions of the product sheet. The second video in the series had 1 review error in total."
