C15 · Video at Scale

C15·M03 Publishing, platform specs, and the analytics loop

Study time: 14 h · Level 4

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Publish videos with correct specs, metadata, thumbnails, captions, and AI disclosure.
  2. Use platform APIs for upload and scheduling, and store the platform ID with the asset.
  3. Read click-through rate, retention curves, and engagement, and map drops and bumps to shots.
  4. Feed analytics back into the hook library, the treatment template, pacing rules, and the routing table.

Key words

retention curve click-through rate platform API AI disclosure analytics loop

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C15, module 03. Publishing, platform specs, and the analytics loop. After this module, you can: 1. Publish videos with correct specs, metadata, thumbnails, captions, and AI disclosure. 2. Use platform APIs for upload and scheduling, and store the platform ID with the asset. 3. Read click-through rate, retention curves, and engagement, and map drops and bumps to shots. 4. Feed analytics back into the hook library, the treatment template, pacing rules, and the routing table. Publishing is the last gate: the file must meet the platform's spec, carry clear metadata, a tested thumbnail, captions, and the AI disclosure that the platform and the law require. Platform APIs upload and schedule, and the platform's video ID goes into the asset record. After release, click-through rate shows how well the thumbnail and title promise; the retention curve shows where viewers leave or rewatch. Map those moments to shot IDs, compare like with like, and turn each finding into a rule for the next production.

Learn

Publish correctly

Publishing is the last gate of the pipeline (C12·M04). Check:

  • Spec per platform: aspect ratio, maximum length, resolution, frame rate, audio (spec_check.py, C09·M04).
  • Metadata: a title with a clear promise, a description with context, chapters, credits, and tags.
  • Thumbnail: one clear face or object, high contrast, few words. The first seconds of the video must keep its promise.
  • Captions: an uploaded caption file (SRT or VTT) in each language (C08·M04, C15·M02).
  • AI disclosure: the platform's altered or synthetic content setting where required, a visible label where the law or the platform requires it, and C2PA content credentials in the file where supported (C16·M03).

Platform APIs

Most platforms offer APIs to upload, set metadata, schedule, and read analytics. Use them for series and variants:

  • store your credentials in a secret manager (C13·M05);
  • after upload, store the platform's video ID with your asset ID;
  • read analytics on a schedule into the same database. The join of platform data with production data (the shot list, the prompt log, the costs) is what makes the loop useful.

Read the data

  • Click-through rate (CTR): the share of people who saw the thumbnail and clicked. It measures the thumbnail and the title.
  • Retention curve: the share of viewers still watching at each second. A steep drop marks a weak moment; a bump marks a rewatched moment.
  • Average view duration and the share at fixed points (3 s, 30 s, the end).
  • Engagement: comments, shares, saves. Compare like with like: the same series, format, length, audience, and time of year. Small samples mislead (C15·M01).

Map moments to shots

A drop at 0:22 is only useful when you know what is at 0:22. With the shot list and its durations, every second maps to a shot ID. Typical findings:

  • a steep drop in the first 3–5 s: the hook does not keep the promise, or it starts too slowly;
  • a drop at a cut: a confusing cut or a broken continuity (C02·M04);
  • a drop before the end card: the payoff came too early, or the end is too long;
  • a bump: a strong or unclear moment; watch it to decide.

Watch for false lessons

Analytics can mislead:

  • Small samples: three videos are not a pattern (C15·M01).
  • Different traffic: a video shown on the home feed and one found by search have different viewers.
  • Seasonal effects: a holiday week changes all numbers.
  • Several changes at once: a new hook and a new thumbnail in the same video cannot be separated. Write each finding with its sample size and the conditions, and test it again before it becomes a fixed rule.

Close the loop

Once a month, review the series: three findings, each with its data. Write each one into the tools that make the next video:

  • the hook library (hook types with their measured hold rates);
  • the treatment template and pacing rules (C03·M02);
  • the routing table (which model for which shot type, C05·M06);
  • the thumbnail rules. Agents (C12) that write scripts and shot lists read these files, so the findings reach production automatically.

Tool walkthrough

Find the drops and map them to shots

python starter/pipeline/retention.py retention.csv --shots shots.json

Export the retention curve from the platform's analytics as time_s,pct. shots.json is your shot list with durations.

Upload with an API (YouTube example)

The YouTube Data API videos.insert method uploads a video with its metadata; the response contains the video ID. Store it:

{"asset_id": "camera_ep03_v2", "platform": "youtube", "platform_id": "<video id>", "published": "2026-10-04T18:00:00Z",
 "variant": "hook=result", "cost_usd": 41.20}

Other platforms (TikTok Content Posting API, Meta Graph API) have their own upload flows and limits; read their current documentation and review rules before you automate posting.

Watch

  • YouTube Help — audience retention in YouTube AnalyticsLearn to read the retention curve and key moments.
  • YouTube Help — disclosing altered or synthetic contentRead when disclosure is required.

Worked example

Retention test (2026-10-04, a 60 s curve with three planted moments, mapped to a 5-shot list):

start 100 %, end 46 % at 60 s; typical drop 0.60 points/s
  held at 3 s: 90 %
  held at 30 s: 61 %
steep drops: 3 s -9.0 (15x typical) S01 | 4 s -9.0 (15x typical) S01 | 22 s -5.0 (8.3x typical) S03
bumps (rewatching): 41 s +2.5 S05

The tool found all three moments and named their shots: a weak hook in S01, a problem in S03 at 22 s, and a rewatched moment early in S05.

Series of 8 explainers: average CTR 3.1 %; a steep drop at 0:04 in 6 of 8. Change: start with the result image (hook type "result first", C02·M05) and cut the intro. The next 4 videos: the first steep drop moved to 0:20; average view duration +35 %. The hook library now has: "result-first: 3-second hold 61 % (n = 4) against 47 % for question hooks (n = 8)".

Lab

Deliverable: C15/M03/ with publishing checklists, the asset records with platform IDs, analytics exports, a retention analysis per video, and a monthly review.

  1. Publish (or prepare for publishing, if you cannot publish publicly) 3 videos of your project with spec checks, metadata, thumbnails, captions, and disclosure.
  2. Upload with an API (or record each manual step that the API would replace). Store the platform IDs with the asset records.
  3. After at least 7 days, export CTR and retention for each video.
  4. Run retention.py with each video's shot list. Write what is at each steep drop and each bump.
  5. Write the monthly review: 3 findings with data, and the change in each tool (hook library, template, routing, thumbnail rules).

Result checklist

  • [ ] 3 publishing checklists, all passed (including disclosure).
  • [ ] Asset records with platform IDs.
  • [ ] Retention analysis per video, mapped to shots.
  • [ ] Monthly review with 3 rule changes.

Self-check quiz

1. The retention curve loses 18 points between second 2 and second 4, against a typical 0.6 points per second. What is the likely problem?

A steep early drop is the most common finding. Test a result-first hook (C02·M05) in the next video.

2. A bump in the curve at 0:41 means what?

Bumps mark the moments that viewers care about. Look at the shot before you decide.

3. Video A has 5.1 % CTR, video B 3.2 %. A is a short, B a 10-minute explainer. What can you conclude?

Benchmarks come from comparable videos, and small samples mislead (C15·M01).

4. Where does the platform's video ID go after upload?

The join between the platform data and your production data is what makes the loop work.

5. Your video shows a realistic person who does not exist, saying things in a news-like style. What must you do on a platform that has a synthetic-content setting?

Realistic synthetic people and events need disclosure (C16·M03).

6. Which thumbnail rule is supported by most platform guidance and testing?

Generate options (C04) and test them with the platform's thumbnail testing where it exists.

7. After 8 videos you find: 'result-first hooks keep 20 % more viewers at 30 s'. What do you do with it?

A finding that is not written into a template is lost.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Monthly review (shape of a strong answer):

Finding Data Rule change
Question hooks lose viewers at 0:03–0:05 steep drops 12–15× typical in 3 of 3 question-hook videos Hook library: result-first is the default; question hooks only with the answer on screen by 2 s
Viewers rewatch the "photo comes true" reveal bumps of +2–3 points at the reveal in 3 of 3 Treatment template: the reveal moves 5 s earlier; a 1 s hold after it
The end card loses 8 points before the CTA drop at end card start End card 4 s → 2 s; CTA in the last shot instead

"CTR (3.4 %, 2.9 %, 3.8 %) varied with the thumbnail; the one with a single face at high contrast was highest. The sample is too small to call it a rule (C15·M01); the next 6 videos test it with the platform's thumbnail test."

  • YouTube Analytics API — reports

C16 · Law, Provenance, and Trust

C16·M01 Copyright and licenses in AI production

Study time: 10 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain the main open legal questions - training data, output ownership, style, similarity - and why answers differ by country.
  2. Read the license of every model file, hosted service, music track, stock asset, and font, and record it.
  3. Keep a rights log that proves the origin of every asset, and audit it before delivery.
  4. Reduce risk in client work with contract clauses and a data rule.

Key words

copyright license rights log human authorship indemnity

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C16, module 01. Copyright and licenses in AI production. After this module, you can: 1. Explain the main open legal questions - training data, output ownership, style, similarity - and why answers differ by country. 2. Read the license of every model file, hosted service, music track, stock asset, and font, and record it. 3. Keep a rights log that proves the origin of every asset, and audit it before delivery. 4. Reduce risk in client work with contract clauses and a data rule. Generative AI raises open legal questions: whether training on protected works is allowed, who owns outputs, and when an output is too similar to an existing work. The answers differ by country and are still changing, so this course gives a method, not legal advice. Read the license of every model file and service you use, save the terms with a date, and keep a rights log for every asset you did not make. Audit the log before delivery, and agree the use of AI with clients in writing.

Learn

This module is not legal advice. Laws differ by country and change quickly. It gives you a working method: know the questions, read the terms, keep records, and ask a lawyer when the stakes are high.

The open questions (as of 2026-10)

  • Training data: many lawsuits against AI companies about training on protected works; some licensing deals (for example music labels with music-generation services in 2026). Results differ by country and case.
  • Output ownership: in the US, the Copyright Office's guidance is that protection needs human authorship. Human selection, arrangement, editing, and human-made parts can be protected; purely generated material without human authorship is not. Other countries have taken different positions in some cases.
  • Similarity: an output that is substantially similar to a protected work, or shows a trademark or a protected character, can infringe, regardless of how it was made.
  • Style: a style is generally not protected, but prompts that name living artists, and outputs that copy a recognizable work, raise legal and ethical risk. Describe features, not names (C06·M03).

Licenses to read

Item What to check
Open model files The license of each file: weights, VAE, text encoder, LoRAs. Apache-2.0, custom community licenses (often with revenue thresholds), research-only.
Hosted models and apps Terms of service: who owns outputs, commercial use, plan limits, attribution, indemnity, use of your inputs for training.
Music The plan's terms: commercial use, streaming, broadcast, territory (C06·M03).
Stock, fonts, LUTs, sound effects The usage license: commercial, editorial only, number of projects, territory.
Client assets The contract: may they be processed with AI, and with which tools?

A workflow is only as free as its most restricted file. The starter kit's lock file (C11·M01) shows a real case: an Apache-2.0 image model whose official template loads a VAE from a non-commercial repository.

The rights log

Write one line per asset that you did not make yourself. Record the ID, source, license or consent, allowed use, and the saved terms or license file. Also record people or brands shown, consent IDs, the date, and an expiry date if there is one. Generated assets have their origin in the prompt log (C04·M01). Together, the two logs prove where every asset came from. Audit them before every delivery.

Document the human contribution

Keep the script, the shot list, the review sheets, the take notes, and the edit history. They show the human authorship (selection, arrangement, editing) that protection may depend on, and they make disputes easier to answer.

When to ask a lawyer

Ask a lawyer before you start in these cases: the work is broadcast or a large campaign; a real person or a brand is shown; a client asks for an indemnity from you; or a license term is not clear. Bring the rights log and the saved terms: a lawyer can then answer quickly.

Client work

Agree in writing:

  • that AI tools are used, and which kinds;
  • whether the client's assets may go to third-party services (the data rule, C13·M05);
  • who owns the deliverables and the intermediate assets (prompts, LoRAs);
  • disclosure and labeling (M03);
  • limits of liability, and any indemnity that you rely on.

Tool walkthrough

Record licenses

python starter/tools/promptlog.py rights --id STOCK-0042 --source "Stock site, image 0042" --license "standard, web and social" \
  --use "background plate, online ad" --file plates/stock_0042.jpg
python starter/comfyui/download_models.py --list        # the license of every starter model file

Audit before delivery

python starter/tools/rights_audit.py --project "The Camera" --registry registry.yaml

The audit runs the prompt-log and rights-log checks, flags risky licenses (non-commercial, editorial only, research, unknown), expired licenses and consents, missing consent files for people, and registry adapters that are expired or not allowed for the project.

Model licenses (as of 2026-10, from the starter lock file)

FLUX.2 klein 4B: Apache-2.0. The FLUX.2 VAE file from the FLUX.2-dev repository: non-commercial. Wan 2.2: Apache-2.0. LTX-2.3 and LTX-2.5: the LTX-2.x Community License (a paid license for companies with annual revenue of US$10 million or more). Gemma encoders: the Gemma terms.

Watch

  • U.S. Copyright Office — Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (reports)Read the summary of Part 2 (copyrightability of outputs).
  • Creative Commons — licenses overviewKnow the meaning of BY, SA, NC, and ND.

Worked example

Rights audit test (2026-10-04) on a small project log:

WARN    STOCK-77: license 'editorial only' - check that it allows this use (background)
WARN    registry leo_v1: not allowed for 'The Camera' (allowed: The Camera (series))
PROBLEM VOICE-ANA: expired on 2026-09-30 - remove the asset or renew the license/consent
PROBLEM FACE-JO: shows people ['Jo'] but has no consent file
PROBLEM registry ambassador_v2: expired on 2026-06-30 - the service must refuse it
3 problems, 2 warnings

Each finding is something a fast manual review misses: an expiry date passed during production, a photo of a person without its consent file, and a stock image licensed for editorial use placed in an ad.

Ad project: 40 generated shots (2 hosted models + 1 open model), 1 generated music track, 1 font, client product photos. The rights log shows: hosted model A allows commercial use on the paid plan (terms saved with the date); model B the same, plus a vendor indemnity; the open model's files are Apache-2.0; the music plan allows streaming; the font is licensed for video; the client contract allows its product photos only on self-hosted models, so those shots were made with the open model.

Lab

Deliverable: C16/M01/ with a license table, a complete rights log, an audit report, and a contract checklist.

  1. List every model file, service, music track, stock asset, font, and LUT used in your project. Record the license of each, and save the terms with the date.
  2. Find at least one file in your workflows whose license differs from the model family's license. Decide what to do.
  3. Complete the rights log; make sure every reference in the prompt log is covered.
  4. Run rights_audit.py. Fix every problem; answer every warning in writing.
  5. Write a one-page contract checklist for AI use in client work.

Result checklist

  • [ ] License table with saved terms and dates.
  • [ ] Rights log complete; the audit has 0 problems.
  • [ ] A file-level license finding and its decision.
  • [ ] Contract checklist.

Self-check quiz

1. An open image model is Apache-2.0, but its official workflow loads a VAE file from a repository with a non-commercial license. Can you use the outputs for a client ad?

Licenses attach to files. The starter lock file shows exactly this case (C11·M01).

2. In the US (Copyright Office guidance, as of 2026-10), what can be protected in an AI-assisted video?

Document your human contribution (script, shot list, edit decisions). Other countries have different positions.

3. An output looks very much like a famous cartoon character. It was made from a text prompt only. Is it safe because a model made it?

How a work was made does not remove infringement risk. Check outputs for recognizable characters, logos, and works.

4. Why save a PDF of a service's terms on the day you use it?

A rights-log line points to the saved terms.

5. What does 'NC' mean in a Creative Commons license?

BY = attribution, SA = share alike, NC = non-commercial, ND = no derivatives.

6. A client's contract says nothing about AI. What do you do before you put their product photos into a hosted model?

Write the data rule into the contract. Many clients allow AI only on self-hosted models for their confidential assets.

7. What is an indemnity in a service's terms?

Some enterprise plans include it. Read the conditions; it does not cover everything.

Item License / terms Saved Allows this project?

flux2-vae.safetensors non-commercial (FLUX.2-dev repository) lock file no → replaced in our workflow with a VAE whose license allows commercial use, re-tested
Video API (plan Pro) outputs owned by us; commercial use; no indemnity terms_2026-10-04.pdf yes
Music track MUS-1 plan Pro: commercial incl. streaming, no broadcast terms PDF yes (online only)
Font desktop + video license license.pdf yes

The voice line was re-recorded with the renewed consent; the stock image was replaced by a generated plate. Second run: 0 problems, 1 accepted warning (editorial-only stock used only in an internal mood board, not in the film)."

C16·M02 Likeness, voice, and consent

Study time: 8 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain personality and publicity rights, digital-replica laws, data protection, and performer agreements as they apply to AI work.
  2. Write and store consent for training, cloning, and depiction, with scope, time, approval, and withdrawal.
  3. Enforce consent in the pipeline - registry expiry, refusals, deletion on withdrawal.
  4. Decide when not to depict a real person at all.

Key words

personality rights digital replica consent record biometric data withdrawal

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C16, module 02. Likeness, voice, and consent. After this module, you can: 1. Explain personality and publicity rights, digital-replica laws, data protection, and performer agreements as they apply to AI work. 2. Write and store consent for training, cloning, and depiction, with scope, time, approval, and withdrawal. 3. Enforce consent in the pipeline - registry expiry, refusals, deletion on withdrawal. 4. Decide when not to depict a real person at all. A person's face and voice are protected in many places: by publicity or personality rights, by new laws on digital replicas of voice and likeness, by data-protection law (faces and voices can be biometric data), and by performer agreements. In AI work, the answer is documented consent: who, what, where, how long, payment, approval, and how to withdraw. Store it, link it to every asset and adapter, and enforce it in code. Some content must not be made at all, with or without a request.

Learn

This module is not legal advice. Rules differ by country and state.

The rights involved

  • Personality and publicity rights: many US states, EU countries, China, and others give people control over the commercial use of their name, image, and voice.
  • Digital-replica laws: newer laws target AI copies of a person's voice and likeness. Example: Tennessee's ELVIS Act (2024) added voice to the state's right of publicity. It also covers making tools available whose main purpose is to produce a particular person's voice or likeness without authorization. Other jurisdictions followed with their own rules.
  • Data protection: face and voice data used to identify a person can be biometric data. Laws such as the GDPR treat it as a special category that often needs explicit consent. This applies to training data and to the models made from it.
  • Performer agreements: union agreements (for example SAG-AFTRA's) require consent and payment for digital replicas of performers.

What consent must say

  • Who: the person (and a guardian for a minor).
  • What: train a likeness LoRA, clone a voice, depict the person in ads, dub them into other languages.
  • Where and how: media, platforms, territories, languages; allowed and forbidden content.
  • How long: a start and an end date; what happens to the models at the end.
  • Payment.
  • Approval: whether the person approves every final use, a sample, or nothing within the scope.
  • Withdrawal: how to withdraw, how fast new uses stop, what happens to published outputs.
  • Disclosure: that outputs are labeled as AI-generated (M03).
  • Signature and date.

Enforce consent in the pipeline

A consent record in a folder is not enough. Connect it:

  1. A rights-log line with the consent file and the expiry date.
  2. A registry entry for every adapter or voice model made from the person, with the allowed uses and the expiry (C14·M03).
  3. The service refuses an expired or out-of-scope adapter.
  4. The rights audit runs before every delivery (M01).
  5. On withdrawal or expiry: delete the models and the training data as agreed, and record it.

Look-alikes and sound-alikes

A generated person who looks or sounds like a real, recognizable person can create the same risk as a direct copy, even if you did not ask for that person. Courts have found sound-alike ads infringing in the past. Check outputs for resemblance to well-known people. If a generated character resembles a real person, change the design. Do not prompt with real names unless the person consents.

Minors, deceased persons, and employees

  • Minors: a guardian signs; keep the scope narrow and the time short; add safeguards (no public training data, strict deletion).
  • Deceased persons: some places protect likeness after death (estates control it). Ask the estate.
  • Employees: consent given to an employer may not be free. Make it optional, and make withdrawal easy when the person leaves.

Never make

  • sexual or intimate content of real people without consent;
  • realistic fake statements or actions of real people presented as real;
  • content that targets or harasses a private individual;
  • the likeness of children without guardian consent and strong safeguards.

A practical rule

If you would not show the person the video before publishing, do not make it.

Tool walkthrough

The consent template

starter/templates/voice_consent.md (C06·M01) covers voice and likeness: scope, time, review, disclosure, payment, revocation, storage. Store the signed record as rights/consent/CONSENT-<name>-<date>.pdf and add a rights-log line:

python starter/tools/promptlog.py rights --id CONSENT-ANA-2026-10 --source "Ana Ruiz (voice actor)" \
  --license "consent record" --use "voice clone, The Camera series, online, until 2027-06-30" \
  --consent-file rights/consent/CONSENT-ANA-2026-10.pdf

Add "expires": "2027-06-30" and "people": ["Ana Ruiz"] to the line; the audit uses both.

Vendor verification

Hosted voice-cloning services usually require a verification step in which the person reads a text. Keep the verification record with the consent.

Watch

  • SAG-AFTRA — AI resources (digital replicas in contracts)Read what performer contracts require for digital replicas.
  • European Commission — data protection (GDPR) overviewNote biometric data as a special category.

Worked example

Brand ambassador campaign. The ambassador consents to: (1) a face and voice LoRA; (2) 20 social videos in 6 months; (3) 8 languages; approval of every final video; withdrawal with 30 days' notice; the models deleted at the end. In the pipeline: the LoRA and voice files carry the consent ID in the registry, with expires: 2027-04-30 and allowed_uses: ["Ambassador campaign 2026-27"]. The rights audit on a test date after expiry reported "registry ambassador_v2: expired … the service must refuse it" (the M01 test), and the adapter service refused it.

A request to refuse: "Make a video of our competitor's CEO announcing a recall." This is a realistic fake statement of a real person. Refused, with the reason in writing; the alternative offered was a comparison ad with their own spokesperson.

Lab

Deliverable: C16/M02/ with a consent record, its rights-log and registry entries, an enforcement test, a withdrawal procedure, and a refusal note.

  1. Write a consent record (adapt the starter template) for a real use in your project: your own voice, or a consenting friend's likeness.
  2. Add the rights-log line and a registry entry with an expiry and allowed uses.
  3. Test enforcement: run rights_audit.py with a date after the expiry, and show that your service (or a check in your pipeline) refuses the adapter.
  4. Write the withdrawal procedure: who receives the request, what stops when, what is deleted, how it is recorded.
  5. Write a refusal note for one harmful request (invent a realistic one), with the reason and an alternative.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Consent record with all fields.
  • [ ] Rights-log line and registry entry linked to it.
  • [ ] Enforcement test: audit fails after expiry; the pipeline refuses.
  • [ ] Withdrawal procedure and refusal note.

Self-check quiz

1. A public figure's speeches are online. Can you clone their voice for an ad without asking?

Public is not the same as permitted. A label does not replace consent.

2. What must a consent record for a voice clone contain?

The starter template (templates/voice_consent.md) has these fields. A lawyer must check it for client work.

3. Why can face and voice data fall under strict data-protection rules?

Data protection applies to the training data and the models made from it, not only to the outputs.

4. The consent for an ambassador's likeness LoRA expired yesterday. What must happen, in the pipeline?

Consent rules must be enforced in code: the registry (C14·M03) and the rights audit (M01).

5. A person withdraws consent for future use. What do you do?

Agree in advance what happens to published material, and follow it.

6. Which content do you never make, even if a client asks?

These cause serious harm, and many are crimes. Refuse them.

7. A practical test before you publish content with a real person's likeness?

If you would not show it to them, it is probably outside the consent.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Withdrawal procedure (shape of a strong answer):

Step Who When
Receive the request (email to rights@studio) and confirm it producer within 2 working days
Mark the registry entry withdrawn: <date>; the service refuses it at once engineer same day
Stop scheduled posts that use the likeness producer same day
Delete the LoRA, the voice model, and the training data; record file hashes and the deletion date engineer within 30 days (as agreed)
Published outputs: removed or kept as the consent record says (here: removed from owned channels within 30 days) producer within 30 days
Log the withdrawal in the rights log producer when done

"Enforcement test: on 2027-05-01 the audit reported the expired adapter; the adapter service returned refused: consent expired 2027-04-30; the delivery gate failed."

C16 · Law, Provenance, and Trust

C16·M03 Disclosure rules, C2PA, and watermarks

Study time: 12 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Apply EU AI Act Article 50 deployer duties and platform disclosure rules to a delivery.
  2. Sign deliverables with C2PA content credentials at the right step, and verify them.
  3. Explain what breaks credentials and watermarks, from measurements.
  4. Build disclosure and signing into the pipeline as an automatic delivery gate.

Key words

EU AI Act C2PA content credentials invisible watermark digital source type

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C16, module 03. Disclosure rules, C2PA, and watermarks. After this module, you can: 1. Apply EU AI Act Article 50 deployer duties and platform disclosure rules to a delivery. 2. Sign deliverables with C2PA content credentials at the right step, and verify them. 3. Explain what breaks credentials and watermarks, from measurements. 4. Build disclosure and signing into the pipeline as an automatic delivery gate. The EU AI Act's transparency duties (Article 50) apply from 2026-08-02: providers of generative systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable way, and deployers who publish deepfakes - realistic content that resembles real people, places, or events - must disclose them clearly. Platforms add their own labels. C2PA content credentials are a signed manifest in the file that records how it was made; any re-encode removes them, so sign last. Invisible watermarks survive some edits and not others. Use both, plus visible labels where required, and gate delivery on them.

Learn

This module is not legal advice. Check the rules of every country where your content is shown.

EU AI Act Article 50 (applies from 2026-08-02)

  • Providers of generative AI systems must mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable way.
  • Deployers (you, when you publish) must disclose deepfakes: image, audio, or video content that resembles real people, objects, places, or events and could falsely appear real. The disclosure must be clear, at the latest at the first exposure. For evidently artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional works, the duty is limited to a disclosure that does not spoil the work.
  • Penalties: for an undertaking, fines of up to €15 million or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(4)).
  • A Code of Practice from the European Commission describes how to mark and label, with more than one marking layer: signed metadata and an invisible watermark. Other jurisdictions have their own rules (for example China's labeling rules for AI-generated content, and US state laws on deepfakes in elections and on intimate images).

Platform rules

Major platforms require a disclosure for realistic altered or synthetic content, through a setting at upload. Some add labels automatically when they detect C2PA credentials or watermarks. Record in the asset record that you set it (C15·M03). Platform rules change often: check the help pages of each platform when you plan a release, and save a copy with the date, as you do with license terms.

C2PA content credentials

C2PA is an open standard for signed provenance metadata. A manifest in the file records who made it, with which tools, from which ingredients, and with which actions; it is signed with a certificate. Viewers and platforms can verify it.

  • Declare how the content was made with an IPTC digital source type: trainedAlgorithmicMedia for generated content, compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia for mixes with captured material.
  • Sign last. Our tests showed that any later ffmpeg step, even a stream-copy remux, removes the manifest. Sign every delivery file after its final encode.
  • Verification shows integrity: one changed byte makes the manifest invalid.
  • Use a certificate from a trusted certificate authority for client work. A test certificate gives "untrusted".
  • Some generators add credentials to their outputs; your edit removes them. Your signature at delivery describes the whole work.

Invisible watermarks

A watermark hides a signal in the pixels (or the audio). Provider watermarks (added by some hosted model providers to their outputs) are designed to survive common edits. You usually cannot add a provider's watermark yourself, and you must not remove it. Our test with a simple open watermark library showed the general point: a watermark survives some processing and is lost in other processing. It is one layer of evidence, not proof.

What credentials do not prove

Valid credentials prove who signed the file and that it has not changed since. They do not prove that the content is true. And a missing manifest does not prove that a file is fake: most real files have none, and many platforms remove metadata on upload. Read credentials as one piece of evidence. Platforms that keep credentials can show a "content credentials" mark to viewers.

The delivery gate

Before a file leaves the studio:

  1. a visible label where the law or the platform requires it;
  2. the platform setting recorded for the publishing step;
  3. valid C2PA credentials, signed with the studio certificate, as the last step;
  4. complete prompt and rights logs (M01). Fail the delivery if any is missing (C12·M04).

Tool walkthrough

Sign, verify, gate

# c2patool: github.com/contentauth/c2pa-rs (releases); set C2PATOOL if it is not on PATH
python starter/tools/provenance.py sign film_web.mp4 --out film_web_signed.mp4 --title "The Camera ep1" \
  --author "Example Studio" --ai generated --cert certs/studio.pem --key certs/studio.key --tsa <time-stamp URL>
python starter/tools/provenance.py verify film_web_signed.mp4
python starter/tools/provenance.py gate film_web_signed.mp4 --record assets/film_web.json

The asset record for the gate holds realistic_people_or_events, platforms, disclosure.visible_label, disclosure.platform_setting, prompt_log, and rights_log.

Inspect with c2patool directly

c2patool film_web_signed.mp4          # the manifest store as JSON, with validation_state

Watch

  • European Commission — Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated contentRead the summary of the marking and labeling commitments.
  • C2PA — Content Credentials (official site)Read 'How it works'.

Worked example

C2PA tests (2026-10-04, c2patool 0.27.22, the sample test certificate, a 6 s H.264 MP4):

File Result
Signed (actions: created with trainedAlgorithmicMedia; edited) Valid (with signingCredential.untrusted: the test certificate)
Signed, then re-encoded with ffmpeg No claim found
Signed, then trimmed with stream copy No claim found
Signed, then remuxed (stream copy, metadata mapped) No claim found
Signed, then one byte changed Invalid: assertion.bmffHash.mismatch

Signing took 0.02 s and added 14 KB to a 3.5 MB file. The gate failed the file twice: for the test certificate, and because the asset record said the video shows realistic synthetic people without a visible label.

Watermark test (an open library, invisible-watermark, a 32-bit payload in a 960 × 1200 image; PSNR about 41 dB, invisible to the eye):

Processing Method dwtDct Method dwtDctSvd
none read read
JPEG quality 90 lost read
JPEG quality 50 lost lost
resize to 50 % and back lost read
crop 10 % of the border lost lost
brightness +20 read read

Short film (fictional, with realistic city shots): end card "Made with generative AI tools: …"; the platform's synthetic-content setting on; C2PA signed with the studio certificate after the final encode; logs archived. EU ad with a realistic spokesperson (consented likeness): a visible "AI-generated" label at the start.

Lab

Deliverable: C16/M03/ with a disclosure decision per deliverable, signed deliverables, verification reports, a break test, and the gate in your pipeline.

  1. For each deliverable of your project, decide: deepfake or not? Which visible label, platform setting, and description text? Write the reasons.
  2. Get c2patool. Sign each delivery file as the last step (use the sample test certificate for practice; note that client work needs a trusted certificate).
  3. Verify each file. Then break one copy: re-encode it, and change one byte of another. Verify again and save the reports.
  4. Add provenance.py gate (or your own gate) to your delivery pipeline (C12·M04). Show one failing and one passing run.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Disclosure decision per deliverable.
  • [ ] Signed files with verification reports.
  • [ ] Break test: re-encode and byte change.
  • [ ] The gate in the pipeline: one fail, one pass.

Self-check quiz

1. Under EU AI Act Article 50, who must disclose a deepfake, and how?

Providers mark outputs machine-readably; deployers disclose deepfakes to viewers. Check the national rules too.

2. What can a breach of Article 50 cost an undertaking?

The €7.5 million / 1 % tier is for supplying incorrect information to authorities, not for Article 50.

3. You sign the master with C2PA, then make the web version with ffmpeg. What happens to the credentials?

Signing is the final step of the delivery pipeline, after every encode.

4. One byte in a signed file changes. What does verification show?

In the test: 'assertion.bmffHash.mismatch'.

5. Verification says 'signingCredential.untrusted'. What does it mean?

The course tests used the c2patool sample certificate, which is untrusted by design.

6. An open invisible watermark survived JPEG at quality 90 and a resize, but not a 10 % crop or JPEG at quality 50. What follows?

Provider watermarks (for example SynthID) are more robust than the simple test method, but no single layer is enough. Never try to remove a provider's watermark.

7. Which digital source type do you declare for a shot made by a video model from a prompt and a key frame?

The IPTC digital source types tell viewers and platforms how the content was made.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Disclosure decisions (shape of a strong answer):

Deliverable Realistic people or events? Visible label Platform setting C2PA
Short film (fiction, stylized night look, invented characters) realistic people, clearly fictional work end card "Made with generative AI" (does not spoil the work) on signed, trainedAlgorithmicMedia
15 s ad with a realistic AI spokesperson (EU) yes "AI-generated" on screen for the first 3 s and in the description on signed
Behind-the-scenes clip (real footage of the team) no generated people none off signed with --ai edited (captured footage with AI edits)

C16 · Law, Provenance, and Trust

C16·M04 Harms, misuse, bias, and professional responsibility

Study time: 10 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Recognize deepfake harms, misinformation risks, and harassment uses, and run a risk review on a request.
  2. Detect and reduce bias in generated people, voices, and stories with explicit casting and pattern reviews.
  3. Estimate the energy footprint of a production's own compute, and report what vendors do not disclose.
  4. Apply a written studio policy to refuse or change harmful work.

Key words

deepfake misinformation bias review energy footprint studio policy

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C16, module 04. Harms, misuse, bias, and professional responsibility. After this module, you can: 1. Recognize deepfake harms, misinformation risks, and harassment uses, and run a risk review on a request. 2. Detect and reduce bias in generated people, voices, and stories with explicit casting and pattern reviews. 3. Estimate the energy footprint of a production's own compute, and report what vendors do not disclose. 4. Apply a written studio policy to refuse or change harmful work. Synthetic video can harm people: deepfakes damage reputations and enable fraud and abuse; realistic fake events mislead even when labeled, because labels are lost when clips are re-posted; content can target individuals. Models also repeat stereotypes in who appears in which roles. A professional studio decides casting on purpose, reviews patterns, measures its footprint, and has a written policy that says what it never makes and how it refuses or changes a request. A short risk review before production catches most problems.

Learn

Harms

  • Deepfakes of real people: reputational damage; fraud (a fake call from a CEO, a fake endorsement); non-consensual intimate content, which is a crime in many places.
  • Misinformation: realistic fake events (disasters, crimes, statements). Even labeled content can be cut and re-posted without its label, and then it circulates as if real.
  • Harassment: content that targets a person or a group.
  • Erosion of trust: when anything can be faked, real evidence is doubted too. Provenance (M03) helps real content prove itself.

The risk review

Before production, answer five questions for every request:

  1. Real people? Is any real person shown or heard? Is there consent for this use (M02)?
  2. Could it be taken as real? Would a viewer who sees a re-posted clip without its label believe it happened?
  3. Who could be harmed? A person, a group, the audience (by deception)?
  4. Bias: who is shown in which roles, and how?
  5. Decision: make it, change the design, or refuse. Record the decision and the reason. Changing the design is often possible: a clearly illustrated or stylized look, a visible label in the picture, real data on screen, no real names.

Bias

Generative models learn from data that over-represents some groups in some roles and under-represents others. Research has shown that text-to-image models amplify demographic stereotypes (for example in occupations). Voices and accents can be stereotyped too. Professional practice:

  • Decide casting explicitly in the bible and the prompts: age, gender, skin tone, body type, accent. Do not leave it to model defaults.
  • Review patterns across many outputs: in the last 50 generated people, who appears in which roles? who is missing?
  • Review stories, not only faces: who is the expert, who is the victim, who speaks.

Footprint

Video generation uses far more compute than text. Estimate the energy of your own compute:

  • energy (kWh) = GPU hours × average GPU power (kW) × overhead (the rest of the machine and cooling; data centers report a PUE of about 1.1–1.6);
  • emissions (kg CO2e) = energy × the grid's emission factor (it varies widely by country, region, and hour). Hosted APIs rarely disclose energy per output: report "not disclosed" with the output seconds, instead of inventing a value. The biggest lever is the number of takes: explore cheaply, and generate finals only for chosen takes (C05·M06).

Fraud and impersonation

Voice clones and face swaps are used in fraud: a fake call from a manager asking for a payment, a fake video of a celebrity selling an investment. Do not build tools or content that make this easier: no unverified voice cloning, no realistic impersonation of real people. If you publish a voice model or an avatar service, verify consent and keep logs.

A studio policy

Write one page and sign it as a team. It says what you never make, what needs consent or a license, and your rules for disclosure, bias review, data handling, and footprint. It also says how anyone can stop a job, how you refuse or change a request, and how you handle misuse of your content. Review it every year. The starter kit has a template (templates/studio_policy.md).

Tool walkthrough

Estimate the footprint

python starter/tools/footprint.py --takes 1200 --takes-gpu-s 60 --gpu-w 700 --grid 0.35 --finished-min 20 --api-output-s 1500

Measure the GPU power during a run with nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.draw --format=csv -lms 1000. Take the grid factor from your grid operator or your cloud region's published data. GPU seconds per take come from your take log or the queue (C05, C12).

The policy and the review

Copy starter/templates/studio_policy.md. Add the risk review (the five questions) to the brief template of C03·M02, so that every project answers it before the treatment.

Watch

  • Partnership on AI — Responsible Practices for Synthetic MediaRead the practices for creators.
  • WITNESS — synthetic media and deepfakes (resources)See how human-rights groups think about synthetic media.

Worked example

Footprint (footprint.py, a 700 W GPU, overhead 1.4, grid 0.35 kg CO2e/kWh, 20 finished minutes):

Practice Takes GPU hours Energy CO2e Per finished minute
Generate every take at final quality 1,200 20.0 19.6 kWh 6.9 kg 0.98 kWh
Explore cheaply, finals for chosen takes (about a third of the GPU time) 400 equivalent 6.7 6.5 kWh 2.3 kg 0.33 kWh

1,500 s of hosted API output: "energy not disclosed by the vendor".

The flood request. Risk review: no real people; could be taken as real news: yes; harm: deception of the public, panic. Decision: change the design to a clearly illustrated style, a visible label "illustration of a possible flood", real flood-risk data on screen, and the donation link. The client agreed. Recorded in the project file.

Bias review. In a 40-shot hospital series, the first draft had 11 of 12 doctors as men in their 40s and all nurses as young women. The bible now specifies the cast of every recurring role; a review of the next 50 people showed a balanced mix that matched the story's setting.

Lab

Deliverable: C16/M04/ with your studio policy, 3 risk reviews, a bias review, and a footprint report.

  1. Adapt the studio policy template to your studio. Have one other person read it and challenge one rule.
  2. Write risk reviews (the five questions and the decision) for 3 requests: one from your project, and two difficult invented ones (one that you change, one that you refuse).
  3. Review the last 50 generated people of your project: roles, age, gender, skin tone, accent. Write what you change in the bible.
  4. Estimate the footprint of your project with footprint.py from your logs. Show the effect of your explore-then-finish workflow.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Studio policy, read and challenged by one other person.
  • [ ] 3 risk reviews, including a changed design and a refusal.
  • [ ] Bias review with bible changes.
  • [ ] Footprint report with the measured inputs.

Self-check quiz

1. A client wants 'a viral video of a flood in our city' to raise donations. What is the main risk, and a good response?

Realistic fake events mislead even with a label, because clips are cut and re-posted. Change the design so the content cannot pass as real.

2. Why is a visible label not enough for a realistic fake event?

Design for the worst re-post: a style that does not look like news footage.

3. In 100 generated 'doctor' shots, 90 are men. What is the professional response?

Defaults are not neutral. Research documents stereotype amplification in text-to-image models.

4. How do you estimate the energy of your own generation work?

In the module example, 1,200 takes of 60 GPU seconds on a 700 W GPU: about 20 kWh; 400 takes: about 6.5 kWh.

5. A hosted video API does not disclose energy per output. What do you report?

Do not invent precision. Report what you know and what you do not.

6. Which change lowers a production's footprint the most?

The number of generations dominates. The same workflow cuts cost and energy.

7. A team member thinks a job breaks the studio policy. What does a good policy say?

A policy without a stop-and-decide process is a poster, not a policy.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A refusal (shape of a strong answer): "Request: a 'leaked' video of a rival company's factory with safety violations, to post anonymously. Risk review: realistic fake event about a real company; intended to be taken as real; harm to the company and its workers; deception of the public. Decision: refused under policy section 1 ('realistic fake events presented as real'). Offered instead: an explainer about safety standards with real, cited data and clearly labeled illustrations. Recorded on 2026-10-04 by the producer."

Footprint report: "Our project: 14.2 GPU hours (queue log) at an average of 520 W (nvidia-smi samples), overhead 1.4, grid 0.30 → 10.3 kWh, 3.1 kg CO2e, 0.52 kWh per finished minute. Hosted API output: 2,140 s, energy not disclosed. Exploring at 640 × 352 with 4-step LoRAs cut our own GPU time by about 60 % against generating every take at final settings."

Program · Level 5

C17 Frontier and Research Practice

50 h · Prerequisites: C01, C05

M01M02M03

About this course

This field changes every month. The skill that lasts is the ability to learn the next thing fast and correctly. This course gives you that method, and a map of where the field is going.

Starter tools for this course (in the starter kit; tested on 2026-10-04):

Tool Use
tools/arxiv_watch.py Pass 0: new arXiv papers for your keywords as a Markdown checklist (M01, M03)
templates/production_note.md The production-note template: claimed, shown, evidence, decision (M01)
tools/model_trial.py One-day model test: usable rate with intervals, Fisher test, cost per usable second, a suggested decision per shot type (M02)
examples/example_scores_10.csv, example_scores_30.csv Simulated score sheets for the M02 worked example

Course outcomes

  1. Read papers, model cards, and technical reports efficiently and critically.
  2. Test any new model in one day with your eval harness.
  3. Explain the main research directions of 2026 and their production impact.
  4. Build a personal system to keep up, and choose a specialization.

Modules

  1. C17·M01 Read papers, model cards, and technical reports 12 h
  2. C17·M02 Test a new model in one day 14 h
  3. C17·M03 Research directions 2026 and your next step 24 h

C17 · Frontier and Research Practice

C17·M01 Read papers, model cards, and technical reports

Study time: 12 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Read a paper in three passes and extract what matters for production.
  2. Read a model card and technical report for capability, limits, and license.
  3. Separate claims from evidence - benchmarks, cherry-picked demos, ablations.
  4. Follow research in English and Chinese sources.

Key words

paper technical report ablation cherry-picking

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C17, module 01. Read papers, model cards, and technical reports. After this module, you can: 1. Read a paper in three passes and extract what matters for production. 2. Read a model card and technical report for capability, limits, and license. 3. Separate claims from evidence - benchmarks, cherry-picked demos, ablations. 4. Follow research in English and Chinese sources. Read a paper in three passes. First, the title, abstract, figures, and conclusion, to decide if it matters. Second, the method and results, to understand what is new. Third, the details, only if you will use or reproduce it. Model cards and technical reports tell you architecture, data, training, limits, and license. Separate claims from evidence: demos are chosen, benchmarks can be gamed, and ablations show what really matters. Many video models come from Chinese labs first, so also follow Chinese sources.

Learn

Three passes

Read research like an engineer who must decide something, not like a reviewer.

  1. Pass 1 (3–10 minutes): title, abstract, the main figure, the results table, the conclusion, and the limitations section. Answer one question: does this touch any shot type in my routing table, or any step in my pipeline? Most papers stop here.
  2. Pass 2 (about 1 hour): the method (what is new, in one sentence?), the experiments (compared to what, on which data, with which metrics?), the ablations, and the limits. Fill a production note.
  3. Pass 3 (hours): the math, the code, the hyperparameters. Only when you will use, reproduce, or build on the work.

Model cards and technical reports

A model release usually comes with a model card or a technical report instead of a peer-reviewed paper. Extract:

  • architecture: the size of the diffusion transformer, the text encoder, the VAE (C01);
  • modes: text, image, video, and audio inputs; first and last frame; references; editing;
  • limits: resolution, duration, frame rate, languages;
  • speed variants: distilled few-step versions, quantized files, VRAM;
  • evaluation: which benchmarks, which human ratings, against which models;
  • the training-data statement and the safety measures;
  • the license of each file. Use the model-card table from C01·M04.

Claims versus evidence

Write two fields in every note: claimed (the authors' words) and shown (what the evidence supports).

  • Demos are selected. Ask how many tries, and which prompts.
  • Benchmarks: which ones? Are they saturated (all models score near the top)? Did the authors introduce the benchmark themselves? Are the metrics the ones that matter for you (motion, identity, text, audio sync)?
  • Human ratings: how many raters, how many prompts, blind or not, who chose the prompts?
  • Ablations: which component gives the gain? If there are no ablations, the paper shows a system, not a cause.
  • Baselines: are the compared models current, and were they run with good settings?
  • Code and weights: released, promised, or not mentioned? Rate the evidence high, medium, or low, with one reason.

From a paper to a production decision

A paper rarely changes your work directly. It tells you what will appear in tools in 3–12 months. Methods that train a small adapter on an existing open model often reach node graphs within weeks; new base models take longer. Write the expected path in the note: "adapter on an open model, code released → test when a node appears".

Sources and a filter

  • Preprint servers and paper aggregators with daily lists: filter them by keywords; a script can do pass 0 for you.
  • Lab blogs and model cards for releases.
  • Chinese-language sources: lab blogs, deep-dive articles on question-and-answer sites, video tutorials, and tech press. Many video models and production methods appear there first. Use a translator; write notes in English.
  • Practitioners: a few researchers and studio engineers who post tests with settings. Keep the list short. Ten good sources read every week are better than a hundred read never.

Tool walkthrough

Pass 0 with a script

python starter/tools/arxiv_watch.py --query "video generation" --query "video diffusion" \
  --query "talking head" --days 7 --max 40 > notes/arxiv_$(date +%F).md

The script calls the public arXiv API (one run per day is enough; it waits 3 s between queries) and writes a Markdown checklist with the first sentence of each abstract. Tick the papers that pass pass 1.

Sources by name (as of 2026-10)

  • English: arXiv (cs.CV, cs.LG, cs.SD), Hugging Face Daily Papers and model cards, lab blogs (Google DeepMind, Meta, NVIDIA, Lightricks, Runway, Luma).
  • Chinese: lab blogs of ByteDance Seed, Alibaba Tongyi (Wan), Tencent Hunyuan, Kuaishou (Kling); Zhihu deep-dive articles; Bilibili tutorials; 36Kr and The Paper.

The note

Copy starter/templates/production_note.md for each item.

Watch

  • S. Keshav — How to Read a Paper (PDF)Read all (3 pages). The three-pass method.
  • Yannic Kilcher — paper explanation videosWatch one video-generation paper explanation.

Worked example

Pass 0 (2026-10-04): arxiv_watch.py --query "video generation" --days 7 --max 20 returned 20 papers from 2026-09-27 to 2026-10-01. Pass 1 (from the abstracts) kept 2 of them.

Note 1 — "Generative Cinematographer: Composing Camera and Object Motion in 3D" (arXiv 2610.02180, pass 1 only).

  • New: lifts one image into an editable 3D scaffold; the artist sets a camera path and moves parts of the subject with 3D handles; guidance maps drive a pretrained video model.
  • Claimed: "consistent camera-relative motion, improved geometric consistency under viewpoint changes".
  • Shown (from the abstract): not yet known; pass 2 must check the baselines and the human ratings.
  • Available how: a guidance branch and LoRA adapters trained on a pretrained Wan model → if code is released, a node-graph port is likely soon.
  • Fits: our "controlled camera + subject move" shots, which we now make with 3D white-box layouts (C05·M05).
  • Decision: pass 2 this week; watch for code.

Note 2 — "MosaiChunk: Compositing Spatio-Temporal Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation" (arXiv 2610.02153, pass 1 only).

  • New: a learned router picks past key-value entries across space and time for a frozen autoregressive generator, so details come back when an object reappears.
  • Evidence to check: the authors introduce their own benchmark (RememBench) → evidence quality at most medium until independent tests exist.
  • Fits: long single takes with revisits (a camera that returns to a set). Not in our tools yet.
  • Decision: watch; re-check in 3 months.

Model card example — LTX-2.5 (2026-08): pass 1 → relevant (open weights, joint audio and video, multishot). Pass 2 → asymmetric dual-stream DiT, Gemma 4 text encoder, distilled variant, INT8 and NVFP4 files; evidence: release notes and demos, few independent evaluations yet; license: the LTX-2.x Community License. Decision: one-day test (M02).

Lab

Deliverable: C17/M01/ with a pass-0 list, 3 production notes (one from a Chinese-language source), and a source list.

  1. Run arxiv_watch.py with keywords for your shot types. Do pass 1 on the list and tick what passes.
  2. Choose 3 items: a paper, a model card or technical report, and a Chinese-language source.
  3. Do pass 1 and pass 2 on each, and write a production note with "claimed", "shown", and an evidence rating.
  4. Write your source list: at most 10 sources, with the day you read each.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Pass-0 list with ticks.
  • [ ] 3 notes with claimed, shown, evidence rating, and a decision.
  • [ ] One source in Chinese, the note in English.
  • [ ] A source list of 10 or fewer.

Self-check quiz

1. You have 40 new papers this week and 3 hours. How do you use the time?

Pass 1 is a filter. Most papers stop there, and that is correct.

2. What is an ablation?

Ablations show which part of the method gives the gain. A paper without them claims more than it shows.

3. A launch page shows 12 perfect clips. What do you write in the 'Shown' field of your note?

Demos are selected best cases. They show what is possible, not the usable rate.

4. A paper reports a gain on a benchmark that the same authors introduced in the same paper. How do you rate the evidence?

A new benchmark can be useful (it measures a new problem) but it is not independent evidence yet.

5. The model card says 'Apache-2.0', and the repository also has a VAE and a text encoder. What do you check?

A workflow is only as free as its most restricted file.

6. Why follow Chinese-language sources?

A large part of the video frontier comes from Chinese labs. Use a translator and write your notes in English.

7. A researcher's post says a new method 'solves long-video consistency'. What do you do?

Posts compress claims. Go to the source before you write a note.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

A strong note (shape):

  • Item: a technical report for a new open video model, 2026-09, English.
  • Read: pass 2, 50 minutes.
  • New: a 4-step distilled variant with audio, at 720p.
  • Claimed: "matches the full model's quality at 8× the speed".
  • Shown: one table with an automatic benchmark (no human ratings for the distilled variant); 3 ablations on the number of steps; no audio evaluation. Evidence: medium for video, low for audio.
  • Available: weights on Hugging Face; the license of the VAE differs from the model license (non-commercial) → flagged.
  • Fits: exploration takes for wides and inserts.
  • Test plan: our eval set v3, 4 shot types × 30 clips each (M02 explains why 30).
  • Decision: test on Friday.

The note is short and skeptical, separates claims from evidence, flags the license, and ends with a test plan and a date.

Go deeper

  • arXiv — cs.CV recent (computer vision)
  • Hugging Face — Daily Papers
  • arXiv API — user manual

C17 · Frontier and Research Practice

C17·M02 Test a new model in one day

Study time: 14 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Run your fixed eval set on a new model with automation.
  2. Compare with your current routing choices using blind scores and cost per usable second.
  3. Decide - adopt, watch, or ignore - with evidence.
  4. Update the routing table and the tool landscape.

Key words

eval harness routing table adoption decision

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C17, module 02. Test a new model in one day. After this module, you can: 1. Run your fixed eval set on a new model with automation. 2. Compare with your current routing choices using blind scores and cost per usable second. 3. Decide - adopt, watch, or ignore - with evidence. 4. Update the routing table and the tool landscape. When a new model appears, do not trust the launch video. Run your fixed eval set from C01 with an automated harness. Score blind, compare with the current models in your routing table, and calculate cost per usable second. Then decide: adopt it for some shot types, watch it, or ignore it. Update your routing table and your tool landscape page. With a good harness, this takes one day.

Learn

Why a fixed procedure

A new video model appears almost every week, each with a launch page of perfect clips. You cannot test every model, and you must not trust launch pages. A fixed procedure answers one question: does this model lower our cost per usable second, or raise quality, for any shot type in our routing table?

Preparation (done in earlier courses)

  • Eval set (C01·M07): cases grouped by shot type (product, dialogue, wide, insert, and others), each with criteria and a usable rule.
  • Backend abstraction (C12·M01): a new model is one new adapter class.
  • Blind scoring (C03·M03): clips renamed to random IDs; a human scores taste and story; a judge model scores objective criteria where it is reliable.
  • Cost tracking: the cost of every clip in the take log.

The day

  1. Adapter (1–2 h): add the model to your backend: an API call or a node-graph workflow.
  2. Run (2–3 h, in parallel): every case of the shot types that matter, with enough clips (see below).
  3. Score (1–2 h): blind, with the same usable rule as the current models.
  4. Analyze (1 h): usable rate per shot type with an interval, a test against the current model, and cost per usable second.
  5. Decide (30 min): adopt for named shot types; watch with a trigger; or ignore.
  6. Update: the routing table, the tool-landscape page with the date, and a short team note.

How many clips

A usable rate from 10 clips has a wide interval: 7 of 10 means "somewhere between about 40 % and 89 %". Random differences between two models are then large. Use a test for two rates (the one-sided Fisher exact test is good for small samples) and know its power: the chance to detect a real difference.

Real difference 10 clips 20 30 40 60 100
50 % vs 80 % 28 % 55 % 73 % 84 % 96 % 100 %
50 % vs 65 % 8 % 13 % 23 % 29 % 46 % 64 %

(Detection rate at p < 0.05, from 2,000 simulated tests per cell with the course tool.) Rules that follow:

  • Use about 30–40 clips per model per shot type that you want to decide on; test fewer shot types instead of fewer clips.
  • A small difference (15 points) needs hundreds of clips: you will usually not detect it in one day, and it rarely changes the routing.
  • "No clear difference" is a result, not a failure: decide on cost, speed, and features.

Decide by shot type

Report each shot type separately. A model can be better for product shots and worse for wides. Compare cost per usable second: total cost divided by the seconds that passed the usable rule. Then:

  • Adopt where it is better (or equal and cheaper);
  • Watch with a trigger (a new version, a price change, a date);
  • Ignore where it is worse.

Keep the eval set healthy

Add cases from real production failures. Retire cases that every model passes. Version the set (v1, v2, …) and keep old results, so that you can show trends.

Tool walkthrough

Analyze the scores

The score sheet is a CSV with one row per clip: model,case,shot_type,seed,usable,seconds,cost_usd.

python starter/tools/model_trial.py scores.csv --incumbent current --candidate x2

For each shot type, the tool prints the usable count, the rate with a 95 % Wilson interval, the cost per usable second, the one-sided Fisher p-value that the candidate is better, and a suggested decision. The decision is a suggestion: you add speed, features, licenses, and taste.

Two example sheets are in starter/examples/ (simulated scores with known true rates; see the worked example).

Choose which models to test

Public blind-vote arenas (for example the llm-stats and Artificial Analysis video arenas) rank models on general prompts. Use them to pick candidates, not to decide: your shot types and your usable rule are different.

Watch

  • llm-stats — Best AI for video creation (blind-vote leaderboard)Use it to choose which new models to test.
  • Artificial Analysis — text-to-video arenaCompare with your own results after the test.

Worked example

The scores are simulated with known true usable rates, so that you can see what the test finds and misses. True rates: current model 50 % product, 55 % dialogue, 40 % wide, at US$0.06/s; candidate "x2" 80 % product, 30 % dialogue, 45 % wide, at US$0.09/s. Clips are 5 s.

Day with 10 clips per shot type (example_scores_10.csv):

Shot type Current x2 p (x2 better) Suggestion
product 7/10 10/10 0.105 watch: no clear difference
dialogue 6/10 3/10 0.965 watch: no clear difference
wide 6/10 4/10 0.911 watch: no clear difference

The real 30-point gain on product shots is not shown with this sample.

Day with 30 clips per shot type (example_scores_30.csv):

Shot type Current x2 $/usable s (current / x2) p (x2 better) Suggestion
product 15/30 23/30 0.120 / 0.117 0.030 adopt
dialogue 16/30 14/30 0.113 / 0.193 0.781 watch
wide 16/30 8/30 0.113 / 0.337 0.992 ignore (worse)

The product gain is detected, at about the same cost per usable second. The true dialogue difference (55 % vs 30 %) was missed in this sample: random results happen, which is why "watch" has a re-test trigger. The wide result shows a model that is clearly worse and more expensive for that shot type.

Decision note: "x2: adopt for product shots (routing updated, 2026-10-04); dialogue: watch, re-test with 40 clips when version 2.1 is released; wides: ignore. Landscape page updated."

Lab

Deliverable: evals/runs/<date>-<model>/ with the clips, the blind key, the score sheet, the model_trial.py report, and a decision note; and eval set v+1.

  1. Choose a model released in the last 3 months that you have not tested, and 2–3 shot types where it could change your routing.
  2. Add the adapter to your backend. Generate 30 clips per shot type with the new model, and the same number with your current model (or reuse recent clips from the same eval cases).
  3. Rename all clips to random IDs; score them blind with your usable rule.
  4. Run model_trial.py. Write the decision note with the numbers per shot type and a trigger for every "watch".
  5. Update your routing table and landscape page. Add 2 new eval cases from failures that you saw.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Run folder with the blind key kept separate.
  • [ ] Report per shot type with intervals and p-values.
  • [ ] Decision note with triggers.
  • [ ] Routing table, landscape page, and eval set updated.

Self-check quiz

1. What makes a one-day model test possible?

C01·M07 (eval set), C12·M01 (backends), C03·M03 (scoring), and model_trial.py.

2. With 10 clips per model per shot type, the candidate scores 10/10 on product shots and the current model 7/10. Is the candidate better?

Small samples give large random differences. The module simulation shows the detection rate per sample size.

3. About how many clips per model per shot type do you need to detect a 50 % vs 80 % usable-rate difference most of the time?

Measured by simulation with the course tool (2,000 runs per size). A 50 % vs 65 % difference needs well over 100.

4. A new model is better on product shots (p = 0.03) at a similar cost per usable second, and worse on wides. Decision?

The routing table is per shot type. One average hides the differences.

5. Why must scoring be blind?

Rename the files to random IDs before scoring; keep the key separate.

6. What does 'watch' mean as a decision?

Keep a watch list with triggers. Without a trigger, 'watch' means 'forget'.

7. Which cost number do you compare between models?

A cheap model with a low usable rate can cost more per usable second than an expensive one.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Decision note (shape of a strong answer):

"Model: a new open video model, version 1.0, tested 2026-10-02 with eval set v4 (3 shot types × 30 clips per model, blind).

Shot type Current New $/usable s p Decision
insert (hands, objects) 14/30 24/30 0.21 / 0.09 0.006 adopt (self-hosted, cheaper)
dialogue 19/30 12/30 0.18 / 0.35 0.98 ignore: lip sync drifts after 4 s
wide 11/30 15/30 0.30 / 0.17 0.21 watch: re-test when the 1.1 release adds the planned camera control

Speed: 95 s per 5 s clip on our 48 GB GPU. License: Apache-2.0 for every file in the workflow (checked). Routing updated for inserts; the landscape page has the date and the license. Eval set v5 adds 2 dialogue cases with long lines, from the failures."

The note gives numbers per shot type, uses enough clips, names a trigger, checks the license, and changes the eval set.

  • Hamel Husain — Your AI product needs evals
  • Wikipedia — Fisher's exact test
