C17 · Frontier and Research Practice

C17·M03 Research directions 2026 and your next step

Study time: 24 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Explain 6 active research directions and their expected production impact.
  2. Build a personal system to keep up (sources, cadence, notes).
  3. Choose a specialization path and plan the next 6 months.

Key words

long-form coherence real-time generation world model specialization

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C17, module 03. Research directions 2026 and your next step. After this module, you can: 1. Explain 6 active research directions and their expected production impact. 2. Build a personal system to keep up (sources, cadence, notes). 3. Choose a specialization path and plan the next 6 months. Six research directions will change production next. Longer coherence makes minutes, not seconds, of consistent video. Real-time and interactive generation makes video that responds to the viewer. World models and 3D-consistent generation give exact space and camera. Joint audio-video models improve speech and sound. Fine control through references, editing, and 3D inputs replaces long prompts. Efficiency through distillation and low-bit formats makes generation cheap. Build a weekly habit to follow these lines, and choose a path for your next six months.

Learn

Six directions

For each direction: what it is, the state in 2026, and what it changes in production.

  1. Long-form coherence. Clips grew from about 5 s (2024) to 15–30 s single takes and native multishot generation (2026). The research problem is memory: when a person or a place leaves the frame and comes back, details must return. Methods select or compress past information (cached keys and values, compact memory tokens) instead of keeping everything. Impact: whole scenes in one generation, fewer joins (C05·M04).
  2. Real-time and interactive generation. Autoregressive models generate chunk by chunk, with a cache, and distillation makes each chunk fast. Interactive "world models" respond to user input (walk, turn, act) at near real-time frame rates; some run on consumer GPUs. The open problems are drift and memory over minutes. Impact: interactive ads and stories, previs that you can walk through, live content.
  3. World models and 3D consistency. Systems generate 3D worlds (for example as Gaussian splats) from text or images, and video models accept 3D layouts as references. Impact: exact cameras, reusable sets, and shots that match across a sequence (C05·M05).
  4. Joint audio and video. One model generates picture, dialogue, effects, and music together, with voice locks from a reference. Research now targets layered, controllable audio (separate parts that you can change) and better sync through reinforcement learning. Impact: fewer separate audio steps; but delivery still needs stems and an M&E mix (C08), so check what you can separate.
  5. Control. Many references, region editing, conversational editing, camera paths, and 3D motion handles for parts of a subject. Impact: director-level control without long prompts; shots that follow a storyboard exactly.
  6. Efficiency. Few-step distillation, adversarial and distribution-matching training, low-bit weights (FP8, NVFP4), and sparse attention. Impact: cheaper exploration, more takes per budget, and large models on smaller GPUs. Test the usable rate: faster models can lose diversity or detail.

Two more lines to watch. Reward-based training uses reinforcement learning on video, with rewards for physics, text, and preference. Evaluation research builds benchmarks for physics, memory, and identity. Both change which models are good at what.

Read directions, not headlines

A direction becomes a production tool in steps: a paper; code; an open adapter or model; a node or an API; a stable version. Track where each item is in these steps. Act at the "node or API" step for experiments, and at the "stable version" step for client work.

A weekly routine (2–3 hours)

  • Monday (30 min): release notes of your 5 main tools.
  • Wednesday (60 min): pass 0 with a script, pass 1 on 5–10 papers (M01).
  • Friday (45 min): one Chinese-language source and one practitioner thread; one production note.
  • Monthly: a one-day model test (M02).
  • Quarterly: update the landscape page and the routing table; retire old notes. Write everything in one notes repository with dates. Notes that nobody can find have no value.

Choose a path

After the program, choose one specialization (see "Next steps and specializations"). Choose where your current strength meets a direction that changes production. Plan 6 months: skills, 2 projects with public results (a repository, a published note series, a film), the sources you follow, and one measurable goal per month.

Tool walkthrough

One query per direction

for q in "long video generation" "real-time video generation" "interactive world model" \
         "joint audio-video generation" "camera control video" "few-step video distillation"; do
  python starter/tools/arxiv_watch.py --query "$q" --days 30 --max 10 >> notes/directions_$(date +%F).md
  sleep 3
done

Products to follow by direction (as of 2026-10)

  • Long takes and multishot: Seedance 2.5 (30 s single takes), Kling 3.0 (up to 6 shots), LTX-2.5 (native multishot).
  • Interactive worlds: Genie 3 (Google DeepMind; about 60 s coherence).
  • 3D worlds: Marble (World Labs; Gaussian splats in .ply/.spz); Seedance 2.5 3D white-box references.
  • Joint audio-video: Veo 3.1, LTX-2.5, Kling 3.0 voice lock.
  • Efficiency: distilled LTX-2.5, NVFP4 files in ComfyUI.

Watch

  • Google DeepMind — Genie 3 blogNote the open problems listed at the end.
  • arXiv — 'Dream machine: the next creative economy' (2026)Read the abstract and introduction; note the predictions.

Worked example

Direction scan (2026-10-04, arxiv_watch.py, last 30 days; titles from pass 0, not yet read):

Direction Example items Step reached
Long-form memory "MosaiChunk" (2610.02153); "Compress to Remember: Learning Compact Memory via On-Policy Distillation for Long Video Generation" (2609.36364); "FrameMorrow" (2609.38839) papers
Real-time and interactive "Waypoint-1.5: A Real-Time Video World Model for Consumer Hardware" (2609.37107); "WorldPlay2" (2609.35560); "Mask Forcing" (2609.09123) papers; some with code
Joint audio-video "Soundwich: Video Generation with Layered and Controllable Audio" (2610.00691); "AV-GRPO" (2609.29816); "HelixWorld: A Real-time Interactive Audio-Visual World Model" (2609.38123) papers
Control "Generative Cinematographer" (2610.02180): 3D camera and motion handles on an open model paper; adapter on an open model
Efficiency "DMAD: Distribution Matching as Adversarial Distillation" (2610.02188); "LongLive-Plug: Once-for-All Distillation" (2609.38154) papers

The scan shows where the field is busy this month: memory for long and interactive video, and distillation. It is a list for pass 1, not evidence of results.

A 6-month plan (pipeline-engineer path):

  • Months 1–2: a custom node and an MCP tool for one control method from the scan, published on GitHub with a test workflow.
  • Months 3–4: serve an open video model with autoscaling and a cost dashboard (C13); publish a one-day test note each month.
  • Months 5–6: a weekly series for a real client with the agent pipeline (C12), with a case study.
  • Routine as above; goal per month: one public artifact.

Lab

Deliverable: C17/M03/ with a direction scan, 6 impact notes, your weekly routine, and a 6-month plan.

  1. Run the direction scan. For each of the 6 directions, choose one 2026 item and do pass 1.
  2. For each, write 3 lines: what it is, the step it reached (paper, code, adapter, node or API, stable), and the production impact for your work.
  3. Write your weekly routine with named sources (English and Chinese) and the time per slot.
  4. Choose a path. Write a 6-month plan with 2 projects, the public result of each, and a measurable goal per month.

Result checklist

  • [ ] Direction scan with dates.
  • [ ] 6 impact notes with the step reached.
  • [ ] A routine with named sources and times.
  • [ ] A 6-month plan with 2 projects and monthly goals.

Self-check quiz

1. Which research direction most reduces the need for long text prompts?

Direct control signals (an image, a path, a mask) carry what words describe badly.

2. What is the main open problem of interactive world models in 2026?

Published systems report about a minute of coherence. Memory methods are an active research line.

3. Why do autoregressive video models matter for production?

This is the basis of real-time and interactive generation. Their problem is drift and lost detail over time.

4. What is the production effect of few-step distillation plus low-bit weights?

Cost per usable second falls if the usable rate holds. Test it (M02); distillation can reduce diversity.

5. A paper shows layered, controllable audio generated with the video. What do you check before you change your sound workflow?

Delivery needs stems and an M&E mix. A research demo is a direction, not a tool.

6. What is the best way to keep up?

A routine beats bursts of intensity.

7. How do you choose a specialization?

IT professionals often start from pipelines and infrastructure, then add one creative strength.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Impact note (shape of a strong answer): "Direction: long-form memory. Item: a memory method for autoregressive video (2026-10, paper with a new benchmark; code not released). Step: paper. Impact for us: our 3-shot kitchen scene now needs 3 generations and 2 joins; a model with memory could do it in one take, with the same cup and window when the camera returns. Action: none now; check the code status monthly; add a 'camera returns' case to the eval set so that we can measure it when a tool appears."

Routine (shape): "Mon 08:30–09:00 release notes (5 tools, RSS); Wed 12:00–13:00 arXiv watch (6 queries) + pass 1; Fri 16:00–16:45 one Chinese source (a lab blog, translated) + one production note; first Friday of the month: one-day model test. Notes in research-notes/ with dates; quarterly landscape update."

A strong answer is specific: named sources, fixed times, the step reached, and an eval-set change, so that a new tool can be tested on the day it appears.

  • World Labs — Marble

Program · Level 5

C18 Capstone Production

100 h · Prerequisites: all courses

M01M02

About this course

The capstone shows everything you learned in one project. You choose one of three briefs (or write your own at the same level). You plan, produce, deliver, and document. The rubric is published, so you can assess yourself before you finish.

Starter tools for this course (in the starter kit; tested on 2026-10-04):

Tool Use
templates/capstone/risk_register.md Risk register with early signs (M01)
templates/capstone/delivery.json, rubric_scores.json The delivery manifest and the rubric score sheet (M02)
tools/capstone_check.py Completeness check of the delivery package: plan, specs, C2PA, captions, stems, logs, write-up, rubric (M02)
All earlier tools qc_gate.py, spec_check.py, rights_audit.py, provenance.py, cost_model.py, model_trial.py

Course outcomes

  1. Respond to a full brief with a complete AI-native production.
  2. Deliver a 2–5 minute film or ad, and a 5-video short-form series made by an automated pipeline.
  3. Document the pipeline, costs, evaluations, rights, and disclosure.
  4. Assess your own work with the published rubric.

Modules

  1. C18·M01 Brief, plan, and pipeline design 30 h
  2. C18·M02 Produce, deliver, document, and assess 70 h

C18 · Capstone Production

C18·M01 Brief, plan, and pipeline design

Study time: 30 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Choose a brief and write a complete production plan.
  2. Design the pipeline - tools, models, routing, gates, infrastructure.
  3. Build the budget, schedule, and risk register.
  4. Get the plan approved at a self-review gate.

Key words

production plan risk register pipeline diagram

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C18, module 01. Brief, plan, and pipeline design. After this module, you can: 1. Choose a brief and write a complete production plan. 2. Design the pipeline - tools, models, routing, gates, infrastructure. 3. Build the budget, schedule, and risk register. 4. Get the plan approved at a self-review gate. Choose one of three briefs: a brand film, a narrative short, or an explainer series. Write a production plan: the treatment, look bible, cast and reference library, shot list, routing table, pipeline diagram, infrastructure choice, budget, schedule, rights plan, and disclosure plan. List the main risks and how you will reduce them. Review the plan against the rubric before you start production.

Learn

Choose a brief

  • A. Brand film (2–3 min) and a series: a launch film for a fictional product, and 5 × 30 s social variants in 2 languages.
  • B. Narrative short (3–5 min) and a series: a short film with 2 recurring characters, and 5 × 45 s episodes of a spin-off.
  • C. Explainer (3–5 min) and a series: a technical explainer with an avatar host, and 5 × 60 s chapter cut-downs in 3 languages.

You can write your own brief at the same level. Every brief must have at least 2 consistent characters (or 1 character and 1 product), and dialogue, native or replaced. It needs music with a clear license, and at least one controlled camera shot (a 3D layout or first and last frames). It also needs localization or variants, and full provenance. Use fictional brands and people, or people who consent in writing (C16·M02).

The plan (one folder, seven parts)

  1. Treatment and script (C02, C03).
  2. Look bible, reference library, and adapter plan (C04, C14): which LoRAs, from which data, with which consent.
  3. Shot list as JSON (C03·M04), with a shot type per shot.
  4. Routing table and budget (C05·M06, C17·M02): a route per shot type, its usable rate and price from your own tests, and caps.
  5. Pipeline diagram (C11–C13): stages, agents, gates, tools, the infrastructure, and what runs without you.
  6. Rights and disclosure plan (C16): the rights log, consents, labels, and signing.
  7. Schedule and risk register.

Budget from usable seconds

For each route: generated seconds = used seconds × handle factor ÷ usable rate. The handle factor (about 1.2–1.3) covers the extra length that you generate and trim. Then cost = generated seconds × price per second. Add images, adapter training, voice, music plans, and storage. Add a reserve of 20–30 %, and set caps in the queue at the budget, not above it.

The pipeline diagram

Draw every stage as a box with its input, its output, its tool, and its gate. Mark which stages run without you (queue, agents, renders) and which need your decision (selects, approvals, the mix). Mark the fallback for every hosted service, and the place where each log is written. The diagram is also the table of contents of your repository: each box points to a folder or a script.

Schedule: human time and machine time

About 70 hours of your time are planned for production (M02). Machine time (generation, training, rendering) runs at the same time, in the background. Order the work by dependencies: adapters before character shots; locked picture before the final mix; final encode before signing. Put review gates in the schedule.

The risk register

For each risk: likelihood and impact (1–3), an early sign, a mitigation before it happens, a response if it happens, an owner, and a status. Review it weekly. The typical AI-production risks are identity drift, vendor or API changes, rights gaps, budget overrun from low usable rates, and GPU shortage.

The self-review gate

Before you generate a final shot, review the plan against the rubric (M02). Ask: could another student run the production from this folder without asking me? Are all routes and prices from my own tests? Does every person and asset have a rights line? Fix the weak parts, then freeze the plan as version 1 with a Git tag. Change it later only by recorded decisions.

Tool walkthrough

Templates

cp -r starter/templates/capstone capstone/templates      # delivery.json, rubric_scores.json, risk_register.md

Budget from your own numbers

Use starter/tools/cost_model.py (C13·M04) for self-hosted routes and your one-day test reports (model_trial.py, C17·M02) for usable rates. Set the caps in pipeline/genqueue.py (C12·M02) to the budget per route.

Freeze the plan

git add capstone/plan && git commit -m "Capstone plan v1" && git tag capstone-plan-v1

Watch

  • StudioBinder — How to write a production scheduleAdapt the idea to an AI production schedule.
  • Curious Refuge — AI film case studies (free start page)Look at how AI short films are presented and credited.

Worked example

Brief B: "Night Shift" (4 min film, and 5 × 45 s spin-off episodes). Used seconds: 240 + 225 = 465 s. Handle factor 1.3. Prices are planning values from the student's own tests (use yours).

Route (shot type) Share Used s Usable rate Generated s Price per s Cost
Dialogue: hosted joint audio-video model 40 % 186 52 % 465 US$0.10 US$46
Inserts: open model on a serverless GPU (US$2/h, 100 s per 5 s clip) 30 % 140 45 % 403 US$0.011 US$4
Wides: hosted model with 3D layout references 30 % 140 33 % 550 US$0.09 US$49
Video total 465 1,418 US$100

Other costs: 2 character LoRAs (about US$6 of GPU time), about 300 key frames (US$12), the music plan (US$10), storage (US$3). Total about US$131; with a 25 % reserve, the cap is US$165.

Risk register (top 3 of 8): R1 identity drift on Leo (L3 × I3; early sign: identity score below 0.5; mitigation: LoRA v4 and the identity gate); R2 the wides route is removed by the vendor (L2 × I3; mitigation: a second route tested on 10 cases); R3 the dialogue usable rate falls below 40 % (L2 × I2; early sign: spend over 50 % with less than 40 % of shots done; response: shorter lines, more coverage from the inserts route).

Pipeline: preproduction CLI → genqueue with caps → character pipeline with the identity gate → studio MCP server → NLE timeline from selects → QC gates (spec check, loudness) → C2PA signing → capstone check.

Lab

Deliverable: capstone/plan/ with all 7 parts, a self-review note, and the tag capstone-plan-v1.

  1. Choose a brief (or write one at the same level).
  2. Write all 7 plan parts. Calculate the budget from used seconds, handle factor, and your own usable rates.
  3. Write the risk register with at least 6 risks, each with an early sign (template: templates/capstone/risk_register.md).
  4. Do the self-review: score the plan against each rubric row, and ask the "another student" question. Fix the weak parts.
  5. Freeze the plan with a Git tag.

Result checklist

  • [ ] 7 plan parts in one folder.
  • [ ] Budget from usable rates, with a reserve and caps.
  • [ ] Risk register with 6 or more risks and early signs.
  • [ ] Self-review note and the Git tag.

Self-check quiz

1. What must the routing table in your plan be based on?

A route without your own numbers is a guess. Re-test any route that is older than 3 months.

2. You need 186 s of usable dialogue. The route has a 52 % usable rate, and you generate 30 % extra length for handles. How many seconds must you generate?

Budget from the usable rate, not from the finished length. This is the most common budget error.

3. What is a risk register?

Review it every week. A risk without an early sign is noticed too late.

4. Which risks are most typical in AI productions?

Each has a known mitigation from the program: LoRAs and gates, backend abstraction, the rights log, and caps.

5. Why a self-review gate before production?

The same logic as approval gates (C03·M02): fix early, where it is cheap.

6. Your plan schedules 70 production hours, and generation alone needs 30 hours of queue time. What do you plan?

Human time and machine time are separate resources. The schedule must show both.

7. Which test proves that the plan is complete?

Use this test at the self-review gate.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Self-review note (shape of a strong answer): "Plan v1 reviewed on 2026-10-04. Story: the treatment has a clear turn at 2:40; the spin-off episodes each have one question and one answer. Routes: all 3 tested in the last month (reports in evals/runs/). Weak parts found and fixed: (1) the wides budget used the launch-page rate; replaced by our test rate of 33 %, which raised the cost from US$22 to US$49; (2) no consent line for the voice of the narrator (a friend): signed consent added, with an expiry; (3) the schedule had the final mix before the picture lock; reordered. Another student read the folder and asked one question (which LUT); the answer is now in the bible. Tagged capstone-plan-v1."

A strong plan is complete enough for someone else to run, uses budgets and routes from your own data, and has a risk register with real mitigations and early signs.

  • PMI — Don't leave home without it: project risk registers
  • Atlassian — risk register template and guide

C18 · Capstone Production

C18·M02 Produce, deliver, document, and assess

Study time: 70 h · Level 5

Outcomes

After this module, you can:

  1. Run the full production through your pipeline.
  2. Deliver all files to specification with QC reports and provenance.
  3. Write a technical write-up with evaluation data and costs.
  4. Assess the result with the rubric and plan improvements.

Key words

deliverables technical write-up rubric showreel

Listen

Transcript (synthetic voice)

C18, module 02. Produce, deliver, document, and assess. After this module, you can: 1. Run the full production through your pipeline. 2. Deliver all files to specification with QC reports and provenance. 3. Write a technical write-up with evaluation data and costs. 4. Assess the result with the rubric and plan improvements. Produce the film and the series with your pipeline. Keep the logs. Deliver masters, platform files, stems, captions, and signed provenance. Write a technical report: model choices with test data, pipeline diagram, costs, usable rates, human time, problems, and fixes. Assess yourself with the rubric. Finish with a showreel and a public portfolio page.

Learn

Production

Follow the plan (M01). Use the pipeline; do not bypass it for "just one quick shot", because that shot then has no log. Work in this order:

  1. Adapters and references first: train and test the character LoRAs; lock the bible.
  2. Key frames and the animatic: check story and timing before you generate motion.
  3. Generation in the background: the queue runs routes with caps while you review.
  4. Selects and the edit: score takes, build the timeline from selects, lock the picture.
  5. Sound: dialogue clean-up, music, effects, mix to the spec; stems and M&E.
  6. Finishing: grade as one film, conform, captions, localization or variants.
  7. Delivery: encode, QC, sign last, verify.

The weekly review

Every week, in 30 minutes: spend against budget per route; usable rate per route; shots done against plan; the risk register (re-score, close, add); and decisions. Write each decision with a date and a reason, and change the plan version. Silent changes make the write-up impossible.

Deliverables

  • The film master (ProRes 422 HQ or better) and the platform versions.
  • The series (and variants or languages as the brief requires).
  • Stems (dialogue, music, effects) and an M&E mix.
  • Captions per language (SRT or VTT).
  • QC reports: spec checks pass for every file.
  • Signed provenance (C2PA, signed last) with the prompt log, the rights log, and the consent records.
  • The pipeline repository, tagged, with a README that reproduces one shot.

The technical write-up (8–12 pages)

  1. Brief and approach.
  2. Pipeline: the diagram and its components.
  3. Model choices with test data.
  4. Costs: planned against actual; cost per usable second; cost per finished minute.
  5. Human time per stage.
  6. Problems and fixes.
  7. Rights and disclosure.
  8. What you would change. Every number must come from a log or a report that is in the repository.

Assessment

Score each rubric row from 1 to 4, with evidence: timecodes, reports, log lines. Ask one peer to score blind to your scores. Where the scores differ by 2 or more, look at the evidence together. Write 3 improvements, each with the change you would make in the plan or the pipeline.

Common problems in the last week

  • A late model change: a route changes behavior or price near the end. Do not re-generate approved shots; finish with what you have, and record it.
  • Credentials lost: a file was re-encoded after signing. Sign again, as the last step.
  • Loudness off by one platform: each platform file needs its own measurement; do not copy the master's numbers.
  • Missing captions for a variant: captions are made per cut, not per project. Plan the last week for checks and fixes only, not for new shots.

Credits and disclosure

List the human roles (writing, direction, editing, sound) and the kinds of AI tools used, with a clear disclosure line (C16·M03). Credit consenting people and licensed music as their licenses require.

Showreel and portfolio

Cut 30–90 s of your best work, the strongest first. Put the disclosure in the credits. Publish a portfolio page with the film, the showreel, the write-up, and the repository link.

Tool walkthrough

Check the package

cp starter/templates/capstone/delivery.json starter/templates/capstone/rubric_scores.json capstone/
python starter/tools/capstone_check.py capstone/delivery.json            # a real delivery: studio certificate
python starter/tools/capstone_check.py capstone/delivery.json --allow-test-cert   # practice only

The tool checks the plan parts, runs spec_check.py on every file against its spec, verifies the C2PA credentials (set C2PATOOL if c2patool is not on PATH), counts caption cues and log lines, checks the write-up sections and the number of measured values, and checks the rubric scores. It proves completeness, not quality.

The other gates

pipeline/qc_gate.py (C12·M04) for every shot, tools/rights_audit.py (C16·M01) before delivery, and tools/provenance.py gate (C16·M03) per file.

Watch

  • Vimeo — Staff Picks (search and study 3 short films)Study the pacing and the credits of strong short films.
  • Content Credentials — verify toolCheck your signed deliverables.

Worked example

Capstone check on a practice package (2026-10-04; a 6 s signed test film, the web spec, sample logs):

First run:

Visual quality + consistency
  ok   deliver/film_web.mp4: 19/19 spec checks
Sound
  FAIL captions deliver/film.de.srt: missing
  FAIL stem deliver/stems/FX.wav
Rights + disclosure
  FAIL deliver/film_web.mp4: content credentials Valid (test certificate), source ['trainedAlgorithmicMedia']
Write-up + evidence
  FAIL write-up: 25 words; missing sections: ['change']
  FAIL write-up: 3 measured values (want 10 or more)
  FAIL rubric scores (self): 1/7 rows
  FAIL rubric scores (peer): 0/7 rows
  FAIL improvements: 1 (want 3)
13/21 checks pass -> NOT READY

After adding the German captions, the effects stem, the missing write-up section with measured values, and both rubric scores: 20/21 (only the test certificate fails); with --allow-test-cert: 21/21, READY. A real delivery signs with the studio certificate.

Brief B results (example): film 4:10; series 5 × 45 s; budget US$148 against a cap of US$165; usable rate 41 % overall (dialogue 52 %, wides 33 %); human time 58 h; cost per finished minute about US$19 (US$148 ÷ 7.9 finished minutes: 250 s of film and 225 s of series). Self-score 4, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3; peer score 4, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 3 (Sound: room tone changes at 2:12 and 3:05; fixed). Improvements: a better LoRA for Leo's wardrobe; sound design earlier; more reaction coverage.

Lab

Deliverable: capstone/ with all deliverables, the write-up, the rubric scores, the showreel, and the portfolio page.

  1. Produce through the pipeline, with weekly reviews and recorded decisions.
  2. Deliver all files; run the QC gates and the rights audit.
  3. Sign every delivery file last, with a trusted certificate if you have one; verify.
  4. Write the technical write-up.
  5. Self-assess and peer-assess with evidence; write 3 improvements.
  6. Run capstone_check.py until it reports READY.
  7. Publish the showreel and the portfolio page.

Result checklist

  • [ ] All deliverables pass QC.
  • [ ] Provenance verified for every delivery file.
  • [ ] Write-up complete, with numbers from the logs.
  • [ ] Self and peer scores with evidence, and 3 improvements.
  • [ ] capstone_check.py: READY.
  • [ ] Showreel and portfolio online.

Self-check quiz

1. Which files together prove how the film was made?

The provenance package (C16). The signature proves the file; the logs prove the origin of every asset.

2. Halfway through production, you have spent 60 % of the budget with 40 % of the shots done. What do you do?

Change the plan by recorded decisions. The weekly review exists to catch this early.

3. capstone_check.py says 'content credentials Valid (test certificate)' and fails. Why?

The same rule as the delivery gate in C16·M03.

4. What makes a technical write-up strong?

Evidence over claims. A reader must be able to check every number in your logs.

5. Your self-score is 4 on every row; a peer gives 2 on Sound. What do you do?

A score needs evidence (timecodes, reports). Disagreement shows where to look.

6. Rubric 'Pipeline + automation: 4' requires:

The C11–C13 standard. The README must reproduce one shot.

7. What goes on the showreel?

Quality over quantity. Viewers decide in the first 10 seconds.

Model answer (open after you do the lab)

Write-up extract: costs (shape of a strong answer):

Route Planned generated s Actual Planned cost Actual Usable rate (plan / actual)
Dialogue 465 512 US$46 US$51 52 % / 47 %
Inserts 403 380 US$4 US$4 45 % / 48 %
Wides 550 690 US$49 US$62 33 % / 26 %

"Wides went over the plan: night exteriors had a 26 % usable rate. Decision on 2026-11-03 (plan v1.2): 4 wides were replaced by 2 inserts and 1 3D-layout shot. Video total US$117 against US$100 planned; project total US$148, within the cap of US$165. Human time 58 h: selects 14 h, edit 12 h, mix 11 h, finishing 9 h, other 12 h. Next time I would test the night-exterior route on 30 clips before planning (C17·M02)."

A professional capstone looks like one piece (no visible model switching), sounds clean, and is fully documented. The write-up reads like an engineering report: decisions, real numbers, and honest limits.

← PreviousCourse overview

Glossary

10GbE
10 Gigabit Ethernet. A network speed of about 1.1 GB/s, enough for a few editors to share high-quality media.
180-degree rule
Keep all cameras on one side of the line of action, so people keep their left and right positions on screen.
3-2-1 backup
Keep 3 copies of data, on 2 types of media, with 1 copy offsite.
A/B test
A test that shows two variants to similar audiences and compares a metric. Change one variable only.
ablation
An experiment that removes one part of a method to measure what that part contributes.
ACES
Academy Color Encoding System. A standard color-management framework for film and TV pipelines.
adapter serving
Keeping a base model loaded and applying LoRAs per request, with a strength, from a cache.
adoption decision
The documented choice to adopt, watch, or ignore a new model, based on test data.
agent
A language model in a loop that chooses and calls tools, reads results, and continues until a goal is done.
agent recipe
A saved, tested instruction set for an agent task that a team repeats.
agentic coding
Coding with an agent that reads files, writes code, runs commands, and fixes errors in a loop.
AI disclosure
Telling viewers that content is AI-generated or altered, with platform settings, labels, and provenance data.
ambience
The background sound of a place, such as traffic, wind, or room hum.
analytics loop
Using audience data from published videos to change the next videos.
animatic
Storyboard frames on a timeline with temporary sound, used to test story and timing.
API format
The ComfyUI workflow export that maps node IDs to inputs. You send it to the server to run a workflow headless.
approval gate
A point in a pipeline where a person must approve before work continues.
arena
A public site where people vote blind between two model outputs. Votes produce a ranking.
aspect ratio
The ratio of frame width to height, for example 16:9 or 9:16.
assembly
The first, complete version of an edit: all chosen shots in script order at planned lengths, before the editor's pass.
async job
An API request that returns a job ID at once; the result is ready later.
attention
The transformer operation where each token takes information from the other tokens that matter to it.
audio-to-video
A generation mode where an audio track conditions the picture, for example for lip sync or music cuts.
audit log
A record of every automated action: time, tool, inputs, result, and cost.
autoscaling
Automatic change of the number of workers based on load, for example queue depth.
avatar
A generated talking person, driven by a script and a voice.
bandwidth-bound
A workload limited by memory speed, for example LLM decoding, which reads all weights for every token.
bias
A systematic pattern in model output, such as stereotypes in who appears in which role.
bias review
A review of many outputs to see who is shown in which roles, and who is missing, followed by changes to the casting.
biometric data
Data about a person's body, such as a face or voice, used to identify them. A special category under laws such as the GDPR.
bit depth
The number of bits per color channel. 10-bit has 1,024 steps and is safer for grading than 8-bit.
bitrate
The amount of data per second in a media file, for example 50 Mb/s.
break-even
The usage level where owning hardware and renting cloud compute cost the same.
budget
The planned spend for a project, shot, or scene, with caps that stop overspend.
budget alert
A notice when spending reaches a share of a budget. It warns after money is spent; queue caps refuse before.
bus
A submix in a DAW: several tracks routed to one channel with one fader and one set of processing. DX, MX, and FX buses become the stems.
C2PA
Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity. An open standard for signed metadata that records how a file was made.
cadence
The rhythm of motion from frame to frame. Repeated frames after a frame-rate conversion make an uneven cadence (judder).
calibration
Comparing an automatic judge with human scores and adjusting it until they agree.
camera angle
The height and direction of the camera relative to the subject, such as low, high, or eye level.
camera control
Model parameters or inputs that set camera moves exactly, instead of words.
camera movement
A change of camera position or direction during a shot, such as a dolly, pan, or orbit.
caption
The text that describes a training image. For a LoRA it starts with the trigger word and describes what varies.
captioning
Writing text descriptions for training images, or making caption files for viewers.
captions
On-screen text of speech and important sounds, for accessibility and silent viewing.
CDN
Content delivery network. Servers in many places that deliver files fast to viewers.
CFG
Classifier-free guidance. A setting that makes a diffusion model follow the prompt more strongly. Too high gives burnt output.
character pipeline
An automated chain from character references to finished, consistent shots of that character.
character sheet
Reference images of a character from several angles, with expressions and outfits.
checkpoint
A saved state of model weights during training, or a full model file.
cherry-picking
Showing only the best results. Normal in demos; test models yourself.
chroma subsampling
Storing color at lower resolution than brightness, for example 4:2:0.
click-through rate
The share of people who saw a thumbnail and title and clicked (CTR).
codec
A method to compress and decompress video or audio, such as H.264, H.265, AV1, or ProRes.
cold start
The delay when a new worker starts and loads a model before it can run jobs.
color space
A definition of colors by primaries, white point, and transfer function, such as Rec.709.
color temperature
The color of light in kelvin. Low values are warm (orange); high values are cool (blue).
Comfy MCP
The official MCP server for ComfyUI (public beta, 2026). It lets agents search and run ComfyUI workflows.
ComfyUI
An open node-graph application for running and combining generative models. Also runs as a server with an API.
compositing
Combining layers of images or video into one final image.
compute-bound
A workload limited by arithmetic speed, for example video diffusion, where many tokens use the same weights in each step.
conditioning
All information that guides generation: text, images, references, structure, audio.
conform
Making all clips in a timeline match the project settings, or relinking an edit to full-quality media.
consent
Informed, specific, documented permission from a person to use their likeness or voice.
consent record
A signed document that says who consents to what use of their likeness or voice, where, for how long, and how to withdraw.
consistency
The same character, product, place, and look across shots.
container
A packaged, isolated software environment, for example a Docker image.
content credentials
C2PA metadata attached to a file that states its origin and edits, with a signature.
context engineering
Choosing what information goes into an LLM's context, in which form, and when.
context window
The maximum number of tokens an LLM can use at one time.
contrast ratio
The ratio of key light to fill light. Higher ratios give darker shadows and more drama.
ControlNet
A model add-on that conditions generation on structure such as depth, pose, or edges.
conversational editing
Editing by a series of instructions, where each builds on the previous result.
copyright
Legal rights over original creative works. Its application to AI training and outputs differs by country.
cosine similarity
A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction, from -1 to 1. Used to compare face embeddings.
cost per usable second
Total generation cost divided by the seconds that pass review. The real cost of generated footage.
coverage
Shots of the same action from several sizes and angles, so the editor has choices.
critique loop
A cycle of draft, critique against a rubric, and revision, with a stop rule.
CTR
Click-through rate. The share of viewers who click a video after they see its thumbnail and title.
CUDA
NVIDIA's software platform for GPU computing. Most AI tools support it first.
custom node
A third-party extension for ComfyUI. It runs code on your machine.
cut-down
A shorter version of an edit, such as 30, 15, or 6 seconds.
data classification
Sorting project data into classes (confidential, personal, internal, public) with a rule for where each class may go.
data protection
Laws about personal data, such as GDPR. Face and voice data can be biometric data.
dataset
The collection of examples used to train or fine-tune a model.
dataset card
A document that describes a dataset: purpose, counts, sources, licenses and consent, known gaps, and allowed uses.
dead-letter queue
Where jobs go after their last failed try, so that a person can look at them.
deepfake
Realistic synthetic media that shows a real person, place, or event that did not happen.
deliverables
The files a project must hand over: masters, platform versions, stems, captions, reports.
delta E
A measure of the difference between two colors (distance in Lab). Below about 2 is hard to see between two shots.
denoise strength
In image-to-image or video-to-video, how much noise is added to the input before generation. Higher changes more.
depth control
Conditioning a model on a depth map to fix the scene layout.
depth of field
The zone of the image that is in focus.
dialogue
The spoken lines of characters.
dialogue edit
Cleaning and joining dialogue: removing clicks and distracting breaths, smoothing joins, matching levels, and filling gaps with room tone.
diffusion
A generative method that learns to remove noise, and generates by denoising random noise step by step.
digital replica
An AI copy of a real person's voice or likeness. New laws and performer agreements require consent for it.
digital source type
An IPTC value that says how content was made, for example trainedAlgorithmicMedia for generated content.
disclosure
Telling viewers that content is AI-generated or AI-altered, by labels or platform settings.
distillation
Training a smaller or faster student model to copy a larger teacher, for example in fewer steps.
DiT
Diffusion transformer. A transformer that removes noise from latent tokens. The core of current image and video models.
dolly
A camera move toward (in) or away from (out) the subject.
dry run
A run that shows planned actions and costs without doing them.
dubbing
Replacing the dialogue of a video with another language.
ducking
Lowering one sound (usually music) automatically while another (usually dialogue) plays, with a sidechain compressor.
duration control
A TTS feature that makes speech fit a given length.
EDL
Edit decision list. A simple text format that lists edits with source and record timecodes.
Elo
A rating system that turns many pairwise votes into a ranking. Used by model arenas.
embedding
A vector of numbers that represents a token or item. Similar meanings are near each other.
energy footprint
The energy that a production uses, mainly from GPU compute.
environment sheet
Reference images of a location from several angles and times, often with a panorama and a plan.
EU AI Act
The European Union law on AI. Article 50 sets transparency duties, such as labels for deepfakes, from 2026-08-02.
eval
An evaluation: a fixed set of test cases with criteria, used to compare models or versions.
eval harness
Code that runs an eval set on models automatically and collects scores.
experiment tracking
Recording configs, data versions, results, and costs for each training run.
exponential backoff
Waiting longer after each failed try (for example 2, 4, 8 s), usually with random jitter, before a retry.
few-shot
Giving a model a few examples of the desired output in the prompt.
ffmpeg
The open command-line tool for converting, editing, and analyzing video and audio.
ffprobe
The ffmpeg tool that reads facts about a media file: streams, codecs, size, frame rate, duration, color tags.
fill light
A softer light that opens the shadows made by the key light.
first/last frame
A generation mode where you give the start frame and the end frame of a clip.
flow matching
A training method where the model learns a velocity from noise to data along straight paths. Allows fewer steps.
focal length
The lens property (in mm) that sets field of view and perspective.
Foley
Sounds of body movement and props (steps, cloth, objects), performed or generated to picture.
frame count rule
The valid frame counts of a video model, set by its VAE time compression. Example: 4n+1 for Wan (81, 121), 8n+1 for LTX.
frame interpolation
Making new in-between frames, for example to convert 16 fps to 24 fps.
frame-accurate trim
A cut at an exact frame. It needs decoding and re-encoding; a stream copy can only cut at keyframes.
gamut
The range of colors that a color space can show, set by its primaries. Rec.709 is small, Rec.2020 is large.
Gaussian splatting
A 3D scene format made of millions of small colored 3D Gaussians. It renders photoreal views in real time.
generated world
A 3D or interactive space made by a world model, such as a Gaussian-splat scene.
GGUF
A file format for quantized model weights (from llama.cpp). Common for low-VRAM use in ComfyUI.
glossary
A list of approved terms and translations, used to keep terminology correct.
GPU
Graphics processing unit. A processor with many cores that runs AI models fast.
GPU rental
Renting a GPU machine by the hour. You pay while it runs, also when it is idle.
gradient descent
The training method that changes each parameter a small step in the direction that reduces the loss.
guardrail
A limit on what an agent can do: permissions, budgets, confirmations.
HDR
High dynamic range. Video with a larger brightness range, for example Rec.2020 with PQ or HLG.
headless
Running software through its API without a user interface.
highlight detection
Finding the best short moments in long content automatically.
hook
The first 1–3 seconds of a video, designed to make the viewer stay.
human authorship
The human creative contribution (writing, selection, arrangement, editing) that copyright protection may depend on in AI-assisted work.
human gate
A pipeline step where a person must approve creative, legal, or cost decisions.
human in the loop
A design where people set goals, review results, and make final decisions.
idempotency
A property where repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once. Prevents double billing on retries.
idempotency key
A unique key for one logical request (for example S07.p2.g4). Repeating the request with the same key returns the first result instead of doing the work again.
identity drift
Gradual change of a character's or product's appearance across shots.
identity score
An automatic similarity score between a generated face (or product) and its reference.
image-to-video
A generation mode that starts from a given image as the first frame.
indemnity
A contract promise by one party to cover certain legal claims, offered by some AI vendors.
inference
Using a trained model to make outputs. The parameters do not change.
infrastructure as code
Defining cloud resources in code files, so they can be created and destroyed reliably.
inpainting
Regenerating only a masked area of an image or video.
input hash cache
Storing outputs under a hash of all their inputs, so a re-run makes only the outputs whose inputs changed.
instruction editing
Changing an image or video with a natural-language instruction while keeping the rest.
interactive video
Video that a model generates in real time in response to user input.
invisible watermark
A signal hidden in pixels or audio that marks content as generated. It survives some edits and is lost in others.
IP-Adapter
An adapter that conditions an image model on a reference image for identity or style.
J-cut
An edit where the sound of the next shot starts before its picture.
joint audio-video
Generation of picture and sound together in one model, so they are synchronized.
JSON schema
A formal description of the structure of JSON data. Used to request and validate structured LLM output.
key frame
An approved still image that defines a shot before motion is generated.
key light
The main light on a subject.
L-cut
An edit where the sound of the current shot continues over the start of the next picture.
latent
The compressed representation of an image or video in which a diffusion model works.
lead room
Space in the frame in the direction a subject looks or moves.
leakage
When a fine-tuned model shows the trained subject or training backgrounds when not asked.
learning rate
The size of each parameter update during training.
least privilege
Giving each person, service, or agent only the rights that its task needs.
license
The legal terms that say how you may use a model, an output, music, or other assets.
license tier
A plan level with specific usage rights, such as commercial or streaming use.
lifecycle rule
A storage rule that moves or deletes objects by age, for example delete temporary files after 30 days.
likeness
A person's recognizable face, body, or voice, protected by law in many places.
lip sync
Matching mouth movement to speech audio, or a model that changes the mouth to match new audio.
LLM as judge
Using a language model to score outputs against a rubric. It must be calibrated against human scores.
LLM judge
An LLM that scores outputs against a rubric. Calibrate it against human judgments before you trust it.
localization
Adapting a video for another language and culture: voice, captions, on-screen text.
long-form coherence
Keeping story, characters, and space consistent over minutes of generated video.
look bible
A document that defines a project's visual rules: palette, light, texture, lenses, references.
LoRA
Low-rank adaptation. Small trainable matrices added to a frozen model to teach it a character, product, or style.
LoRA evaluation
Testing a LoRA for fidelity (identity), flexibility (new prompts), and leakage (no-trigger prompts), and in the real pipeline.
LoRA rank
The size of the LoRA matrices. Higher rank gives more capacity and a larger file, and can overfit faster.
LoRA strength
A multiplier that sets how much a loaded LoRA changes the model, typically 0.4 to 1.0.
loss
A number that measures how wrong a model's prediction is during training.
LUFS
Loudness Units relative to Full Scale. A loudness measure that matches human hearing. Platforms set targets in LUFS.
LUT
Look-up table. A file that maps input colors to output colors, used for conversions and looks.
M&E
Music and effects mix. The full mix without dialogue, used to make foreign-language versions.
machine-ready script
A script with standard tags and fixed descriptors that tools can parse directly.
mask
An image that marks which pixels an operation should change.
match cut
A cut that links two shots by shape, motion, or idea.
matte
A grayscale image that defines transparency for compositing.
MCP
Model Context Protocol. An open standard that connects AI applications to tools and data through servers.
MCP client
The part of a host application that connects to one MCP server and gives its tools to the model.
MCP server
A program that exposes tools, resources, and prompts to AI applications through MCP.
media asset management
A system that stores media with IDs and metadata so people and tools can find and reuse it.
memory bandwidth
How fast data moves between GPU memory and compute units, in GB/s.
mesh
A 3D surface made of triangles, with textures and materials.
metadata
Data about a file: origin, settings, rights, technical properties.
minimum detectable effect
The smallest change that a test is planned to detect; it sets the sample size.
misinformation
False information that spreads as if true, including realistic synthetic video.
MLX
Apple's machine-learning framework for Apple silicon.
model
A function with many parameters that maps an input (for example a prompt and noise) to an output (for example a video).
model card
A document that describes a model: architecture, data, uses, limits, and license.
model registry
A managed list of models and adapters with versions, evaluations, and rights.
models.lock
A file that lists each model file of a workflow with its URL, size, SHA-256 hash, and license. It makes downloads repeatable and shows license conflicts.
MoE
Mixture of experts. A model with several expert sub-networks; a router uses only some of them for each token or step.
morphing
An artifact where faces or objects change shape unnaturally during a clip.
motion control
Inputs that set how subjects or the camera move, such as motion references or parameters.
motivated light
Light that seems to come from a real source in the scene.
motivated movement
A camera move that has a story reason, such as following action or revealing information.
multi-agent
A system where several specialized agents work on parts of a task.
multi-shot
Generation of several connected shots in one request, with shared cast and space.
music generation
Making music with AI models from a text brief.
NAS
Network-attached storage. A shared storage server on the local network.
native audio
Sound that a video model generates together with the picture.
NeRF
Neural radiance field. A neural network that stores how a 3D scene looks from every direction.
NLE
Non-linear editor. Editing software that stores edits as references and never changes the source media.
node graph
A visual program made of connected nodes, such as a ComfyUI workflow.
noise reduction
Removing unwanted background noise from audio.
null test
Adding the stems, subtracting the mix, and measuring what is left; a residual near silence proves that the stems add up to the mix.
NVMe
A fast SSD interface. Used for models, caches, and active projects.
object storage
Cloud storage for files as objects in buckets, such as S3-compatible storage.
observability
Metrics, logs, and traces that show how a system performs.
offload
Moving parts of a model to CPU memory when GPU memory is too small.
on-screen text
Text that appears in the picture, such as signs, titles, or graphics.
OpenTimelineIO
An open timeline format and Python library for exchanging edits between tools.
orchestrator
The component that moves work between stages and agents in a pipeline.
outpainting
Extending an image or video beyond its frame, for example to change aspect ratio.
overfit
When a model learns its training data too exactly and loses flexibility.
overfitting
Training too long or too strongly, so the model copies training details and loses flexibility.
pacing
The speed and rhythm of an edit, set mainly by shot length.
panorama anchor
A 360° image of a location used as a reference to keep the space consistent.
paper
A research publication that describes a method and its results.
paper edit
A list of chosen lines and shots in story order, made before the cut.
parameter
One of the numbers inside a model that training sets.
patch
A small block of an image or video (in space and time) that becomes one token.
per-output API
A model API billed per output, such as per image or per video second.
personality rights
Rights that protect a person's name, image, and voice from unauthorized commercial use.
personalization
Making versions of a video for specific audiences or people.
photogrammetry
Reconstructing 3D geometry from many overlapping photos.
pipeline diagram
A diagram of the stages, tools, agents, and gates of a production system.
pipeline metrics
Measures of a production system: cost and human minutes per finished minute, rejection rate per gate, lead time.
plan-approve-act-review
The cycle for agent sessions: the agent proposes steps, a person approves them, the agent acts on a copy and logs every change, and the change is checked against a diff.
planar tracking
Tracking a flat surface through a shot (position, scale, rotation, perspective), so a logo or screen can be pinned to it.
platform API
A platform's programming interface for upload, metadata, scheduling, and analytics.
previs
Previsualization. A rough version of shots or scenes made to plan the production.
product sheet
Reference images of a product from all sides, with logo and material details.
production pipeline
The ordered stages that turn a brief into delivered video.
production plan
The complete plan for a project: creative, technical, budget, schedule, rights, risks.
project memory
A file in a repository that gives an agent stable project rules and commands.
prompt adherence
How exactly a model follows the prompt.
prompt grammar
A fixed order of prompt elements: cinematography, subject, action, context, light, sound, style.
prompt log
A record of each generation: model, prompt, seed, settings, references, cost, date.
proxy
A small, light copy of media used for fast editing.
publishing API
A platform API for uploading videos and setting metadata.
QC
Quality control. Checks of deliverables against specifications: format, color tags, loudness, defects.
quality gate
An automatic check that an output must pass before the next stage.
quantization
Storing model parameters with fewer bits to save memory and often time.
queue
A list of jobs that workers process in order.
RAID
A method that combines disks for speed or protection against disk failure. It is not a backup.
real-time generation
Generating frames as fast as they are played.
reference
An input (image, video, or audio) that shows the model what an element must look or sound like.
reference image
An image given to a model to control identity, style, or composition.
reference latent
A reference image that the VAE encodes and attaches to the conditioning, so the model can copy identity, objects, or places from it.
reference-to-video
A generation mode that uses references to make new shots with the same elements.
reframe
Changing the crop of a shot for another aspect ratio, often with subject tracking.
region editing
Editing only a selected area of a video.
relight
Changing the lighting of an existing image or video.
reproducibility
The ability to make the same output again from the same inputs and versions.
resource
In MCP, read-only data that a server exposes to the client.
responsible use
Using AI in ways that avoid harm, respect rights, and are transparent.
restyle
Changing the visual style of footage while keeping its motion and performance.
retention
How long viewers keep watching. The retention curve shows where they leave.
retention curve
The share of viewers still watching at each second of a video.
retry
Repeating a failed request, usually with backoff.
reverb
The sound reflections of a space. Also an effect that adds them.
review
Checking outputs against the specification and deciding keep, fix, or regenerate.
review and approval
A process and tool for comments and approvals on cuts and versions.
rights log
A record of the source, license, restrictions, and consent for every asset.
risk register
A list of project risks with likelihood, impact, owner, and mitigation.
risk-based review
Review effort that follows the cost of an error: full human review for high-risk content, samples for low risk.
room tone
The quiet background sound of a space, used to fill gaps in dialogue.
roto
Rotoscoping: making a matte for a moving object frame by frame; AI masks now do most of it.
rotoscoping
Making a mask that follows a subject frame by frame.
rough cut
An early version of an edit with the right shots in order, before fine timing.
routing
Sending each job to the model or service that fits it best.
routing table
A table that maps shot types to models, modes, and limits.
rubric
A set of criteria with defined levels used to score work.
rule of thirds
A composition guide that places subjects on lines dividing the frame into thirds.
safe zone
The part of the frame that a platform's interface does not cover. Keep captions and key picture content inside it.
sample grid
One image with renders of the same prompts and seeds for each checkpoint, to compare checkpoints side by side.
sampler
The method that takes each denoising step, such as Euler or DPM++.
sandbox
A limit on what a tool may touch, for example only paths inside the project folder.
scale to zero
Stopping all workers when there are no jobs, so idle time costs nothing.
scene extension
Continuing a generated clip from its last frames to make a longer shot.
scopes
Measurement displays for video levels and color: waveform, parade, vectorscope.
screen direction
The left-to-right or right-to-left direction of movement and looks, kept consistent across cuts.
secrets
Sensitive values such as API keys, stored in a secrets manager, never in code.
seed
The number that fixes the starting noise of a generation, so it can be reproduced.
selects
The takes marked as good enough for the edit.
serverless GPU
GPU compute that starts containers on demand and bills per second of use.
setup and payoff
An element shown early in a story that returns with meaning later.
shot list
A list of all shots with size, angle, lens, move, action, and duration.
shot matching
Grading shots so that they look continuous within a scene.
shot size
How much of the subject the frame shows, from extreme wide to extreme close-up.
shot specification
The complete description of one shot, used to prompt and to review.
showreel
A short video of your best work, used in a portfolio.
sidecar metadata
A small file next to a media file (for example JSON) with its prompt-log ID, rights status, and technical data.
sidechain
A method where one signal (dialogue) controls processing of another (music ducking).
sound design
Creating and layering sounds to support story and emotion.
sound effects
Specific sounds for events, such as doors, impacts, or vehicles.
specialization
A focused career path after the program.
spot instance
Cheaper cloud compute that the provider can stop at any time.
stem
A submix of one part of the soundtrack (dialogue, music, or effects), full length from the same start, so the parts add up to the mix.
stem separation
Splitting a mix into parts such as voice, music, and effects.
stems
Separate submixes of a final mix, such as dialogue, music, and effects.
step
One denoising iteration in diffusion generation.
story structure
The shape of a story: situation, change, tension, release.
storyboard
A sequence of frames that shows each planned shot.
structured output
LLM output in a fixed machine-readable format, such as JSON that matches a schema.
structured prompt
A prompt written as structured data (for example JSON) with one field per element.
studio policy
A one-page, signed team document that says what the studio never makes, what needs consent, and how to stop or refuse a job.
style guide
Rules per language or brand: formality, units, dates, names, caption style.
style reference
A reference image that controls style, palette, or texture only.
subgraph
A group of ComfyUI nodes packaged as one reusable unit with named inputs.
SynthID
Google DeepMind's invisible watermark for AI-generated content.
system prompt
Stable instructions that set an LLM's role, rules, and output format.
technical report
A detailed document from a lab about a model's design, training, and results.
technical write-up
A report that documents a production with decisions, data, costs, and limits.
template
A reusable structure with fixed and variable parts.
tempo
The speed of music in beats per minute (BPM).
temporal consistency
Stability of objects, light, and detail from frame to frame.
tensor cores
GPU units for fast low-precision matrix math used by AI models.
test media
Media generated for tests (test patterns, tones) at known sizes, rates, and lengths, so that results can be asserted.
text encoder
The model part that turns the prompt into embeddings. Often a large language model.
text-to-video
A generation mode that makes video from a text prompt only.
thumbnail
The still image that represents a video in feeds and search.
tiled decode
Decoding a latent in tiles to reduce peak memory.
timecode
An address for each frame in HH:MM:SS:FF.
timeline
The sequence of edits on video and audio tracks in an editor. Each edit references part of a media file (source in/out) and places it in time (record in/out).
token
The unit a transformer processes: part of a word, an image patch, or a block of video or audio.
tool call
A structured request from a model to run a named tool with given inputs.
tool design
Defining tool names, descriptions, schemas, and results so agents use them correctly.
track layout
A standard order and grouping of tracks in an edit or mix session.
tracking
Following the motion of points or surfaces in a shot, to attach other elements to them.
training
The process that sets a model's parameters from data.
transcript editing
Editing video by editing its transcript text.
transfer function
The curve that maps signal values to brightness, such as gamma, PQ, HLG, or log.
transformer
A neural network architecture built on attention. The base of current LLMs and DiTs.
treatment
A one-page description of the idea, structure, tone, and look of a video.
trigger word
A unique token that activates the subject a LoRA learned.
true peak
The highest level of an audio signal, including peaks between samples, in dBTP.
TTS
Text-to-speech. A model that turns text into spoken audio.
turnaround
Views of a character or object from front, side, back, and three-quarter.
Unreal Engine
A real-time 3D engine used for games, previs, and virtual production.
upscaling
Increasing resolution. Generative upscalers add new detail that may be invented.
VAE
Variational autoencoder. It compresses images or video into a latent and decodes latents back to pixels.
variant
One version of a templated video, defined by one row of data.
vectorscope
A scope that shows hue and saturation of the image.
vendor abstraction
One interface over several vendors, so a vendor change is a configuration change.
video editing model
A model that changes an existing video from an instruction.
video-to-video
A generation mode that transforms a source video while keeping its motion.
virtual production
Filmmaking with real-time 3D environments, for example on LED walls with tracked cameras.
voice clone
A synthetic copy of a real person's voice. Requires consent.
voice design
Creating a synthetic voice from a text description.
voice lock
Keeping a character's voice the same across generations, using a voice reference.
VRAM
The memory on a GPU. Model weights and activations must fit in it.
watermark
A mark in content that identifies its origin. Invisible watermarks can survive editing.
waveform
A scope that shows brightness levels across the frame.
webhook
An HTTP call that a service sends to your endpoint when an event happens, such as job completion.
WebSocket
A network connection that stays open, so a server can send events (such as progress) to a client.
weights
The stored parameter values of a model.
Whisper
A family of open speech-recognition models that make transcripts, also with timestamps.
white box
A simple grey 3D block-out of a scene used to plan cameras and layout.
withdrawal
When a person takes back consent. New uses stop, and models and data are deleted as the consent record says.
workflow
A fixed sequence of steps in code, as opposed to an autonomous agent. In ComfyUI, a saved graph.
world model
A model that generates an explorable or interactive space, not only a fixed clip.

How to study

Order

Do the levels in order. Inside a level, you can do the courses in any order, unless a course lists a prerequisite.

Level Courses Focus
L1 C01–C03 How the models work, screen language, LLMs and agents
L2 C04–C07 Image, video, audio, and 3D/world generation
L3 C08–C10 AI-native editing and finishing
L4 C11–C15 Pipelines, orchestration, infrastructure, fine-tuning, scale
L5 C16–C18 Law and provenance, frontier research, capstone

Each module

  1. Outcomes. Read them first. They tell you what you must be able to do.
  2. Listen. A short spoken summary (synthetic voice). The transcript is below the player.
  3. Learn. The concept text. It uses no product names.
  4. Diagram. The structure of the idea in one picture.
  5. Watch. Selected videos and pages, with a note on what to look at.
  6. Worked example. Real prompts, settings, and decisions, step by step.
  7. Lab. Do it. Each lab gives a deliverable and a result checklist.
  8. Quiz. Each answer shows an explanation.
  9. Model answer. Compare it with your result after the lab.
  10. Go deeper. Primary sources: papers, model cards, official docs.

Your production repository

Make one Git repository for the whole program, for example ai-video-lab/. Put every lab result in it:

ai-video-lab/
  C01/  C02/  ...  C18/
  prompts/          # prompt log: every prompt, model, seed, settings, cost
  rights/           # rights log: sources, licenses, consent records
  evals/            # your model comparison sets and results
  pipelines/        # code, ComfyUI workflows, agent configs

Rule: every generated asset has a line in the prompt log. Every asset that you did not make has a line in the rights log. You use these logs in C16 and in the capstone.

Time

About 1,010 hours in total (74 modules). At 15 hours a week, this is about 16 months. At 40 hours a week, it is about 6 months. The site adds up these numbers from the module pages.

When a tool changes

Tools in labs change often. If a lab tool is not available:

  1. Read the "Tool landscape" page for the current alternative.
  2. Use the same concept and the same result checklist with the alternative.
  3. Write the change in your prompt log.

Requirements by level

These are the tools and resources that each level needs. All prices are estimates as of October 2026.

Entry knowledge (assumed)

  • Command line, Git, and a package manager.
  • Read and change Python and JSON. Call a REST API with curl or Python.
  • Basic cloud use (one of AWS, GCP, Azure) and Docker.

Level 1: C01–C03

Item Requirement
Computer Any modern laptop.
Software Python 3.11+, Jupyter (local, or Google Colab).
AI access One frontier LLM with API access (for example Claude, GPT, Gemini). An MCP-capable client (for example Claude Desktop or Claude Code).
Budget About US$20–50 per month.

Level 2: C04–C07

Item Requirement
Computer Any modern laptop. Local generation is optional at this level.
AI access Credits on 2–3 hosted generators, or one aggregator API (fal.ai or Replicate) that serves many image, video, and audio models. A voice/music account (for example ElevenLabs).
3D A free Unreal Engine install, or a browser-based Gaussian-splat viewer.
Budget About US$100–300 for the level. Video costs about US$0.05–0.15 per generated second. Plan to generate about 5 times more than you use.

Level 3: C08–C10

Item Requirement
Computer 16 GB RAM or more, SSD with 200 GB free.
Editing DaVinci Resolve (free). For the native MCP labs: Resolve Studio (one-time licence) or Adobe Premiere (subscription, has an MCP server).
Audio Fairlight (inside Resolve) or a DAW (Reaper is low cost).
Budget One licence or subscription + LLM access.

Level 4: C11–C15

Item Requirement
GPU Local: NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB VRAM minimum, 32 GB recommended (RTX 5090 class). Or cloud: rented GPU (H100 about US$3–5/hour; A100 or L40S cheaper). Apple silicon works for some labs, but most open video models run best on CUDA.
Software Docker, ComfyUI, Python, ffmpeg.
Cloud One cloud account with object storage. One GPU rental or serverless GPU account (for example RunPod, Modal).
Budget Cloud path: about US$150–400 GPU time for the level (LoRA training is the largest part).

Level 5: C16–C18

Item Requirement
Tools Everything from Level 4. c2patool (free, open source) for content credentials.
Budget Capstone: about US$100–300 generation and GPU time.

What happens without a local GPU

Every Level 4 lab has a cloud path. The concepts and result checklists are the same. The cloud path also teaches you cost control, which is a core skill.

Tool landscape, October 2026

This page lists the current tools by category. It changes every quarter. The concept text in the modules does not depend on it. Facts marked (V) are checked on a primary or trade source. Other facts are reported by several sources but are not checked.

Video generation: hosted

Model Vendor Strong points (as of 2026-10)
Kling 3.0 / 3.0 Omni Kuaishou #1 in the blind-vote text-to-video arena (V). Up to 6 shots per generation, each 3–15 s, with shot size and camera move for each shot. Native audio with a voice locked from a reference.
Seedance 2.5 ByteDance 30 s in one take, native 4K, native audio, up to 50 references (images, audio, 3D white models, style), 10-bit color, region editing (V). In CapCut and Jimeng (即梦).
Veo 3.1 + Flow Google Cinematic realism, 4K, native 48 kHz audio, "Ingredients" (reference images), scene extension, Scene Builder.
Gemini Omni Flash Google Any-to-any model. Edit video by conversation. SynthID watermark on every clip. API about US$0.10/s.
Runway Gen-4.5 + Aleph 2.0 Runway Aleph edits existing video: remove objects, relight, add elements, restyle. Also inside Adobe Firefly.
Luma Ray3 / Ray3 Modify Luma Native 16-bit HDR. Video-to-video on actor footage.
Sora 2 OpenAI API removed 2026-09-24 (V). Use this as a case study for vendor risk.

Video generation: open weights (local or rented GPU)

Model Key facts
Wan 2.7 (Alibaba) Apache 2.0. 27B MoE. T2V, I2V, reference-to-video with voice clone, instruction editing. 1080p, 15 s, first/last frame.
Wan 2.2 / 2.6 Smaller variants run from about 8 GB VRAM (5B GGUF). Wide LoRA support.
LTX-2.5 (Lightricks) 22B audio+video DiT, multishot, 4K HDR, distilled few-step variant, INT8 and NVFP4 builds, day-one ComfyUI (V). About 32 GB VRAM with FP8.
HunyuanVideo 1.5 (Tencent) 80 GB full; about 24 GB INT8; lower with FP8 + tiling.

Image generation

GPT Image 2 (top of the image arenas, Sept 2026), Nano Banana Pro / Nano Banana 2 (Google, strong editing, 4K), FLUX.2 (open weights; FLUX.2 Klein is the small variant), Midjourney V8.x (style), Kling Image 3.0, Seedream (ByteDance).

Audio

  • Voice, dubbing, avatars: ElevenLabs (TTS, voice clone, dubbing, Avatars), HeyGen (Avatar IV, lip-synced dubbing in 175+ languages), Synthesia.
  • Music: Suno v6 (2026-09-09, licensed training data), ElevenLabs Music v2.5 (2026-09-11, licensed). Licenses differ by plan.
  • Open TTS: IndexTTS-2 / 2.5 (duration control for dubbing), CosyVoice 3 (0.5B, about 4 GB VRAM, Apache 2.0), Qwen3-TTS. Fish Audio S2 weights are for research only.

LLMs and agents

Frontier families: Claude (Anthropic), GPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google). Open weights: Qwen, DeepSeek. Agent coding tools: Claude Code, Codex. Rankings change monthly. Use LMArena and Artificial Analysis, then test on your own task (C03).

Editing and finishing

  • DaVinci Resolve 21.1: native MCP server in Resolve Studio (Sept 2026) (V). Assistants can organize timelines, rename, grade, apply LUTs, add markers, render, and check delivery specs.
  • Adobe Premiere 26.5: Firefly AI Assistant (agent) for bins, renames, markers, first cut, storyboard to video. Generate Video, Sound Effects, Soundscape, and Music. An MCP server is reported.
  • Bridges: Jumper (MCP for Premiere, Resolve, Final Cut, Avid), EditAssist.
  • Others: Final Cut Pro, Avid Media Composer, Descript (transcript editing), CapCut (social, Seedance inside).
  • Finishing: After Effects, Nuke, Fusion, Blender, Topaz (upscale and interpolation), iZotope RX, Pro Tools, Fairlight.

Pipelines

  • ComfyUI: the standard node graph for open models. Comfy MCP (public beta) connects Claude, Codex, and Cursor to ComfyUI workflows. Local community MCP servers also exist.
  • Model APIs: fal.ai, Replicate (many models, one API), and vendor APIs.
  • Higgsfield: multi-model studio, with an MCP server.
  • Training: musubi-tuner (kohya-ss), AI Toolkit (ostris), fal LoRA trainers.

Infrastructure

  • Local GPU: RTX 5090 (32 GB), RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB). Apple Mac Studio M5 Max (up to 128 GB) and M5 Ultra (up to 512 GB unified memory) are very good for editing and LLMs, and slower for most video diffusion. DGX Spark and Strix Halo give 128 GB unified memory in a small box.
  • Cloud GPU (mid-2026 list prices): RunPod H100 about US$2.89/h; Modal H100 about US$3.95/h base; fal H100 about US$4.50/h (raw GPU), and per output about US$0.05 per video second; Replicate H100 about US$5.49/h.

Law and provenance

  • EU AI Act Article 50: transparency duties apply from 2026-08-02. Deepfakes need a clear label at first exposure. The Code of Practice asks for more than one marking layer: C2PA signed metadata + invisible watermark.
  • Platform rules (YouTube, TikTok, Meta) add their own AI labels.
  • Google SynthID is on Google model output. C2PA Content Credentials can be added with c2patool.

Chinese ecosystem (useful to follow)

Kling (可灵), Jimeng / Seedance (即梦), Wan / Tongyi Wanxiang (通义万相), Hunyuan (混元), Vidu. There is a large "AI short drama" (AI短剧 / AI漫剧) industry with an industrial pipeline: engineered script → storyboard → image assets → video → edit. Many tutorials are on Bilibili and Zhihu.

Next steps and specializations

After the capstone, choose one path. Each path gives the next skills, the primary sources to follow, and a first project.

1. AI Director

  • Next skills: directing actors for performance capture; advanced story structure; longer-form continuity (10+ min); music video and ad formats.
  • Follow: festival AI-film tracks; Curious Refuge case studies; vendor showcase channels (Runway, Kling, Google Flow).
  • First project: a 5-minute narrative with 3 recurring characters and one location built as a 3D world.

2. Creative Technologist / Pipeline Engineer

  • Next skills: custom ComfyUI nodes in Python; your own MCP servers; queue systems; evaluation harnesses.
  • Follow: ComfyUI blog and GitHub; Model Context Protocol specification; Banodoco community; posts from ComfyUI and practitioners on X.
  • First project: an open-source MCP server that controls one creative tool, with tests.

3. Generative Media Infrastructure Engineer

  • Next skills: Kubernetes GPU scheduling; model serving (TensorRT, torch.compile, xDiT, sequence parallel); cost observability; multi-region storage.
  • Follow: NVIDIA developer blog; vLLM and SGLang (multimodal serving); cloud vendor GPU docs.
  • First project: serve an open video model behind an autoscaling endpoint with a cost dashboard (cost per output second).

4. Model Fine-Tuning Specialist

  • Next skills: dataset curation at scale; captioning models; video LoRA and full fine-tune; distillation; evaluation design.
  • Follow: musubi-tuner and AI Toolkit repos; Hugging Face Diffusers docs; arXiv cs.CV (video generation).
  • First project: a brand-safe product LoRA for one open video model, with an eval report.

5. AI Finishing Artist (color, VFX, sound)

  • Next skills: ACES deep dive; Nuke compositing; Houdini basics; Dolby Atmos mixing.
  • Follow: Blackmagic training and certification; Foundry learning; Mixing Light; Netflix Partner Help Center (delivery specs).
  • First project: a finishing pass that combines generated and real shots without visible difference.

6. Localization and Scale Producer

  • Next skills: dubbing quality control; cultural adaptation; variant testing; platform APIs.
  • Follow: platform creator docs; dubbing vendor research blogs.
  • First project: one video, 10 languages, lip-synced, with a QC report and cost per language.

7. Research Engineer: video generation

  • Next skills: PyTorch; diffusion and flow-matching math; distributed training; reading and reproducing papers.
  • Follow: arXiv (cs.CV, cs.LG); open model technical reports (Wan, LTX, HunyuanVideo); CVPR, ICCV, NeurIPS, ICLR.
  • First project: reproduce one ablation from an open video model paper at small scale.

How to keep up (for every path)

  1. Once a week: read release notes of the 5 tools you use most.
  2. Once a month: run your fixed eval set (C17) on any new model.
  3. Once a quarter: update your own tool landscape page.
  4. Follow both English and Chinese sources. Many video models and pipelines come from Chinese labs first.
